# P R E F A C E .

---

For the present edition of the *Súrya-siddhánta* <note>The "Sun-Treatise," one of the most significant ancient Sanskrit texts on astronomy.</note> and commentary nine MSS. <note>Abbreviation for manuscripts.</note> have been collated.

Of the mere text I had four copies :

*A.* Borrowed from Pandit <note>A Hindu scholar or learned master of Sanskrit.</note> Rájájí, of Benares : venerable in appearance, and almost without an error ; but defective, in the first part, by the whole of the opening chapter and about half of the second.

*B.* Belonging to Traváḍí Lajjás'ankara Pandit, of Benares : generally correct.

*C.* From the library of the Asiatic Society of Bengal, being No. 81 : of little value : in the Bangálí character <note>The script used for writing the Bengali language.</note>.

*D.* Likewise from the library of the Asiatic Society of Bengal, being No. 77 : almost useless : in the same character with *C*.

Of the commentary, exhibiting the text at large, I used five copies, of which three are more or less imperfect ; namely :

*a.* It belongs to Pandit Náráyaṇa Bhaṭṭa, of Benares : moderately correct.

*b.* Procured from Traváḍí Lajjás'ankara Pandit, of Benares : much more faulty in the first part than in the second.

*c.* A MS. belonging to the Asiatic Society of Bengal, being No. 81 : in the first part, nearly related to the corresponding portion of *b* ; in the latter, wanting all the thirteenth chapter but its beginning and end : of scarcely any worth : in the Bangálí character.

*d.* Lent to me by Paṇḍyá Indrají Durlabhají, of Benares : contains only the first part ; and of thus much the seventh and

# Salutations to the Supreme Soul.
## Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings"
### The Surya Siddhanta <note>The "Sun Canon," a foundational Sanskrit treatise on Indian astronomy.</note>

->I bow to the curved-trunk god <note>Ganesha</note>, the son of Shiva,<-
->who grants wisdom to man and by whose memory<-
->one attains the obstacle-free completion of desired tasks.<-

->Victory to my parents, Gejiba and Lallaji, the embodiments of Mother Parvati and Lord Shiva,<-
->from whom five sons were born, who are the causes of the world of light <note>referring to their expertise in Jyotisha or astronomy/astrology</note>.<-

->I bow to my brother Krishna, the wise world-teacher,<-
->whose speech was a place of trust for the Universal Emperor Jahangir <note>original: "Sārvabhauma-Jahāngīra"; this refers to the Mughal Emperor Jahangir, indicating the commentator lived in the early 17th century</note>.<-

->Having thoroughly examined various texts, I, Ranganatha,<-
->compose this commentary on the Surya Siddhanta, titled "The Illuminator of Hidden Meanings."<-

Now, a certain sage—desiring to relate the true reality as he knows it, consisting of the dialogue between the Man-who-is-part-of-the-Sun and Maya the Asura <note>Maya is the traditional architect of the Asuras who receives the astronomical knowledge from a representative of the Sun God</note> to the other sages who are curious about the motions of the planets—records the auspicious salutation to Brahma. This was performed for the obstacle-free completion of the narration and serves as instruction for his students:

> Salutations to Brahma, whose form is inconceivable and unmanifest, 
> who is beyond the three qualities <note>the Gunas: sattva, rajas, and tamas</note> yet is the soul of all qualities, 
> the embodiment who is the support of the entire universe. || 1 ||

"To Brahma" means to the Lord who pervades the universe because of His vastness and limitlessness; the meaning is that He is the one established by sacred scriptures in passages such as "From this very Self, space was produced." "Salutations" implies a specific mental and intellectual devotion characterized by the actions of body and speech...

<meta>This page begins the commentary on the Surya Siddhanta, a foundational Sanskrit treatise on Indian astronomy. It focuses on the opening invocation and the philosophical nature of the divine.</meta>

# The Surya Siddhanta

->I bow to that supreme essence, which draws forth and elevates...<- <note>The commentator is explaining the opening salutation of the text, breaking down the grammatical and philosophical meaning of "bowing" to the divine.</note>

One might ask: if the sky itself is all-pervading, why is a specific deity invoked? To this, the author responds: **"To the forms who are the support of the entire universe."** This means He whose forms are Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva—the agents of creation, preservation, and destruction—serves as the foundation for the entire world, both stationary and moving. Since the physical sky lacks these conscious roles, the divine is distinct.

One might then suggest that it is proper to meditate upon the form of such a being. To this, the author says: **"To Him whose form is inconceivable and unmanifest."** He is "inconceivable" because He cannot be the object of meditative focus. The reason for this is His "unmanifest form." Because His true nature is not perceptible or manifest, a humble salutation (bowing) is the only appropriate response.

Why is His form unmanifest? The author explains: **"To Him who is without qualities."** This means He is beyond the three *gunas* <term>Gunas: the three fundamental qualities of nature—Sattva (goodness), Rajas (passion), and Tamas (darkness)</term>. Since manifest forms require these qualities, His lack of them renders Him unmanifest.

Does this imply He has no nature at all? The author clarifies: **"To Him whose essence is quality."** Here, "qualities" refers to eternal knowledge and bliss which constitute His very self. This aligns with the sacred scripture <note>original: "Shruti"</note> which states: *"Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinity."* Thus, while He is directly "without qualities" (in a material sense), He is indirectly the "essence of quality" (in a spiritual sense). How else could the creation of the universe be possible?

As the Lord Himself has said:
> "Leaning upon My own nature, I send forth again and again
> this entire multitude of beings, who are powerless under the control of nature."
> <note>This is a quotation from the Bhagavad Gita, Chapter 9, Verse 8.</note>

So say the other commentators. || 1 ||

Now, regarding the concern that this work might be merely a human invention—

<summary>This page provides a philosophical commentary on the opening verse of the Surya Siddhanta, defining the Supreme Being as both the support of the universe and an inconceivable, quality-less essence that manifests as Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva.</summary>
<keywords>Surya Siddhanta, Brahma, Vishnu, Shiva, Gunas, Brahman, Bhagavad Gita, Indian Astronomy, Unmanifest, Inconceivable</keywords>

<meta>This page begins the commentary on the second and third verses of the Surya Siddhanta, following the introductory invocation. It establishes the mythological origin of the astronomical knowledge being presented.</meta>

## Accompanied by the *Gudharthaprakashaka* <note>The "Exposition of the Hidden Meaning," a famous 17th-century commentary by Ranganatha.</note>

To prevent any doubts and intending to describe the beginning of the dialogue, the author first states in two verses that the demon Maya performed penance.

->When but a small part of the *Krita* Age <note>The first and most virtuous of the four world ages (Yugas) in Hindu cosmology.</note> remained, a **Great Demon** named Maya,<-
->desiring to know the supreme, holy, and secret primeval knowledge, the highest wisdom,—<-
->the foremost of the limbs of the Veda, in its entirety, which is the cause of the motion of the stars—<-
->performed most difficult penance, while worshiping the Sun.<-

"Maya" is the name of a certain great *Daitya* <note>A race of giants or titans in Vedic mythology, often translated as "demons" or "asuras."</note>. He performed *Tapas* <note>Ascetic penance involving self-discipline, meditation, and physical austerity to gain spiritual power or knowledge.</note>, which consists of rules for the mortification of one's own body through recitation of mantras, fire offerings, and meditation to please a chosen deity. The performance of penance by the *Daityas* is well-known at every step in the *Puranas* <note>Ancient Indian texts containing mythology, history, and cosmology.</note>. 

Now, since their performance of penance is usually famous for being directed toward a specific chosen deity, one might ask: "Toward which god did he direct his penance?" To this, the author says: "While worshiping." He was serving Vivasvan, who is Narayana <note>A name for the Supreme Being, here identified with the Sun God.</note> presiding over the solar orb. 

One might then ask: "Knowing this deity to be the enemy of the *Daityas*, how could he worship him to achieve his own desires? Surely one's own benefit cannot be achieved from an enemy; otherwise, the very nature of enmity would be contradicted." To this, the author provides an adjective for the penance: "Most difficult." This means it was possible to perform only through extreme suffering and intense hardship. And so, it is famous in hundreds of instances in the *Puranas* that the Lord, being uniquely affectionate toward his devotees, is well-pleased by such penance and fulfills the desires even of the *Daityas*. This is the sense of "worshiping in that manner."

Now, since the mention of this particular demon's penance is not found anywhere in the usual accounts of *Daitya* penances in the *Puranas*, how can his penance be known as authoritative? To this, the author says: "When but a small part remained..." <note>Referring to the end of the Golden Age, implying this is a specific historical tradition within the astronomical lineage.</note>

---

\* <margin>An alternative reading is "named Mayo."</margin>

# The Surya Siddhanta

In the age-cycle known as the *Krita Yuga* <note>The first and golden age of the world in Hindu cosmology</note>, the word "and" implies the inclusion of the dawn and twilight periods of that age. Therefore, it refers to the specific *Krita* quarter-age together with its preceding dawn and succeeding twilight. The conclusion is that this does not refer to the mere *Krita* age as described in other texts. With a small amount of time remaining within that twilight period—meaning, as the intended *Krita Yuga* was nearing its end—Mayasura performed his penance. The sense is that the fact that Mayasura performed penance just recently <note>relative to the cosmic cycle being discussed</note> is established by the direct evidence known to all people, and does not require the authority of other scriptures.

Now, one might ask: why did Mayasura perform penance? Even a dull-witted person does not act without a purpose. To answer this, the author provides an adjective for Mayasura: **Desiring to know.** "Knowledge" here refers to the science <term>Shastra: a systematic body of teaching or sacred scripture</term> by which things are known; thus, he performed penance for the sake of gaining scientific knowledge. 

What is that science? The author provides a qualification for that knowledge: **Of the lights.** This refers to the cause of the motion of the planets and stars situated in the region of the *Pravaha* wind <note>In ancient Indian cosmology, the celestial bodies are moved by a specific cosmic wind called Pravaha</note>. Since roots meaning "to move" also mean "to know," the result is that he was desiring to know the science of light <term>Jyotisha: Astronomy/Astrology</term>, which explains the knowledge of the positions, movements, and measurements of the heavenly bodies. 

One might argue that such great effort is not necessary for the knowledge of astronomy, as it is known by all the Sages and is not difficult to grasp. To this, the author says: **Entire.** This means the complete science of astronomy. The idea is that, thinking with the mind of a Daitya <note>A race of titans or giants; Mayasura was their architect</note> that "because the Sages are human, my knowledge from them might not be complete or accurate," he sought to serve the Lord—the one who knows the reality of the entirety of the difficult science of astronomy, who is not a deceiver, who is all-knowing, and the Great Teacher.

Furthermore, one might suggest that it is not proper for an Asura <note>A titan or non-divine being</note> to engage with the science of astronomy because it would lack a spiritual result for him. To this, the author says: **A limb of the Veda.** It is a *Vedanga* <note>One of the six auxiliary disciplines of the Vedas, specifically astronomy</note>. Since the fruit of the "limb" is the same as the fruit of the "body" (the Veda itself), and that fruit is Liberation <term>Moksha: release from the cycle of rebirth</term>, it is proper to engage in this study.

<summary>This page explains the opening context of the Surya Siddhanta, detailing how the figure Mayasura performed penance at the end of the Golden Age (Krita Yuga) to receive the complete, divine science of astronomy directly from a divine source.</summary>
<keywords>Surya Siddhanta, Mayasura, Jyotisha, Astronomy, Vedanga, Krita Yuga, Vedic Science, Moksha</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the introductory commentary on the Surya Siddhanta, specifically the "Gudhartha-prakashaka" (The Illuminator of Hidden Meanings). It establishes the divine authority of astronomy/astrology as a limb of the Vedas.</meta>

# Accompanied by the Illuminator of Hidden Meanings

Therefore, it generates spiritual merit because it is included among the fourteen branches of knowledge <note>The fourteen Vidyas include the four Vedas, six Vedangas, Puranas, Nyaya, Mimamsa, and Dharma Shastras</note>, such as the Puranas and Logic.
Now, one might ask: "How is this a limb of the Veda?" To this, the author replies: "It is supreme."

->This Time is the Lord Vishnu, infinite, the Supreme Lord.<-
->Since He is worshipped through this [science], who else is considered more worthy of worship?<-

Because it explains Time, it is excellent and thus a limb of the Veda <term>Vedanga: literally 'limb of the Veda,' referring to six auxiliary disciplines used to understand and perform Vedic rituals</term>. The intention here is to distinguish it from the Puranas and other texts. Now, one might ask: "Since there are six limbs of the Veda, such as Grammar, why is there a specific focus on this one?" To this, he replies: "It is the goal." It is the best among the six limbs of the Veda. Why? Because it is "the highest."
It is the primary limb, meaning the "eye." Just as a person without eyes is unable to act, this science of light <term>Jyotish-shastra: the traditional Indian system of astronomy and astrology</term> is the most excellent among the limbs of the Veda. Furthermore, one might say: "Even so, such great effort to gain this knowledge is not justified." To this, he replies: "It is a secret."

> Knowledge indeed came to the Brahmin and said: "Protect me, I am your treasure. Do not speak of me to the scornful, the crooked, or the undisciplined; thus may I remain powerful."

According to this scripture <note>original: "Shruti," referring to the Vedas or Upanishads</note>, it means it must be kept secret. Thus, because this science is determined to be a precious gift, such great effort was made to obtain it. || 3 || Then, the Sun, being pleased, gave this to Maya <note>Maya is the great architect and asura who received the revelation of the Surya Siddhanta</note>, as he says:

->Gratified by that penance, and being pleased with him who sought a boon,<-
->The Sun himself gave the motion of the planets to Maya. || 4 ||<-

"Himself" means by his own accord. "Pleased" means he is of the nature of happiness. Alternatively, it means the beautiful, visible Sun, being satisfied, even though he dwells within the solar orb. He was "gratified" or extremely satisfied by that "penance" <term>Tapas: intense spiritual discipline or austerity</term> which was very difficult to perform. To him [Maya]...

<summary>This passage argues for the spiritual supremacy of astronomy (Jyotisha) as the "eye" of the Vedas and describes how the Sun God, pleased by the rigorous penance of the sage Maya, revealed the secrets of planetary motions.</summary>
<keywords>Surya Siddhanta, Vedanga, Jyotisha, Time as Vishnu, Maya, Sun God, Tapas, sacred knowledge</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the introductory narrative of the Surya Siddhanta, focusing on the moment the Sun God agrees to reveal astronomical secrets to the demon Maya.</meta>

# The Treatise of the Sun
<note>original: "Surya-Siddhanta"</note>

To the one named Maya, the Asura <note>A class of powerful beings in Hindu mythology, often translated as 'demons' or 'titans'</note>. To him, who was a seeker of a boon and desired to know the science of the stars <term>Jyotish-shastra: the traditional Indian system of astronomy and astrology</term> according to his own wish; to that seeker of astronomical knowledge. He gave the "conduct" or the knowledge of the planets—those celestial bodies situated within the procreative winds of space. He gave it "excellently" <note>original: "prakarshena"</note>, meaning in its entirety and according to its true essence. || 4 ||

Now, one might ask: how did this Sun, even to his own enemy who had come for refuge, speak these words for the sake of his own duty? To translate the actual words spoken by the Sun directly to Maya, the author first provides this introductory context to show the connection.

## The Illustrious Sun Spoke:

This means that the Sun, shining brilliantly with masses of light, replied to the Asura Maya. Otherwise, the connection between the fourth and fifth verses would be inconsistent. What did he say? He repeats these auspicious words:

> Your intention is known by me, for I have been gratified by your penance.
> I shall give you the knowledge based on Time, the great conduct of the planets. || 5 ||

O Maya, your "intention"—your desire in the form of a wish to know the science of the stars—is known by me, the Sun, even though it was unspoken by you; it was known instinctively. What follows from that? My success is not merely through this, therefore he says: "I." By the repetition of "to you," I shall give to you the knowledge, the scripture based primarily on Time <note>original: "kalashrayam"</note>. The "great conduct" refers to the immeasurable movements of the planets situated in the procreative winds. The resulting meaning is: the science of the stars which explains the positions and motions of the planets. I, residing within the solar orb, shall give it. Now, lest you think these words to a Daitya <note>A descendant of Diti; another term for the Asura race</note> might be deceptive, he describes his own character as non-deceiving...

<column-break/>

**Vocabulary**
*   **Surya-Siddhanta:** The "Established Doctrine of the Sun," a foundational Sanskrit text on astronomy.
*   **Mayasura:** Maya the Asura, a legendary architect and scientist of the non-gods.
*   **Jyotish-shastra:** The sacred science of light, encompassing astronomy and time-keeping.
*   **Grahanaam:** Of the planets (including the Sun and Moon in this system).
*   **Kalashrayam:** Depending on or grounded in Time.
*   **Toshita:** Gratified or pleased.
*   **Tapasa:** Through penance or ascetic heat/effort.
*   **Graha-sthiti:** The stationary position or longitudinal placement of a planet.

## Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings" <note>original: Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka; this is the title of the commentary by Ranganatha</note>

He explains the reason for recounting what was previously stated. "Gratified," he says. Because (for) he is extremely pleased by the penance and worship performed by you, he says, "therefore I give." And so, the sense is that by the power of your actions, and because of my affection for my devotees, I have set aside our natural enmity <note>Maya is an Asura (demon), traditionally the enemies of the Devas (gods) like Surya</note> and have shown compassion to you, just as Prahlada was shown compassion; you are not to be deceived. || 5 ||

Now, a doubt arises: since the Sun is always blazing with heat, how could Maya be able to stand in his presence for the duration of the teaching? Or, how could the Sun, who is in constant motion, cease his wandering to engage in a dialogue with Maya? Therefore, since giving the knowledge directly seems impossible, how could he say "I give"? To answer this, he repeats the Sun's subsequent words:

> No one can endure my brilliance, nor do I have a spare moment.
> This person, who is a partial manifestation of myself, will tell you everything in its entirety. || 6 ||

O Maya, this person standing before you will tell you the entire Science of the Stars <term>Jyotiḥśāstra: the traditional Sanskrit term for astronomy and astrology</term> in its entirety. But will he speak the truth? To this he says: "A partial manifestation of myself." This means he is related to me, the Sun, or born from me. Thus, the sense is that he will speak only the truth to you, who have received my compassion. By this, the meaning of "I give" mentioned in the previous verse is clarified as "I shall give through my own partial manifestation."

But why should you not speak it yourself? To this he says: "No." No living being is a "bearer of brilliance"—that is, capable of enduring the heat—of me, who resides in the solar disc <note>original: Sūryamaṇḍala</note>. Thus, the sense is: "How could you, being unable to stay near me for a long time, hear it from me?"

But what if Maya says, "By the power of my own penance, I am able to stay near you for a long time and will hear it from you"? To this he says: "To tell." For me, who am constantly revolving due to the Prohibitive Wind <term>Pravahavāyu: in ancient Indian cosmology, the celestial wind that keeps the planets and stars in constant motion</term> and who, by my own power, am never still, to speak...

# The Surya Siddhanta
<note>original: "सूर्यसिद्धान्तः" - The "Sun Treatise," the foundational text of Indian astronomy.</note>

A "moment" <term>kshana: a brief unit of time</term> does not exist as a static entity. Because of the constant motion of the celestial spheres, it is impossible for anything to remain in a single fixed position. 
And so, because you are stationary and I am in constant motion, it is impossible for us to remain together for a long duration; therefore, your hearing the teaching directly from me is impossible. You do not have the power to occupy my station to make such hearing possible. This is because there is no divine command from the Lord for you to do so. || 6 ||

Now, concluding the report of the Sun's words, the author introduces the dialogue between the Sun-man <term>Suryansha-purusha: a personified portion or partial incarnation of the Sun God</term> and the demon Maya <term>Mayasura: the great architect and scientist of the Asuras</term>.

> Having spoken thus, the God disappeared after commanding a portion of himself. 
> That person then spoke these words to Maya, who stood before him bowed with palms joined in reverence. || 7 ||

"The God" refers to the one residing in the solar orb. "Having spoken thus" means having said what was previously recorded. "Commanding a portion of himself" refers to the Sun-man; the Sun God ordered him, "You must tell Maya the entire greatness of the planets." Without such a command, how could he speak to Maya? The implied conjunction "and" should be understood here. "Disappeared" means the Sun-man <note>The commentator likely means the Sun God himself here</note> became invisible to the eyes. Now the text returns to the main subject: "That person." 
The Sun-man, commanded by the Sun, spoke the following words to the demon Maya. Now, one might ask: "It is said one should not speak unless asked; how then did he speak to Maya without being questioned?" To answer this, the text provides two descriptions of Maya: "bowed" and "with palms joined." "Bowed" means he was humble, performing a prostration with intense devotion and faith. "With palms joined" <term>pranjali: the gesture of folding hands</term> indicates he stood with his mind focused, his hands pressed together at the tips—a physical sign of his mental state. This clearly describes a "bodily salutation" <term>kayika-namaskara</term> involving a bowed head and joined hands. The implication is that by this gesture, which says, "Lord, I bow to you, please favor me and tell me this," Maya effectively asked, and thus the Sun-man spoke to him. || 7 || Now, the promised dialogue—

# Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings" <note>original: "Gudharthaprakashaka", the title of Ranganatha's famous 17th-century commentary</note>

Desiring to speak the knowledge to Maya in this translation, the person who is an incarnation of a fragment of the Sun <note>original: "Suryamsha-purusha"</note> says: "Listen carefully to what I say."

->“Listen with a single-minded focus to that supreme knowledge which was spoken<-
->previously by the Sun himself to the great seers in age after age.” (8)<-

O Maya! One whose mind is fixed on only one thing—that is, you, having withdrawn your mind from other subjects and giving your mind to my words—listen to this science of astronomy <note>term: "Jyotish-shastra" (the traditional Indian science of stars, mathematics, and time-keeping)</note>. The meaning is: make it perceptible to yourself through the union of the soul and the sense of hearing. 

Now, lest you think, "You are speaking something of your own invention," he explains the connection of that word "previously" and so on. That supreme knowledge, which is like an eye <note>The Vedas describe astronomy as the "eye" among the six limbs of Vedic knowledge</note>, refers to the science of astronomy. To the question of when this was spoken in the distant past, he says: "In age after age" <note>original: "Yuge Yuge"</note>. This implies it was spoken to the great sages in every Great Age <note>term: "Mahayuga" (a cosmic cycle of 4,320,000 years)</note>. 

"By the Sun himself" means directly, without an intermediary. The word "himself" is used to exclude the possibility of there being any other intermediary for those sages, just as I am an intermediary for you now because a direct conversation with the Sun is difficult. Because those sages had brought the Supreme Lord under their control through the power of their penance, and their will was unimpeded due to His grace, they were able to enter the solar orb <note>original: "Mandala-adhishthana"</note>. Thus, the sense is that what was spoken by the Sun is being told to you, not something of my own invention. (8)

Now, since what is spoken by the Sun might not be identical in every age, one might ask: "Which age's science are you teaching?" Otherwise, if it were spoken only once, the phrase "in age after age" would be illogical. To this, he says:

->“This is that very same ancient science which the Sun <note>original: "Bhaskara" (The Light-Maker)</note> spoke previously.<-
->Only the difference in time exists here due to the revolution of the ages.” (9)<-

# The Surya Siddhanta

->The Science of Light <note>original: "Jyotish-shastra"; refers to the traditional Indian system of astronomy and astrology</note> which I am about to speak to you is that which was spoken by the Sun himself.<-

By using the word "indeed," it is implied that this is a direct transmission of what the Sun spoke, and not something based on my own imagination. It is called "primordial" because it was spoken by the Sun in the earliest times. Now, one might argue that even a text spoken by the Sun in a more recent Age <note>original: "Yuga"; a vast cycle of time in Hindu cosmology</note> could be considered "ancient." To address this, the text clarifies the meaning of "primordial" by saying: "That which..." This means the science which the Sun spoke first, before which nothing else was spoken. He "proclaimed" it—meaning he spoke it with great excellence and in full detail to the Sages.

And so, because there is no reason to go beyond the first revelation, and because that first revelation was the most detailed, the later versions—which are merely summaries of what was already established—are set aside. The intention here is to teach the science as it was given in the First Age.

One might then ask: "Does this mean the versions of the Sun's science given in subsequent Ages are useless?" To this, the author says: "Of the Ages..." By the revolution and constant repetition of the Great Ages <note>original: "Mahayugas"; a cycle of 4,320,000 years</note>, the only difference in the various versions of the Sun's teachings is "merely that." This refers to the "Difference of Time"—the interval created by time itself. The time of a later scripture is different from the time of an earlier one; the difference lies in the era, not in the fundamental methods taught in the scriptures.

Thus, because the motion of the planets <note>original: "Grahachara"</note> undergoes slight variations due to the power of Time, the Compassionate One <note>the Sun deity</note> spoke as if providing a new scripture in different Ages. He did this to establish those specific variations in planetary motion for the sake of the worldly dealings of the people living at that time. Therefore, the later scriptures are not useless.

The underlying sentiment is this: "I have accepted the planetary motions established in the Sun's science for the current Age, and I have set aside the motions from the primordial version as they no longer serve a practical purpose; yet, I am teaching you the very essence of what He spoke." Furthermore, even within a single Age, if differences are observed in the planetary motions during intermediate periods, learned scholars of those times establish those differences and compose new treatises. This correction or difference added to the original text is known as the "Seed" <note>original: "Bija"; a technical term for the astronomical correction applied to mean longitudinal positions of planets to make them match observations</note>...

<summary>This page introduces the Surya Siddhanta, explaining that while the core astronomical truths are eternal and divine, the specific calculations for planetary motions must be updated (the "Bija" correction) to account for the passage of vast cosmic cycles or Yugas.</summary>
<keywords>Surya Siddhanta, Jyotish-shastra, planetary motion, Mahayuga, Bija correction, Hindu astronomy, time cycles</keywords>

# Accompanied by the "Light on the Hidden Meaning" <note>original: Gudharthaprakashaka; the title of the commentary by Ranganatha</note>

...they say. Because ancient texts have been lost, the dialogue between the Sun God and the Sages <note>original: Suryarshi-samvada</note> is also not seen nowadays; however, one should not doubt this text due to its lack of current fame, as its authority is established by sacred tradition. || 9 || Now, having introduced the "divisions of time," the author first desires to define Time itself and thus classifies it:

->Time is the destroyer of worlds; another Time is that which is used for calculation.<-
->That [calculable time] is twofold due to being gross or subtle; it is called Measurable and Immeasurable.<- || 10 ||

Time is of two kinds. One is Time that is an indivisible, continuous rod <note>representing eternal, linear time</note>, established by the evidence of other sacred scriptures. It is the "destroyer of worlds"—"worlds" here refers to living beings and, by extension, even inanimate objects. Although Time is also the cause of their birth and maintenance, it is called the "destroyer" here to emphasize its ultimate power and because destruction is the finality of all things. By saying "destroyer," birth and maintenance are also implied, for otherwise, destruction would be impossible. Therefore, it is said in other texts:

> Time creates all beings; Time sweeps away all creatures.

The other, or second type of Time, is "divided time" <note>original: khanda-kala</note>. It is "calculable" <note>original: kalanatmaka</note>, meaning it is an object of knowledge. The sense is that it is capable of being known or measured. This second, calculable Time is also of two types. The author explains this: "due to being gross or subtle," meaning through greatness and smallness. "Measurable" <note>original: murtta; literally 'having form'</note> refers to that which has a defined magnitude. "Immeasurable" <note>original: amurtta; literally 'formless'</note> is the time different from that, as described by those who know the truth. The word "and" <note>original: ca</note> in the verse connects the causes to their effects in order: thus, great time is Measurable, and minute time is Immeasurable. || 10 || Now, demonstrating the two aforementioned divisions by their nature, and desiring to explain the first division, the author speaks of two further sub-divisions.

# The Surya Siddhanta

> That which begins with a breath is called "measurable" time, while that which begins with an atom is known as "unmeasurable" time. *
> Six breaths make one *vināḍī* <note>approximately 24 seconds</note>, and sixty of those are known as a *nāḍikā* <note>approximately 24 minutes</note>. || 11 ||

A "breath" (*prāṇa*) is the time taken for one inhalation and exhalation by a healthy person sitting at ease; it is also defined as the time required to pronounce ten long syllables. This breath is the starting point of "measurable" (*mūrta*) time. That which begins with a "trifle" (*truṭi*)—including units like the *tatpara*—is contained within a single breath and is designated as "unmeasurable" (*amūrta*) time <note>original: "amūrta-sañjña"</note>. Now, because unmeasurable time is unsuitable for practical use and is secondary to the measurable time that constitutes it, the author sets aside the explanation of its divisions. Instead, focusing on measurable time as the primary subject for practical application, he describes the *pala* and the *ghaṭī*. By "six breaths," one *pala* <note>also called a vināḍī</note> is formed. Sixty of these *palas* are declared by those who know the truth of time to be one *ghaṭikā*. || 11 ||

Now, he describes the day and the month:

> Sixty *nāḍīs* are proclaimed to be one sidereal day and night.
> Thirty of those make a month; likewise, a civil month is measured by sunrises. || 12 ||

By sixty *ghaṭīs*, a sidereal <note>relating to the stars</note> day and night is declared. By the use of the word "but" (*tu*), it is implied that since the day and night are sidereal, the *ghaṭīs* composing them are also sidereal. This is because the circle of the stars <note>the zodiac</note> completes one revolution in these sixty *ghaṭīs*. A sidereal month consists of thirty such sidereal days. Since there are various systems of measurement, he defines the nature of the civil (*sāvana*) month. "Likewise," thirty days and nights—specifically those bounded by the rising of the sun, measured from one sunrise to the next—constitute a civil month.

<term>Nākṣatra: Sidereal, or measured by the stars.</term>
<term>Sāvana: Civil, or measured by sunrises.</term>

...is a civil month. || 12 || Now, after defining the lunar and solar months, and while describing the year, the author speaks of the divine day:

->A lunar month is formed by lunar days; likewise, a solar month is defined by the sun's transit.<-
->Twelve months make a year, which is called a single day of the gods. || 13 ||<-

In the same way <note>referring to the previous verse's count of thirty</note>, a lunar month <term>Aindava: relating to the moon</term> consists of thirty lunar days <term>Tithi: a lunar day, roughly 1/30th of a synodic month</term>. In the sacred sciences, this is primarily explained as ending either with the new moon or the full moon. However, in this specific treatise, the month ending with the new moon is considered primary. A month calculated from any desired lunar day is considered secondary.

By the transit—that is, the period of time marked by the sun's entry into a zodiac sign—a solar month is described by those who know the measurements of time. A transit <term>Sankranti: the moment the sun enters a new zodiacal sign</term> is the time when the center of the solar disc moves into the starting point of a zodiac sign.

Twelve months make a year. It should be understood that the year is measured by the same standard used for the months; thus, a year related to solar months is a solar year. A "day"—meaning a full day and night—is called "divine," meaning it belongs to the heavens. The meaning is that those who know the truth of measurements state that a solar year is the measure of a single day and night for the gods. || 13 ||

Now, a question arises: since the day and night of the gods has been mentioned, why has the day and night of the demons not been mentioned? Providing the answer to that, the author speaks of the year of the gods and demons:

->For the gods and the demons, day and night are mutually reversed.<-
->Six times sixty of those make a divine year, and likewise a year for the demons. || 14 ||<-

The plural is used because there are many gods and demons. "Mutually" means "each other." "Reversed" means "by inversion." Regarding "day and night," the meaning is this: what is day for the gods is night for the demons. What is night for the gods is day for the demons. What is day for the demons is night for the gods. What is night for the demons...

That is called a day of the gods. # Accompanied by the Illuminator of Hidden Meanings

By the measure of years: "by two, three, four, and the oceans" <note>original: "dvicisugāgaraiḥ"; a mnemonic where 'oceans' represents the number 4</note>. Following the rule that "numbers move from right to left," this results in four hundred and thirty-two. When multiplied by "ten thousand" <note>ayutena</note>, the total is known to be four million, three hundred and twenty thousand <note>4,320,000 years, the length of a Mahāyuga or Great Age</note>.

Now, regarding the specific durations of the quarters within a Great Age: since no specific different measures are initially heard, one might assume they are equal based on the logic that "what is not specified should be equal." However, the text denies that each is simply a fourth part of the Great Age. 

**Of the Kṛta and the others:** This refers to the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages. 
**By the arrangement of the pillars of Dharma:** <term>Dharmapāda-vyavasthayā</term> <note>The "feet" or pillars of righteousness/morality</note>. The following arrangement or status should be understood, rather than an equal duration of time. The meaning is this: In the Kṛta Age, Dharma has four pillars; therefore, its duration is the greatest. Then, in the Tretā Age, because Dharma possesses only three pillars, the duration of the Tretā is shorter in proportion. Similarly, because Dharma possesses two pillars and one pillar in the Dvāpara and Kali ages respectively, their durations are proportionately shorter than the Kṛta and Tretā. Their measures are not equal. || 16 ||

Now, if a Great Age consists of ten parts in total (the sum of all the pillars of Dharma), then what is the specific measure of each? By using the rule of proportion with the previously mentioned figures, the author explains the specific knowledge of the measures of the Kṛta and other ages:

---

-> A tenth part of the Age, multiplied by four, three, two, and one, <-
-> is in order the duration of the Kṛta and the other ages. <-
-> A sixth part of each belongs to their respective dawns and twilights. <- || 17 ||

---

The "tenth part of the Age" refers to one-tenth of the previously mentioned 4,320,000 divine years. This part is multiplied fourfold, and then by four, three, two, and one in sequence. The result is the measure of the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali ages respectively. 

One might ask: in the Law Books of Manu <note>the Manusmṛti</note>, the measures of the Kṛta and others are given in divine years as 4,000, 3,000... <note>The text cuts off here, likely preparing to explain the addition of "sandhyā" or transitional periods</note>.

# The Surya Siddhanta

100 | 12000 | <note>These figures refer to the total years in a Great Age or Mahayuga.</note> However, there appears to be a contradiction here, as the measurements for these ages are given as 4,800; 3,600; 2,400; and 1,200 years. To resolve this, the text states: *In the sixth part.* This means that one-sixth of the total duration represents the sum of the two "twilight" periods—the dawn at the beginning and the dusk at the end.

Thus, for the measurements I have stated: 4,800; 3,600; 2,400; and 1,200; their sixth parts are 800; 600; 400; and 200 respectively. These figures represent the combined duration of the opening and closing twilights for each respective age. Half of each figure represents a single transition period <term>Sandhikala (the 'junction' or transition period between two cosmic ages)</term>.

The individual transition periods at the start and end of each age are therefore 400, 300, 200, and 100 years. By subtracting these, the "pure" duration of the ages mentioned in other texts is revealed, excluding their twilights.

| Age (Yuga) | Dawn (Sandhi) | Core Duration | Dusk (Sandhi) | Total |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Krita (Golden Age)** | 400 | 4,000 | 400 | 4,800 |
| **Treta (Silver Age)** | 300 | 3,000 | 300 | 3,600 |
| **Dvapara (Bronze Age)** | 200 | 2,000 | 200 | 2,400 |
| **Kali (Iron Age)** | 100 | 1,000 | 100 | 1,200 |

Therefore, there is no contradiction; my stated figures include the transition periods because they are inherently connected to and contained within their respective ages. // 17 //

Next, to determine the duration of a <term>Kalpa (an eon, or a 'Day of Brahma')</term>, the text explains the measurement of a <term>Manvantara (the reign of a Manu, a progenitor of humanity)</term> and its transition period:

-> Seventy-one cycles of the ages are here called a Manvantara. <-
-> At its end, a transition period is declared, equal to the number of years in the Golden Age, which is a Great Flood. <- // 18 //

"Seventy-one cycles of the ages" refers to seventy-one <term>Mahayugas (Great Ages)</term>. In this context of "measured time," a Manvantara is the duration between the start of a Manu's reign and its completion. This is explained by those expert in the different divisions of time. When that Manu's reign reaches its conclusion, there is a transition period equal to the years of the Golden Age (Krita Yuga) <note>original: "Kritabda-sankhya", meaning 4,800 divine years</note> which manifests as a <term>Jalaplava (a cosmic deluge or great flood)</term>.

# The Surya Siddhanta
<note>The Surya Siddhanta is one of the oldest and most significant Sanskrit treatises on Indian astronomy, traditionally attributed to a revelation from the Sun God.</note>

Four hundred and three divine years have passed. The implied meaning is that within these divine years, Brahma <note>The creator deity in Hindu cosmology</note> completed the work beginning with the calculation of the planets and ending with the arrangement of the *Pro-vaha* winds <note>The celestial winds believed to drive the motion of the stars and planets</note>.
|| 24 || Now, the author explains the cause of the planets' apparent eastward motion:

->Moving westward with great speed along with the stars,<-
->the planets, being outpaced, lag behind as if falling back,<-
->each remaining in its own orbit. || 25 ||<-

Afterward, or rather, by repeating their cycle toward the western direction along with the stars <note>the constellations or *nakshatras*</note>, the planets—such as the Sun and others—move continuously due to the swift force of the *Pro-vaha* winds. While moving in their own respective orbits, they are "outpaced" or defeated by the stars because the stars move faster. The underlying sense is that they become "heavy," as if out of shame. "Equally" means uniformly; the word "only" is used to exclude any more or less variation. They "lag behind," meaning they appear to be suspended or trailing toward the east from their original positions. Just as one who is ashamed stays behind and does not go forward, so do the planets. By the word "but," it is implied that there is a decrease in this "heaviness" for the planets starting from Saturn down to the Moon, following the order of their orbits. Saturn is the heaviest; Jupiter is slightly less so; then Mars, and so on in order. He whose orbit is large has greater heaviness, and he whose orbit is small has a corresponding lightness of weight.

This is what is being said: Brahma established the physical sphere of the stars within the *Pro-vaha* wind. Inside that, Saturn and the others were placed in their own celestial spheres, aligned with the starting point of the zodiac—the region of Aries—near the junction star Revati <note>Zeta Piscium, the traditional zero-point of the Indian zodiac</note> located on the ecliptic within the physical stellar sphere. The ecliptic <term>Kranti-vritta: the apparent path of the Sun across the celestial sphere</term> is connected to the celestial equator at the points of Aries and Libra; the two points of the ecliptic are separated by three signs from these intersection points...

<summary>This page explains the ancient Indian astronomical theory of planetary motion, suggesting that planets only appear to move eastward because they are slower than the rapidly rotating sphere of stars moving westward.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical explanation of planetary motion and celestial spheres, specifically focusing on the mechanics of why planets appear to move differently than the fixed stars.</meta>

->Accompanied by the *Illuminator of Hidden Meanings*<-
<note>original: "Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka," the title of the commentary by Raṅganātha on the Sūrya Siddhānta.</note>

The circle consisting of the twelve zodiac signs is the path of the planets, defined by the twenty-four degrees of northern and southern declination starting from Capricorn and Cancer. The celestial equator <note>original: "viṣuvad-vṛtta"</note>, however, stays centered between the poles and passes directly over the terrestrial equator <note>original: "nirakṣa-deśa," the place with no latitude</note>. This celestial sphere of the fixed stars <note>original: "nakṣatra-gola"</note> is rotated once every sixty sidereal hours by the impact of the Provector wind <note>term: "pravaha-vāyu" - in ancient Indian cosmology, this is the cosmic wind responsible for the daily rotation of the heavens</note>. 

The planets also revolve due to the impact of the internal winds within that sphere, yet they do not move exactly in unison with the points of the ecliptic <note>term: "krānti-vṛtta" - the "circle of declination" or the sun's path</note> such as Aries. This is because the winds are subtle, their impact is slight, and the planetary bodies themselves are heavy. Consequently, a "lagging" <note>original: "lambana," here referring to the retrograde-like falling behind the stars rather than parallax</note> of the planets is observed from those positions. For this reason, a planet does not rise at the same time as the stars on the following day; rather, because the planet has been lagged by the wind, it rises later as it moves upward. 

This lagging is consistent for Saturn and the other planets because their weight corresponds to their specific orbits, and the density or impact of the winds also corresponds to those orbits. One might argue that since the winds act in accordance with the poles, the lagging of the planets should occur along the celestial equator and not the ecliptic. If that were so, the calculations for declination and the revolutions <note>term: "bhagaṇa" - a full orbit or revolution through the zodiac</note> through the twelve signs of the ecliptic mentioned later would be inconsistent. However, there is no inconsistency: even if a planet is lagged by the wind while moving along an equatorial path, it is projected by a vertical line onto the nearest point of the ecliptic within the planetary sphere. This is what is meant by the phrase "moving in their own paths"—they move along orbital paths within the celestial sphere that follow the ecliptic. This is the summary. // 25 //

Because of this, the eastward motion of the planets is established in the world; regarding this, he says:

> Therefore, their motion is eastward; through their daily revolutions,
> their speed appears different due to the size of their orbits.
> Thus, they traverse the parts of the zodiac. // 26 //

# The Treatise of the Sun

Therefore, from this very dependence <note>original: "avalambana"; referring to the gravitational or positional dependence of the celestial bodies</note>, the forward motion of those planets—that is, the state of those whose movement is toward the eastern direction—is established. This eastward motion of the planets is produced by the nature of their parallax <note>original: "lambana"; here used to describe the displacement or motion relative to the observer</note>. People who are ignorant of the true causes, perceiving this motion directly, imagine it to be produced by an inherent power of the planets. To answer how great that motion is, the author says: "By revolutions."

The daily motion, consisting of this eastward movement, is determined by the revolutions to be mentioned hereafter. When the planetary revolutions are obtained by the solar days <term>Surya-savana: a natural day measured from sunrise to sunrise</term> related to the calculation of time produced by those revolutions, then the motion for a single day is to be known through proportion. 

Now, an objection arises: since the revolutions of the planets are not equal, the daily motion of each planet is different; therefore, the previous statement that planetary motion is of the nature of a single "parallax" or displacement is incorrect, because such displacement should be uniform. To this, the author responds: "By virtue of the circumference." 

The circumference refers to the periphery of the orbit <term>kaksha-paridhi: the circular path traveled by a planet</term>. By virtue of that—in accordance with it—this planetary motion is different and not uniform. This is the intended meaning: the displacement of the planets is not in a uniform space, but rather in their own respective orbits. In those respective regions, the minutes of arc <note>original: "kala"; 1/60th of a degree</note> which are equal in number are the minutes of motion. However, these minutes represent a small physical distance in a large orbital circle and a large physical distance in a small orbital circle, because all orbital circumferences are marked with the same 21,600 minutes of the circle <note>the standard division of a circle in Indian astronomy</note>. 

As for the revolutions, they depend entirely on the motion: the planet whose orbital circle is large has fewer revolutions, and the one whose orbital circle is small has many. The motion produced from that follows the same principle; thus, there is no contradiction. 

But why is a varying motion accepted instead of a uniform motion? To this, he says: "By virtue of that." By virtue of the different speeds, the planets "enjoy" <note>original: "bhunjante"; a technical term meaning to pass through or occupy</note> the limbs, which are the zodiac signs <term>Rashi: a 30-degree arc or sign of the zodiac</term> and the lunar mansions <term>Nakshatra: the 27 sectors of the ecliptic</term>. And so, the point is that this specific motion is useful for knowing the planets' occupation of signs and so forth, whereas a uniform motion would not be. || 26 ||

Now, while explaining the distinction in the occupation of the asterisms, he describes the nature of the revolutions to be mentioned.

## Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings" <note>The *Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka*, a famous commentary by Raṅganātha on the *Sūrya Siddhānta*</note>

The word "then" <note>implied in the transition</note> indicates a distinction from what was previously stated. The specific meaning is that a planet with fast motion traverses the signs in a very small amount of time, whereas a planet with very slow motion traverses them over a long period; thus, the enjoyment of an equal number of signs and degrees does not occur in the same amount of time for slow and fast-moving planets. "By the revolution of those signs" means by their rotation. Since there are twelve signs in the Ecliptic <term>Krāntivṛtta: the sun's apparent path in the sky</term>, a "Revolution" <term>Bhagaṇa: a full circle of 360 degrees</term> is the completion of the circle's passage by those divisions. It means that the place from which a planet starts moving and to which it returns is called a "Revolution," consisting of the twelve signs.

Now, since a revolution could potentially start from any point on the Ecliptic, which specific place is the beginning? To this, he says: "At the end of the constellation Revatī" <note>original: *pauṣṇānte*</note>. Because at the beginning of creation, Brahma placed all the planets in the Ecliptic at a position near the junction star of the Revatī constellation <note>Zeta Piscium</note>, the movement of the planets is measured from that limit. The meaning is that the location immediately following the junction star of Revatī serves as both the beginning and the end point of the circle. || 27 ||

One might ask: the name "Revolution" is applied to the cycle, but is it also applied to the individual signs? To clarify this, he describes the nature of a Revolution under the guise of defining technical terms:

> Sixty seconds make a minute; sixty of those make a degree. Thirty of those degrees make a sign, and twelve of those signs make a Revolution. || 28 ||

Just as the "breath" <note>prāṇa</note> is the primary unit in the measurement of concrete time, so too are "seconds" <term>vikalā: 1/60th of a minute</term> the primary unit in the measurement of space. Sixty of these make one "minute" <term>kalā: 1/60th of a degree</term>. Sixty minutes...

# The Treatise of the Sun

Experts in the definitions of spatial measurement state that a "portion" is called a degree. A "sign" <note>Zodiac sign or Rashi</note> consists of thirty of these degrees. There are exactly twelve of these signs in total. The word "exactly" is used here to exclude any other number, such as three or four. Thus, by using the term "totality," and because the term "revolution" is applied even to a single part of the circle, the previous statement is justified. || 28 || Now, wishing to describe the revolutions, the author first states the revolutions of the Sun, Mercury, and Venus, as well as the "conjunctions" <term>shighrochcha: the points of highest velocity or 'fast apogees' used in calculating planetary positions</term> of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.

<gloss>4,320,000</gloss>
> In an Age, the revolutions of the Sun, Mercury, and Venus, 
> and of the conjunctions of Mars, Saturn, and Jupiter, 
> moving eastward, are four-zeros-teeth-oceans. || 29 ||

In a Great Age <term>Mahayuga: a vast cycle of 4,320,000 solar years</term>, for the Sun, Mercury, and Venus, there are four "vacuums" <note>zeros</note> occupying the places from the units to the thousands. Then, from the ten-thousands to the millions place, there are the "teeth" <note>32</note> and the "oceans" <note>4</note>. Thus, the solar years of an Age—measured as four, three, two, and zero followed by three more zeros <note>4,320,000</note>—are the number of revolutions, which are completions of the twelve signs of the zodiac. This same number applies to the conjunctions of Mars, Saturn, and Jupiter. The word "and" in the verse should be understood as a connective. Here, the order is not based on the planetary orbits or their movement, as Jupiter's position is central; rather, it follows the independent requirements of the calculation. 

One might ask: since these points have no physical bodies in the sky and cannot be suspended, and thus have no motion, how can "revolutions" be attributed to them? To this, the author says: "moving eastward." They move toward the east. Even though these points are invisible, they possess an eastward motion, so there is no error in stating their revolutions. The determination of their true nature and characteristics will be explained in the Chapter on True Positions. || 29 ||
Now, he states the revolutions of the Moon and Mars.

For Venus’s fast-apex: six (6), seven (7), rules (2), twins (2), sky (0), and mountains (7). <gloss>7,022,376</gloss>
For Saturn: serpents (8), six (6), five (5), flavors (6), Vedas (4), and the moon (1). || 32 || <gloss>146,568</gloss>

The revolutions of the invisible, eastward-moving fast-apex of Venus are 7,022,376. By this, the interpretation of "mountains" as seventy-one or eleven is rejected. For the physical orb of Saturn, the revolutions are 146,568. || 32 || Now he states the revolutions for the Moon’s nodes and its apogee.

> The revolutions of the Moon’s apogee <note>The point in the orbit farthest from Earth</note> in a Great Age are 488,203.
> <gloss>488,203</gloss> Moving in reverse, the revolutions of the Node <note>The Rahu or ascending node</note> are 232,238. || 33 ||

The revolutions of the Moon’s slow apogee <term>Mandocca: the point of slowest orbital velocity</term>, which moves eastward and is visible in its effects, amount to 488,203 in a Great Age. Regarding the Node—specifically the Lunar Node—because of its proximity, the revolutions of this invisible form move "leftward" or westward. These revolutions, consisting of complete circuits through the twelve signs of the zodiac, amount to 232,238 in a Great Age. The mention of the "Great Age" <term>Yuga: a cycle of 4,320,000 years</term> here is to distinguish these figures from the calculations used for the Kalpa <note>a much longer cosmic period</note> which will be discussed later regarding planetary apogees and nodes. Since the revolutions of planetary apogees and nodes do not occur identically in every Age, they are mentioned here in the context of this specific Age. The determination of the nature and direction of the apogees and nodes will be made clear in the chapter on True Motion <note>Spashta-adhikara</note>. || 33 ||

Now, to understand the nature of sidereal days in a Great Age, the author explains the nature of the civil days of the planets and the method for knowing their number:

> <gloss>1,582,237,828</gloss> The sidereal revolutions are 1,582,237,828.
> The terrestrial risings of the planets in an Age are their own sidereal risings diminished by their own revolutions. || 34 ||

Although the stars <note>Nakshatras</note> have no motion of their own, they appear to revolve due to the Provahe wind <term>Pravaha-vayu: the celestial wind believed to drive the stars westward</term>; the number of their revolutions is equal to the number of sidereal days. Therefore, the term "leftward" (westward) mentioned previously applies here as well. These revolutions number 1,582,237,828. Now, one might ask: since the planets also revolve and rise due to the force of the Pravaha wind, how are their specific days to be known? To this, he says: "The risings." By the word "rising" <term>Udaya</term>, we mean the day, derived from the definition of the period from one rising to the next. Thus, these stated sidereal days, when diminished by the planets' own previously mentioned revolutions, result in the "own-risings" <note>the civil or solar days for that specific planet</note>.

### Accompanied by the *Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka* <note>The "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings," a famous 17th-century commentary by Ranganatha.</note>

Each planet's own <term>civil days</term> <note>Sāvana-divasa: a day measured from sunrise to sunrise.</note> occur within a Great Age. By the term "in a Great Age," it is meant that at any desired time, the <term>sidereal days</term> <note>Nākṣatra-divasa: days measured by the rotation of the stars.</note> and the various civil days of the planets are determined by the planetary revolutions and their longitudinal movements. However, it is indicated that signs multiplied by five, degrees and so on multiplied by ten, and minutes should be subtracted in the place of <term>ghaṭīs</term> <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes.</note>; otherwise, because they are of different types, the difference cannot be logically established.

Here is the <term>mathematical proof</term> <note>Upapatti: the logical or geometric derivation of a formula.</note>: If there were no dependence on the eastward motion of the planets, then because the rising of a planet and the rising of a star would have the same cause, there would be no difference between sidereal and civil days. Therefore, because civil days are separated from sidereal days by the <term>lag</term> <note>Lambana: here referring to the relative slowing or parallax-like delay caused by the planet's own motion.</note> of the planets, the planetary civil days in a Great Age are fewer than the sidereal days by the number of revolutions of that lag. This is because the <term>pro-vaha</term> <note>The "pro-vaha" wind is the mythological/cosmological force in Indian astronomy that drives the celestial sphere westward.</note> does not make them equal to the westward motion of the revolutions. Thus, the statement "the risings of the stars" <note>Bhodaya: referring to verse 34 of the Surya Siddhanta.</note> etc., is proven. By this very logic, it is also established that the sum of the revolutions and the civil days equals the sidereal days. || 34 ||

Next, he states the nature of lunar months and <term>intercalary months</term> <note>Adhimāsa: extra months added to the lunar calendar to keep it synchronized with the solar year.</note>, which is the cause for knowing their quantity:

->The lunar months are the difference between the revolutions of the Sun and the Moon.<-
->Those lunar months, when diminished by the solar months, the remainders are the intercalary months. || 35 ||<-

The difference between the revolutions of the Sun and the Moon constitutes the months of the Moon; these are the lunar months. These are "diminished by the solar months"—here, by applying the word "but" <note>original: "tu"</note> from the verse, they are diminished by the solar months (which will be described later as the Sun's revolutions multiplied by twelve). The remaining lunar months that are left over are precisely the intercalary months and no others. By this, the lunar nature of intercalary months is clarified. 

Here is the mathematical proof: A lunar month consists of thirty <term>tithis</term> <note>A lunar day, or 1/30th of a synodic month.</note> and lasts until the end of the <term>conjunction</term> <note>Darśānta: the moment of the new moon when the Sun and Moon meet.</note> of the Sun and Moon. Compared to a solar month, which is defined by the Sun traversing twelve signs...

# The Surya Siddhanta

The determination <note>original: "siddhih"</note> of time is achieved solely through the interval between the Sun and the Moon. How else could the conjunction of the Sun and Moon, which occurs at the end of a new moon <note>original: "darshante"</note> and involves their slow motion, occur again at the end of the next new moon? Indeed, a difference of twelve zodiac signs constitutes one revolution's difference; therefore, a lunar month is established by this difference in revolutions. The extent to which lunar months exceed solar months is defined as the "intercalary months" <term>Adhimasa: extra months added to the lunar calendar to keep it synchronized with the solar year</term>. This nature is defined here because of its utility in the calculations to be explained later. || 35 ||

Now, the author explains the nature of the "omitted days" <note>original: "avama"</note> and the solar civil days which are to be discussed.

> By subtracting the civil days from the lunar days, the "loss of lunar days" is found.
> The time from one sunrise of the Sun to the next sunrise are the "earth-civil days." || 36 ||

This means: from the lunar days <note>the lunar days to be mentioned hereafter</note>, having subtracted <note>original: "projhya"</note> the civil days, the remainder is the "accumulation of lunar dates" <note>original: "tithichayah"</note>. In these lunar dates, there is a "loss" or deficiency equal to the remainder of the civil days. Alternatively, the term "tithi" <note>lunar day</note> implies that the civil day is a "loss" from the lunar day; this nature is defined for its utility in future calculations. 

Now, one might ask: since civil days for all planets were mentioned previously <note>in the section "revolutions of the earth," etc.</note>, whose days should be taken here? In response, under the guise of describing the nature of the Sun's civil days, the author says: "From sunrise..." The period of time beginning from the moment of the Sun's rise until the moment of its next immediate rise is one day. Such days are "earth-civil days" <note>original: "bhumi-savana-vasarah"</note>. They are called "earth days" because sunrise is perceived in relation to the Earth, and they are also "civil days" <note>savana</note>. Thus, by using the terms "civil" and "earth" without further qualification, it is implied that these refer only to the Sun's days and not to those of other planets, as the others lack such specific designation. || 36 || 

To the question of "how many are there," the author next provides their quantity and the quantity of lunar days.

# The Treatise of the Sun

Since the revolutions <term>bhagana; the complete orbital cycles of a planet</term> cannot be fully accounted for within a single Age <term>Yuga; a cycle of 4,320,000 years</term>, it is necessary to state the revolutions for a Kalpa <term>a vast cosmic period consisting of 1,000 Yugas</term>. One might ask why these revolutions and other periods were not stated for the Kalpa at the very beginning. To this, the author replies:

> The intercalary months, the omitted lunar days, the sidereal, lunar, and solar days—these, when multiplied by one thousand, become the revolutions and other periods in a Kalpa. || 40 ||

These previously mentioned "revolutions and others"—meaning the list beginning with revolutions—are as follows: the intercalary months <term>adhimaasa; extra months added to align lunar and solar years</term>, the omitted lunar days <term>unaraatra; days dropped to maintain the lunar calendar</term>, and the sidereal, lunar, and solar days. Each of these is related to its respective day-count. For instance, "the sidereal days of the stars," "the lunar days," and "the solar days" <note>The text refers to specific numerical mnemonics used in previous verses to denote these large figures</note>. Solar months should also be included here. These are stated as the revolutions in a Kalpa when multiplied by one thousand, because a Kalpa consists of a thousand Ages. The intent is that they were originally stated for a single Age for the sake of brevity. || 40 ||

Now, in two verses, while stating the revolutions of the slow-moving apogees <term>mandocca; the point in an orbit furthest from the Earth</term> of the Sun and other planets, he introduces the revolutions of the nodes <term>paata; the points where a planet's orbit crosses the ecliptic</term>.

> In a Kalpa, the revolutions of the Sun’s apogee, moving eastward, are 387; of Mars, 204; of Mercury, 368; || 41 ||
> Of Jupiter, 900; of Venus, 535; and of Saturn’s apogee, 39. Now, for the nodes, moving westward: || 42 ||

The terms "moving eastward" and "in a Kalpa" apply to each planet up to the apogee of Saturn. In a Kalpa, the revolutions of the Sun’s apogee, which moves with a forward motion, are measured as seven, eight, and three <note>original: "saptāṣṭavahnayaḥ" (387) read from right to left in the Katapayadi system</note>... [the text continues to list the nodes of Saturn].

# The Treatise of the Sun (Surya Siddhanta)

In this context, to dispel the slight doubt as to why the revolutions of the Moon’s apogee and nodes were not mentioned here, the author reminds us of what was stated previously. Regarding the "revolutions": the revolutions of the Moon’s <term>Mandocca</term> <note>the lunar apogee, or the point where the moon is furthest from Earth</note> and <term>Pata</term> <note>the ascending node, where the moon crosses the ecliptic</note> were indeed stated in this chapter during the previous discussion of planetary revolutions in a <term>Yuga</term> <note>an immense cycle of time</note>. The word "certainly" is used to dismiss any idea of forgetfulness; they were declared in the verse beginning with "The Moon's apogee..." etc. || 44 ||

Now, wishing to explain the calculation of the planetary positions at a desired time, the author provides three verses to determine the years elapsed since the end of the <term>Krita Yuga</term> <note>the Golden Age, the first of the four world ages</note>. This is necessary for calculating the <term>Ahargana</term> <note>the total count of elapsed days since a fixed epoch</note> based on the time elapsed in the current planetary motion.

> Having summed the time of the six <term>Manus</term> <note>progenitors of humanity; there are 14 in a cosmic day</note> along with their respective <term>Sandhis</term> <note>twilight periods or transitional intervals between ages</note>,
> and including the <term>Sandhi</term> at the beginning of the <term>Kalpa</term> <note>a cosmic day of 4.32 billion years</note>, as well as that of the Manu Vaivasvata; || 45 ||
> [Multiply] by the number of elapsed <term>Yugas</term>, and likewise adding this current <term>Krita Yuga</term>;
> then, having subtracted the time of creation previously mentioned in divine measurement; || 46 ||
> In the count of solar years, these are known to have passed at the end of the <term>Krita Yuga</term>:
> Zero, zero, zero, zero, two, seven, three, five, nine, and one. || 47 ||

<margin>1,953,720,000 <note>This marginal number likely represents a calculation of elapsed years, though the OCR digits 125702 appear to be a partial or misread inventory number</note></margin>

The time of the six Manus in solar years, together with their "twilights" (<term>Sandhis</term>)—which are six intervals each equal to the length of a <term>Krita Yuga</term>—along with the twilight at the beginning of the <term>Kalpa</term> (the <term>Krita</term>-sized interval connected to the start of the cosmic day), are all to be integrated. The word "but" in the text serves to dismiss the idea that only half of the lifespan is considered. Furthermore, the elapsed <term>Yugas</term> of the seventh Manu, known as Vaivasvata, are twenty-seven; these are combined. Likewise, the <term>Krita Yuga</term> belonging to the current twenty-eighth cycle is added as having already passed.

# Page 32
## Accompanied by the *Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka* <note>The "Revealer of Hidden Meanings," a famous commentary by Raṅganātha on the Sūrya Siddhānta.</note>

-> <-

Then, from the established doctrine <term>Siddhānta; a formal astronomical treatise</term>, the time of creation—specifically the time required for the process of creation expressed in years—is indicated by the divine measurement previously mentioned. It was stated that "divine years are multiplied by one hundred" using the previously mentioned figures <note>original: "kṛtādrividā," referring to specific numerical codes used in Sanskrit astronomy</note>. The essential meaning is that the number of solar years is calculated by multiplying the divine years by three hundred and sixty. By this, it is made clear that the unification mentioned earlier is done by the standard of solar years, not by the standard of divine years. 

The word "and" <note>original: "ca"</note> should be understood here in the sense of addition, after having "discarded" or subtracted [the creation period]. These remaining years—amounting to 1,706,400,000 <note>The text uses word-numerals: kha (0), abhra (0), kha (0), abhra (0), dvi (2), sapta (7), tri (3), śara (5), atidhṛti (18/19) - representing a massive epochal number</note>—should be known as having passed at the end of the quarters of the Golden Age <term>Kṛta Yuga; the first and longest of the four world ages</term>. 

Now, it might seem that stating "of the six Manus" <note>Manu: a progenitor of humanity; there are 14 in one Day of Brahma</note> and so on is a repetition, since the combined time from the beginning of the Kalpa <term>Kalpa; a Day of Brahma, lasting 4.32 billion years</term> has already been stated. One might argue that the previous mention was to understand the total age of Brahma, while this mention is for the purpose of calculating planetary positions <term>Grahasādhana; the mathematical determination of a planet's place in the sky</term>. Otherwise, one might wrongly attempt to calculate planetary positions from the total elapsed age of Brahma. 

It is right to calculate planetary positions from the elapsed age of Brahma, and we accept that. If it were otherwise, since the planetary cycles exist from the birth of Brahma until his end, it would be impossible to calculate planetary positions due to a lack of knowledge of the elapsed years since the start of Brahma's day. But this is not so. 

By the statement that "the Kalpa causes the destruction of all beings at the end of a thousand Great Ages," it is said that the planetary cycles are destroyed at the end of Brahma's day, and the planetary cycles are created at the beginning of that day. Therefore, it is only the years elapsed since the beginning of Brahma's day that are useful for planetary motion, not the years of Brahma's total lifespan. If the planets did not exist, there would be no point in calculating them. 

Therefore, the elapsed years useful for planetary motion have been calculated again within the Day of Brahma. However, the years elapsed since the start of the Day of Brahma must be reduced by the "time of creation's delay"—the period from the very start of the Day until the actual moment planetary motion begins. These "years since creation" are what are actually used for planetary calculations. Otherwise, if one tried to calculate planetary motion during that internal period of creation when the planets were not yet moving, it would lead to errors. This explains the necessity of stating the time of creation.

# The Surya Siddhanta

<note>original: "सूर्यसिद्धान्तः" - The Sun's Treatise, the foundational text of Indian astronomy.</note>

This is the direction of the argument, as there is no inconsistency. For instance, 360 solar years make one divine year. These multiplied by twelve thousand make a Great Age <note>original: "Mahayuga", a cycle of 4,320,000 years</note>, which is 4,320,000 years. This multiplied by seventy-one is the measure of a Manu period, 306,720,000 years. This multiplied by six is the measure of six Manu periods, 1,840,320,000 years. This, combined with seven "sandhis" <note>twilight periods between ages</note> each equal to the measure of a Golden Age <note>original: "Krita Yuga"</note> (1,728,000), which totals 12,096,000, results in 1,852,416,000. Adding twenty-seven Great Ages (116,640,000) results in 1,969,056,000. Adding the Golden Age of the current cycle (1,728,000) results in the total elapsed years of the Kalpa <note>original: "Kalpagata-varsha"</note>, which is 1,970,784,000. Subtracting the time spent in creation (47,400 divine years multiplied by 360, equaling 17,064,000), the elapsed years used for calculating planetary motions at the end of the Golden Age are 1,953,720,000. || 47 ||

Now, the author explains the method for calculating the "Heap of Days" <term>Ahargana: the total number of civil days elapsed from a fixed epoch to a desired date</term> at a given time, and then the determination of the lords of the day, month, and year in four verses:

"From that point onward" means after the end of the Golden Age. The number of solar years elapsed at the desired time is added to the years arising from the end of the Golden Age...

## Accompanied by the *Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka* <note>The "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings," a famous commentary by Raṅganātha on the Sūrya Siddhānta.</note>

The previously mentioned figures, such as the "four voids" <note>original: "khacatuṣka"; referring to the number 40,000 used in epoch calculations</note> and so on, when properly applied, result in the elapsed Solar Years at the desired time. These are converted into months—meaning they are multiplied by twelve. At the desired time, these are combined with the elapsed months starting from the bright half of the month of Madhu <note>The month of Chaitra, marking the beginning of the lunar year</note> up to the limit of the <unclear>Solar</unclear> bright half. 

If an intercalary month <term>Adhimāsa: an extra month added to the lunar calendar to keep it in sync with the solar seasons</term> falls within these elapsed months, it should not be counted separately here, as it is considered part of the subsequent month and that specific month is treated as having sixty days. These resulting months are placed in two positions. Multiplied by the Intercalary Months of an Age <term>Yuga: a vast cosmic cycle of time</term> and divided by the Solar Months of an Age, the resulting whole intercalary months are added to the total. 

Note that if a "true" intercalary month has occurred but is not obtained through this calculation, one should add one to the calculated intercalary months. Conversely, if a "true" intercalary month has not occurred but is obtained by the calculation, one should subtract one. Otherwise, the calculated <term>Ahargana: the total number of civil days elapsed from a fixed epoch to a given date</term> would differ by an interval of thirty days. 

These resulting months are then converted into days—meaning they are multiplied by thirty. These are then increased by the elapsed lunar days <note>tithis</note> starting from the first day of the bright half of the current month. These are placed in two positions. In one position, they are multiplied by the Omitted Days <note>Avamas</note> of an Age and divided by the Lunar Days of an Age. The resulting whole omitted days are subtracted from the other position. The result is the Civil <note>Sāvana</note> Day-Count <note>Ahargana</note> at midnight at the location of Laṅkā <note>The terrestrial equator, used as the prime meridian in Indian astronomy</note>.

From this calculated Day-Count, starting from the Sun, the Lords of the Day, Month, and Year are determined. He describes the knowledge of the Lord of the Day: "By seven..." This Day-Count is reduced by multiples of seven; the remainder determines the result. From that remainder, the Lord of the Day—the master of the weekday—is found, starting with Sunday. It follows that the next one is the current Lord of the Day. 

The rationale <note>upapatti</note> here is as follows: In converting Solar Years into months, the solar months related to the time from the beginning of creation up to the end of the intercalary month...
