## The Surya Siddhanta
<note>original: "Surya Siddhanta" — The "Sun Precept," a foundational Sanskrit treatise on Indian astronomy.</note>

If one asks why the sum of the fractional lunar months <term>Lunar month: the period between two new moons, roughly 29.5 days</term> related to the time between the start of the month of Chaitra <note>The first month of the Hindu lunar calendar</note> and the end of the period equals twelve times the elapsed solar years at the beginning of Chaitra—listen to the explanation. It is undisputed that twelve times the solar years equals the number of solar months <term>Solar month: the time it takes the sun to pass through one zodiac sign</term> at the start of a solar year.

When these are combined with the calculated fractional intercalary months <term>Intercalary month (Adhimasa): an extra month added to the lunar calendar to keep it synchronized with the solar seasons</term>, they become the fractional lunar months at the start of the solar year. At the beginning of Chaitra, these become whole (integer) lunar intercalary months by removing the fractional parts. This is because the fractional remainder represents the time difference between the start of Chaitra and the start of the solar year. When these whole intercalary months are subtracted, the remaining lunar months at the start of Chaitra are proven to be equal to twelve times the solar years, as previously stated.

By adding these whole intercalary months, the total measure of lunar months at the start of Chaitra is established. To find the desired time, the months elapsed since the bright half of Chaitra are added. By this logic, the criticism that "lunar months since Chaitra cannot be added to solar months (twelve times the solar years) because they are of different types" is refuted.

According to the stated method, since lunar months are indeed present there, the addition is possible as they are of the same type. We did not perform the previous addition ourselves; rather, it is self-evident because it takes the form of twelve times the solar years.

Now, these whole intercalary months must be added. From the fractional solar months elapsed from the beginning of creation until the last fallen intercalary month, the whole lunar intercalary months are derived using a proportion: "If the solar months of an Age <note>Yuga: a vast cosmic cycle of time</note> yield the intercalary months of an Age, then how many do these specific solar months yield?" Because they are calculated from solar units, they are lunar. Now, to know the fractional part of the intercalary month at the desired time: "If the lunar months of an Age yield the intercalary months of an Age, then how many are yielded by these fractional lunar months situated between the last intercalary month and the desired time?" Since no full intercalary month has occurred in that interval, the result is a solar fraction—

In this calculation, the lunar months of the age act as the multiplier and the solar months of the age act as the divisor. Since the lunar months in the multiplier and divisor cancel each other out as equals, the result is: the desired lunar months multiplied by the age's intercalary months and divided by the age's solar months. The result is the intercalary fraction in lunar terms.

Now, since it is impossible to know the specific solar and lunar months separately, one cannot easily find the intercalary month and its fraction. However, if there is a single divisor but different numerators and multipliers, then the sum of the desired solar and lunar months is known. This sum, multiplied by the intercalary months of the age and divided by the solar months of the age, gives the intercalary months as the quotient. The remainder—the fractional part—is not useful for calculating the "heap of days" <term>Ahargana: the total number of elapsed days from a fixed epoch to a given date</term>. In that calculation, only the whole intercalary months are necessary to add, as they represent the deficiency <note>the gap between solar and lunar years</note>. Thus, the count of lunar months from the beginning of Creation <note>Srishtyadi</note> up to the desired month is established.

However, many scholars argue that because the solar months (calculated as solar years multiplied by twelve) are unknown from the start of the solar year to the desired time, one should simply add the known elapsed lunar months starting from the month of Chaitra. But in those desired solar months, there is an excess consisting of the intercalary remainder. By discarding that remainder and adding only the whole intercalary months, a continuous sequence is maintained. They claim that the calculation of intercalary months is based on the lunar system because they accept the desired solar months as being increased by that intercalary remainder.

This view should be reflected upon. Continuity is achieved simply by adding the intercalary months—derived from the pure desired solar months—to those solar months which are increased by the intercalary remainder. Otherwise, by the rule of proportion, if the intercalary months of the age are multiplied by the remainder and divided by the solar months of the age, the remainder would increase. After dividing these by seven and discarding the quotient, the remainders identify the Lord of the Month and the Lord of the Year in sequence. <note>This refers to the planetary rulers assigned to specific time divisions in the Hindu calendar.</note>

## Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings"

The calculation of the Lord of the Day <note>Varesvara</note> follows the order previously mentioned starting with the Sun. The calculation of these two <note>the Lord of the Month and the Lord of the Year</note> is also based on that same sequence. Here is the underlying logic: From the beginning of creation, one solar-civil month <note>Saurasavana-masa</note> consists of thirty day-and-night cycles. The Sun is its lord because the Sun is the ruler of the first day of that month. Similarly, at the start of the second month, Mars is the ruler of the day; therefore, Mars is the Lord of the Second Month. Thus, between each successive Lord of the Month, there is an interval of two <note>skipping two days in the weekly sequence</note>. This is because when thirty days are divided by seven <note>the days of the week</note>, the remainder is two.

In the same way, one solar-civil year <note>Saurasavana-varsha</note> consists of three hundred and sixty day-and-night cycles. The Sun is its lord because the Sun is the ruler of the first day of the year. At the start of the second civil year, Mercury is the ruler of the day; therefore, Mercury is the Lord of the Second Year. Thus, between each successive Lord of the Year, there is an interval of three. This is because when three hundred and sixty days are divided by seven, the remainder is three.

To determine how many months and years have passed in the current era, the total number of elapsed days <term>Ahargana</term><note>literally "heap of days"</note> is divided by thirty to find the elapsed months, and by three hundred and sixty to find the elapsed years. Since there is a shift of two days per month, the elapsed months are multiplied by two and one is added to find the current Lord. Since there is a shift of three days per year, the elapsed years are multiplied by three and one is added to find the current Lord. Because there are seven days in a week, these results are divided by seven; the remainders, starting from the Sun, indicate the Lords of the Month and Year. || 52 ||

Now, he describes the movement of the planets:

> The total number of elapsed days, multiplied by the planet's own revolutions and divided by the number of terrestrial days in a cycle, results in the mean position of the planet in revolutions and its fractions. || 53 ||

The "total number of elapsed days" <note>Ahargana</note> is multiplied by "its own revolutions"—meaning the specific number of revolutions assigned to that planet within a Great Age <term>Yuga</term> or a Kalpa <note>an immense cosmic time cycle</note>. Then, by the "terrestrial days" <note>Kuvasara</note>—

To this, he says: "The others have not reached zero degrees." The remaining apogees and nodes, which are described as <term>slow-moving (mandacarinah)</term> <note>having very low angular velocity</note> and were previously mentioned in terms of their total revolutions, have not—at this end of the Golden Age—reached a state of "zero degrees" (niranshatvam) or a lack of degrees. 

Furthermore, stating their positions in signs and degrees would be cumbersome. Because they move so slowly, a position calculated once remains useful for a thousand years. Since there is no necessity for constant calculation, their derivation from the elapsed years of the Silver Age has been disregarded—this is the point. 

However, if they are to be calculated from that point, they must be added to their respective <term>epochs (kshepakas)</term> <note>initial positions or constants used in astronomical calculations</note>. The epoch constants (in signs, degrees, minutes, and seconds) are:
The Sun’s apogee: 0s 7° 28' 12"
Mars: 2s 21° 14' 24"
Mercury: 5s 7° 4' 48"
Jupiter: 0s 6° 0' 0"
Venus: 11s 13° 21' 0"
Saturn: 4s 20° 13' 12"
The Node of Mars: 8s 11° 10' 12"
Mercury: 8s 11° 16' 48"
Jupiter: 8s 7° 56' 24"
Venus: 4s 17° 25' 7"
The Node of Saturn: 4s 10° 13' 12"
In this manner, the planets are to be calculated for any desired time from their respective...

# The Surya Siddhanta
<note>original: "Surya Siddhanta" — The "Sun Treatise," one of the most foundational ancient Indian texts on astronomy.</note>

First, the knowledge of the *yojana* <note>A traditional Indian unit of distance, roughly 5 to 9 miles.</note> must be established. || 58 || Now, in order to bring about the calculation of the longitudinal correction <term>deshantara-phala: the correction applied to planetary positions to account for the observer's distance from the prime meridian</term> for the planets, the author speaks of the Earth's circumference, preceded by a statement on the Earth's diameter which serves as its basis.

## The diameter of the Earth is twice eight hundred yojanas.
## The square root of ten times the square of that is the Earth's circumference. || 59 ||

Eight hundred doubled is sixteen hundred *yojanas*; this is the Earth's diameter <note>original: "bhukarna" — literally "Earth-ear" or "Earth-diagonal," used here for diameter</note>. It is the diameter of the terrestrial globe, the line passing through the center of the circular circumference. By saying "doubled," it is indicated that eight hundred is the measure of the straight line from the center to the circumference <note>the radius</note>. Just as the radius of a planetary orbit is treated as a "diagonal" in calculations, so too is this Earth-diameter. The word "but" <note>original: "tu"</note> implies that although this may contradict the *Puranas* <note>Ancient Hindu religious texts which often give much larger, mythological dimensions for the Earth</note>, it is established by the authority of tradition supported by direct observation.

From this, he explains the knowledge of the circumference. "From the square of that": from the square of the Earth's diameter (the product of the number multiplied by itself), multiplied by ten, take the square root. The method for finding what number multiplied by itself produces this result (the square root) is well-known in other mathematical treatises. This result is the Earth's circumference.

Here is the mathematical proof: Since the radius <note>original: "trijya"</note> is measured as 3438 <margin>represented by the mnemonic "Gaja-Agni-Veda-Rama": Elephants (8), Fires (3), Vedas (4), Rama (3) read right-to-left as 3438</margin>, and the diameter is twice the radius, the circumference for that diameter is equal to the minutes in a circle, which is 21,600. Therefore, for any given diameter, what is the circumference? The multiplier is 21,600 and the divisor is 6876 <note>twice 3438</note>. When these are simplified, the divisor becomes 1 and the multiplier is approximately 3 and 1/8th. Thus, the diameter multiplied by this gives the circumference.

In this context, the Divine Author <note>referring to the Sun God, the traditional revealer of this text</note> has squared the value to facilitate the calculation, resulting in 9;52;12. For the sake of simplicity, the value of 10 was adopted here, as the difference is very slight. Since it is said that one should "multiply a square by a square," the square of the diameter is multiplied by ten, and the square root of that result yields the diameter multiplied by the square root of ten. Although using ten instead of the precise square results in a "gross" <note>approximate</note> calculation, it is nonetheless used for supreme...

->Accompanied by the *Exposition of the Hidden Meaning*<- <note>original: "Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka," the name of the famous commentary by Raṅganātha</note>

The compassionate Lord, for the benefit of the world and to simplify the calculations, has accepted this. > The Earth's own corrected circumference is found by multiplying [the equatorial circumference] by the sine of latitude and dividing by the radius. By that [corrected circumference], the daily motion of the planet multiplied by the distance of longitude is divided. || 60 ||
> The result, in minutes of arc and so on, should be subtracted from the planets if the observer is to the East. If the location is to the West of the prime meridian, it should be added; thus the planets are corrected for one's own location. || 61 ||

The hypotenuse of the equinoctial shadow <note>original: "akṣakarṇa"</note> is the square root of the sum of the squares of twelve and the equinoctial shadow. The radius multiplied by twelve and divided by this [hypotenuse] results in the sine of the colatitude <term>Lambajya: the sine of the angle between the zenith and the celestial equator</term>. The circumference of the Earth multiplied by this and divided by the radius—measured here as 3,438 <note>original: "gaja-agni-veda-rāma" or 8-3-4-3</note>—results in the "corrected circumference of the Earth" <term>Sphuta-bhuparidhi</term> pertaining to one's own local country. 

The daily motion of a planet <note>original: "gati"</note> is multiplied by the "difference of longitude" <note>the distance in yojanas between the prime meridian and the local place</note> and divided by that corrected circumference of the Earth. The result is in minutes of arc and so on. If the local place is situated in the eastern direction from the prime meridian line, that result should be subtracted or diminished from the planetary positions. If the local place is situated in the western direction from the prime meridian line, the result should be added or joined to the planets. This is to be done by the calculator. Those resulting planets then become "local" <note>original: "svadeshajah"</note>. Because the previously calculated "heap of days" <term>Ahargana: the total days elapsed since the start of the epoch</term> was calculated for the location of Lanka <note>the traditional Indian prime meridian</note>...

# The Surya Siddhānta
<note>original: "Sūrya Siddhānta" — The Sun's Treatise, a foundational text of Indian astronomy.</note>

Because the planets calculated from that <insert>the base text</insert> pertain to the location of Lanka <note>Lanka is the traditional reference point on the equator for Indian astronomers, representing zero latitude and zero longitude.</note>. Here is the mathematical rationale: Although the Earth is ball-shaped <note>original: "kandukākāratvena" — like a ball or globe</note> and its circumference is uniform everywhere, making a "true circumference" <term>sphuṭa-paridhi: the corrected circumference of the Earth at a specific latitude</term> seem impossible, we assume the equatorial region <term>nirakṣa-deśa: the "region without latitude," or the equator</term> to be the center. The stated Earth's circumference applies only to those equatorial regions. Elsewhere, following that logic, the circles become smaller and smaller toward the north and south, resulting in a diminished circumference at one's own location, which is called the "true circumference."

Thus, at ninety degrees—at the North Pole <note>original: "Meru"</note> and the South Pole <note>original: "Vaḍavā"</note>—there is a total absence of circumference. At the equator, the circumference is stated to be at its maximum. Therefore, where the latitude <term>akṣāṃśa</term> is at its maximum of ninety, the colatitude <term>lambāṃśa: the complement of latitude (90 minus latitude)</term> is absent. Where there is no latitude, the colatitude is at its maximum of ninety. The nature of latitude and colatitude will be explained further on.

And so, as the circumference decreases in accordance with the decrease in colatitude, a proportion is established: if the stated Earth's circumference corresponds to the maximum colatitude of ninety degrees, what then corresponds to the colatitude of one's own location? Although this proportion is logical, it is ignored by some because proportions cannot be directly applied to the degrees of a circle. Since the use of sines <term>jyā: the chord-half or sine used in Indian trigonometry</term> is accepted by all, the maximum sine <term>trijyā: the radius of the calculation circle</term> is used as the standard. The sine of the colatitude <term>lamba-jyā</term> is used as the desired value. Thus, the calculation for the "true circumference" is rightly and logically stated.

The rationale for the difference in longitude <term>deśāntara: the longitudinal distance between two places</term> is as follows: the planet calculated for Lanka must be adjusted for one's own location, specifically for the point on the equator that lies directly south or north on the same meridian. For this, it is necessary to know the distance in leagues <term>yojana: a traditional unit of distance, roughly 8-9 miles</term> between the observer's meridian and the equatorial reference point. This is essential for those observing from Lanka. Just as the circumference diminishes, that distance also diminishes. The distance between one's own location and the prime meridian <note>The line passing through Lanka and Ujjain</note> is calculated upon one's own local circumference. By the proportion—if this distance in leagues exists on the local circumference, what would it be on the equatorial circumference?—the distance between the observer's meridian and the equator is known. Then, in the time between two sunrises, the Sun traverses the Earth's circumference...

## Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings" <note>The Gudharthaprakashaka, a famous 17th-century commentary by Ranganatha on the Surya Siddhanta, a foundational Sanskrit astronomical text.</note>

The planets traverse their respective orbits at their own specific velocities, measured in minutes of arc <term>kala <note>A unit of angular measurement where 60 minutes equal one degree.</note></term>. Based on the previously mentioned circumference, if the planetary motion in minutes is known, then the distance in <term>yojanas <note>An ancient Indian measure of distance, roughly 8 to 15 kilometers.</note></term> between the prime meridian at Lanka <note>In ancient Indian astronomy, Lanka refers to a theoretical point on the equator at zero longitude, not necessarily the modern island of Sri Lanka.</note> and one's local equatorial position is calculated. By the rule of proportion, since the multipliers and divisors of the stated circumferences are equal, the distance in yojanas between the prime meridian and one's local meridian, multiplied by the planetary motion and divided by the earth's circumference, results in the "longitudinal correction" <term>deshantara <note>Literally 'difference of place'; the correction applied to planetary positions to account for the observer's longitude relative to the prime meridian.</note></term> in minutes of arc.

Although the longitudinal correction could be derived through a single proportion—asking: "If the total circumference of the sky corresponds to the daily motion, what does the distance between the prime meridian and the local meridian correspond to?"—the author has instead provided a two-step proportion. This was done to assist those of very dull intellect who might not understand how a result pertains to the equatorial region without explicitly mentioning the "equatorial place" <term>niraksha-desha <note>Literally 'a place without latitude,' i.e., a point on the terrestrial equator.</note></term>.

The reasoning for the application of this correction is as follows: If one's local equatorial position is to the east of Lanka, midnight at that local position occurs earlier than midnight at Lanka. This is because, due to the force of the <term>pravaha <note>The 'prohibitive' or 'pro-vaha' wind, which in ancient cosmology was believed to drive the celestial spheres from east to west.</note></term> wind, the sun rises earlier in the east. Therefore, to find the planet's position for that earlier local time from the position calculated for the later Lanka time, the correction must be subtracted. Conversely, if the equatorial position is west of Lanka, midnight occurs later than at Lanka; thus, to adjust the earlier Lanka-based planetary position to the later local time, the correction must be added.

It should be understood that for the "nodes" <note>The points where a planet's orbit crosses the ecliptic.</note> which are subtracted from a full circle, this correction is applied in reverse. Because the local meridian and the local equatorial point share the same north-south line, their midnights are identical. Therefore, the planetary positions calculated for the local equatorial midnight remain valid and unchanged for the observer's actual local midnight. All of this is logically established. || 61 ||

Next, the author describes the nature of the Prime Meridian <term>rekha <note>Literally 'the line'; the zero-longitude meridian passing through Ujjain and Lanka.</note></term> and names certain locations situated upon it.

# Accompanied by the *Gudharthaprakashaka* <note>The "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings," a famous commentary by Ranganatha on the Surya Siddhanta.</note>

When the "emergence" <note>original: *unmilana*; the moment the moon begins to reappear from the Earth's total shadow</note> occurs—meaning at that specific time—then the desired location of the observer stands to the East of the central meridian <note>The prime meridian, traditionally passing through Ujjain</note>. If the text reads "observed emergence" <note>original: *drksiddham*</note>, it refers to the emergence as seen by the naked eye. If this happens before the calculated time—meaning without surpassing it—then it is in the East. By the word "and," if the emergence of the moon occurs after the calculated time, then the observer's location stands in the Western direction.

Now, one might ask: why is the time of "emergence" specifically taken here, out of all the phases like contact, clearance, immersion, and emergence? To this, the author says: "In this way." Or, by another method, from the "immersion" <note>original: *sammilana*; the moment the moon is completely covered by the shadow</note>. Following the mathematical methods described in the chapter on Lunar Eclipses <note>original: *chandra-grahana*</note>, if the immersion occurs after the calculated time, the location is to the East of the central meridian; if the immersion occurs before the calculated time, the location is to the West. The word "even" is used for emphasis. Thus, the emergence and immersion times are used to determine the displacement.

The mention of "emergence" is illustrative; the author ignores the first contact and final clearance because they are difficult to perceive with certainty at the very beginning and end. Instead, the author uses immersion and emergence—the middle phases of the eclipse—because they can be determined with certainty.

Next, he explains how the longitudinal result <note>original: *deshantara-phala*</note> is established by means of the distance in *yojanas* <note>A traditional unit of distance, roughly 8-9 miles</note>. Between those two—the observed time of emergence/immersion and the mathematically calculated time—one should take the difference in *ghatis* <note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note>. One should then multiply the Earth's circumference <note>original: *bhuparidhi*</note> as observed at one's own location—calculated by methods such as "multiplying by the sine of latitude"—by that difference. Dividing that product of the corrected circumference by sixty, the resulting *yojanas* indicate the distance to the East or, alternatively, the *yojanas* situated in the Western division. This is the circumference of one's own country...

# The Treatise of the Sun

The limit is the distance from the circular region of one's own location to the prime meridian <note>original: "rekhā-desha," referring to the zero-longitude line passing through Ujjain</note>. This is the meaning. It should be understood by the mathematician—this is the implied remainder of the sentence. The result is the distance in <term>yojanas</term> <note>a traditional Indian unit of distance, roughly 8-9 miles</note> between the prime meridian and one's own location. With those distance-yojanas, the mathematician should calculate the "longitudinal correction" <note>original: "deshāntara-phalam"</note> in minutes of arc <note>original: "kalā"</note>, following the method previously described, such as "multiplied by the longitudinal difference." Because of the word "hi" <note>a Sanskrit particle often used for emphasis or to indicate a reason</note>, the corrective process is the same because the nature of the calculation is identical.

Here is the underlying logic <note>original: "upapatti"</note>: Without the longitudinal correction, the planetary calculation corresponds only to the prime meridian. Therefore, the times of the beginning and end of eclipses <note>original: "unmīlana-sammīlana," literally the opening and closing of the celestial eyes</note> calculated through mathematics are accurate for the prime meridian. If one's own location is in the eastern division, the times of sunrise and other events occur first at one's own location and later at the prime meridian. Since a lunar eclipse occurs simultaneously for all locations, the time of contact <note>the start of the eclipse</note> occurs after the time calculated for the prime meridian. Similarly, if one's own location is in the western division, the times of sunrise and other events occur first at the prime meridian and later at one's own location; thus, the time of contact occurs earlier than the time calculated for the prime meridian.

Therefore, what was stated in the previous verse and a half is perfectly established. The difference between the time (measured in <term>ghatikās</term> <note>a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note>) of sunrise at one's own location and at the prime meridian is established as the "longitude-difference ghatikās." Since the Sun traverses the earth's circumference in the time between two sunrises, the proportion is: if the earth's circumference at one's latitude corresponds to sixty <term>ghatikās</term>, then what distance corresponds to the difference in time? By this proportion <note>original: "anupātena"</note>, the distance in yojanas between the prime meridian and one's own location is found. From these known values, the longitudinal correction is determined. It should be noted that because a solar eclipse does not occur simultaneously at all locations, this knowledge cannot be obtained through the timing of its phases in the same way as described above. || 65 ||

Now, he speaks of the knowledge of the time when the weekday begins.

# Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings" <note>The *Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka*, a famous 17th-century commentary by Raṅganātha on the Surya Siddhanta.</note>

In a desired location situated to the east of the prime meridian <note>The "prime meridian" in Indian astronomy traditionally passed through Ujjain and Lanka.</note>, the start of the weekday—meaning the beginning of the day's lord—occurs after midnight by the number of *nadis* <note>A *nadi* or *ghati* is a unit of time equal to 24 minutes.</note> of longitude calculated previously. The underlying logic <term>upapatti: mathematical proof or rationale</term> is as follows: The time of sunrise in Yamakoti <note>A mythical city on the equator to the east of Lanka.</note> is identical to the moment of midnight in Lanka, which marks the commencement of the planets' motions. When considering when this occurs in one's own local region to the east or west of the meridian, that midnight occurs after or before the local midnight by the measures of longitude. This is because midnight at the equator and midnight at one's local meridian occur simultaneously only if they are on the same longitude. Thus, the statement "the start of the weekday..." is logically established.

Now, if it is asked: "Why is this knowledge of time mentioned? It seems to lack a practical purpose," the answer is no. Because the planet is calculated for a specific moment using the "count of days" <term>ahargana: the number of elapsed days from a fixed epoch</term>, knowing that specific time allows us to find the difference between local midnight and that epochal time. By applying a "motion correction" <term>chalana: adjusting a planet's position based on time elapsed</term> using that interval, the planet previously calculated is brought to the local midnight position. This serves to satisfy those of slow understanding <note>A common pedagogical phrase in Sanskrit commentaries for providing simplified or step-by-step proofs.</note>. Furthermore, there is "brevity" <term>laghava: the principle of parsimony or mathematical efficiency</term> because, by knowing that time, one avoids the need for a separate longitude correction <term>deshantara-samskara</term> for the planet. Therefore, the subsequent instruction on "motion correction" to establish the planet's position at the desired time is consistent. By this, from that midnight—meaning the midnight at the equator consisting of fifteen *ghatikas*—in the northern hemisphere, from the sun's sunrise, measured by the ascensional difference...

# The Surya Siddhanta

In the southern hemisphere, the result is that the time is earlier by the amount of the ascensional difference <note>The 'ascensional difference' or 'Chara' refers to the difference between the time of sunrise at the equator and at a specific latitude.</note> from sunrise. The explanation that the start of the weekday occurs at a time increased or decreased by the longitudinal difference <note>original: 'deshantara'</note> between eastern and western regions—thereby indicating the start of the day based on sunrise in Lanka <note>Lanka is the traditional prime meridian in Indian astronomy, located on the equator.</note>—is rejected. This is because the word "that" refers to what was previously mentioned, making the reference to "midnight" illogical, as a period of fifteen ghatikas <note>A 'ghatika' is 24 minutes; 15 ghatikas equal 6 hours.</note> is not commonly known by the term "midnight." Since the venerable Lord stated that the calculation of the elapsed days <note>original: 'ahargana'</note> is based on midnight at Lanka, the rule for knowing the start of the weekday at one's own location would be inconsistent. Furthermore, there is a lack of consistency with the practical start of the weekday based on sunrise at Lanka. || 66 ||

Now, the author describes the method for calculating the instantaneous position of a planet <note>original: 'tatkalika'</note>:

-> Multiply the daily motion by the desired ghatikas and divide by sixty; the result is in minutes and so on. <-
-> Subtract this from the planet's position if the time has passed, or add it if the time is yet to come, to find the instantaneous position. <- || 67 ||

The daily mean motion of the planet is multiplied by the desired ghatikas <note>The time elapsed since the last known position.</note> that have passed or are remaining from the time the planet's position was last calculated. This product is divided by sixty, resulting in minutes of arc and so on. If the desired time is in the past (elapsed), the result should be subtracted from the planet's position. If the desired time is in the future (yet to come), the calculator should add it to the planet's position. Thus, the planet becomes "instantaneous"—known for the specific desired moment.

**The Proof:**
The logic <note>original: 'upapatti'</note> here is a proportion: if the planet moves by its daily motion in sixty civil ghatikas, then how much does it move in the desired elapsed or remaining ghatikas? By this calculation, the planet is increased or decreased by its motion to become the instantaneous planet. It should be noted that for the "Node" <note>The ascending node of the moon or a planet.</note> which is subtracted from the circle, the process is reversed <note>Because nodes move retrograde (backward) compared to planets.</note>. The mean planet moved in this way is more accurate than the calculated true planet...

# Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings"

The motion of the planets has been described here to indicate that if the calculation is made clear, it becomes precise. <note>Verse 67</note>

Now, the author states the value of the maximum latitude <term>vikshepa: the angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the ecliptic</term> of the Moon:

->The Moon is deflected by its node, north or south,<-
->from the end of its own declination by the eightieth part of the minutes of the zodiac.<- <note>Verse 68; original: "bhacakraliptāśītyaṃśaparamaṃ..."</note>

The Moon <note>original: "anuṣṇagu," literally 'the one with cool rays'</note>, following the path of the arrow-circle <term>iṣuvṛtta: the secondary circle used to measure latitude</term> from the end of its own declination, is drawn by a cord-like force toward the nearest point on the ecliptic. Thus, from that position—the specific point on the ecliptic reached by its own motion—it is deflected by its node <term>pāta: the ascending or descending node where the orbit crosses the ecliptic</term> toward the north or the south. By that "cord," it is cast away <note>original: "vicyipyate," meaning moved or deflected</note>; the node does not allow the lunar disk to remain exactly on the ecliptic at the point of its own longitude. The meaning is that the lunar disk is moved a certain distance away from that spot along a north-south line. By using the specific term "the one with cool rays" (Moon), it is also indicated that because the Sun lacks a node, its disk remains exactly on the ecliptic at its own longitude and is never deflected.

The author then provides the specific measurement for this maximum north-south latitude. "Of the zodiac": of the minutes <term>liptā: arcminutes</term> of the twelve signs, which measure twenty-one thousand six hundred (21,600). The "eightieth part" of these is the maximum. This results in two hundred and seventy minutes <note>21,600 divided by 80 = 270' or 4.5 degrees</note>. The result is that the maximum latitude of the Moon is 270'. Some explain here that since the Sun has no "arrow" (latitude), and the zodiac is the fifth orbit from it, and the Moon's orbit is the eighth from that, the division of the zodiacal minutes by eighty (the product of five, eight, and two for the two directions, north and south) represents the Moon's deflection...

"Two-ninths of that" refers to taking a ninth part of the Moon's maximum latitude <note>The Moon's maximum latitude was previously established as 270 minutes; one-ninth is 30 minutes</note>. Doubling that results in 60 minutes <note>1 degree</note> as the maximum distance. This is the amount by which Jupiter is deflected north or south by its node. Mercury, Venus, and Saturn are each deflected by four times that ninth part, or 120 minutes <note>2 degrees</note>, by their respective nodes, moving them away from the path of the ecliptic.

Some explain the reasoning here as follows: since the Moon's disk is 33 minutes, and Jupiter's disk is 7 minutes, a latitude of twice the ninth part is appropriate for Jupiter. Because Mars is situated below Jupiter, a triple maximum latitude is given. Because Mercury and Venus have small and large disks respectively and are situated even lower, a quadruple maximum latitude is assigned to them equally. Even though Saturn is in a very high orbit, because of its slow motion, a maximum latitude equal to that of Mercury and Venus is considered appropriate. || 69 ||

These, when multiplied by ten, give the values in order for the Moon and the following planets...

The mean values for the celestial latitude <note>original: *vikshepa-kala*; the angular distance of a planet north or south of the ecliptic</note> of the Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn are given according to the order of the days of the week. Since the personified fragment of the Sun <note>the *Suryansha-purusha*, a divine being sent by the Sun God</note> spoke only what was originally declared by the Sun to the sage Maya, this text is rightly called the *Surya Siddhanta* <note>The Established Doctrine of the Sun</note>. Thus ends the Chapter on Mean Motions in the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings" <note>original: *Gudharthaprakashaka*</note> composed by the astronomer Ranganatha, son of the venerable Ballala, the sovereign among all calculators.

These entities previously mentioned—named the Fast-Apogee <note>*shighrochcha*; related to planetary anomaly/conjunction</note>, the Slow-Apogee <note>*mandochcha*; the point where a planet is furthest from Earth</note>, and the Node <note>*pata*; the intersection of orbits</note>—are specific living forces that cause the motion of the Sun and other planets. One might argue that motion occurs simply due to Time itself, and therefore these entities are not the cause; to address this, the text says "of Time..." <note>implying they are specific manifestations or "bodies" of Time</note>.

## The Treatise of the Sun

The nature of time as previously established, and the fact that these entities—being the embodiment of time—act as the cause of planetary motion, is not impossible. This is the underlying sentiment. Now, one might ask: since time is embodied in units like *ghatis* <note>a traditional unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note>, and these entities do not possess that specific form, how can they be called the "embodiment of time"? To this, the author replies: **They are dependent on the zodiacal revolutions.** This means they occupy regions associated with the circles of the planetary spheres, following the ecliptic <note>the sun's apparent path</note> located in the celestial sphere, and are composed of the signs of the zodiac. Furthermore, since the movement of planets through these signs is produced solely by the power of time, these entities—being identical to that movement—are the embodiment of time. This is the meaning.

But why are they not seen? To this, he says: **They are of invisible form.** Because they possess bodies made of wind <note>aerial or gaseous</note>, they are unmanifest and therefore not perceptible to the senses. Thus, because of the existence of the planets' "high points" <term>ucca: the apogee or perihelion where a planet is furthest or nearest</term> and other factors, the mathematical operation for determining true positions is produced. || 1 ||

Now, he explains how the "high point" <note>ucca</note> among these two (the apogee and the node) acts as the cause of motion:

->Bound by those reins of wind, by those beings with right and left hands,<-
->the planets are pulled forward and backward toward their own directions, according to their proximity.<- || 2 ||

The planets, which possess physical discs, are bound by "reins" or ropes made of wind belonging to those spirits known as the "high points" <note>ucca</note>. By those spirits, using their right and left hands—the mention of hands and fingers implies the use of both hands—the planetary disc is pulled "forward and backward" (meaning along the eastern and western paths) toward the spirit's own direction, depending on how close the planet is.

The intention is this: The "high points" and nodes of the planets reside in their respective places on the ecliptic, which serves as the orbit within the celestial sphere. There, a cord in the shape of a puller, distinct from the *Provector* wind <term>pravaha-vayu: the cosmic wind believed to drive the celestial spheres westward</term> and composed of wind, moves of its own accord while vibrating in its place. This cord is threaded through the eastern and western sides of the planetary disc...

# The Surya Siddhanta

The meaning is that because the motion of the planets is of a different nature, it is appropriate to understand their movement accordingly; thus, the "true motion" <note>original: *spashtakriya*; the calculation of a planet's actual observed position versus its mean or average position</note> of the planets is established. Or rather: if one asks how the attraction of the planets is possible by means of "wind-ropes," since those ropes are sparse and lack the density required for pulling, the author says: *It is called Pravaha.* The wind, which acts as a circular cord in the shape of the orbit held in the two hands of the deity of the *Ucca* <note>the 'Ucca' refers to the apogee or an astronomical slowing/pulling point, personified here as a deity</note>, is called *Pravaha* because of its connection to the *Pravaha* wind. This is not the same as the *Pravaha* wind that causes the westward diurnal rotation. It impels, moves, and drives those planets toward its own *Ucca*—that is, toward the station of the deity of the *Ucca*. By the word "but" <note>original: *tukārāt*; indicating a nuance in the Sanskrit particle 'tu'</note>, it is meant that when a planet is to the east of the *Ucca* station, the wind moves the planet with a westward motion; when it is to the west, the wind moves the planet with an eastward motion. And so, the orbit-shaped cord rotates in such a way at various times that it is said to be "pulled by the deities"—this is a figurative way of saying they are drawn toward the *Ucca*. Therefore, he says that the "true motion" of the planets is produced. *Pulled to the east and west:* the planets, pulled toward the eastern and western directions by the deities of the *Ucca*, attain a "distinct kind" of motion, a mode of movement different from their mean <note>average</note> motion. Therefore, the calculation is not managed by mean motion alone. || 3 || Now, he clarifies what was said regarding being pulled forward and backward:

> A deity known as *Ucca*, when situated in the half-revolution <note>180 degrees or six signs</note> in front of the planet, pulls the planet forward (eastward). When situated in the rear half-revolution, he likewise pulls the planet backward (westward). || 4 ||

The being known as *Ucca* situated in the six signs of the eastern portion from the planet's position pulls—attracts—the planetary disk toward the eastern direction, toward himself. *Situated in the other half* means the being known as *Ucca* situated in the six signs of the western portion from the planet's position. He attracts the planetary disk toward the western direction, toward himself, in the same manner. || 4 || Now, he states the result established by what was said previously.

# The Treatise of the Sun

Because it is impossible to calculate the celestial latitude of a planet through mere existence, the author says: "Rahu." The deity presiding over the position of the node is Rahu, a specific living entity; the Moon's node is the specific Daitya <note>A class of celestial beings or "demons" in Vedic cosmology</note> named Rahu. According to its etymology, it is called "Rahu" because it "leaves" or "abandons" (rahati) the planet. || 6 || Now, he clarifies this:

->The node, situated in the latter half of the revolution, deflects the planet<-
->toward the north; situated in the former half, it pulls it toward the south. || 7 ||<-

The node (Rahu), when situated in the "latter half" (the six signs forming the western division from the planet's position), deflects the planetary disk toward the north from its position on the ecliptic by the measure of its latitude. When situated in the "former half" (the six signs forming the eastern division from the planet's position), it pulls or deflects it toward the southern direction. || 7 || Now, he describes the specific case for Mercury and Venus:

->In the case of Mercury and Venus, when the node is similarly situated relative to the <term>Apex of Swift Motion</term> (shighrocha),<-
->then, due to the attraction of that Apex, those two are deflected as previously described. || 8 ||<-

Regarding Mercury and Venus, the term <term>Apex of Swift Motion</term> <note>original: "shighrocha"; refers to the point in a planet's orbit where its motion appears fastest, used in Indian astronomy to account for heliocentric motion within a geocentric model</note> is used here in the singular to represent the class. The <term>Node</term> <note>original: "pata"</note> is also used in the singular to represent the class. "Similarly" means at whatever time the node is situated within the latter or former halves of the revolution; the word "and" implies "by the two nodes at that time." Those two, Mercury and Venus, are deflected toward the south and north respectively, according to the sequence of the former and latter halves. Now, one might ask: since the nodes situated in such a way relative to the Apex have no direct connection, how can they deflect Mercury and Venus to the south or north? Otherwise, there would be an undue extension of logic due to a lack of common substratum. Therefore, he provides the reason: "Due to the attraction of that Apex..."

Because of the "pull" of those fast-apogees, there is a swift attraction from those nodes by the deities presiding over the nodal positions...

<meta>The page contains official stamps from the Government of India, Ministry of Culture (top left) and a CSL library logo (top right).</meta>

This means that the planets are moved by the force of attraction from the "wind-strings" <note>The text uses the metaphor of 'wind-strings' (vayu-sutra) to describe the invisible forces or tethers that pull planets toward their orbital peaks</note> of their respective slow-moving apsides.
Mercury and Venus are deflected in the north and south directions as previously described. Here, by the word "Node" <term>Pata: the point where a planet's orbit crosses the ecliptic</term>, one should understand the node as adjusted by the full circle. Otherwise, while the calculation of the center based on the planet's highest point is logically established, the calculation based on the "swift-moving" center <note>original: "shighrocha," referring to the second equation of center in Indian astronomy</note> would not be logically consistent. Thus, the general description of celestial latitude <term>Vikshepa: the angular distance of a planet north or south of the ecliptic</term> for all planets was stated separately for Mercury and Venus to show the difference in their nodes. Indeed, in no other theory is the deflection of the two apsides perceived such that one should fear the total contradiction of what was previously stated. And the reason for stating the difference in nodes is:

->The revolutions of the nodes stated here as *jha-bhṛ-kho-sr*<-
->Are greater than the revolutions of the swift-centers;<-
->Stated as small for the sake of ease, when joined with the moving center,<-
->The nodes of those two should be made to correspond to the read cycles.<-

This is the direction indicated by the teacher Bhaskara <note>Bhaskaracharya (1114–1185 AD), one of the most significant Indian mathematicians and astronomers</note>. || 8 || This being the case, since there is no difference between the two "Apside-Deities," why is the resulting correction <term>Phala: the 'fruit' or equation of center used to find the true position of a planet</term> not the same for the Sun and the Moon? To this, he says:

# Because of the greatness of its orb, the Sun is pulled away only slightly.
# Because of the smallness of its orb, the Moon is pulled away much more than that. || 9 ||

In the case of the Sun, because of the greatness—the heaviness—of the orb or disk <term>Bimba: the visible disk of a celestial body</term>, the maximum correction is very small compared to other planets. The word "only" is used for emphasis; it is "pulled away" or attracted by the power of the Apside. The Moon, because of the smallness of its orb—the lightness of its disk—is pulled by the power of the Apside to a maximum correction much greater than that of the Sun. || 9 || Now, he explains that because Mars and the others have even smaller bodies, a greater correction than these two is possible:

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of planetary motion, specifically addressing why the five planets (Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn) behave differently than the Sun and Moon due to their smaller size and the influence of "deities" at their orbital high points.</meta>

->Accompanied by the *Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka* <note>The "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings," a famous commentary by Raṅganātha on the Surya Siddhanta</note><-

## Mars and the others, due to the smallness of their bodies, are pulled by the deities known as the "Fast" and "Slow" High Points, becoming very distant and highly accelerated. || 10 ||

The five planets—Mars and the others—because of the smallness of their bodies <note>original: *alpamūrtitvāt*</note>, meaning their smaller disk size, are pulled very far by the deities named the Fast High Point <term>Śīghrocca: the point of conjunction/apogee related to orbital velocity</term> and the Slow High Point <term>Mandocca: the apogee related to the planet's own elliptical anomaly</term>. Therefore, they are "highly accelerated," meaning they attain extreme velocity. The meaning is that due to the lightness of their disks and the attraction of these two high points, they produce large "greatest equations" <note>The mathematical correction needed to find a planet's true position from its mean position</note>.

Now, one might ask: for the Sun and Moon, it is logical that their motion is produced by the movement of the *Pravaha* wind <note>A cosmic wind described in ancient Indian cosmology that drives the celestial spheres</note> which deviates from the circular shape of their orbits. But for Mars and the others, since each has two high points, and it is possible for these to attract them without the medium of wind, how can we accept that their motion is produced by a wind moving differently from the circular orbit? 

Because the positions of the two high points are not in the same place, a single atmospheric sphere <note>original: *vāyu-maṇḍala*</note> cannot naturally be the support for two simultaneous, opposing motions. Therefore, for Mars and the others, the two deities of the Fast and Slow High Points are designed to pull the planetary disks <note>original: *grahabimba*</note> along the path of their cords <note>imaginary lines of force</note> by their own power. 

There is no need to imagine the movement of an atmospheric sphere here. Even for the Sun and Moon, there is no harm in accepting this same mechanism. The idea of an atmospheric sphere is not strictly necessary, despite previous statements about "wind-reins." When it was said they are "bound by wind-reins," it was to support the description of the planets' positions—that they remain connected by a straight line to their respective celestial spheres within the westward-turning *Pravaha* wind. That statement was not meant as a physical cause that would lead to logical inconsistencies. 

By imagining "High Point Deities," the production of a single result—in the form of the two-fold corrective calculations—is consistent with how these deities pull the planets in space by their own power. Consequently, the idea that the "cord" is physically woven into the planetary disk or the circular orbit is also rejected; otherwise, the equal or opposing pulls from the two high points would result in the snapping of that circular cord-mandala. || 10 || Now, he concludes this topic:

<summary>This passage explains that the five planets are more easily influenced by gravitational-like "pulls" from their orbital apogees (deities) because of their small size, and argues that these forces are divine/energetic rather than purely atmospheric.</summary>

# The Treatise of the Sun

> Therefore, a very great addition or subtraction <note>original: "dhanarṇam"; refers to the mathematical correction applied to a planet's mean position to find its true position</note> occurs for them due to the power of their motion. Being pulled by these [forces] in this manner, they move through the sky, impelled by the provector wind. || 11 ||

Now, following the previous explanation of the pull exerted by the "slow" points <note>the apogees</note>, a very great result—an addition or subtraction—occurs for these planets, such as Mars and the others, due to the power of their motion (the movement produced by that pull). 

One might ask: "Why is this movement produced by the pull not directly visible to the eye?" To this, the author says: *Being pulled...* These planets, such as Mars, being pulled in the manner described by the deities of the high points <note>apogees</note> and nodes, move through the sky—within the sphere of the heavens—while being struck by the wind. This refers to the constant westward-flowing provector wind <note>term: "Pravaha-vayu"; in ancient Indian cosmology, this is the cosmic wind that drives the celestial spheres</note>. 

The inner meaning is this: Just as the eastward motion produced by the support [of the spheres] is not directly perceived, so too this irregular movement of pulling—which is essentially a modification of that eastward motion—is not perceived because of the overwhelming force of the rotation caused by the provector wind. || 11 ||

Next, the author describes how the resulting single motion of the planets (Mars and the others), produced by these combined causes of motion, is of eight distinct types:

> Retrograde, somewhat retrograde, transverse, slow, very slow, even, 
> as well as very swift, and swift; thus the motion of the planets is eightfold. || 12 ||

For the planets starting with Mars (excluding the Sun and Moon), the resulting motion is of eight types. Among these, the six types from "retrograde" to "even" are mentioned, along with the two motions "very swift" and "swift." The word "as well as" indicates the combination. The specific nature of these will be clarified later. || 12 ||

Now, he categorizes this eightfold motion into two broader divisions:

> Among these, very swift, swift, slow, very slow, and even 
> are known as the five types of "direct" motion; that which is retrograde is [divided into] retrograde and somewhat retrograde. || 13 ||

Among those eight types of motion, the five types from "very swift" to "even" [are grouped together]...

# The Surya Siddhanta

From the first half-sine <note>original: "prathama-jyārdha"; the sine of 3° 45' or 225 minutes</note>, subtracted by the quotient obtained by dividing that same first half-sine—since there is no other preceding value—and then adding that result to the first half-sine, the second half-sine is derived. The first value doubled is one less. To calculate the third and subsequent values, the previously mentioned method is applied. "By the first" means by the sum of the first half-sine. In this manner, by dividing the established sums by the first value, the resulting quotients are used to increase the segments; these segments, when added to the immediately preceding established half-sine sums, produce the next established sums.

For example:
The first segment is 225. Divided by the first (225), the result is 1.
The second segment is 449. Divided by the first, the result is <gloss>2</gloss> 2 <note>The gloss clarifies the numerical value</note>; here, a fraction greater than half is treated as one, according to the traditional practice of the school.
The first segment (225) minus the sum of the quotients (1) equals 224. Adding this to the second segment (449) results in the third: 671.
Similarly, this (671) divided by the first segment gives a result of <gloss>3</gloss> 3.
Adding this to the previous sum of quotients (3) results in 6.
The first segment (225) minus this total sum of quotients (6) equals 219.
Adding this (219) to the third (671) results in the fourth: 890.
Similarly, this (890) divided by the first segment gives a result of <gloss>4</gloss> 4.
The segment representing the difference in sines, which is the first segment minus the previous quotients (219), is reduced by this 4 to become 215.
Adding this (215) to the fourth results in the fifth: 1105.
And so on for the rest.

Now, since an infinite number of segments could theoretically be produced by this method, the rule for the number of segments is stated. "By the teeth" <note>The word 'khu' or 'danta' refers to the number 32 or 24 in different systems; here it specifies 24</note>. Thus, twenty-four half-sine sums are to be calculated, and no more. On this point:

-> From the twenty-first, the twentieth, the sixth, and the fifteenth, <-
-> and from the seventh, the twelfth, and the seventeenth, an additional half is considered. <-

It should be noted that in the context of the *Brahma Siddhanta* <note>A major astronomical treatise by Brahmagupta, c. 628 CE</note> mentioned here, a fraction greater than half is not necessarily taken as one. Since the mathematics remains unaltered, one might ask why the established sums were not simply listed in order. To this, he says: "In order..." These established sums, in sequence—

# Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings" <note>original: "Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka," a famous commentary on the Surya Siddhanta</note>

These shall be explained immediately hereafter. Here is the logical proof: On level ground, a circle should be drawn and marked with the minutes of a revolution <note>21,600 minutes or 'kalā'</note>. It should be divided into four parts by two lines representing the horizontal and vertical diameters. There, by counting equal divisions on both sides of the point where the vertical line meets the circumference, a string tied between those two points represents the "full chord" of the full arc measured by those double divisions in the circle. 

In this mathematical system, since we only use the "half-chord" from the vertical line, the half of that [full chord] is the "half-chord" <term>jya</term><note>The Sanskrit 'jya' literally means 'bowstring'. While we translate it as 'sine', it refers to the length of the semi-chord in a circle of a specific radius, not just the trigonometric ratio.</note> of that half-arc. Thus, in a quadrant of the circle, the desired half-chords of the desired degrees—which take the form of half-arcs—are to be calculated starting from the vertical line. 

In this regard, the Lord <note>referring to the Sun God, the traditional author of the text</note>, by His own will, has envisioned twenty-four sines within a quadrant of the circle measuring three signs <note>90 degrees</note>. The knowledge of these is based on the marking of the minutes of the circle. The radius of that circumference is the final sine of three signs. The calculation of the diameter is done by the following proportion: If for a circumference measuring 3,927 <note>original: 'bhanandāgni'</note>, the diameter is 1,250 <note>original: 'khabāṇasūrya'</note>, then what is the diameter for a circumference of the circle's minutes <note>21,600</note>? 

As follows: The circle's minutes (21,600) multiplied by 1,250 equals 27,000,000. This divided by 3,927 results in a diameter of 6,876. Half of this is the final sine: 3,438. 

Now, regarding the distinction between the arc and the sine in a circle: although they are unequal, the Lord, considering that some small part of the circle must be [effectively] straight—otherwise a mustard seed could not stay still on an emblic myrobalan fruit <note>a metaphor for a spherical object; if no part were flat, nothing could rest upon it</note>—determined that the sine of that very small part is equal to the arc itself.

->A ninety-sixth part of a circle appears like a straight staff.<-

This is according to the <term>Statement of Shakalya</term> <note>An ancient authority often cited in astronomical texts</note>. The first sine is calculated as 225 minutes, which is the eighth part of the minutes in one sign <note>30 degrees or 1,800 minutes</note>, representing the twelfth part of the circle's minutes. This is the measure of the first arc; therefore, the twenty-four desired sines are spaced by this interval. Now, because the twenty-four sines increase successively, it is visible through the marking of sines on the circle that the differences between them—the segments—decrease successively. Similarly, in summary: These stated <term>tabular sines</term> <note>original: kramajyārdhapiṇḍa; the half-chord values</note>, when subtracted individually from the <term>radius</term> <note>original: vyāsārdha or trijyā; the maximum sine value</note> in reverse order—starting from the penultimate value back to the first—become the <term>tabular versed sines</term> <note>original: utkramajyārdhapiṇḍa; the "stepped-out" or coversine values</note> in sequence.

For example, the twenty-fourth sine value was stated as "form, fires, essence, qualities" <note>3531</note>. When the value "wealth, fires, actions, fires" <note>3438, the radius</note> is reduced by the preceding value, the remainder is seven, which is the first tabular versed sine. Likewise, the twenty-third value subtracted from the final value <note>the radius</note> gives the second tabular versed sine. Proceeding in this manner, there are twenty-four tabular versed sines.

Here is the <term>rationale</term> <note>original: upapatti; mathematical proof or logic</note>: The versed sine is the difference in the form of an "arrow" <note>original: bāṇa; the segment of the radius between the arc and the chord</note> between the sine and the arc. Although it is not strictly possible to have a "half-arrow" in the same way one has a "half-chord" <note>sine</note>, it is proper to call them "versed sine values" rather than "half-versed sine values." Nevertheless, following the technical terminology of the Divine Revelation <note>referring to the Sūrya Siddhānta as spoken by the Sun God</note>, because the versed sine represents the full portion of the "arrow" when the arc-arm is absent, it is called a "half-versed sine."

Furthermore, it is clearly seen in the quadrant of a circle that when all sines are marked, the amount by which the sine of certain degrees is less than the radius is the versed sine of the complementary degrees. Therefore, to find the versed sines using the sequence of the stated sines, the stated values are subtracted from the radius in reverse order. This is the logic behind the phrase "subtracting..." etc. || 22 ||

Now, in the following five verses, the author records the previously established tabular versed sines.

These are the established values of the versed sines <note>Utkramajya-pindas</note> as previously determined. The mountain <note>Mahidhra</note> refers to the fixed values. In the absence of the sine of the base <note>Bhujajya</note>, because the versed sine of the upright <note>Kotyutkramajya</note> is at its maximum, the radius <note>Trijya</note> minus the zero-sine is the maximum versed sine value. The word "only" <note>original: "eva"</note> implies that this is not done in the second and third operations; rather, in those steps, the **Manda-phala** <note>the equation of the center, or correction for elliptical orbits</note> is what must be calculated.

The underlying logic <note>original: "upapatti"</note> is as follows: From the point on the orbital circle where the planet's mean position corrected for its slow anomaly <note>original: "manda-spashta"</note> is located, the physical body of the planet <note>original: "graha-bimba"</note> is pulled toward itself by the deity residing at the point of the fast anomaly <note>Shighrocca</note> using a "cord" held in their hand. This pull occurs across a distance equal to the sine of the maximum fast anomaly. 

Because of this, from the "slow-clear" position on the circle marked with zodiacal degrees, the planet's body moves in a direction opposite to the path of the orbit, at a distance from the fast anomaly point known as the fast center, within the circle called the **Shighra-nichocca-vritta** <note>the epicycle of the fast anomaly</note>. 

There, as before, the sine and cosine of the latitude are the base and perpendicular from the horizontal line of the orbit. When the center is in the signs beginning with Capricorn, the cosine is added to the radius. When in the signs beginning with Cancer, the radius is diminished by the cosine. This forms the perpendicular <note>koti</note> representing the straight-line distance between the planet on the epicycle and the horizontal line of the planet's orbit. The distance between the base of this perpendicular and the center, which lies within the horizontal line of the orbit, is equal to the sine of the latitude <note>bhujaphala</note>; this is the base <note>bhuja</note>. The cord from the center of the Earth to the planet is the diagonal hypotenuse <note>karna</note>. 

The square root of the sum of the squares of this base and perpendicular gives the hypotenuse. Where this hypotenuse-cord meets the orbital circle, that is the "clear" or true longitude of the planet. The rule of proportion <note>original: "anupata"</note> is: if at the end of the Shighra hypotenuse the result is the sine of the latitude, what is it at the end of the radius? The arc of this result is the **Shighra-phala**, which is the difference between the "slow-clear" position and the true longitude. Now, to know the center of the epicycle, the "slow-clear" knowledge is necessary. Therefore, the Shighra...

# The Surya Siddhanta

Clear knowledge through the correction of planetary equations. In this context, the mean planet corrected by the calculated <term>Mandaphala</term> <note>Equation of Center; the correction for the planet's elliptical orbit</note> is called the "Slow-True" planet. To achieve a precise true position, it is necessary to apply corrections to the mean planet. First, the <term>Mandaphala</term> derived from a mean planet that has already been adjusted by the <term>Shighraphala</term> <note>Equation of Apex; the correction for the observer's relative position, similar to parallax or the Earth's motion</note> is more accurate. Therefore, the <term>Mandaphala</term> is applied to the mean planet already adjusted by the <term>Shighraphala</term> to bring it closer to the true position. (42) Now, one might ask: since the Sun and Moon lack a <term>Shighraphala</term>, how is their true position determined? Answering this, the text clarifies the process for Mars and the other planets.

-> For the Sun and Moon, there is only one "Slow" operation; for Mars and the others, it is now stated: <-
-> The "Fast," the "Slow," then the "Slow" again, and the "Fast"—these four are in sequence. (43) <-

For the Sun and the Moon, there is only one "Slow" (<term>Manda</term>) operation. Because they lack a "Fast" (<term>Shighra</term>) equation, their true position is determined solely by the <term>Mandaphala</term>. The word "one" implies that the <term>Mandaphala</term> is calculated only once; because the center of their slow-apsis circle is known directly from the mean planet, no further operations are required—this logic is clear. Next, the process for Mars and the other planets is described. What was mentioned previously is now explained with clarity. He says: "The Fast," etc. First, the <term>Shighraphala</term> calculated from the mean planet is applied to the mean planet. From this result, the <term>Mandaphala</term> is calculated and applied. From that result, a second <term>Mandaphala</term> is calculated and applied to the mean planet to produce the "Slow-True" (<term>Mandasphuta</term>) position. Finally, the <term>Shighraphala</term> is calculated from that and applied. Thus, there are four operations in sequence; this is the meaning of the previous statement. (43)

Now, he mentions a specific detail here:

-> Apply half of the "Fast" equation to the mean, and then half of the "Slow" equation; <-
-> Then apply the full "Slow" equation to the mean planet, and finally the full "Fast" equation. (44) <-

## Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings" <note>original: "Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka," the title of Raṅganātha's commentary on the Sūrya Siddhānta</note>

Half of the calculated "conjunction correction" <term>Shīghraphala: the correction for the planet's orbital position relative to the Sun</term> should be applied to the mean planet. From this, the half-correction related to the "equation of center" <term>Mandaphala: the correction for the planet's elliptical eccentricity</term> is calculated—meaning half of the calculated equation of center. Likewise, it should be applied to that very value from which it was calculated. The resulting meaning is that it should be applied to the value already corrected by half the conjunction correction. From this, the full equation of center is calculated and applied to the mean planet; this becomes the "mean-true" planet <term>Mandaspashta: the planet's position corrected only for eccentricity</term>. From this, the full conjunction correction is calculated. The word "and" <note>Sanskrit: 'ca'</note> implies a conjunction of operations. Therefore, it should be applied to the mean-true planet. By the word "only" <note>Sanskrit: 'eva'</note>, it is emphasized that a planet determined by this stated method is the "true" planet <note>Spashta</note> and not otherwise.

Now for the rational proof <note>original: "Upapatti"</note>: The equation of center is truly accurate when calculated from the true position, but the true position itself depends on the equation of center. Because of this mutual dependence, calculating an extremely precise equation of center is difficult. However, the Lord <note>referring to the Sun God, the revealed author of the Sūrya Siddhānta</note>, for the sake of providing a close approximation, calculated the equation of center from the "half-true" position, which is more precise than an equation of center calculated merely from the mean planet. The "half-true" position is the mean planet corrected by half of both corrections. Even here, because half of the equation of center calculated from a position corrected by half the conjunction correction is somewhat more precise, this method is justified, starting with "half of the conjunction correction in the mean..." and so on. (Verse 44)

Now, one might ask: how should the application of these two corrections be performed? To this, he says:

> if the anomaly is in the half-circle beginning with Aries, the correction in minutes
> is additive; if in the half-circle beginning with Libra, it is subtractive. (Verse 45)

In the conjunction process and the eccentricity process for all planets—the word "and" indicates the combination—the correction in the form of arc-minutes should be added if the anomaly <term>Kendra: the angular distance between the planet and its apsis</term> is within the six signs beginning with Aries <note>the first 180 degrees of the orbital circle</note>. It should be subtracted if the anomaly is within the six signs beginning with Libra <note>the latter 180 degrees</note>. The word "and" here serves to establish the rule. The word "only" <note>Sanskrit: 'eva'</note> is used to exclude any difference in the rules for addition and subtraction, even if the methods for deriving the two corrections differ.

Now for the rational proof: It was stated previously that when there is a forward-pulling force, the correction for the planet is additive, and when there is a backward-pulling force, it is subtractive. In that context, when the anomaly is taken from the planet to its high point <note>apsis</note>...

# The Surya Siddhanta

In the case of the eastward pull, the center begins with Aries <note>the first sign of the zodiac</note>; in the case of the westward pull, the center begins with Libra. Thus, what was stated previously is logically established. || 45 || Now, the author describes the "difference of the arms" <term>bhujantara: the correction for the equation of time due to the eccentricity of the ecliptic</term> for the planets:

> The daily motion of a planet, multiplied by the Sun’s "arm-result" <note>the result of the sine of the anomaly, or the equation of center</note> and divided by the minutes of the entire circle of the constellations, yields minutes which should be applied to the planet in the same manner as the Sun. || 46 ||

The true motion of the Sun and other planets is multiplied by the Sun’s "arm-result" <note>original: mandaphala</note> expressed in minutes of arc. This is then divided by the total minutes in the twelve signs of the zodiac—which amounts to 21,600 <note>original: bhacakra-kalika</note>. The resulting minutes are to be applied to the planet (the Sun or others) "in the same manner as the Sun"—meaning, according to whether the Sun’s equation of center is additive or subtractive. The word "but" <insert>implied in the grammatical structure</insert> indicates they should also be adjusted when negative.

The logic <note>original: upapatti</note> here is as follows: Since the "heap of days" <term>ahargana: the total number of days elapsed from a fixed epoch</term> is based on a uniform mean measurement, the positions of the planets derived from it are established for the time of mean midnight. At mean midnight, the point on the ecliptic <note>original: krantivrtta</note> occupied by the mean Sun is on the lower meridian.

However, true midnight—defined as the intersection of the point on the ecliptic occupied by the *true* Sun with the lower meridian—occurs at a different time, either before or after mean midnight, depending on whether the equation of center is positive or negative. Therefore, because of the time interval corresponding to the minutes of the equation of center, the planet's position is slightly different at the time of true midnight compared to the time before or after it. By this calculation, the planets are adjusted to their positions at the time of true midnight.

The previous argument—that this correction does not apply to the Sun because the Sun is already at true midnight—is hereby refuted. If one were to argue that other planets are at mean midnight while the Sun is at true midnight, it would contradict the fact that all are derived from the same "heap of days" and must therefore be simultaneous.

### The Treatise of the Sun

In the calculation, the result derived from the anomaly <note>the difference between the planet's position and its apogee</note>—which is the velocity of the center in the form of its own motion minus the motion of the slow-point <note>apogee</note>—is the velocity correction. This must be applied to the motion itself. This is stated as "in the motion of the Moon" to avoid a method to be explained later; otherwise, the "true" status would apply only to the velocity of the center and not to the actual motion of the Moon. || 47 || Now, by means of two verses, he explains the "slow-clear" velocity <term>Mandaspaṣṭagati: the corrected angular velocity of a planet after accounting for its elliptical orbit</term> of the planets, preceded by the calculation of the velocity correction which indicates the underlying theory.

> The correction to the planet's motion should be performed as in the "slow-process" <note>Manda-karman: the calculation for the planet's equation of the center</note> for the planet. The motion is multiplied by the difference of the sine-intervals, and then divided by two hundred and twenty-five <note>original: "tattva-netra" (225), using the Katapayadi system where 'tattva' is 25 and 'netra' is 2</note>. || 48 ||
> This is then multiplied by its own "slow-circumference" <note>Manda-paridhi</note> and divided by the degrees in a circle <note>360</note>; the resulting minutes are added in the signs beginning with Cancer, and subtracted in the signs beginning with Capricorn. || 49 ||

In the "slow-process" means for the purpose of the operation for the slow-velocity correction. Just as in the method for bringing out the planet's slow-correction—by multiplying by the circumference and dividing by the degrees of the circle to find the arc—the velocity correction of the planet is to be calculated from the planet's motion. The meaning is that just as the planet's slow-correction is calculated from the sine of the center's arm <note>the anomaly</note>, so this velocity correction is calculated from the planet's motion. To explain: since the difference in the planet's slow-correction over one day is the planet's slow-velocity correction, the result derived from the difference between two sines over one day results in the slow-velocity correction. Because the difference between two centers is the "center-velocity" <note>Kendragati</note>, the difference between those two sines is the sine-table interval <note>Jyāpiṇḍāntara</note> defined by the measure of two hundred and twenty-five <note>original: "tattvāśvi"</note>, converted into minutes of motion. He says exactly this: "multiplied by the difference of the sine-intervals." The mean motion of the planet is the same as the velocity of the center, because the motion of the apogee is extremely small. "Multiplied by the difference of the sine-intervals" means multiplied by whatever sine-table interval occurs during the calculation of the sine of the arm.
