# The Surya Siddhanta:

> Divide the product by the variable hypotenuse; when the hypotenuse is greater than the radius, add the result to the velocity. When it is less, subtract it; if the result is greater than the velocity itself, subtract the velocity from it, and the remainder is the retrograde motion. || 51 ||

Having previously established the <term>slow-corrected velocity</term><note>Sanskrit: mandaspaṣṭagati; the velocity of a planet after accounting for its elliptical orbit but before the solar correction</note>, one should subtract it from the velocity of the <term>fast anomaly</term><note>Sanskrit: śīghrocca; the point representing the Earth's motion or the sun's influence</note>. Regarding the resulting difference, for the sake of consistency between the radius and the variable hypotenuse in the rule of three, it should be understood that the term <term>radius</term><note>Sanskrit: trijyā; the standard sine of 90 degrees used as a constant in Indian trigonometry</note> here refers to the <term>cosine of the second fast-correction</term><note>Sanskrit: dvitīya-śīghraphala-koṭijyā</note>. Multiply by the difference. The result obtained there should be divided by the second <term>variable hypotenuse</term><note>Sanskrit: calakarṇa; the distance from the Earth to the planet</note>. 

The resulting value should be added to or subtracted from the slow-corrected velocity depending on whether the second variable hypotenuse is greater or less than the radius (the cosine of the fast-correction). This yields the <term>true velocity</term>. Now, one might ask: when the correction for the fast anomaly is greater than the slow-corrected velocity, the subtraction would seem impossible—how then do we determine the true velocity? This is not an impossible scenario. When a planet is near its <term>perigee</term><note>Sanskrit: nīca; the point in the orbit closest to Earth</note>, the variable hypotenuse is smaller than the difference of the cosine, and the correction can indeed exceed the slow-corrected velocity. To this, the text says: "if [the result is] greater." Subtract the slow-corrected velocity from the larger correction; the remainder is the <term>retrograde motion</term><note>Sanskrit: vakragati; the apparent backward motion of a planet in the sky</note>, also called reverse motion or westward motion. Thus, there is no error in the logic. The mathematical rationale is as follows:

> The velocity of the fast anomaly, multiplied by the sine of the difference between the correction degrees and ninety, and divided by the hypotenuse, should be subtracted from its own fast velocity to find the true planetary velocity. If the subtraction is reversed, the remainder is the retrograde motion.

This quote from the <term>Siddhanta Shiromani</term><note>A major 12th-century astronomical treatise by Bhaskara II</note> follows the tradition of the Elder Vashistha Siddhanta. The detailed proof of this precise method is explained in its commentary. There, the first half of the verse is stated to determine the <term>velocity of the fast anomaly</term><note>Sanskrit: drākkendrabhukti</note>. This velocity is multiplied by the cosine of the correction and divided by the hypotenuse.

# Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings" <note>original: "Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka," a famous commentary on the Sūrya Siddhānta</note>

The result derived from the velocity of its own fast apex <note>term: śīghrocca - the point of highest velocity in the planetary cycle, often corresponding to the sun's position</note> must be subtracted. First, to perform the subtraction with a common denominator, the hypotenuse <note>term: karṇa - the distance from the earth to the planet</note> is used as a multiplier for the velocity of the fast apex. Furthermore, since the velocity of the fast apex is composed of the sum of the velocities of the center <note>term: kendra - the anomaly or angular distance</note> and the planet, and the result was subtracted in two parts within the central velocity itself, the difference is found between the central velocity multiplied by the cosine of the result <note>term: phala-koṭijyā</note> and the central velocity multiplied by the hypotenuse. 

Because the difference of products is equal to the product of the difference, and for the sake of mathematical simplicity, the central velocity is multiplied by the difference between the cosine of the result and the hypotenuse, then divided by the hypotenuse. This explains the derivation up to the point of the remainder. 

Now, when the hypotenuse is equal to the cosine of the result, the velocity is established as equal to the slow-corrected velocity <note>term: manda-spaṣṭa-gati - the velocity corrected for the planet's elliptical orbit but not yet for its relation to the sun</note>, and thus there is no correction. If the hypotenuse is smaller, the result is greater than the velocity of the fast center; when that is subtracted from the velocity of the fast apex, the velocity of the fast center is eliminated, and the excess—which takes the form of the velocity correction—is ultimately subtracted from the slow-corrected velocity. 

If the hypotenuse is larger, the result of the previous method is less than the velocity of the fast center. When that is subtracted from the velocity of the fast apex, the deficit results in a true velocity that is greater than the slow-corrected velocity. Thus, by taking the velocity of the fast center in place of the velocity of the fast apex, the result produced is indeed the velocity correction. This is added or subtracted from the slow-corrected velocity depending on whether the hypotenuse is larger or smaller than the cosine of the result. This explains the section ending with "is less." 

If the negative correction is greater than the slow-corrected velocity, the remainder from the reverse subtraction is the "westward velocity" <note>term: paścima-gati - retrograde motion</note>, which is the true velocity. Everything here is flawless.

## The Treatise of the Sun

When the rays of the gods at the <term>apogee</term><note>The highest point in an orbit</note> are slackened, the body of the planet is pulled by cords of air. Its body—the visible disk—is drawn to the left or right by the deity; at that time, <term>retrograde motion</term><note>original: "vakragati"; the apparent backward movement of a planet in the sky</note> occurs. The idea is this: a planet separated by less than three signs can be pulled by the gods with slack, circular cords. However, a planet separated by more than three signs cannot be so pulled. Therefore, at the point where the equation of the center becomes negative, the planet begins its retrograde movement. Because the force of the pull is not increasing, it is possible for the object to move downward along its circular path. || 52 ||

Furthermore, since it is seen in a circle that the radius diminished by the versed sine of the arm is the sine of the upright, the radius of the diurnal circle is the radius diminished by the versed sine of declination. <note>Technical Vocabulary:
- **Sine of declination (Krāntijyā):** The distance of a planet from the celestial equator.
- **Radius of the diurnal circle (Dyujyā):** The radius of the path a star or planet takes across the sky in 24 hours.
- **Radius (Trijyā):** The standard radius used in Indian trigonometry, usually 3438 minutes.
- **Equinoctial shadow (Viṣuvadbhā):** The shadow cast by a 12-digit gnomon at noon on the day of the equinox.
- **Earth-sine (Kṣitijyā):** A specific line in the geometry of the celestial sphere used to find the difference between the rising of a planet on the horizon vs. the equator.
- **Respirations (Asavaḥ):** A unit of time; one respiration equals 4 seconds of sidereal time.</note>

# The Surya Siddhanta

> The arc of that [the sine of the ascensional difference] is to be added and subtracted respectively from the fourth part of the day-and-night circle when the declination is northern, to find the half-day and half-night. || 62 ||
> When the declination is southern, the process is reversed. These values doubled are the total lengths of the day and night. For the fixed stars, the same applies using their own declination as modified by their latitude. || 63 ||

The sine of declination <note>original: "Krāntijyā"</note> is multiplied by the twelve-digit shadow of the gnomon <note>A vertical pillar used to measure shadows</note> at noon on the day of the equinox <note>original: "Viṣuvaddina"</note> and divided by twelve; the result is the "earth-sine" <note>original: "Kujyā"</note>. That earth-sine is then multiplied by the radius and divided by the radius of the diurnal circle <note>original: "Dyujyā"</note>; the result is the sine of the ascensional difference <note>original: "Charajyā"</note>. The arc of that sine, expressed in breaths <note>Asavaḥ; a unit of time equal to four seconds</note>, constitutes the ascensional difference <note>original: "Charāsavaḥ"</note>.

In the fourth part of the total daily rotations of the planet in question—that is, one quarter of the total daily breaths—placed in two separate positions: if there is northern declination <note>original: "Uttarakrānti"</note>, the breaths of the ascensional difference are to be added and subtracted. These results are declared by the experts in time to be the half-day and half-night respectively.

If there is southern declination <note>original: "Dakṣiṇakrānti"</note>, the half-day and half-night are reversed: where it was subtracted, that is the half-day, and where it was added, that is the half-night. By the word "but" <note>referring to the particle 'tu' in the verse</note>, these half-values when doubled give the total measure of the day and the measure of the night for the planet itself.

He [the author] states that the measures of day and night for the fixed stars <note>original: "Nakṣatra"</note> are also to be calculated by the aforementioned method. Regarding the phrase "with latitude" <note>original: "Vikṣepa..."</note>: using the calculated declination of the star's polar longitude, and adding or subtracting the star's latitude depending on whether the directions are the same or different, one should determine the day and night measures for each specific star.

Here is the geometric proof <note>original: "Upapatti"</note>: The twelve-digit gnomon is the vertical side, the equinoctial shadow is the horizontal side, and the hypotenuse of the latitude is the diagonal. In another known triangle, the sine of declination is the vertical side, the earth-sine is the horizontal side, and the hypotenuse is the latitude-hypotenuse. Thus, where the vertical is twelve, the horizontal is the equinoctial shadow; where the vertical is the sine of declination...

# Accompanied by the Illuminator of Hidden Meanings

<note>The title refers to the commentary by Ranganatha on the Surya Siddhanta, a foundational Sanskrit astronomical text.</note>

The <term>Kujyā</term><note>Earth-sine; the distance between the horizon of a specific location and the celestial equator measured along the diurnal circle.</note> is determined by the proportion of the sine of the latitude. Its true nature is the sine of the portion of the diurnal circle situated between the equatorial horizon and the local horizon, measured according to the <term>Dyujyā</term><note>The radius of the diurnal circle of a planet.</note>. By the proportion of the <term>Trijyā</term><note>The radius of the standard sine table, usually 3438 minutes.</note>, that sine is called the <term>Carajyā</term><note>Ascensional difference; the difference between the time of sunrise at the equator and at a specific latitude.</note>. 

The calculation follows this proportion: if the <term>Kujyā</term> is measured by the <term>Dyujyā</term>, what would it be when measured by the <term>Trijyā</term>? The result is the <term>Carajyā</term>. The arc of that value represents the <term>Carāsavaḥ</term><note>Ascensional difference measured in 'asus' or respirations; 1 respiration equals 4 seconds of time.</note> in the segment of the diurnal circle. 

In the Northern Hemisphere, because the local horizon lies below the equatorial horizon, the <term>Carāsavaḥ</term> are added to the quarter of the day-length <note>measured from the meridian to the equatorial horizon</note> to find the half-day, and subtracted to find the half-night. In the Southern Hemisphere, because the local horizon lies above the equatorial horizon, they are subtracted from the half-day and added to the half-night. Thus, all is proven regarding the sine of declination and so forth. // 63 //

Next, the author describes the method for bringing forth <note>calculating</note> the <term>Nakshatra</term><note>Lunar mansion; one of 27 divisions of the ecliptic.</note> of a planet:

> **The span of a Nakshatra is eight hundred minutes; likewise, seven hundred and twenty for a Tithi.**
> **The elapsed minutes of the planet divided by the span gives the Nakshatras; the remainder and the daily motion give the days and so forth.** // 64 //

The span of a <term>Nakshatra</term> consists of eight hundred minutes of arc. In this context, he also mentions the span of a <term>Tithi</term><note>A lunar day; 1/30th of a lunar month.</note>. He says "Sky-twins-mountains" <note>A Sanskrit numerical code (bhūta-saṅkhyā): Sky=0, Twins=2, Mountains=7, read right-to-left as 720.</note>. This means the span of a <term>Tithi</term> consists of seven hundred and twenty minutes. 

For whichever planet the knowledge of the <term>Nakshatra</term> is desired: the signs of that planet should be multiplied by thirty to get degrees, then multiplied by sixty to get minutes, according to the standard definition. These total minutes are divided by the span of a <term>Nakshatra</term> <note>800</note>. The quotient represents the <term>Nakshatras</term> already passed by the planet. The remainder represents the minutes already traversed within the current <term>Nakshatra</term>. 

From this, he explains how to find the elapsed time in days: By the "motion" <note>bhukti</note>. By dividing the remainder by the planet's daily motion in minutes, the elapsed days and so forth are achieved. Similarly, by subtracting the remainder from the total span and dividing by the motion, the remaining days <note>until the planet enters the next mansion</note> are achieved. 

The proof here is as follows: In the full revolution of the circle of constellations, there are twenty-seven <term>Nakshatras</term> beginning with Ashvini...

# The Surya Siddhanta
<note>The Surya Siddhanta is one of the most important early Sanskrit texts on Indian astronomy, dating in its current form to approximately the 4th-5th century CE.</note>

...the planets [starting from Ashvini] based on their motion. The total minutes of the circle for the twenty-seven lunar mansions <term>nakshatras; the 27 divisions of the sky along the ecliptic</term> are measured as twenty-one thousand and six hundred <note>21,600 minutes, which equals 360 degrees</note>. By proportion, what is the extent of a single lunar mansion? The extent is eight hundred minutes <note>21,600 divided by 27</note>. Similarly, for a lunar day <term>tithi; a 30th part of a lunar month</term>, since there are thirty parts in a lunar month and a lunar month is established by one complete revolution of the distance between the Sun and the Moon: if the extent of thirty lunar days is the full circle of minutes, what is the extent of one lunar day? By proportion, the extent is seven hundred and twenty minutes <note>21,600 divided by 30</note>.

Now, if eight hundred minutes make one lunar mansion, then how many are made by the minutes traveled by a planet? By this proportion, the result gives the lunar mansions passed by the planet starting from Ashvini. The remaining minutes represent the portion of the current lunar mansion already traversed by the planet. By subtracting this from the total extent, the remainder is the portion yet to be traversed. From these two, using the planet's daily motion—if one day equals the daily motion, then what do the desired minutes equal?—one obtains the days and other units already passed or remaining. In this way, the daily lunar mansion should be known from the Moon. || 64 ||

Now, in this context, he describes the calculation of the "Yogas" <term>Yoga; an astrological period defined by the combined longitudinal motion of the Sun and Moon</term>:

> From the sum of the minutes of the Sun and Moon, the Yogas are found by dividing by the extent of a mansion.
> The past and future portions, multiplied by sixty and divided by the sum of their daily motions, give the time in ghatikas. || 65 ||

From the minutes of the sum of the Sun and Moon (calculated according to the standard definitions of signs and degrees), the Yogas—Vishkambha and the others—are found by dividing by the "extent." This means dividing by the previously mentioned extent of a mansion <note>800 minutes</note>. The extent of each individual Yoga is equal to this measure. By subtracting this from the total sum, the number of completed Yogas is found. That Yoga whose extent cannot be further subtracted is the "current" one. The meaning is: the minutes divided by the extent give the past Yogas, and the next one is the current one. 

Regarding the remainder: the portion already passed and the portion remaining (found by subtracting the passed portion from the total extent), he explains the method for calculating the time in <term>ghatikas; a traditional unit of time equal to 24 minutes</term>. He says "past and future." The word "and" implies both. The minutes should be multiplied by sixty and then divided by the sum of the daily motions of the Sun and Moon (expressed in minutes). The result is the number of *ghatikas* past or remaining.

Because of the word "but/however," they occur in the halves of the lunar days in sequence. *Kimstughna* is the fourth. Then—

"Then," meaning after the completion of the fixed Karanas, the seven known as "mobile" Karanas—beginning with Bava and ending with Bhadra—occur from the second half of the first lunar day of the bright fortnight until the end of the month. Now, one might ask: which Karanas occur from the fifth day onwards? To this, he says: "In a month." Among the seven mobile Karanas starting with Bava, each one occurs eight times within a month (defined here as the thirty lunar days minus the time occupied by the fixed Karanas). One might argue: since it was stated that the four fixed Karanas occupy half a lunar day each until the first half of the bright fortnight, and the mobile Karanas were mentioned generally, perhaps there is only one rotation of them until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight? ->One should assign the duration of half a lunar day to all Karanas.<-
->This is declared to be the precise motion of the sun and other celestial wanderers. || 69 ||<-

One should assign an equal duration of half a lunar day <note>original: "tithyārdha-bhoga"</note> to each of the seven mobile Karanas. This is the established rule of the scripture—

# The Treatise on the Sun

Now, the Chapter on the Three Questions is explained. In this context, because a teacher’s desire to explain does not arise without a question, and without that desire, students cannot gain knowledge, the "Three Questions" refers to the inquiry into the three elements: direction, place, and time. The method for knowing direction is described in four verses:

> On a stone surface leveled with water, or on a smooth floor coated with hard plaster, one should draw a circle with a radius of a desired number of digits related to the gnomon. <note>The gnomon, or 'Shanku', is a vertical pillar used in ancient astronomy to measure shadows.</note> || 1 ||
> 
> In the center of that circle, one should place a gnomon imagined to be twelve digits in height. Where the tip of its shadow touches the circle in the forenoon and afternoon halves of the day— || 2 ||
> 
> —one should mark those two points on the circle, named East and West. Between those two points, a North-South line should be drawn using a "fish" figure. <note>A 'Timi' or fish figure is a geometric construction using intersecting arcs to find a perpendicular line.</note> || 3 ||
> 
> Between the North and South directions, an East-West line is drawn using another fish figure. The intermediate directions <note>North-east, South-east, etc.</note> are likewise established through the points between the main directions. || 4 ||

Regarding the commencement of determining directions: first, on a stone surface leveled with water—meaning made as flat as the surface of water—or, in the absence of that, on a floor made smooth by hard plaster <term>Vajralepa: a traditional Indian durable lime-plaster or cement</term> or by pounding, one should draw a perfect circle. The radius should be a desired number of digits, using the same units of measurement as the gnomon's digits. This means the line of the circle's circumference should be equidistant from the center at all points. 

Then, in the center—meaning the middle point of that circle—one should place a gnomon. This gnomon is a wooden rod with a flat top and a circular circumference, marked with twelve equal divisions or digits. Then, during the forenoon and afternoon halves of the day...

<meta>This page continues the technical explanation of astronomical orientation, specifically focusing on the "Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka" (The Illuminator of Hidden Meanings), a commentary on the Sūrya Siddhānta. # Accompanied by the Illuminator of Hidden Meanings

In the first and second parts of the day, one should mark the points where the tip of the shadow cast by the fixed gnomon <note>original: "śanku"; a vertical pillar used in ancient astronomy to measure time and direction</note> touches the circumference of the circle. In the first part of the day, as the shadow continually decreases, it enters the circle at a certain point; in the latter half of the day, as the shadow continually increases, it exits the circle at another point. Having marked these two points of entry and exit on the circumference line of the circle, designating them as the "East" and "West" points respectively, a line should be drawn between them using a "fish" <note>original: "timi" or "matsya"; a geometric construction formed by the intersection of two circles, resembling the shape of a fish, used to ensure a perfect perpendicular</note>. This line becomes the North-South line.

The "fish" is created by taking the distance between the two points as the radius and drawing two circles centered on those two points. The area contained within the intersection of the circumferences of these two circles forms the fish-shape. In this construction, one intersection point is the "mouth" (formed by clearing away the outer parts of the circles) and the other intersection is the "tail" (formed by clearing the other two parts of the circles). The line defined by the mouth and the tail is the North-South line. From the East point, the right-hand end of the line points South; from the West point, the right-hand end of the line points North. Afterward, the initial circles and the fish-shape should be erased. The gnomon should also be removed from its place, leaving only the North-South line—this is the intended meaning.

Then, in the middle space between the North and South directions, using the North-South line as the radius and the North and South points as centers, one should again create circles and a "fish" as described before. By this means, the East-West line should be drawn. The end of the line near the original East point is East, and the end near the West point is West. By erasing the fish-shape, the East-West line is also established. Finally, from the intersection point of these lines, one should redraw the original circle mentioned at the start of the direction-finding process. Where the lines meet the circumference of that circle, those are the cardinal directions; thus, the four directions are established within the circle relative to its center.

# The Surya Siddhanta

In that same manner. Just as the East-West line was established by means of the North and South points, it is done by that same method. The word "only" is used here to exclude other methods. "Indeed" is used for emphasis. The intermediate directions <note>the corners, such as Northeast or Southwest</note> are to be properly determined by means of "fish" figures <note>term: <term>matsya</term> (fish); a geometric construction where two intersecting circles create a lens shape resembling a fish, used to draw perpendicular lines</note> produced between two immediate cardinal directions using small circles. These should be known by the points where the lines and circles intersect.

Now, the underlying logic <note>term: <term>upapatti</term>; a proof or rational explanation</note>: The two points where the horizon and the East-West circle <note>the prime vertical</note> intersect are located in the East and West directions. There, the knowledge of the East-West division is gained through the rising and setting of the sun. The knowledge of where the East-West circle meets the horizon is gained by knowing the rising and setting points of the sun when it is at the intersection of the celestial equator and the ecliptic <note>the equinox</note>, because the celestial equator is connected to the intersection points of the East-West horizon circle.

However, on any other day, the rising and setting of the sun occur to the North or South by the distance of the amplitude <note>term: <term>agra</term>; the angular distance of the sun from the true East at sunrise</note>. Because the horizon is vast and distant, it is impossible to gain precise knowledge of East and West simply by observing the sun's rising. Therefore, to know this in one's desired location, a circle mimicking the horizon is drawn on a desired level surface. 

Even then, because the shadow is of infinite length at sunrise, its tip cannot touch the circumference of the circle. But as the sun moves higher, the shadow shortens. At the moment the shadow enters the circumference of the circle, the "base" <note>term: <term>bhuja</term>; the distance from the East-West line</note> for that time (which will be explained later) should be applied in reverse as a sine-segment. Where the versed sine <note>term: <term>utkramajya</term></note> touches the circumference, that point is West of the gnomon's position. This is because the shadow falls to the North or South of the East-West line by the distance of the "base," and because the shadow falls in the direction opposite to the sun. Similarly, in the afternoon, as the sun moves lower...

## Accompanied by the *Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka* <note>The "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings," a famous commentary by Raṅganātha on the Surya Siddhanta</note>

As the shadow increases, at whatever point and time it exits the circumference of the circle drawn around the gnomon <note>The *śanku* or gnomon is a vertical rod used to track the sun's movement</note>, the "instantaneous base" <term>bhujā: the distance between the shadow's tip and the east-west line</term>—which will be described later—should be applied in reverse as a half-chord. From that position, the versed sine <note>The *utkramajyā* or versed sine is a trigonometric function used here to find the exact point on the circle's edge</note> is applied; where it touches the circumference, that is the **East** of the gnomon's position. The line connecting these is the **East-West line**. This is understood through the observation of the gnomon, and similarly, the knowledge of the East-West line of a place is gained through the observation of the shadow.

To explain: where the shadow enters the circle is the **West**, and where it exits is the **East**. However, because the entry and exit cannot happen at the same time, the shadow's western position at the time of entry is a physical reality, but the eastern exit is impossible at that same moment. Likewise, at the time of exit, the eastern position is real, but the western entry is impossible. To achieve a simultaneous calculation, one of the two marks must be adjusted by the difference between the two "instantaneous bases." In this case, the eastern mark should be moved in the direction of the sun's declination <term>ayana: the northward or southward path of the sun</term> by the number of digits <note>angulas</note> representing the difference between the bases. Alternatively, the western mark may be moved in the opposite direction of the declination.

The resulting line is the East-West line for the center of the circle. This is identical to the East-West line established by placing a gnomon in the center and applying the "base" to the entry and exit marks as previously described. This is stated in the *Siddhānta Śiromaṇi* <note>The "Crown of Treatises," a 12th-century work by the mathematician Bhāskara II</note>:

Out of compassion for the world, the Lord <note>referring to the divine origin of the Surya Siddhanta</note> did not mention the adjustment of a single point because the difference is very small; for the sake of ease, the entry and exit points were simply called "West" and "East," even if slightly imprecise. # The Surya Siddhanta
<note>original: "सूर्य्यसिद्धान्तः" - The "Sun Treatise," one of the most important historical texts on Indian astronomy.</note>

In the desired location, the East and West directions are to be established. Between these, the North-South line is formed by the line passing through the two points of the "middle fish" <note>The 'matsya' or fish is a geometric shape formed by the intersection of two circles, used to find perpendicular lines.</note>. It is correctly stated that the East-West line lies between the North and South directions, passing through the center of that fish. 

Now, an objection is raised: If the North-South line is derived from the fish formed by the East and West points, and the line touching those East-West points is already established by the distance between them, then re-calculating it seems redundant. Otherwise, the North-South line itself would be inconsistent. 

To this, we reply: It is true. Some say the re-calculation of the line touching the East-West points is specifically to define the segments of the North-South line. However, the reality is this: the center—the intersection of the North-South and East-West strings—is essential because the previously mentioned circle will be used in future steps. Since the diameter of that circle is greater than the distance between the East-West points, the line between those points must be extended at both ends; that extended line becomes the East-West line within the circle. Because a line might sometimes curve above or below a single point, it is more accurate to establish the full line from the start. By using the line passing through the "mouth" and "tail" of the fish <note>The vertices of the lens-shaped intersection</note>, which is longer than the distance between the points, the resulting straight line is much longer and more precise. Therefore, re-calculating the East-West line in this manner is the superior method.

In the same way, by using four "small fish" created between the two adjacent cardinal directions, four strings establish the intermediate corner directions <note>North-East, South-East, South-West, and North-West</note> within the circle. Thus, the eight directions are established around the center of the desired location. // 4 //

Next, he describes the position of the shadow at a given time relative to the intersection of these directional strings:

-> The shadow at a desired time is known by the digits <term>angulas</term> <note>A traditional unit of measurement, roughly the width of a finger.</note> marked on those side-strings. <- // 5 //

# The Surya Siddhanta
<note>original: "Surya Siddhanta" — The "Sun Precept," one of the foundational astronomical treatises of ancient India.</note>

The circle is also that thread. Because the east-west circle is designated as the prime vertical <note>original: "samamandala" — the great circle passing through the zenith and the east/west points</note>, the line representing it is called the prime vertical line. Similarly, the east-west circle of a place with no latitude is called the celestial equator <note>original: "vishuvat-mandala"</note>. Since it is attached to the east and west points, the east-west thread is established as its middle thread; thus, the east-west thread is also designated as the celestial equator. It should be noted that the designations of the ecliptic <note>original: "kranti-vritta"</note> and the vertical circle <note>original: "drig-vritta"</note> are not mentioned here because they are moving <note>variable</note> and only occasionally connect to the east-west points. || 6 ||

In the square, this is the interval measured in digits <note>original: "angula"</note>, which is equal throughout. Now, the amplitude of the hypotenuse-circle is discussed. Here is the proof: the amplitude of the hypotenuse-circle of the "arm" is called the amplitude when refined by the equinoctial shadow...

# Accompanied by the Illuminator of Hidden Meanings

Because in the southern hemisphere, the northern <term>Bhujā</term><note>The 'arm' or side of a triangle, here referring to the distance of the shadow from the east-west line</note> is greater than the <term>Palabhā</term><note>The equinoctial midday shadow, used to determine local latitude</note>, the <term>Agrā</term><note>The amplitude; the distance between the east-west line and the rising/setting point of a celestial body</note> is the <term>Bhujā</term> minus the <term>Palabhā</term>. Since the latitude line lies to the north of the east-west line in the middle of the <term>Bhujā</term>, the distance between the two lines is the <term>Agrā</term>, in the form of the <term>Bhujā</term> minus the <term>Palabhā</term>. Similarly, in the northern hemisphere, because the northern <term>Bhujā</term> is less than the <term>Palabhā</term>, the <term>Agrā</term> is the <term>Palabhā</term> minus the <term>Bhujā</term>. This is because the <term>Palabhā</term> line is further north from the east-west line than the <term>Bhujā</term> line; thus the distance between the two lines is the <term>Agrā</term> of the hypotenuse circle. Furthermore, because the southern <term>Bhujā</term> is less than the <term>Palabhā</term>, the <term>Agrā</term> is the <term>Bhujā</term> plus the <term>Palabhā</term>. Since the <term>Bhujā</term> and <term>Palabhā</term> lines are respectively south and north of the east-west line, the interval between them is the sum of the <term>Palabhā</term> and the <term>Bhujā</term>. Because the <term>Palabhā</term> is a substitute for the <term>Shankutala</term><note>The distance from the center of the dial to the shadow line</note>, it is always considered northern; to say otherwise due to the shadow's connection is incorrect. In the celestial sphere, the <term>Shankutala</term> is southern, and the shadow exists in the direction opposite to the observer. Therefore, the calculation of the latitude line to the south of the east-west line due to the southern <term>Bhujā</term> is explained according to the movement of the equinoctial shadow. || 7 ||

Now, in this context, the author explains how to find the hypotenuse from a known shadow, and the verification thereof:

> ->The square root of the sum of the squares of the gnomon and the shadow is the hypotenuse. Subtracting the square of the gnomon from the square of this [hypotenuse], the square root is the shadow; the gnomon is found by the reverse.<- || 8 ||

The square root of the sum of the squares of the twelve-digit <term>Shanku</term><note>The gnomon or vertical pillar used to cast shadows for astronomical measurement</note> and its shadow is the <term>Chāyā-karna</term><note>The shadow-hypotenuse; the distance from the tip of the gnomon to the tip of the shadow</note>. Now, he describes the method for finding the shadow as a form of verification. "Of this": from the square of the shadow-hypotenuse, subtract the square of the gnomon (which is 144, as 12 squared is 144), and the square root is the shadow. He then mentions the verification of the shadow-hypotenuse by another method. "The gnomon": by the reverse—meaning the opposite of the method for finding the shadow—subtract the square of the shadow from the square of the shadow-hypotenuse, and the square root [is the gnomon].

# The Treatise of the Sun
<note>original: "Surya-Siddhanta"</note>

...this is the meaning. The gnomon <note>a vertical pillar used to cast a shadow for measurement</note> should be twelve digits <note>original: "dvadasangula"</note> in height. Here is the mathematical proof: The twelve-digit gnomon is the vertical side <note>original: "koti"</note>, the equinoctial shadow is the horizontal side <note>original: "akshabha-bhuja"</note>, and the square root of the sum of their squares is the hypotenuse; thus, the equinoctial hypotenuse is established.

Now, a question arises: why did the Lord, the All-Knowing One, describe the calculation of the hypotenuse from a desired shadow after having already established the directions? This is especially curious since the solar amplitude <note>original: "agra"; the distance of the sun from the east-west line at sunrise</note> and other factors have been stated independently. One should not argue that this was stated merely to determine the solar amplitude without mathematical error. Such an argument fails because the knowledge of the "arm" <note>original: "bhuja"; the north-south distance of the shadow</note>—which is to be explained later—depends on the solar amplitude, and the solar amplitude in turn depends on the "arm." This creates a logical fallacy of mutual dependence <note>original: "anyonyashraya"</note>. Furthermore, recalculating what is already known through mathematics would be useless.

One might suggest that by using a pointer equal in length to the "arm," the end of the desired shadow is known. By knowing the shadow's end on the circumference of a circle centered on the gnomon (placed at the intersection of the directional lines), the "arm" is mathematically determined by the distance to the east-west line, thus avoiding mutual dependence. However, even then, it is improper for the All-Knowing Lord to make a statement without purpose. Even a dull-witted person does not speak without a reason. The solar amplitude and the "arm" are not strictly necessary for the basic determination of directions, which would justify their mention here. 

Moreover, since the calculation of the hypotenuse given here is identical to the mathematical calculation to be described later, its inclusion here seems misplaced. Unlike the *Crest-Jewel of Siddhantas* <note>original: "Siddhanta Shiromani," a famous 12th-century work by Bhaskara II</note>, which uses the shadow's hypotenuse for determining directions through observation, the hypotenuse mentioned here does not seem to serve that immediate purpose. 

Could it be that these four verses, beginning with "the square wall," were interpolated by some slow-witted person and not spoken by the Lord? No, that is not the case. When the solar amplitude—which is the basis for determining the "arm"—is established through the method described here, the directions are correctly established. Thus, the calculation of the solar amplitude is for the purpose of verifying the accuracy of the directional determination. Furthermore, the hypotenuse is calculated so that one may verify the accuracy by comparing it with the result obtained through the ratio: "If the radius of the diurnal circle yields this amplitude, then what does the radius of the celestial sphere yield?"

# The Surya Siddhanta

Multiply that sine by three and divide by ten; the resulting degrees are known as the precession <note>original: "ayana". This refers to the shifting of the equinoxes over time</note>. From the planet corrected by that precession, one calculates the declination, the shadow, the half-duration of daylight, and so forth. || 10 ||

The "circle of stars" refers to the zodiacal belt, the ecliptic, which is joined with groups of lunar mansions <note>original: "nakshatras"</note> fixed at the ends of rods measuring the celestial latitude. In a Great Age <note>original: "Mahayuga"</note>, in the eastern direction, it oscillates thirty times—meaning the number thirty multiplied by twenty, which equals six hundred. It "hangs down" or oscillates from its position on the sphere supported by the poles. By using the term "oscillates" <note>original: "parilambate"</note>, the author indicates that there is no complete revolution of the stellar sphere; otherwise, this would have been mentioned in the chapter on mean motions in the context of planetary revolutions. Furthermore, by saying it "hangs down," it is implied that it returns to its original position, and similarly, it is suggested that it oscillates toward the west from its central position. Thus, by the will of God, the stellar sphere first moves a certain number of degrees to the west, then returns to its original state, then moves the same number of degrees to the east, and returns again—this constitutes one unique revolution. Therefore, "eastward" is just an illustrative direction. The failure to explicitly mention the westward oscillation is due to the state of the alignment at the time of the dialogue. Here, the reading "thirty times" <note>original: "triṃśatkṛtve"</note> is an error in the text.

->For in an Age, the stellar sphere oscillates eastward six hundred times.<-

This is because the previous reading contradicts the *Soma Siddhanta* <note>An ancient astronomical text attributed to the Moon-god</note>, and because the *Brahma Siddhanta* states, "the sphere moved behind that." From the total number of elapsed days <note>term: Ahargana (the count of days since the beginning of the epoch)</note> multiplied by six hundred and divided by the number of solar terrestrial days in an Age, the result is obtained in revolutions. Discarding the full revolutions, the remaining signs and degrees are converted into a "arm" <note>term: Bhuja (the distance from the nearest equinox or solstice)</note>. Those degrees of the "arm" multiplied by three and divided by ten are to be known as the degrees of precession. The essential meaning is: the degrees of the "arm" multiplied by three and divided by ten equals the precession <note>original: "ayanāṃśa"</note>. From that corrected...

# Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings" <note>Sanskrit: Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka, a famous commentary on the Sūrya Siddhānta</note>

By adding or subtracting those <term>precession values</term><note>Sanskrit: ayanāṃśa; the angular distance representing the shifting of the equinoxes</note> from the planet—due to the eastward and westward movement of the <term>zodiac wheel</term><note>Sanskrit: bhacakra</note>—one understands the longitudinal shift. One should calculate the <term>declination</term><note>Sanskrit: krānti; the angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator</note>, the <term>shadow</term><note>Sanskrit: chāyā</note>, and the <term>ascensional difference</term><note>Sanskrit: caradala; the difference between a planet's actual rising and the 6 o'clock position</note> according to whether the planet is within or outside the six signs of the <term>solstitial point</term><note>Sanskrit: ayanagraha</note>. This is not done solely from the planet's mean position.

The <term>shadow</term> will be explained later; the <term>ascensional difference</term> (cara) was mentioned in the previous chapter. By the word "etcetera," the movement of the solstices and the <term>visibility correction</term><note>Sanskrit: dṛkkarm; a calculation to determine when a planet actually becomes visible on the horizon</note> are included. Although one could simply say "<term>declination</term> is derived from the corrected planet," and mentioning others is technically redundant since they depend on it, the specific mention of <term>declination</term> implies that for the sake of knowing the <term>declination</term> alone, it must be calculated from the planet as adjusted by precession. The mention of <term>shadow</term> and <term>ascensional difference</term> serves to indicate that <term>declination</term>—which is the basis for other calculations—must be derived from the corrected position to avoid using the uncorrected solar position.

Here is the rationale: By the will of the Supreme Lord, the <term>ecliptic</term><note>Sanskrit: krāntivṛtta; the sun's apparent path</note> moves along its own path from the west by twenty-seven degrees, increasing gradually. Then, turning back, it returns to its original position, and from that spot, it moves twenty-seven degrees to the east. Thus, the point of the <term>ecliptic</term> that rested at the intersection of the <term>ecliptic</term> and the <term>celestial equator</term><note>Sanskrit: viṣuvadvṛtta</note> at the beginning of creation—which is near the star <term>Revati</term><note>Zeta Piscium, the traditional zero-point of the Hindu zodiac</note> and serves as the limit for the previously calculated <term>planetary longitude</term><note>Sanskrit: grahabhoga</note>—has moved either east or west along the path of the <term>ecliptic</term>.

On the <term>celestial equator</term>, however, either the western or eastern part of that section has moved. At the <term>intersection point</term><note>Sanskrit: sampāta; the equinox</note>, there is no <term>declination</term> because there is no north-south distance between the two circles. But at the previous intersection point, because there is now a north-south distance between them, <term>declination</term> is produced. Therefore, calculating <term>declination</term> from the <term>planetary longitude</term> as it stands (without correction) is inconsistent; it is proper to calculate <term>declination</term> from the <term>planetary longitude</term> measured from the current <term>intersection point</term>. To find that <term>planetary longitude</term> measured from the current intersection, one takes the <term>planetary longitude</term> measured from the original intersection (as described in the previous chapter) and adjusts it by the degrees of the interval between the current intersection and the original intersection points on the <term>ecliptic</term>—these are called the <term>precession values</term> (<term>ayanāṃśa</term>). These values represent the eastward or westward shift of the original intersection point...

# The Treatise of the Sun

The property of the hypotenuse mentioned here is shown to be useful for what follows. At that time, because the Sun is situated on the equatorial circle, the term "equinoctial shadow" <note>original: "vishuvat-prabha"; the shadow cast by a vertical gnomon at noon on the day of the equinox</note> is used. || 12 || Now, the author describes the method for bringing forth the colatitude and latitude.

->The two sines <note>the "sine" here refers to the Indian 'jya', a chord-half</note> multiplied by the gnomon and the shadow, and divided by the equinoctial hypotenuse, || 13 ||<-
->are the sines of colatitude and latitude. Their arcs are the colatitude and latitude, which are always southern.<-

The two radius-values <note>the standard radius used in calculations</note> placed in two positions are multiplied by the gnomon and the shadow: in one place multiplied by twelve <note>the standard height of the gnomon in Indian astronomy is 12 digits</note> and in the other by the previously mentioned equinoctial shadow. Both are then divided by the equinoctial hypotenuse <note>the hypotenuse formed by the 12-digit gnomon and its equinoctial shadow</note>. The results are, in order, the sine of colatitude and the sine of latitude. The arcs of these two sines are respectively the colatitude and latitude, which in both hemispheres are always in the southern direction. 

The logic here is as follows: In the meridian circle, the distance between the celestial equator and the observer's prime vertical is the latitude. In the meridian circle, the distance of the celestial equator from the southern horizon is the colatitude. Both are south of one's own prime vertical in the upper sphere. Their sines are the sine of latitude and sine of colatitude. These form the base and the upright <term>bhujā and koṭi; the two sides of a right-angled triangle</term> where the radius is the hypotenuse. By the rule of proportion: if in the triangle of the equinoctial hypotenuse, the upright and base are twelve and the equinoctial shadow, then what will they be when the radius is the hypotenuse? From these two proportions, the sines of colatitude and latitude are found, and their arcs are the colatitude and latitude. This is proven. || 13 || 

Now, he describes the calculation of latitude from the midday shadow in two verses.

->The midday shadow is the base; the sine of three signs <note>the radius, as three signs equal 90 degrees</note> multiplied by that, || 14 ||<-
->and divided by its own hypotenuse, gives the minutes of the arc of zenith distance. These are north if the base is south,<-
->and south if the base is north. These are then combined with the minutes of the Sun's declination. || 15 ||<-

If the directions are different, they are added; if the same, they are subtracted; the result is the latitude in minutes.

## Accompanied by the *Illuminator of Hidden Meanings* <note>original: "Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka," a famous 17th-century commentary by Raṅganātha on the Sūrya Siddhānta</note>

The <term>sine of the base</term> <note>the horizontal shadow length</note> multiplied by the <term>radius</term> <note>the standard radius of the celestial sphere, usually 3438 minutes</note> and divided by the <term>hypotenuse of the noon shadow</term> results in the arc of the result. This is known as the "minutes of zenith distance." These minutes are considered "Southern" when the base—the form of the noon shadow—is situated to the south of the East-West line. They are "Northern" when the base is to the north. The word "and" <note>Sanskrit: 'ca'</note> serves to establish this rule of orientation.

Those minutes of zenith distance and the previously mentioned <term>minutes of solar declination</term> <note>the sun's distance north or south of the celestial equator</note> are added together if they are in different directions. If they are in the same direction, they are subtracted to find the difference. The word "and" again establishes this arrangement. The result is the <term>minutes of latitude</term> <note>the observer's distance from the equator</note>.

Here, the Lord <note>referring to the divine origin of the Sūrya Siddhānta</note> has provided the mathematical proof through the designation of the "base." To explain: just as the noon shadow is the base for a <term>gnomon</term> <note>a vertical pillar used for timekeeping</note> of twelve digits or for the hypotenuse of the noon shadow, so too is the zenith distance the interval of the Sun on the meridian circle from the <term>zenith</term> <note>the point directly overhead</note> at noon. The sine of that distance is the "sine of zenith distance."

In the proportion: if for the hypotenuse of the noon shadow, the noon shadow is the base, then for the radius-hypotenuse, what is the base? The result is the sine of the zenith distance. Its arc, being expressed in minutes, is called the "minutes of zenith distance." Because these relate to the planet <note>the Sun</note>, their direction is opposite to the direction of the shadow.

Now, if the degrees of declination and the degrees of latitude are in the same direction, the zenith distance is their sum; therefore, the southern zenith distance minus the southern declination equals the degrees of latitude. If the declination and latitude are in different directions, the zenith distance is the difference. If the zenith distance is southern, then because it is the latitude minus the declination, the latitude is found by adding the northern declination. If the zenith distance is northern, then because it is the declination minus the latitude, the latitude is the northern declination minus the zenith distance. Thus, the logic is perfectly established.

However, some practitioners, by taking the "base," calculate the southern or northern base at any desired time from the East-West line to the shadow. By treating this as a "near-noon shadow" and calculating its hypotenuse, they derive the minutes of zenith distance in the same manner...

In the three signs starting with Libra <note>the third quadrant</note>, the true Sun is known by adding six signs to the calculated arc. **The mathematical logic <term>Upapatti</term> is as follows:**
When the declination and latitude are in the same direction, the zenith distance is their sum. If the latitude is south and less than the declination, the declination is south. In different directions, the latitude minus the declination is the southern zenith distance; by this, the latitude is reduced and the declination is north. If the latitude is less than the declination and the zenith distance is north, then the latitude plus the zenith distance is the northern declination. 

The sine of this is the sine of declination <term>Krāntijyā</term>. If the maximum sine of declination corresponds to a radius-sine, then what [longitude] does this specific sine correspond to? The result is the sine of the Sun's longitude including precession <term>Sāyanārka-bhujajyā</term>. Its arc is the Sun's longitude. Because the "arm" <term>Bhuja</term> <note>the distance from the nearest equinoctial point</note> is symmetrical across the four quadrants:
1. In the first quadrant (Aries etc.), the "arm" itself is the Sun.
2. In the second quadrant (Cancer etc.), because the "arm" is the Sun subtracted from six signs, the Sun is six signs minus the "arm."
3. In the third quadrant (Libra etc.), because the "arm" is the Sun minus six signs, the Sun is the "arm" plus six signs.
4. In the fourth quadrant (Capricorn etc.), because the "arm" is the full circle minus the Sun, the Sun is the full circle minus the "arm."

Thus, by this inverse process, everything is easily understood. || 18 ||

# The Treatise of the Sun

->The correction for the slow motion of the Sun is applied repeatedly in reverse to find the mean Sun.<-

From the true Sun obtained through calculation, the correction for the slow motion <note><term>Mandaphala</term>: the equation of center, used to account for the elliptical nature of an orbit</note> is applied repeatedly and in reverse <note>original: "vamam" (leftward/inverse)</note> to the true Sun to arrive at the mean Sun as derived from the count of days <note><term>Ahargana</term>: the total number of elapsed days since the start of the current cosmic epoch</note>. This is the meaning: by treating the true Sun as the mean, and calculating the correction from the previous peak of slow motion <note><term>Mandocca</term>: the apogee or the point where the planet is furthest from Earth</note> as previously described, one applies the positive or negative correction inversely to the true Sun to find the mean Sun. From this result, the correction is calculated again and applied inversely to the true Sun, repeating this process until the values no longer change <note>This describes an iterative mathematical process to find a stable value</note>. Thus, while the true Sun is found from the mean Sun by a single application of the correction, finding the mean Sun from the true Sun requires multiple inverse applications.

The reasoning here is as follows: the mean Sun, when adjusted by the correction derived from it, becomes the true Sun. Conversely, the true Sun adjusted inversely by that same correction becomes the mean. However, when calculating the mean Sun from the true Sun, the exact mean is initially unknown, making it impossible to know the exact correction derived from it. Therefore, by treating the true Sun as the mean, one calculates an approximate correction; applying this inversely to the true Sun yields a value closer to the mean. By repeating this, the correction becomes increasingly precise until it matches the correction that would be derived from the mean Sun itself. Everything stated here is flawless.

->The sine of declination, multiplied by the equinoctial hypotenuse and divided by the gnomon-sine, yields the amplitude. [Verse 22]<-
->The sun’s amplitude, multiplied by the desired hypotenuse and divided by the middle hypotenuse, becomes its own.<-

The sine of the sun's declination <note>original: "kranti-jya"</note> is multiplied by the equinoctial hypotenuse <note>original: "aksha-karna"; the hypotenuse of a shadow cast at the equinox</note> and divided by the gnomon-sine <note>original: "shanku-jiva"</note>. Here, the "gnomon" refers to a vertical pillar of twelve digits <note>the standard unit of measure in ancient Indian astronomy</note> in length. The resulting value is the sun's shadow. By extension, this applies to the planets as well. This amplitude <note>the angular distance of a celestial body from the east or west point of the horizon</note>, when multiplied by the hypotenuse of the shadow at the desired time and divided by the "middle hypotenuse"—meaning the radius <note>original: "trijya"; literally the "sine of three signs" or 90 degrees</note>—results in the "own amplitude" <note>the amplitude specific to that moment's shadow</note>. 

The mathematical proof is as follows: In the sphere, the sine of declination is the perpendicular side, the amplitude on the horizon is the hypotenuse, and the "earth-sine" <note>original: "kujya"</note> is the base. In this triangle, if a perpendicular of twelve <note>the gnomon</note> gives the equinoctial hypotenuse, then what hypotenuse does the sine of declination give? By this proportion, the amplitude is found. Furthermore, by the proportion "if this is the value in the circle of the radius, what is it in the circle of the hypotenuse?", the amplitude for the specific shadow-hypotenuse is established. [Verse 22]

Next, the calculation of the "base" <note>original: "bhuja"; the north-south distance of the shadow from the east-west line</note> is described in two verses:

->In the southern hemisphere, the sun's amplitude added to the equinoctial shadow is the northern base. [Verse 23]<-
->In the northern hemisphere, subtract the amplitude from the equinoctial shadow; the remainder is the northern base.<-
->By the reverse, the base becomes southern in the interval between east and west. [Verse 24]<-
->The midday base is always known as the midday shadow.<-

The sun's amplitude at the desired time, in the southern hemisphere <note>original: "yamya-gola"</note>, is added to the equinoctial shadow <note>original: "vishuvad-bha" or "palabha"</note>; the sum is the "base" in the northern direction. In the northern hemisphere <note>original: "uttara-gola"</note>, one should subtract the amplitude from the equinoctial shadow; the remainder is the base in the northern direction...

It establishes the geometric relationship between the celestial sphere and the local horizon through proportional reasoning.</summary>

The result is the <term>base</term> <note>Sanskrit: *bhujā*; the north-south component of a shadow's position</note>. Now, if the <term>amplitude</term> <note>Sanskrit: *karṇāgrā*; the distance of the sun's rising point from the east-west line</note> cannot be subtracted from the <term>equinoctial shadow</term> <note>Sanskrit: *palabhā*; the shadow cast by a vertical pole at noon on the equinox</note>, how is the base to be calculated? To this, the author says: *By reversal.* By subtracting the equinoctial shadow from the amplitude, the remainder becomes the southern base. Now, one might ask whether the base is southern or northern; to this, he says: *In the distance between east and west.* This means the base is the southern or northern distance from the east-west line. 

However, since the second limit was not mentioned and the distance is not well-known, one might ask: "From the east-west line, the distance of *what* is the base?" He answers this under the guise of describing the nature of the midday shadow: *At midday.* The base at the time of midday is always said to be the midday shadow. Thus, it is clarified that the base is the distance by which the tip of the shadow is south or north of the east-west line.

The mathematical rationale <note>Sanskrit: *upapatti*</note> is as follows: The distance by which the foot of the <term>gnomon</term> <note>Sanskrit: *śaṅku*; a vertical pillar used for timekeeping</note> is south or north of the east-west line is the north-south base of the planet. The gnomon is the perpendicular line from the planet to the plane of the horizon. Here, this base is produced by the combination of the <term>gnomon-projection</term> <note>Sanskrit: *śaṅkutala*; the distance from the rising-setting line to the foot of the gnomon</note> and the amplitude. 

The gnomon-projection is the southern distance of the gnomon's foot from the rising-setting line located on the diurnal circle. The amplitude, however, is the distance from the east-west line to the rising-setting line, being north or south according to the north or south <term>declination</term> <note>Sanskrit: *gola*; refers to the celestial hemisphere</note>. In the direction opposite to the planet, the gnomon-projection is northern and the amplitude is in the opposite direction; their combination as the base is visible on the celestial sphere. 

This refers to the *Great Gnomon* <note>Sanskrit: *mahāśaṅku*; the sine of the altitude</note>. By the proportion "If this is for the Great Gnomon, what is it for a gnomon of twelve digits?", the base is found from the east-west line to the tip of the shadow. When the amplitude and gnomon-projection are calculated for a twelve-digit gnomon, their combination yields that same base. There, the amplitude was calculated previously. As for the gnomon-projection for a twelve-digit gnomon: the equinoctial shadow is the base, the Great Gnomon is the <term>perpendicular</term> <note>Sanskrit: *koṭi*</note>, the gnomon-projection is the base, and the <term>hypotenuse</term> <note>Sanskrit: *karṇa*</note> is the <term>diagonal of the shadow</term> <note>Sanskrit: *hṛti*</note>. In this triangle of twelve...

By the proportion: "If the equinoctial shadow <note>palabhā: the shadow cast by a 12-digit gnomon at noon on the equinox</note> is the base for the gnomon's upright, then what is the base for the great gnomon's upright?" one brings forth the base of the gnomon. Because the multipliers and divisors are equal in the proportion regarding what this is for a twelve-digit gnomon compared to a great gnomon, only the name "equinoctial shadow" remains. 

In the southern hemisphere <note>dakṣiṇagola: when the sun is south of the celestial equator</note>, because the latitude is north and thus in the same direction, the sum of the equinoctial shadow and the tip is the northern base. In the northern hemisphere <note>uttaragola</note>, because the latitude is south and thus in a different direction, the difference between the equinoctial shadow and the tip is the base; therein, if the equinoctial shadow remains, it is the northern base, and if the latitude remains, it is the southern base. Since the shadow at midday takes the form of a base, the base at the time of midday is the midday shadow; all this is logical. // 24 //

Now, having spoken of the hypotenuse of the shadow situated on the meridian <note>yāmyottaravṛtta: the north-south circle</note>, he explains the hypotenuse of the shadow situated on the prime vertical <note>pūrvāparavṛtta: the east-west circle</note> by two methods:

## The sine of colatitude and the sine of latitude, multiplied by the equinoctial shadow and the twelve-digit gnomon respectively, // 25 //
## and divided by the sine of declination, are the two hypotenuses when the sun is at the prime vertical.

The sine of colatitude <note>lambajyā</note> and the sine of latitude <note>akṣajyā</note> are multiplied respectively by the equinoctial shadow and twelve; both are divided by the sine of declination <note>krāntijyā</note>. The results (indicated by the word "but") are the two hypotenuses connected to the visible shadow when the sun is in the prime vertical <note>samamaṇḍala</note>; in both cases, it results in the shadow-hypotenuse. 

Here is the derivation: The circle that follows the east-west direction above the zenith is called the prime vertical. This is the calculation of the shadow-hypotenuse for an object situated there. If the equinoctial hypotenuse is the hypotenuse for the equinoctial shadow as a base, then what is the hypotenuse when the sine of declination is the base? This is because, for the prime vertical gnomon, the sine of declination is the base, and the prime vertical gnomon and the "earth-sine" <note>kujyā</note> subtracted from the "total day-radius" <note>taddhṛti</note> are respectively the hypotenuse and the upright. From this, using the rule "multiply the radius by twelve and divide by the gnomon measure," the calculation is performed.

There is no well-known qualifying characteristic in this method to prevent such over-application. # Page 26
## The Treatise of the Sun

When the northern <term>declination</term><note>The angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator.</note> is less than the latitude of the observer, then the midday hypotenuse is calculated using the Sun's declination at the <term>prime vertical</term><note>The vertical circle passing through the east and west points of the horizon.</note>. However, this is not the actual midday value. The result obtained by multiplying the <term>equinoctial shadow</term><note>The shadow cast by a vertical gnomon at noon on the day of the equinox.</note> by the radius and dividing it by the midday sine of amplitude—derived from the midday hypotenuse—is the <term>hypotenuse of the shadow</term><note>The distance from the tip of the gnomon to the tip of its shadow.</note> of the planet's disk when it is situated on the prime vertical.

By specifying "northern" here, it is clearly stated that this calculation is not performed for southern declination, because the disk of the planet situated on the prime vertical is not visible <note>In the northern hemisphere, a body with southern declination never crosses the prime vertical above the horizon</note>. Otherwise, if the declination were small in the southern hemisphere, the prime vertical <term>gnomon</term><note>The vertical pillar used to cast a shadow for astronomical measurements.</note> would be visible, and there would be no reason to exclude it.

### The Mathematical Proof

The reasoning here is as follows: From the midday shadow hypotenuse (which is theoretical at the moment of entering the prime vertical), if a twelve-digit gnomon gives that hypotenuse, then what would the <term>radius</term><note>The standard trigonometric sine-radius used in ancient Indian astronomy, often 3438 minutes.</note> give? This yields the instantaneous "middle gnomon." If the equinoctial shadow is the base for a perpendicular of twelve, then what is the "base of the gnomon" for the perpendicular of the great gnomon? 

By canceling out the two twelves, the product of the equinoctial shadow and the radius, divided by the middle hypotenuse, is obtained. If the middle gnomon is found by this base, then what is the "prime vertical gnomon" found by the base of the <term>amplitude</term><note>The angular distance of a rising or setting celestial body from the east or west point of the horizon.</note>? The product of twelve, the amplitude, and the middle hypotenuse is divided by the middle hypotenuse and the equinoctial shadow. This is because the prime vertical gnomon and its associated "right sine" act as the perpendicular and hypotenuse. 

When calculating the shadow hypotenuse from this using the previous method, the two twelves cancel out. The product of the middle hypotenuse, the equinoctial shadow, and the radius is divided by the amplitude and the middle hypotenuse. By canceling the equal multipliers and divisors (the middle hypotenuse), the result is established. One cannot simply assign values at will. 

Furthermore, by reducing the dividend and divisor by the radius, the "midday amplitude" is established in the place of the divisor (being the middle hypotenuse multiplied by the amplitude and divided by the radius). Thus, it is said to be "divided by the midday amplitude." In the place of the dividend, the product of the middle hypotenuse and the equinoctial shadow is not calculated for the southern hemisphere because the planet is not visible there. Even in the northern hemisphere, if the declination is greater than the latitude, the calculation is not performed because it is impossible for the body to enter the prime vertical, as it remains within the polar circle of the prime vertical. This is only possible when the declination is small.

Again, for a second time, from the multiplier of twelve. The word "and" <note>Sanskrit: *ca*</note> implies a collection. The word "but" <note>Sanskrit: *tu*</note> indicates the sequence of the day's halves. In the forenoon, it refers to the Southeast and Northeast (in southern/northern progression), and in the afternoon, to the Southwest and Northwest. This is known as the "Corner Gnomon" <note>Sanskrit: *Kona-shanku*</note>. The square root of the difference between the squares of the corner gnomon and the radius is called the <term>sine of zenith distance|drig-jya</term>.

> as the value of the unknown quantity.

> two equal sides <note>an equation</note> must be diligently formed,
> by subtracting, adding, multiplying, or dividing.

# The Surya Siddhanta

Based on the rule of equalizing the two sides of an equation, the value of the corner gnomon <term>Konashanku; the gnomon's shadow when the sun is at an intermediate direction like Northeast or Southwest</term> is to be determined. Let the unknown value be $x$ <note>original: "ya 1", an abbreviation for "yavattavat," the standard Sanskrit term for an unknown variable, similar to "x"</note>.
If a gnomon of twelve units is the vertical side <term>Koti</term> and the equinoctial shadow <term>Palabha; the shadow cast by a vertical gnomon at noon on the equinox</term> is the horizontal side <term>Bhuja</term>, then what is the horizontal side for the corner gnomon? The base of the corner gnomon is thus: $x \cdot \text{Palabha} \cdot 1/12$ <gloss>1/12</gloss>.

In the southern hemisphere <term>Dakshinagole</term>, the horizontal side is this value added to the amplitude <term>Agra; the distance of the sun at rising from the east-west line</term>: $(x \cdot \text{Palabha} \cdot 1 + \text{Agra} \cdot 12) / 12$ <gloss>12/12</gloss>.
In the northern hemisphere <term>Uttaragole</term>, the horizontal side is the difference with the amplitude. If it is north of the prime vertical, the side is the amplitude minus the gnomon's base: $(x \cdot \text{Palabha} \cdot 1 - \text{Agra} \cdot 12) / 12$ <gloss>12/12</gloss>. If it is south of the prime vertical, the side is the gnomon's base minus the amplitude: $(x \cdot \text{Palabha} \cdot 1 - \text{Agra} \cdot 12) / 12$ <gloss>12/12</gloss>.

From the center of the north-south and east-west lines of the corner, the hypotenuse of a square equal to the side is the sine of the zenith distance <term>Drigjya; the sine of the angular distance from the zenith to the sun</term>. Thus, twice the square of the side equals the square of the sine of the zenith distance.
In the southern hemisphere: $(x^2 \cdot \text{Palabha}^2 \cdot 1 + x \cdot \text{Palabha} \cdot \text{Agra} \cdot 24 + \text{Agra}^2 \cdot 144) / 72$ <gloss>144/72</gloss>.
In the northern hemisphere: $(x^2 \cdot \text{Palabha}^2 \cdot 1 - x \cdot \text{Palabha} \cdot \text{Agra} \cdot 24 + \text{Agra}^2 \cdot 144) / 72$ <gloss>144/72</gloss>.

Now, the square of the sine of the zenith distance is also equal to the square of the radius <term>Trijya</term> minus the square of the corner gnomon ($x^2$). Setting these sides as equal and clearing the denominators, the arrangement <term>Nyasa</term> for clearing the sides is:

->In the Northern Hemisphere: $\{ x^2 \cdot \text{Palabha}^2 \cdot 1 - x \cdot \text{Palabha} \cdot \text{Agra} \cdot 24 + \text{Agra}^2 \cdot 144 \}$ Now,<-
->$\{ 72 \cdot \text{Radius}^2 - 72 \cdot x^2 \}<-

# With the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings" commentary

By this [method], since it is equal to half the square of the radius <note>original: "trijyā-varga-ardha"; the radius in Indian trigonometry is typically 3438 minutes</note>, it is maintained as such for the sake of simplifying equal multipliers. Even there, for the purpose of a single multiplication, it is established that half the square of the radius, diminished by the square of the amplitude <note>original: "agra-varga"; the sine of the distance of the rising sun from the east point</note>, is multiplied by one hundred and forty-four. However, when the amplitude is greater than the sine of one and a half signs <note>45 degrees</note>, the square of the amplitude diminished by half the square of the radius, multiplied by one hundred and forty-four, becomes negative.

Now:

->When a remainder exists starting with the square of the unknown,<-
->then multiply both sides by a desired [number] and add<-
->something so that the side of the unknown becomes a square;<-
->then, by the root of this [side] and by the same operation<-
->on the side of the known,<-
->the value of the unknown is indeed obtained.<-

According to this statement, in order to find the root of both sides, a division by the coefficient of the square of the unknown must be performed. The coefficient of the square is the square of the side <note>bhuja</note> increased by two; when the side of the unknown is divided by this, the "square of the unknown" <note>term: yāvattāvad-varga; literally "as many as" squared, the standard term for $x^2$ in Sanskrit algebra</note> is established in the first place. In the second place, by the statement "the equinoctial shadow multiplied by twelve and the sine of the amplitude, divided by that [coefficient]," the result is called the "quotient" <note>term: phala</note>. This quotient, doubled and multiplied by the unknown, is positive or negative according to the North or South celestial hemispheres. When the side of the known is divided, it is called the "surd" <note>term: karaṇī</note>, which is positive or negative depending on whether the amplitude is less or greater than the sine of one and a half signs. Then, to find the root, the square of the "quotient" (which is half the coefficient of the unknown) is added to both sides. On the side of the unknown, after adding and taking the root, the first term is the "unknown" <note>yāvattāvad</note> and the second term is the "quotient," positive or negative in the North and South hemispheres. For example: $x + q$ or $x - q$. In the North hemisphere, the unknown may be negative: $-x + q$. In either case, because a "middle unknown" name is impossible, the root of the side of the known is the square root of the "surd" combined with that square [of the quotient].

# The Surya Siddhanta

<page-num>93</page-num>

In the case where the sine of one and a half signs <note>original: "sārdharāśijyā"; referring to the sine of 45 degrees</note> is greater than the amplitude, or when it is greater, the square root of the result of the calculation <note>original: "karaṇūnasya phalavargasya mūlam"; referring to the square root of the difference of squares in the sine formula</note> is used. And so, even if the previously mentioned logic regarding "from half the square of the radius minus the square of the amplitude" fails when the sine of 45 degrees is greater:

->Whenever in the process of subtraction<-
->the value to be subtracted cannot be taken from the other,<-
->the rule is as stated, but by reversed subtraction;<-
->the wise must then turn addition into subtraction.<-

Following this method stated by Bhaskara <note>Bhaskara II, the 12th-century mathematician</note>, whether the square of the amplitude is subtracted from the square of the sine or vice versa, there is no error in the relationship of "lesser" or "greater." Now, for the sake of further refinement, the placement of the two sides of the equation is shown.
In the Southern Hemisphere <note>original: "dakṣiṇagole"</note>:

| Unknown (ya) | 1 | Result (pha) | 1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Square of Unknown (ya-varga) | | Root (pa) | 1 |

Because the square root of the result of the calculation is less than the result itself, the placement of those sides is also:

| Unknown (ya) | 1 | Result (pha) | 1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Square of Unknown (ya-varga) | | Root (pa) | 1 |

Here, using the rule "with one unknown" <note>referring to the *Ekavyakta* method of algebra</note>:
"Divide the remaining known value by the remaining unknown coefficient; the result is the value of the unknown quantity."
By this, in the first position, the root is subtracted from the result, which is logical.
In the second position, the result is subtracted from the root; however, the Lord <note>the divine author of the Surya Siddhanta</note> did not mention this "negative" corner shadow.
This is because a negative state is a reversal of position. In the upper sphere <note>the visible celestial hemisphere</note>, what is reversed or below the horizon is not visible, so its description is not required. Nor is it necessary to describe it just because it might be "visible" in the lower hemisphere. Since we are calculating for the sake of determining the shadow for someone in the upper hemisphere, and a shadow there is impossible in that case, it is irrelevant. In the Northern Hemisphere <note>original: "uttaragole"</note>, however:

| Unknown (ya) | 1 | Result (pha) | 1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Square of Unknown (ya-varga) | | Root (pa) | 1 |

or

| Unknown (ya) | 1 | Result (pha) | 1 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Square of Unknown (ya-varga) | | Root (pa) | 1 |

In the first position, the root added to the result is logical. In the second position, the root subtracted from the result was not mentioned by the author because it is not useful for the shadow calculation, as the square root of the result of the calculation is less than the result itself.

This is because the radius is the distance in the diurnal circle's semi-diameter from the <term>unmaṇḍala<note>the equatorial horizon</note></term> to the meridian line. And because the ascensional difference sine lies between those two meridian lines, as the unmaṇḍala stays above or below the horizon in the north or south respectively.

In the diurnal circle of the planet, at a position separated by the <term>hour angle<note>original: "nataghaṭī," time from noon</note></term> on both sides of the intersection of the meridian and the diurnal circle, that line is the full sine of the hour angle.
