That value, contained within the upper diameter of the meridian, is the <term>desired divisor<note>original: "iṣṭahṛti"</note></term> calculated by the proportion of the <term>radius of the diurnal circle<note>original: "dyujyā"</note></term>. 

The result of the desired divisor multiplied by the diurnal radius and divided by the radius is the <term>cheda</term>. From this, the proportion is: if the cosine of latitude is the upright side for a hypotenuse equal to the radius, then what is the upright side for a hypotenuse equal to the desired divisor? By this proportion, the desired gnomon is found. From this, the sine of zenith distance, the shadow, and its hypotenuse are established by the stated method; thus, the explanation is complete. || 35 ||

# The Treatise of the Sun

->The radius multiplied by the desired shadow and divided by its hypotenuse<-

<note>Verses 36–38. These verses describe the trigonometric process of converting a physical shadow measurement back into time (measured in "asavas" or respirations).</note>

The radius <term>Trijya; the radius of a standard circle, usually 3438 minutes</term> multiplied by the shadow at the desired time and divided by the hypotenuse of that shadow results in the sine of the zenith distance <term>Drigjya; the sine of the angular distance from the zenith</term>. The square root of the value obtained by subtracting the square of the sine of the zenith distance from the square of the radius—the word "and" here implies the constant relationship between these terms—is the desired gnomon <term>Shanku; the vertical shadow-casting pillar, here representing the sine of the altitude</term>. 

That specific gnomon, multiplied by the radius and divided by the sine of the local colatitude <term>Lambajya; the sine of the angle between the pole and the zenith</term>, results in the "divisor" <term>Cheda</term>. That divisor, multiplied by the radius and divided by the radius of the diurnal circle <term>Dyujya</term>, results in a unique "sine of altitude" <term>Unnatajya</term>. This is not the actual arc of the time elapsed. 

When the "antya" <term>the sum of the radius and the sine of the terrestrial latitude</term> associated with the diurnal circle is decreased by this calculated sine of altitude, the arc of the remainder is found using the versed sines <term>Utkramajya; the "sines of the reverse order" used to find arcs near the horizon</term>. Following the methods mentioned previously regarding the totals of versed sines, if the remainder exceeds the radius, the arc of the excess is found via the R-sine tables and added to the versed sine arc. In this manner, the calculated units <note>asavas</note> represent the time elapsed since sunrise in the morning or the time remaining until sunset in the afternoon. 

The logic here is easily understood as the inverse of the previously mentioned rules. In this context, the "divisor" converted to the scale of the radius is the "desired antya," though it is not strictly a sine in the traditional sense. Because the diameter of the diurnal circle does not align perfectly with the rising-setting line, this is referred to as the "sine of altitude" due to its close approximation. # With the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings" Commentary
<note>original: "Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka" — this is the title of the famous commentary by Raṅganātha on the Sūrya Siddhānta.</note>

...it was stated that the lower part should be considered equal to the elevated time-chord. Otherwise, if the bow-string <note>the chord</note> were to result in an elevated time, the portion starting with "lessened by that" would be rendered useless. This is the general direction of the argument. || 38 ||

Now, in one and a half verses, the author explains the method for finding the Sun's position through the sine of declination <term>Krāntijyā: the sine of the angular distance of a celestial body from the celestial equator</term> using the amplitude of the shadow at a desired time.

> The sine of the colatitude multiplied by the amplitude of the shadow at the desired time, and divided by the digits of its own hypotenuse, results in the sine of declination. That, multiplied by the radius and divided by the sine of maximum declination || 39 ||
> Its arc is the "field" in signs and so on; the Sun is located there according to the quadrants.

The sine of the colatitude <term>Lambajyā: the sine of the angle between the zenith and the celestial pole</term> is multiplied by the amplitude of the hypotenuse <note>the distance of the shadow's tip from the east-west line</note> at the desired time. The word "but" <note>original: "tu"</note> is used to exclude the sine of the altitude. When this is divided by the number of digits in the hypotenuse of the shadow at that moment, the result is the sine of declination. That sine of declination is multiplied by the radius and divided by the sine of the maximum declination <note>approximately 24 degrees in ancient Indian astronomy</note>. The arc of that result is the "field" or position in signs and so on—essentially the "sine-arm" <note>original: "bhuja"</note>. Based on the four quadrants identified by the <unclear>marks</unclear>, the Sun is produced in that specific quadrant. Following the prescribed rules—such as subtracting from the sign of Cancer or from the half-circle—the true Sun is found.

The derivation is as follows: If for a hypotenuse-amplitude we get a specific value, what would it be for a radius-amplitude? In the ratio where the sine of colatitude is the vertical side for a radius-hypotenuse, what would the vertical side be for a shadow-hypotenuse? By this proportion, since the two radii (as multiplier and divisor) cancel each other out, the sine of declination is equal to the sine of colatitude multiplied by the desired hypotenuse-amplitude and divided by the hypotenuse. Since the method for bringing forth the Sun from this has been stated previously, it is very easy to understand and is repeated here for clarity. || 39 ||

Now, he describes the path of the shadow's rotation:

# The Treatise of the Sun
<note>original: "Surya Siddhanta"</note>

On the desired day, in the middle, eastern, and western sections, at the distance of the "arm" <note>the 'bahu' or 'bhuja' refers to the north-south distance of the shadow tip from the east-west line</note>, marks are made within the circle at the distance of the arm from the east-west line. This is the meaning: from the center point of the east-west line, one mark is made at the distance of the arm-inches; a second mark is made in the eastern section at the distance of the arm-inches corresponding to that specific time; and a third mark is made in the western section at the distance of the arm-inches corresponding to that other time. Thus, on a single day, at three different times, three marks are made at their respective arm-distances from the east-west line.

By using the intersection of two "fish" figures <note>a 'matsya' or fish is a geometric construction where two intersecting arcs create a lens shape, used to find perpendiculars or centers</note> formed from the adjacent marks—that is, by producing a "fish" from each pair of marks—the intersection of the two central lines passing through the mouth and tail of each "fish" is found. From that point where those lines, extended according to their path, meet: with a "three-touching string" <note>a string or radius that touches all three points</note>. With a radius measured by the string touching the three marks, a circle is rotated which becomes the path of the shadow. This means the tip of the shadow at any time between the first and last observations will fall upon the circumference of that circle.

Here is the mathematical proof: Since the shadow tip is at the distance of the "arm" from the east-west line, and having identified three shadow tips, to find the center of the circle that touches them, the north-south lines passing through the middle of the adjacent marks are found via the two "fish" constructions. Since the center must be equidistant from the points on the circumference, and the midpoints between the marks must relate to the circumference, those lines necessarily meet at the center. Thus, the intersection of the lines from the midpoints of each pair of adjacent marks is established as the center of that circle.

To find the meridian line <note>the true north-south line</note>, two "fish" are used. It is no wonder that a circle drawn from that center touches all three points. However, it must be noted that because the shadow tip moves in accordance with the Sun's motion, its path is not a perfect circle, as the diurnal circle changes every moment. Otherwise, the variation in declination <note>the Sun's angle relative to the celestial equator</note> would not be accounted for. Therefore, the shadow tips falling on a single circular circumference—

Rotation is not possible. Nevertheless, because the calculated tips of the shadows must necessarily exist on a single circle, the fact that the shadow-tips falling within that interval lie on its circumference is accepted—despite a slight discrepancy—by the compassionate Lord <note>Referring to the divine origin of the Surya Siddhanta</note>. This was taught so that one might know the position of a shadow-tip even without seeing it, by observing the positions of shadow-tips at other times. This is useful for determining the <term>Agra-bhuja</term> <note>The amplitude of the shadow, used to find the sun's position</note> and other values necessary for knowing the Sun's zodiacal position when the Sun is covered by clouds or other obstructions at the desired time. ## Accompanied by the *Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka* <note>The "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings," a famous commentary by Raṅganātha on the Sūrya Siddhānta.</note>

Regarding the rising times <term>udayāsavaḥ; literally 'rising breaths', where one breath equals 4 seconds of time</term> of the zodiac signs: in order to find the specific rising time for each individual sign, one must subtract the preceding values from the subsequent ones. This is established by the previous rules starting from "the product of the radius and the sine of three signs" up to "these are the rising times at Laṅkā." Here, the term "Laṅkā" should be interpreted as referring to any location on the Earth's equator <term>nirakṣadeśa; literally 'the place without latitude'</term>. Since the geometric configuration of the celestial sphere is identical for all equatorial locations, there is no obstacle to applying this method to any such place. Otherwise, one would be forced to apply a longitudinal correction <term>deśāntara-saṃskāra</term>—just as one does for planets—to find the values for one's specific equatorial meridian. The correction for local rising times <term>carasaṃskāra; the adjustment for the 'ascensional difference' caused by the observer's latitude</term> is explained immediately hereafter. The mathematical derivation for the values starting with "six, eight, and seven" <note>original: "svāgāṣṭaya"; a mnemonic for the number 1686</note> follows the same logic as previously stated. || 42 || Now, in half a verse, the author describes the local rising times derived from these.

-> The local rising times are found by subtracting the local ascensional difference segments. || 43 || <-

These are now established. The "ascensional difference segments" <term>carakhaṇḍa</term> are produced in relation to one's own specific country. By calculating the total ascensional difference for the signs starting with Aries according to the prescribed method, and then subtracting them sequentially from one another as described before, one obtains the segments for the signs from Aries to Gemini. When the equatorial rising times are diminished by these segments, they become the "desired rising times"—that is, the rising times for the first three signs (Aries, Taurus, and Gemini) at the specific latitude where those segments apply. The proof for this is as follows:

> Aries through Gemini rises in fifteen nadis <note>A nadi is 24 minutes; 15 nadis equal 6 hours or 90 degrees</note>.
> When the Sun is in the northern hemisphere, they rise in that time minus their respective ascensional differences.

According to this statement by Bhāskara <note>Bhāskarācārya, the 12th-century mathematician and astronomer</note>, the knowledge of each individual rising time depends on the individual ascensional difference. Since an individual difference is a "segment," the logic is sound. || 43 || Next, he describes the rising times for the remaining signs.

# The Surya Siddhanta
<note>original: "Surya Siddhanta" — The "Sun Precept," a foundational Sanskrit treatise on Indian astronomy.</note>

->The three signs beginning with Cancer, when added to their respective values in reverse and direct order, *<-
->become the desired rising times for the six signs beginning with Libra when taken in reverse order †. || 44 ||<-

From that difference, the rising times at the equator <term>Lankodaya-asavah</term><note>The time taken for a zodiac sign to rise at the Earth's equator, measured in 'asu' or respirations (1 asu = 4 seconds of time).</note> for Aries and the following signs are placed in reverse order—Gemini, Taurus, and Aries. These are then added to their three respective <term>charakhandas</term><note>Ascensional differences; the correction factors used to adjust equatorial rising times to a specific local latitude.</note> placed in reverse order of their rising. The three signs beginning with Cancer and ending with Virgo thus have their known rising times determined. Now, the author explains the method for knowing the rising times of the remaining six signs.

"In reverse order": These six signs mentioned, from Aries to Virgo, are taken in reverse order—Virgo, Leo, Cancer, and so on. The word "only" <note>original: "evakaro"</note> is used to exclude the direct order of Aries, Taurus, etc. The six signs beginning with Libra become the desired known rising times for one's own locality. Thus, it is established that the rising time of Virgo is that of Libra; the rising of Leo is that of Scorpio; the rising of Cancer is that of Sagittarius; the rising of Gemini is that of Capricorn; the rising of Taurus is that of Aquarius; and the rising of Aries is that of Pisces. The mathematical proof here:

> From the end of Virgo to the end of Sagittarius, by the measured time-units of the rising,
> When the planet <insert>Mars</insert> is rising or situated above, then by those called the 'ascensional differences' (chara),
> Subtracting those from the previously elapsed portions, whether at the end of Virgo or the end of Pisces,
> By the practice of subtracting the ascensional differences, the equatorial risings become the local risings.

This is easily understood through the statement of Bhaskara <note>Bhaskara II, a 12th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note>. || 44 || Now, to calculate the <term>Lagna</term><note>The Ascendant; the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon at a specific time.</note> as a positive or negative value for a desired time, the author speaks of the elapsed and remaining rising times.

->The elapsed and remaining rising times should be calculated from the time desired from the Sun.<-
->The elapsed and remaining degrees, multiplied by their respective local rising times and divided by thirty (thirty). || 45 ||<-

# Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings."

From the Sun calculated for the desired time <note>the specific moment for which an astrological chart is being cast</note>, the elapsed and remaining time-units <note>original: "asavas," a unit of time equal to one respiration or 4 seconds</note> are produced. How are these elapsed and remaining units to be calculated? To this, the author says: "Multiplied by the rising periods of their own signs." The degrees already traversed by the Sun in the sign it occupies are the "elapsed degrees," and those remaining until the end of the 30-degree sign are the "remaining degrees." These elapsed and remaining degrees of the Sun, multiplied by the local rising periods <note>term: "udayāsu" - the time it takes for a zodiac sign to rise above the horizon at a specific latitude</note> of that sign and divided by thirty, result in the elapsed and remaining time-units respectively.

The logic <note>original: "upapatti"</note> here is as follows: At the time the ascendant <note>term: "Lagna" - the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</note> is to be calculated, the Sun must also be calculated for that exact moment; otherwise, the calculation of the instantaneous ascendant would not be accurate. For this purpose, the elapsed and remaining time-units of the sign occupied by the Sun must be determined. This is because that specific sign is rising from the moment of sunrise until the desired time, spanning both the prior and subsequent periods. Furthermore, the knowledge of the ascendant is easily obtained by counting the rising periods of the subsequent signs. Therefore, the proportion is: if thirty degrees correspond to the total rising time-units, then how many time-units correspond to the elapsed and remaining degrees? 

Since these rising periods are derived from the zodiacal signs starting from the intersection points <note>the equinoxes</note>, the Sun must be adjusted by the precession of the equinoxes <note>term: "ayanāṃśa" - the longitudinal difference between the tropical and sidereal zodiacs</note>. Otherwise, the Sun would not properly correspond to the stated rising periods of the signs, leading to inconsistency. For this very reason, the Great Teacher Bhāskara <note>Bhāskarācārya, the 12th-century mathematician-astronomer</note> stated:

->The declination must be calculated from the Sun plus the precession,<-
->and the elapsed and remaining times of the planets must indeed be calculated likewise.<-

Now, a doubt arises: should the elapsed and remaining time-units not be calculated from the Sun's position at sunrise? After all, that sign is rising from sunrise until the desired time. The sign is not necessarily rising exactly at the desired time such that its elapsed units should be calculated then. Nor are the units calculated from the instantaneous Sun applicable to the period starting from sunrise, because the instantaneous Sun was not at that position at sunrise. If so, why did the venerable and omniscient Bhāskara and others say it should be calculated from the Sun at the desired time? To this, it is replied: Regarding the rising periods...

# The Treatise of the Sun

Because of the nature of the celestial sphere, sidereal ghatis <note>A ghati is a unit of time equal to 24 minutes; sidereal time is measured relative to the stars rather than the sun</note> established by the principles must be used. Everywhere, the calculated ghatis are civil <note>original: "sāvana"; solar or civil days measured from sunrise to sunrise</note> in nature. Converting them to sidereal time is necessary, otherwise, the calculation of the ascendant <note>term: Lagna; the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</note> would be incorrect. For that purpose, using the secret method of "multiplying by the respirations of the rising signs," etc., the respirations <note>term: asu; a unit of time equal to 4 seconds, or the time taken for one breath</note> produced by the daily motion of the planets are added to the sixty civil ghatis to find the sidereal equivalent. By the rule of proportion, one determines how much should be added to the desired civil ghatis to make them sidereal. 

In this process, if the rising respirations of the fractional parts of the signs are eighteen hundred minutes, then by the proportion "what are the respirations for the elapsed time," the multipliers and divisors of the eighteen hundred rising respirations cancel out because they are equal. The remaining motion <note>original: "cālana"</note> is then added to the Sun. The civil ghatis themselves remain unchanged. Thus, the Sun at the desired time—at which time the ascendant is calculated—makes the previously taken civil ghatis effectively sidereal. This was correctly stated by the Lord <note>referring to the divine source of the Sūryasiddhānta</note>. This is also the intention behind the statement by the teacher Bhāskara <note>Bhāskarācārya, a famous 12th-century mathematician and astronomer</note>:

->If the desired ghatis for calculating the ascendant are civil,<-
->they become sidereal by calculating the position of the Sun for that specific time.<-
->For here, the sidereal risings must be subtracted from similar units;<-
->this is not achieved if the conversion to sidereal time is not performed.<-

Thus ends verse 45. Now, he explains the method for calculating the arc of the ascendant from the desired ghatis using two verses:

> From the respirations of the desired ghatis, one should subtract the remaining portion of the sign to be passed <note>original: "bhogya"</note>.
> Likewise, subtract the rising respirations of the subsequent signs; but in the reverse case, subtract those already passed. || 46 ||
> If there is a remainder, multiply it by thirty and divide by the "unpurified" sign <note>the sign whose duration could not be fully subtracted</note>.
> The result, subtracted from or added to the signs, is the ascendant on the horizon at that time. || 47 ||

### Accompanied by the *Illuminator of Hidden Meanings* <note>original: "Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka," a famous commentary on the Sūrya Siddhānta</note>.

From the breaths <note>term: Prāṇa (breath). A unit of time equal to 4 seconds; 6 breaths make one Vināḍī</note> of the desired time—that is, the ghatikas <note>term: Ghaṭikā. In the manner described, from the remaining breaths of the desired time, one should subtract the "elapsed breaths" and the rising times of the "elapsed signs" in reverse order. The rising time of a sign that cannot be fully subtracted is called the "incomplete sign." The remainder is multiplied by thirty and divided by that sign's rising time. The text implies that if there is no remainder, no further calculation is needed as the result would be zero. By adding or subtracting the resulting degrees and minutes to the sign's boundary, one determines the exact point on the ecliptic <note>term: Krāntivṛtta. The circular path of the Sun across the sky</note> that is touching the eastern horizon at the desired moment. This point, connected by the line of the horizon, is the *Lagna* <note>term: Lagna. The Ascendant; the specific point of the zodiac rising in the East at a given time</note> for that time.

For the purpose of making predictions, just as planets are measured from the starting point near the junction star of Revatī <note>the star Zeta Piscium, marking 0° in the sidereal zodiac</note>, the *Lagna* should also be taken from that same point. Therefore, it is self-evident that the resulting *Lagna* should be adjusted by the precession <note>term: Ayanāṃśa. The longitudinal difference between the tropical and sidereal zodiacs</note> in reverse, though this was not explicitly stated. One should not argue that because the precession adjustment for the Sun was not mentioned earlier, the *Lagna* should remain as it is. For the purpose of calculating planetary positions at a specific time, the Sun's precession adjustment is already implied, as it is necessary for calculating declination, shadows, and the half-duration of daylight. Now, if one argues that the Lord <note>the divine author of the text</note> did not explicitly mention the reverse precession adjustment, and therefore the *Lagna* should be taken from the equinox <note>term: Sampāta</note> for predictions—while the Sun requires the adjustment only for the sake of calculating the *Lagna* because rising times are measured from the equinox—that is not correct.

# The Surya Siddhanta
<note>The Surya Siddhanta is one of the foundational Sanskrit treatises on Indian astronomy, dating back to the 4th-5th century CE.</note>

->Subtracting or adding the degrees, that point on the horizon is the Ascendant.<-

By repeating the half-verse and the words "east and west" found at the beginning of the previous verse, it is established by the Lord’s <note>original: "bhagavataḥ"; referring to the divine source of the text</note> own words that the Ascendant <term>Lagna; the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</term> is found by sequentially subtracting or adding the degrees of the precession of the equinoxes <term>ayanāṃśa; the longitudinal difference between the tropical and sidereal zodiacs</term> as the cycle moves east and west. 

The logic here is as follows: When subtracting the elapsed or remaining time-units <term>asu; a unit of time equal to four seconds</term> from the desired time-units <note>ghatikā; a unit of 24 minutes</note>, it is understood that the sign occupied by the Sun is not necessarily the Ascendant. Then, by subtracting the rising times of the subsequent or preceding signs, it is understood that a fully "cleared" sign is not the Ascendant. Rather, that sign whose rising time cannot be fully subtracted is the one rising on the horizon at the desired time. 

To determine which specific degree of that sign is rising, a proportion is used: if thirty degrees correspond to the total rising time of the uncleared sign, then how many degrees correspond to the remaining time-units? Through this method of calculating elapsed or remaining portions, the specific degrees of the rising sign are established. In this context, the remaining degrees subtracted from thirty give the elapsed degrees of the rising sign. Thus, the Ascendant is formed by the remaining degrees from the "uncleared" sign. The elapsed degrees added to the count of elapsed signs also result in the Ascendant. 

The inverse correction for the precession of the equinoxes is performed to align the calculation with the planetary positions. Otherwise, for the purpose of predicting results, the planets must be taken as corrected by the precession. Thus, everything is faultless. || 47 ||

From the nectar <note>referring to the clarity of the teaching</note>. Using the rising periods of the zodiac signs at the equator <note>term: Nirakṣadeśarāśyudayāsu — the time it takes for signs to rise at the terrestrial equator, used as a universal constant in Indian astronomy</note> as previously described, one should subtract or add the calculated degrees of the signs to the Sun, depending on whether the time is before or after the meridian <note>term: Prāk-paścima-nata — eastern or western hour angle</note>. The intention is as follows:
If the time is in the east <note>before noon</note>, one should take the time-units <note>Asus</note> of the hour angle and subtract the elapsed rising periods of the sign currently occupied by the Sun. Then, subtract the rising periods of the preceding signs. Multiply the remainder by thirty and divide by the rising period of the next sign to be subtracted. The resulting degrees and the number of signs subtracted should be taken from the Sun to find the Meridian House.

Similarly, if the time is in the west <note>after noon</note>, one should subtract the remaining rising periods of the sign occupied by the Sun from the time-units of the hour angle. Then, subtract the rising periods of the subsequent signs. Multiply the remainder by thirty and divide by the rising period of the next sign. The resulting degrees and the number of signs should be added to the Sun to find the Meridian House. Even when the desired time is less than the elapsed or remaining portion of the current sign, the time-units multiplied by thirty and divided by the rising period of the Sun's sign, when subtracted from or added to the Sun, yield the Meridian House. By this same method, the Ascendant <note>Lagna</note> can also be calculated.

Now for the rationale:
The point of the ecliptic <note>term: Krāntivṛtta</note> which is intersected by the upper meridian <note>term: Yāmyottaravṛtta</note> is the Meridian House. To calculate this, the "hour angle" <note>term: Natakāla</note> is the duration in ghatis <note>units of 24 minutes</note> by which the Sun has moved from the meridian at the desired time. In the eastern and western hemispheres, it is designated as "east" or "west." The eastern hemisphere <note>term: Prākkapāla</note> lasts from midnight until midday. The western hemisphere <note>term: Paścimakapāla</note> lasts from midday until midnight. In the case of an eastern hour angle, because the Sun is east of the meridian, the zodiacal portion east of the Sun is what touches the meridian; therefore, it is calculated by subtracting from the Sun using the hour angle. In the case of a western hour angle, because the Sun is west of the meridian, the portion ahead of the Sun...

# The Surya Siddhanta
<note>original: "Sūryasiddhānta"; the "Sun-Treatise," one of the most important historical texts of Indian astronomy.</note>

From the Ascendant <term>Lagna; the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</term> at midnight, and following the sequence of the Sun’s position, the calculation is performed using the "bent" hours <note>original: "nata-ghaṭī"; hours measured from the meridian</note>. In that context, because the desired meridian circle is fixed at an interval of fifteen hours, it must be calculated using the rising periods at the equator <note>original: "nirakṣodaya-asubhiḥ"</note>. The reasoning for the remaining operations is quite clear, so this is the summary. || 48 || Now, he describes the method for determining time:

> From the remaining portion of the lesser sign, and the elapsed portion of the greater sign,
> and the sum of the rising periods of the intervening signs, the determination of time is achieved. || 49 ||

Immediately following this: between the Ascendant and the Sun, take the one that is the absolute minimum and calculate its remaining rising periods <note>original: "bhogya-asūn"</note>; then take the one that is greater and calculate its elapsed rising periods <note>original: "bhukta-asūn"</note>. Adding these together with the rising periods of the intervening signs—meaning the zodiac signs situated between the Sun and the Ascendant—the calculation is complete. The word "and" <note>original: "ca"</note> implies the summation. By combining these in the manner described, the "attainment of time" occurs.

The logic here is as follows: Since the greater always follows the lesser, the time remaining for the lesser sign to rise, plus the rising times of the signs in between, plus the time already elapsed for the greater sign, establishes the total time interval between those two points. || 49 || Now, he explains how to know whether the time calculated from the Ascendant and the Sun falls within the day or the night:

> When the Ascendant is less than the Sun, it is the remainder of the night; when greater than the Sun, it is day.
> When greater than the Sun plus half the zodiac circle, it is after sunset. || 50 ||

When the Ascendant is "less" than the Sun (within a range of three signs), the time determined by the previous method occurs during the remainder of the night <note>the pre-dawn hours</note>. When the Ascendant is "greater" than the Sun (within a range of six signs), the time determined occurs during the day. When the Ascendant is greater than the Sun plus six signs <note>half the zodiac or 180 degrees</note>, the time calculated using the Sun and the Ascendant (plus six signs) occurs after sunset—meaning during the night. By this, the elapsed time of the night is found.

Similarly, at sunset, the time is established as being during the night if the Ascendant is greater than the Sun plus six signs <note>Adding six signs (180 degrees) to the Sun's position gives the point currently setting on the western horizon</note>. # The Treatise of the Sun

> Six thousand and five hundred <note>Sanskrit: *sārdhāni ṣaṭsahasrāṇi*</note> are the leagues <term>yojanas: a traditional Indian measure of distance, roughly 5 to 9 miles</term> of the Sun.
> The diameter of the Moon's orb is four hundred increased by eighty * ॥ 1 ॥
> Multiplied by the true daily motion and divided by the mean daily motion, they become true.

Six thousand with a half—a half-thousand being five hundred—making six thousand five hundred leagues is the diameter <term>viṣkambha: the width or diameter of a circle</term> of the Sun's orb, which is spherical in form. The diameter of the Moon's spherical orb is four hundred plus eighty <note>480 yojanas</note>. These two diameters, when multiplied by the planet's own true motion <note>instantaneous velocity</note> and divided by its own mean motion <note>average velocity</note>, become the "true" or apparent diameters. In this mathematical system, the learned treat the diameter itself as the disk. 

The reasoning here is as follows: because the planet wanders in its mean orbit at a distance equal to the radius <term>trijyā: the sine of the radius</term>, the diameter measured there is the "mean" diameter. Since the mean motion is accepted there with little difference, the proportion is: if this is the diameter for the mean motion, what is it for the true motion? Thus, the disk appears larger when the planet is at its perigee <note>lowest point, moving faster</note> and smaller at its apogee <note>highest point, moving slower</note>, due to the maximum and minimum variations in velocity ॥ 1 ॥ 

Now, while calculating the Sun's disk relative to the Moon's orbit, the author explains the calculation of the diameters in terms of time <note>arc-measure</note> with a verse and a half:

> The Sun's diameter multiplied by its own revolutions and divided by the Moon's revolutions ॥ 2 ॥
> Or multiplied by the Moon's orbit and divided by the Sun's orbit †,
> Is the diameter in the Moon's orbit. Divided by fifteen, these are the minutes of the measure ॥ 3 ॥

The Sun's diameter, the true diameter mentioned previously, is multiplied by its own revolutions <note>the number of times the Sun orbits in an eon</note> and divided by the Moon's revolutions; or alternatively, by the Moon's orbit which will be described...

# Accompanied by the "Illuminator of the Hidden Meaning" <note>The *Gudharthaprakashaka*, a famous 17th-century commentary by Ranganatha on the Surya Siddhanta</note>

When the solar diameter is multiplied by the solar orbit and divided by the lunar orbit (as will be described), the "true" solar diameter as it appears in the celestial sphere occupied by the Moon is determined. Then, the number of <term>yojanas</term> <note>a traditional Indian measure of distance, roughly 8-9 miles</note> of that diameter, when divided by fifteen, results in the measure of the minutes of arc <note>arcminutes</note> of the disc diameters of the Sun and Moon. 

The logic <note>original: "upapatti"</note> here is as follows: If the total minutes in a circle <note>21,600 arcminutes</note> correspond to the total yojanas of the lunar orbit, then how many yojanas are in a single minute? In the lunar orbit, one minute of arc equals fifteen yojanas. Therefore, because the Moon is situated in its own orbit, its true diameter in yojanas divided by fifteen gives the minutes of its disc diameter. Similarly, in the solar orbit, one minute of arc equals two hundred and fifty yojanas; thus, the true solar diameter divided by that number gives its diameter in minutes. 

Because the Sun is seen from a great distance from the world as if it were in the lunar sky—and because it cannot be perceived with a distinct, separate distance by the naked eye—the solar disc diameter is calculated according to the scale of the lunar orbit. This is achieved through a proportion: "If this is the diameter in the solar orbit, what would it be in the lunar orbit?" This is a mathematical abstraction <note>original: "avastubhuta," meaning not physically real but mathematically useful</note> calculated for the sake of computation. In reality, the solar sphere does not reside in the lunar orbit; if it did, it would lead to the absurdity of the Moon having a twelve-minute motion during a solar eclipse. 

Now, the true solar diameter is multiplied by the lunar orbit (defined by the lunar revolutions) and divided by the solar orbit (defined by the solar revolutions). Since the "celestial orbit" <note>khakaksha</note> values in the multiplier and divisor cancel each other out, the result is the diameter multiplied by the solar revolutions and divided by the lunar revolutions. This method was stated first because of its importance, even though the orbits were not previously mentioned. Thus, the solar disc diameter established in the lunar orbit, when divided by fifteen, results in the minutes of the solar disc diameter. This is logically explained. || 3 ||

Next, he establishes the Earth's shadow, which is necessary for eclipses, in two verses:

-> The true lunar motion multiplied by the Earth's diameter and divided by the mean motion, <-
-> results in the "Cone" <note>the length of the shadow cone</note>; the difference between the Earth's diameter and the true solar distance. || 4 || <-

To convert this segment into arc-minutes, the radius <term>Trijya: the sine of the radius</term> is the multiplier and the lunar distance is the divisor. Since the true and mean motions of the Moon act as equal multipliers and divisors, they cancel out. By simplifying the radius and the mean lunar distance, the divisor is separately stated as fifteen. ## Accompanied by the *Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka*.

The difference between the Earth’s diameter <term>Bhūvyāsa</term> and the mean solar disk <term>Madhyārka-bimba</term> in units of distance <term>Yojanas</term> has the Sun’s true motion and mean motion as its multiplier and divisor <note>The ratio of true to mean motion is used to scale the apparent size of the celestial bodies</note>. For the Moon and the Sun, their mean distance-cords <term>Yojana-karṇa</term> are likewise the multiplier and divisor respectively. In that context, for the sake of simplification, the diameters of their disks in *Yojanas* are taken in place of the distance-cord. Although it might seem improper to use the disk diameters since they do not strictly follow the mean distance-cords of the Sun and Moon, the error is accepted because the difference is negligible.

Regarding the diameters of the Moon and Sun: as stated in the "Chapter on the Terrestrial Sphere" <term>Bhūgolādhyāya</term>, the orbit multiplied by the Earth’s radius and divided by the Earth’s circumference gives the distance-cord. This applies even more so to the radius of that orbit. Even there, when taking the true solar disk in *Yojanas*, it is established that the mean solar disk in *Yojanas* is multiplied by the Sun’s true motion and divided by the Sun’s mean motion. 

One should not argue: "By the aforementioned method, the Sun’s true and mean motions are the multiplier and divisor for the *difference* between the Earth’s diameter and the mean solar disk, not just for the disk itself; how then is the Earth’s diameter established as such by the phrase 'the diameter of the earth'?" This is because the Lord <note>Referring to the divine author of the Sūrya Siddhānta</note> has accepted the Earth’s diameter exactly as it stands, due to the very small difference it makes. By the statement "the difference between the Earth’s diameter and the true solar distance," the terms "mean" and "true" apply to both, and because of the proximity to the solar distance, the "trueness" <note>The corrected or instantaneous value</note> of the Earth’s diameter is established in the same manner as the solar disk.

Now, the result obtained from this section, subtracted from the Earth’s diameter, gives the *Yojanas* of the Earth’s shadow <term>Bhūbhā</term>. To convert this into minutes of arc <term>Kalā</term>, the radius <term>Trijyā</term> is the multiplier for the other part of the Earth’s diameter, and the true distance-cord—which is the Moon’s mean distance-cord multiplied by the mean motion and divided by the true motion—is the divisor. Here, by reducing the multiplier and divisor (the radius and the mean distance-cord), the number fifteen remains in the place of the divisor, and the Moon’s true and mean motions act as the multiplier and divisor; thus, the calculation is well-proven. Because the Earth’s shadow follows the form of a needle <note>a cone</note>, the first section is subtracted from the second; it is rightly said that the Earth’s shadow in *Yojanas*, divided by fifteen, results in the value in minutes and so on. If, however, in the phrase "the Sun's disk diminished by the Earth's diameter," one starts from the mean disk—

# The Surya Siddhanta
<note>The Surya Siddhanta is one of the foundational Sanskrit texts of Indian astronomy, dating back to at least the 6th century CE.</note>

### The Treatise on the Sun

Regarding the previous statement: if we first take the <term>apparent solar disk</term><note>The visible size of the sun as seen from Earth</note>, then because the <term>true diameter of the Earth</term><note>original: "mahivyasa"</note> is not yet established, the difference between the Earth's diameter and the <term>true solar distance</term><note>original: "sphutarka-shravana"</note> is taken exactly as heard in the tradition, which is correct. 

However, in that case, the <term>mean and true motions of the Sun</term>—which act as the divisor and multiplier for the solar disk minus the Earth's diameter—should have been mentioned. The Lord <note>referring to the divine author of the text</note> did not mention them because the difference is negligible. One should not argue that the "mean yojanas" <note>a traditional unit of distance, roughly 8-9 miles</note> of the Sun and Moon were used in the calculation rather than their "true distances," and therefore the mean and true motions were omitted as multipliers. Such an argument fails because it would imply the omission of the "needle" <note>the cone of the shadow</note> generated by the Moon's true distance in yojanas. 

Furthermore, one cannot claim that using the Moon's mean distance creates a large error (thus requiring the true distance), while using the Sun's mean distance creates only a small error. If one uses the <term>mean solar disk</term> in yojanas, the <term>true solar distance</term> cannot be logically derived. Nor can it be argued that while each error is small, they combine into a large error, making it necessary to use the Sun's motion in at least one place. There is no logical necessity <note>original: "vinigamana-virahat"</note> for this. 

Previously, the Sun's true and mean motions were the multiplier and divisor for the solar disk alone, not for the Earth's diameter. But in the final calculation, where both are involved, it is more appropriate to use the Sun's motion to distinguish between the "gross" and "precise" values. 

If it is argued that by using the Moon's motion for the first part of the Earth's diameter, the "needle" is explained, and thus for the second part (the true solar disk minus the Earth's diameter), the Sun's motion is implied—this is not correct. In the context of this commentary, there is no authority for assuming the Sun's motion, nor is there a logical occasion for it. Otherwise, one might as well assume the Moon's motion here too. 

By this logic: if the Earth's diameter is calculated by the Moon's mean motion, then what is it by the Moon's true motion? This gives the "true" segment of the Earth's diameter known as the "needle." Then, if the other segment (the true solar disk minus the Earth's diameter) is compared to the Moon's disk, the second true segment is found. The difference between these two true segments...

# Accompanied by the *Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka* <note>The "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings," a famous commentary on the Sūryasiddhānta</note>.

The claim that the Earth's shadow is "clear" <note>term: *spaṣṭa* (clear/true/corrected); refers to the mathematically corrected value of a planet's position or size</note> is dismissed as everything has been properly accounted for. There is no proof for establishing their "clearness" through the two proportions mentioned, nor is there any occasion for such "clearness" to arise. Furthermore, the mean diameters of the Moon and Sun cannot be logically established in that manner. 

However, Jñānarāja Daivajña <note>A prominent 16th-century Indian astronomer</note> stated in the *Siddhāntasundara*: Having realized in his heart that the "clearness" of the Earth's diameter in its conical form <note>term: *sūcī-rūpa* (needle-shaped or conical); refers to the cone of the Earth's shadow</note> was untenable, he took the Earth's diameter as the first segment. Then, by using the proportions of the Sun's corrected diameter minus the Earth's diameter against the mean distance, and by reducing the result by the final difference, he generated the multipliers and divisors for the mean diameter. He accepted both segments. He then calculated: "If the minutes of the Moon's mean distance are equal to the radius, then what are they for these two?" By repeating the result of the proportion and using fifteen as the divisor in place of the standard measure, he declared the difference between them to be the Earth's shadow (*bhūbhā*).

As stated in his text:

> The Moon's diameter, multiplied by the difference between the diameters of the Sun and the Earth, and divided by the Sun's diameter; 
> The Earth's diameter minus that result is the Earth's shadow. 
> That value, divided by one hundred and sixty-one <note>original: *śarendu* (arrows = 5, moon = 1; read right-to-left as 15)</note>, results in the minutes of the shadow.

In this passage, the Sun's diameter is expressed in yojanas <note>A traditional unit of distance, roughly 8-13 kilometers</note> of the corrected solar orb, not the mean yojanas. The commentator Cintāmaṇi <note>Jñānarāja's son and commentator</note> maintains that the multipliers and divisors for the lunar and solar orbs are in mean yojanas, not corrected yojanas. This is because it would otherwise contradict the *Sūryasiddhānta* <note>The "Sun Treatise," the foundational text of Indian astronomy</note>, which serves as the authority. This is stated because even with that logic, the result cannot be established. 

Furthermore, regarding what the commentator Cintāmaṇi said about calculating the mean diameter of the Earth's shadow: "By treating the mean distances themselves as the multipliers and divisors since there is no difference in the result, one obtains the mean diameter. Even if the original author did not say so, one should calculate the 'clearness' by the proportion: 'If this is the result for the difference in mean motions, what is it for the difference in true motions?'" This is not proper, as the Earth's shadow is not actually produced by the influence of the difference in those motions. Otherwise, if it were calculated by the motion...

# The Treatise of the Sun
<note>original: "Surya Siddhanta"</note>

...because the Earth's shadow is calculated from the actual angular diameters of the Sun and Moon <note>literally "the solar and lunar orbs"</note> without modification. That argument is incorrect.

### The true motion of the Moon, multiplied by the Earth's diameter and divided by the mean motion...

Since this is established by the logic stated in the *Treatise of the Sun* and not otherwise specified, we must take the Earth's diameter <term>Bhu-vyasa: the physical diameter of the Earth used as a baseline for calculating the shadow cone</term> as it is, without modification. Enough of this elaborate searching for faults in others' arguments. // 5 //

Now, he describes the characteristics of the two types of eclipses:

## At six signs from the Sun is the Earth's shadow; when the Moon's node is equal to that, or equal to the Sun itself,
## An eclipse occurs, even if the node is a few degrees more or less. // 6 //

The Earth's shadow is located at a distance of six signs <note>180 degrees</note> from the Sun, because it is always in the direction opposite to the Sun. When the Moon's node <term>Pata: the points where the Moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic</term> is equal to that position (the Sun plus six signs), or alternatively, when the Moon's node is equal to the Sun's position, an eclipse of the Moon or Sun respectively occurs. 

Now, one might ask: does an eclipse occur even if they are not exactly equal? To this he says: "a few degrees more or less." Even if the Moon's node is a few degrees greater or less than the Sun (or the Sun plus six signs), an eclipse still takes place. Thus, there is no error. For a lunar eclipse, these degrees are fixed at twelve for certainty. For a solar eclipse, however, it is roughly seven degrees, due to the adjustment for the "sixth part of the degrees of zenith distance" <note>referring to parallax adjustments</note>. 

The reasoning here is as follows: when the Moon's node is equal to either the Sun plus six signs or the Sun alone, there is an absence of celestial latitude <term>Shara: the angular distance of a planet north or south of the ecliptic</term> for the Moon, because it is at the node. At that time, the Moon enters the Earth's shadow, and an eclipse occurs. Similarly, even when latitude exists, if it is less than the "half-sum of the diameters" <term>Manaikya-khanda: the combined radii of the two celestial bodies, the threshold for contact</term>, a portion of the orb will be within the Earth's shadow and an eclipse occurs. In the same way, when latitude is absent or less than the half-sum of the diameters, the lunar orb becomes the coverer of the solar orb; however, in that case, the latitude is adjusted by parallax <note>original: "nati"</note>. Thus, what has been stated is well-reasoned. // 6 //

Now, one might ask: when exactly do these occur? He next describes the timing of these two eclipses...

# Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings" <note>The *Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka*, a famous 17th-century commentary by Raṅganātha on the *Sūrya Siddhānta*</note>

**At the moment of the New Moon's end, the Sun and Moon are equal in signs and other divisions. At the end of the Full Moon, they are equal in degrees and minutes, but separated by half the zodiac.** **(7)**

The Sun and Moon produced at the time of the New Moon's end <note>Sanskrit: *amāvāsyānta*</note> are equal in their components, starting from their zodiac signs. At the end of the Full Moon <note>Sanskrit: *paurṇamāsyante*</note>, the Sun and Moon are equal in degrees and minutes but are separated by six signs <note>180 degrees</note>. Thus, at the end of the New Moon, because the Sun and Moon are in the same position (though one may be above or below the other), a solar eclipse <term>Sūryagrahaṇa: an eclipse of the sun</term> occurs. At the end of the Full Moon, because the Moon and the Earth's shadow are in the same position, a lunar eclipse <term>Candragrahaṇa: an eclipse of the moon</term> occurs. 

By this, it is indicated that in the previous verse, where it mentioned "the Moon's node," one should not take both the Moon and the Moon's node together, as that would make this verse redundant. The logic here is: at the end of the New Moon, there is a conjunction because there is no east-west distance between the Sun and the Moon, making them equal. At the end of the Full Moon, they are equal in degrees etc., but at an interval of six signs because they are separated by half the zodiac circle. **(7)** Now, he explains the calculation of the Sun, Moon, and Moon's node at the end of the lunar phase <note>the *parvan*, or syzygy</note>.

**By the result of the elapsed or remaining hours of the lunar phase, the two [Sun and Moon] become equal in minutes when subtracted or added. The Node at that time is calculated differently.** **(8)**

Those two, the Sun and the Moon—using the hours <note>Sanskrit: *nāḍī*, a unit of 24 minutes</note> of the lunar phase that have either passed or are yet to come from the time the Sun and Moon were calculated—one applies their own "result" <note>the distance traveled based on their specific velocity</note>. 

> The daily motion multiplied by the desired hours and divided by sixty gives the result in minutes and seconds.

This is brought forward from what was stated in the "Chapter on Mean Motion." By subtracting or adding that result according to whether the time is past or future, they become equal in minutes <note>Sanskrit: *samaliptau*</note> at that moment. Although it would be appropriate to say "equal in degrees," the term "equal in minutes" is used to highlight that they have been calculated through their respective velocities and apogees to be perfectly coincident in longitude.

# The Surya Siddhanta
->Page 58<-

The <term>Node</term><note>Sanskrit: *Pāta*; the point where the orbit of a planet or the Moon intersects the ecliptic</note>, when increased or decreased by the result of its own motion—applied in reverse order due to its retrograde nature—becomes the value for that specific time, namely the end of the <term>Lunar Day</term><note>Sanskrit: *Parvānta*; the exact moment of the New Moon or Full Moon</note>. The reasoning for this is found in the verse on "displacement." At the end of the lunar day, because of the difference in degrees, there is an equality in minutes and so forth. Because the Node is subtracted from the full circle <note>360 degrees</note>, its motion is treated as the opposite of the other planets. || 8 ||

Now, the author explains the purpose of the <term>Disks</term><note>Sanskrit: *Bimba*; the visible circular area of the Sun, Moon, or Earth's shadow</note> mentioned previously:

> **The Moon, situated below, acts like a cloud to cover the Sun.**
> **Moving eastward, the Moon enters the Earth's shadow; thus, the shadow becomes its coverer. || 9 ||**

The Moon is the coverer of the solar disk. One might ask: since both are present in the sky, why shouldn't the Sun cover the Moon? To this, the text says: *situated below*. According to the chapter on orbits to be discussed later, the Moon's orbit is below the Sun's orbit; therefore, only the Moon can be the coverer. An object situated above cannot be a coverer, which is why the Sun does not cover the Moon. 

One might then argue that covering cannot occur without being in the same orbit. To this, the text says: *like a cloud*. Just as a cloud situated below covers the Sun, so does the Moon. Moving toward the east, the Moon enters into the Earth's shadow. For this reason, this Earth-shadow becomes the coverer of the Moon. 

The underlying meaning is that in a solar eclipse, the disks of the Sun and Moon are utilized, whereas in a lunar eclipse, the disks of the Moon and the Earth's shadow are utilized. The reasoning is as follows: at the end of the New Moon, the Moon is below the Sun, and thus the Moon covers the Sun. As for Mercury and Venus, they do not act as coverers because their disks are too small. Since there are no planets below the Moon, the Sun's rays—blocked by the Earth at a distance of six signs <note>180 degrees, or directly opposite the Sun</note>—do not fall upon the lunar sphere. Thus, the lusterless Moon enters the Earth's shadow, and the Earth's shadow becomes its coverer. || 9 ||

Now, the author describes the calculation of the <term>Eclipse Magnitude</term><note>Sanskrit: *Grāsa*; literally 'the bite' or the portion of the disk obscured</note>.

<meta>This page continues the technical explanation of eclipse calculations, specifically focusing on the magnitude of the eclipse (obscuration). Institutional stamps from the Ministry of Culture and the Central Secretariat Library are present on the physical folio.</meta>

->Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings" <note>original: "Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka," the name of the commentary</note><-

Subtract the moon’s instantaneous <term>latitude</term> <note>original: "vikṣepa," the angular distance of a celestial body from the ecliptic</note> from half the sum of the diameters of the <term>eclipsed body</term> <note>original: "khādya"</note> and the <term>eclipsing body</term> <note>original: "chādaka"</note>. The remainder is called the "obscured portion" <note>original: "channa"</note>. * || 10 ||

That which is covered is the **eclipsed body**. In a **solar eclipse**, it is the Sun; in a **lunar eclipse**, it is the Moon. That which covers is the **eclipsing body**. In solar and lunar eclipses, these are the Moon and the Earth's shadow, respectively. From half the sum of their previously calculated diameters (in minutes of arc), one should subtract the **latitude** (in minutes, etc.) of the Moon at that moment, calculated as previously described. The remaining value is the measure of the "obscured portion"—the extent of the disk of the eclipsed body that is covered by the eclipsing body. This is called the **magnitude of the eclipse** <note>original: "grāsa-rūpa," literally 'the form of the bite'</note> by those **learned in the principles of eclipses**.

The logic <note>original: "upapatti"</note> here is as follows: At the moment the edges of the eclipsed and eclipsing disks touch (the beginning or end of the eclipse), the distance between the centers of the disks is equal to the sum of their respective <term>radii</term> <note>original: "bimba-khaṇḍa," literally 'disk-parts'</note>. This is derived from the diameter measurements in minutes of arc. For the sake of simplicity and ease of calculation, this is taken as **half the sum** of the diameters. As the eclipsing body enters further, the "bite" (magnitude) increases. Since the two bodies are separated by their latitude at the end of the lunar month or full moon, if the latitude is less than the sum of the radii, the disks overlap. That difference is the **magnitude of the eclipse**. || 10 ||

Next, the author explains how to determine if an eclipse is total, partial, or if no eclipse occurs at all:

If that [obscured portion] is greater than the body to be eclipsed, the eclipse is total; otherwise, it is partial. If the **latitude** is greater than half the sum of the diameters, an **occurrence of an eclipse** <note>original: "grāsa-sambhava"</note> is not possible. || 11 ||

If that **measured obscuration** is greater than the diameter of the body to be eclipsed, then for that reason, the **eclipse** is "entire" or total.

† <margin>An alternative reading for "in that" is "greater than the measure of the eclipsed body."</margin>

# The Treatise of the Sun
<note>original: "Surya Siddhanta"</note>

Otherwise, if the amount of the eclipse <note>the portion of the disk covered</note> is less than the diameter of the body being eclipsed, the eclipse will be partial. If the latitude <note>the angular distance of the moon from the ecliptic</note> is greater than the sum of the radii of the two bodies, an eclipse is impossible; no eclipse will occur. Here is the proof: if the eclipse amount is greater than the body being eclipsed, there is a total eclipse; if less, it is partial. If the latitude exceeds the sum of the radii, the disks cannot touch, resulting in an absence of an eclipse. || 11 ||

Now, he describes the half-duration and the half-duration of total obscuration in two verses:

->The sum and the difference of the diameters of the eclipsed and eclipsing bodies are each halved.<-
->From the squares of these two, subtract the square of the latitude; the square roots of the remainders, || 12 ||<-
->multiplied by sixty and divided by the difference between the daily motions of the Sun and Moon,<-
->give the results in minutes of time for the half-duration and half-total-obscuration respectively. || 13 ||<-

The sum and the difference of the measures of the eclipsed and eclipsing bodies should be halved and placed in separate locations. These are necessary for further calculations should errors arise in subsequent steps. From the squares of these—the square of half the sum and the square of half the difference—subtract the square of the latitude. Take the square roots of both results, multiply them by sixty, and divide by the difference in the velocities <note>daily motion</note> of the Sun and Moon in minutes. The results obtained from the sum and difference respectively are the <term>Half-Duration</term> <note>Sthityardha: half the time from first contact to last contact</note> and the <term>Half-Total-Obscuration</term> <note>Vimardardha: half the time the body is completely covered</note> in units of time <note>Ghatis/Nadikas</note>.

Here is the proof: The time from the start of the eclipse to the end is called the <term>Duration</term> <note>Sthiti</note>. One half of it is from the start to the middle of the eclipse, and the other half is from the middle to the end. At the moment the edges of the disks touch, the <term>Sum of the Radii</term> <note>Manaikyakhanda</note> is the hypotenuse, the latitude at the time of contact or separation is the upright side, and the distance between the tip of that latitude and the tip of the latitude at the middle of the eclipse is the base <note>the horizontal side of the right-angled triangle</note>. This geometric figure allows for the calculation of that segment. Similarly, in a total eclipse, the time between the immersion and the emergence is the "crushing" <note>total obscuration</note>; therein...

# Accompanied by the *Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka* <note>The "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings," a famous commentary by Raṅganātha on the Sūrya Siddhānta</note>

From the moment of the middle of the eclipse <note>the maximum point of obscuration</note>, during the interval of the duration of total darkness <term>sammīlana-unmīlana-kālāvadhi-khaṇḍe: the period between the start of total obscuration and the start of the moon's reappearance</term>, the distance between the centers of the eclipsed body <note>the Moon</note> and the eclipsing body <note>the Earth's shadow or the Moon in a solar eclipse</note> is the hypotenuse, which is equal to the difference of the semi-diameters. The instantaneous latitude <note>celestial latitude</note> is the base of the triangle. The difference between the squares of these two is the square of the upright side, which represents the east-west distance on the circle of deflection. This is the geometric figure.

"Immersion" <term>sammīlana</term> is the completion of the covering of the eclipsed disk. "Emersion" <term>unmīlana</term> is the beginning of the exit of the fully covered disk from the eclipsing body. In those instances, the latitude at the middle of the eclipse is taken as an approximation for the times of contact, separation, immersion, and emersion. The statement in the previous verse—that the square root of the difference between the squares of the hypotenuse and the base is the upright—is thus proven.

Since the middle of the eclipse occurs when there is no east-west distance between the centers of the two disks, the rule of proportion is applied: if sixty ghatis <note>a ghati is 24 minutes</note> correspond to the difference in motion, then how much time corresponds to the minutes of the calculated upright side? This gives the half-duration of the eclipse. In a lunar eclipse, because the Earth's shadow follows the Sun's motion, the Sun's motion is used; this proves what was stated in the second verse. // 13 //

Now, he explains in two verses that the half-duration of the eclipse and the half-duration of total darkness must be calculated repeatedly <note>through iteration to achieve precision</note>.

> The motions [of the planets] multiplied by the half-duration in ghatis and divided by sixty,
> result in minutes and so forth. These should be subtracted for the [start of] the eclipse and added for the separation, repeatedly. // 14 //
> With the latitudes [calculated from those positions], the half-duration of the eclipse and the half-duration of total darkness
> should be calculated repeatedly. Otherwise, for the node, the resulting minutes should be applied inversely. // 15 //

The motions of the Sun, Moon, and the nodes, multiplied by the ghatis of the half-duration and divided by sixty, result in minutes. For the sake of the half-duration of contact, these are subtracted from the Sun and Moon at the start of the eclipse; for the sake of the half-duration of separation, they are added at the end. In the case of the Moon's node, the result in minutes derived from the half-duration is applied inversely <note>because the nodes move in retrograde/reverse direction</note>.

# The Surya Siddhanta

->The Treatise of the Sun<-

If the result produced by one's own calculation is otherwise <note>meaning, if it differs from the observed reality</note> or reversed, it should be added for the cause of the **half-duration of the first contact** <term>Sparsha-sthyardha: the time from the start of the eclipse to the maximum obscuration</term> and subtracted for the cause of the **half-duration of the release** <term>Moksha-sthyardha: the time from maximum obscuration to the end of the eclipse</term>. This is done by means of their respective "deflections" <note>latitudes</note>, which are the minutes of the arc of the latitude <term>Shara-kala</term> brought forth from the positions of the Moon and its Node at those specific times. The plural "deflections" is used because of the many minutes involved; it refers to the two specific deflections <note>at contact and release</note>.

The "half-duration" <term>Sthiti-dala</term> must be calculated repeatedly. Here, the word "repeatedly" is applied once to the half-duration of the contact and a second time to the half-duration of the release. Therefore, the half-duration of the contact is to be perfected by the latitude derived from the Moon and its Node as calculated for the time of contact, using the previously mentioned method. Similarly, the half-duration of the release is to be calculated by the latitude derived from the Moon and its Node at the time of release.

Both of these must be done repeatedly <note>iteratively</note>. By moving the middle positions of the Moon and its Node using the calculated half-duration of contact, and then finding the latitude again, one refines the half-duration of contact until there is no further difference <note>until the calculation converges</note>. In the same way, by moving the middle positions of the Moon and its Node using the calculated half-duration of release, and finding the latitude again, one refines the half-duration of release until no difference remains.

Now, one might ask: since the method for the half-duration of the eclipse and the **half-duration of total obscuration** <term>Vimardhardha</term> is said to be the same, why was the repeated calculation for the half-duration of total obscuration not explicitly mentioned? To this, the text says: "The half-duration of total obscuration." Just as with the calculation for the half-duration of contact and release, the half-duration of the start of totality and the half-duration of the end of totality must be calculated repeatedly until they are refined.

Just as the "minutes of the half-duration" were taken, here the minutes of the half-duration of total obscuration are taken to find the start and end of totality. Through this repeated process for each, the true half-durations of the start and end of totality are established. The mathematical proof is as follows: the previously described geometric figure depends on the latitudes at the times of contact, release, immersion, and emergence. Since these are unknown at the start, the "rough" half-duration and half-totality are first produced by taking the latitude from the middle of the eclipse...

### Accompanied by the *Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka* <note>The "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings," a famous commentary by Raṅganātha on the Sūrya Siddhānta.</note>

Because the occurrence of these [eclipses] happens between the preceding and succeeding times, the <term>latitude</term> <note>original: "vikṣepa"; the angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the ecliptic</note> calculated from the moon and its <term>node</term> <note>original: "pāta"; the point where the moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic</note> moving at that time is instantaneous but approximate. This is because it is derived from an approximate <term>half-duration</term> <note>original: "sthityardha"; half the total time from the start to the end of an eclipse</note>. Therefore, the half-duration brought forth from this, though finer than the previous calculation, is still considered approximate; thus, it must be calculated repeatedly to achieve precision. It should be understood that the half-duration represents the time from the first contact to the middle, or from the middle to the end, because the "touching" and "releasing" of the sky <note>the celestial bodies</note> occurs at the moments of immersion and emersion. || 15 || Now, he describes the times for the middle of the eclipse, the first contact, and the final separation.

->**At the end of the true lunar day, one should declare the middle of the eclipse.**<-
->**Subtracting the half-duration minutes gives the start; adding them gives the end. || 16 ||**<-

At the end of the <term>true lunar day</term> <note>original: "sphuṭa-tithi"; the precise moment when the sun and moon are in opposition or conjunction</note>—the word "but" <note>original: "tu"</note> is used to exclude the times before or after it—one should state the middle of the eclipse, which is the completion of the maximum obscuration. To prevent the confusion of some who might think this occurs at the end of the *mean* lunar day <note>calculated from average speeds</note>, the word "true" is used. The "grasping" or first contact <note>original: "grāsa"</note> occurs at the end of the lunar day minus the half-duration minutes. The "release" or separation <note>original: "mokṣa"</note> occurs at the end of the lunar day plus the half-duration minutes. The word "but" serves to establish the specific rule that the times of contact and separation are derived from the half-duration.

The reasoning here is as follows: At the end of the lunar day, there is no longitudinal difference between the eclipsed body and the eclipsing body <note>original: "chādya-chādaka"</note>. The contact of the disks at that union is greater than at the preceding or succeeding times; therefore, this is the time of the middle of the eclipse. However, some say:

> The end of the phase is indeed calculated from the distance between the marks of the Sun and Moon;
> But the meeting of the disks does not happen exactly then, because the Moon stays at the end of its latitude.
> Therefore, at the end of the lunar day brought forth from the Moon refined by the <term>ecliptic deviation</term> <note>original: "āyana-dṛṣṭi"; a correction for the tilt of the Earth's axis</note>,
> The union of the disks occurs—how is it that the ancients did not know this? We do not know.

## The Treatise of the Sun

By this reasoning, some scholars here dispute the <term>middle of the eclipse</term><note>Sanskrit: madhyagrahanam; the moment of maximum obscuration</note>. That is not correct. In the absence of an east-west difference, and because a conjunction exists, the middle of the eclipse is appropriate right there at the north-south difference of the two <term>Kadamba lines</term><note>The vertical lines passing through the poles of the ecliptic</note>. Otherwise, if one accepts a conjunction on the polar axis or the prime vertical, there would be a failure of logical consistency. The conjunction of the two planets as they are found is accepted only via the Kadamba line. The "visibility operation" is taught for the sake of visual conviction. Because the two eclipses are inherently visible to the eye, and because of the non-visibility of the two planets <insert>during the eclipse</insert>, and so forth—this is the summary. The <term>first contact</term><note>Sanskrit: sparsha; the beginning of the eclipse</note> occurs at the time of the middle of the eclipse minus the half-duration of the eclipse in <term>ghatis</term><note>A unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note>. The <term>release</term><note>Sanskrit: moksha; the end of the eclipse</note> occurs at the subsequent time by adding the half-duration of the release. This is established because the two half-durations represent the interval from the middle. || 16 ||

Now, he describes the times of <term>total immersion</term><note>Sanskrit: nimilana; the start of totality</note> and <term>emergence</term><note>Sanskrit: unmilana; the end of totality</note> in the case of a total eclipse.

->In the same manner, subtracted and added by the half-duration of total obscuration,<-
->Are the two called immersion and emergence in a total eclipse. || 17 ||<-

In a total eclipse, it is "in the same manner." This means just as the first contact and release occur at the end of the lunar day <note>tithi</note> when modified by the half-duration. The word "exactly" <note>original: "eva"</note> excludes any other method. By the half-duration of the immersion and the half-duration of the emergence, respectively subtracted from and added to the end of the lunar day, the moments named immersion and emergence occur. The logic here: since the half-duration of obscuration <note>Sanskrit: mardardha</note> is the interval from the middle time, immersion and emergence occur respectively when that duration is subtracted or added, but only in a total eclipse. In a partial eclipse, these do not exist because the very nature of totality is contradicted. || 17 || Now, he describes the calculation of the <term>perpendicular arc</term><note>Sanskrit: kotiliptika</note> to find the amount of obscuration at a desired time.

->By the half-duration minus the desired time, for the Sun and Moon,<-
->One should multiply the difference in their daily motions; the result divided by sixty is the perpendicular arc in minutes. || 18 ||<-

# Accompanied by the *Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka* <note>The "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings," a famous 16th-century commentary by Raṅganātha on the Sūrya Siddhānta.</note>

One should multiply the difference in motion between the Sun and the Moon (expressed in minutes of arc) by the desired time units <note>ghatikās; 1 ghatikā = 24 minutes</note> elapsed since the beginning of the eclipse, provided these are not greater than the half-duration of the contact. The logic here is as follows: At the desired time, the distance between the centers of the eclipsed and eclipsing bodies is the hypotenuse; the celestial latitude at that time is the "arm" <note>bhuja; the side opposite the angle</note>; and the distance between the tip of the latitude at that time and the tip of the latitude at the middle of the eclipse along the circle of latitude is the "base." If one objects to this, we say no: the minutes derived from the half-duration of contact minus the desired time units are established as the "base." This is because the half-duration units were previously established from the base at the time of contact. || 18 ||

Now, he describes a specific rule regarding solar eclipses:

-> In an eclipse of the Sun, the minutes of the base-arc are multiplied by the mean half-duration, <-
-> and divided by the corrected half-duration; these are known by the wise as the corrected base-minutes. || 19 || <-

In a solar eclipse, the minutes of the base-arc calculated in the manner previously described—which are derived from the corrected half-duration of the solar eclipse—are multiplied by the "mean half-duration" <note>the duration calculated from the corrected latitude alone, without parallax</note> and divided by the "corrected half-duration" <note>the duration as modified by parallax, as taught in the chapter on solar eclipses</note>. The result is the corrected base-minutes, according to those who know the truth of solar eclipses. 

The logic here is: In a solar eclipse, the interval between the middle of the eclipse and either the contact or the separation is the half-duration. Because that duration is adjusted by the sum or difference of the parallax in longitude <term>lambana; the apparent shift in position due to the observer's location on Earth</term>, the base-minutes derived in the usual way correspond to the corrected half-duration. However, the required minutes must correspond to the half-duration produced by the corrected latitude. This is because the geometric figure related to the "base" exists within the field of the half-duration. Since the corrected half-duration <note>which includes parallax</note> does not arise from that specific geometric field, a correction is necessary. Otherwise, there would be no need to mention the adjustment of the latitude-derived half-duration by the parallax. Therefore, these values arrived at via the corrected half-duration...
