# Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings"
<note>original: "Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka," a famous commentary by Raṅganātha</note>

The degrees of deflection <term>valanāṃśa; the angle between the ecliptic and the prime vertical</term> are the distance by which the east-west directions of the ecliptic <term>krāntivṛtta</term> are turned toward the north or south from the east-west directions of the prime vertical <term>samavṛtta</term>. To calculate this, one first finds the "latitudinal deflection" <term>akṣavalana</term>, which is the distance by which the directions of the celestial equator <term>viṣuvadvṛtta</term> are turned from the directions of the prime vertical toward the north or south.

To explain: Consider a circle passing through the poles of the prime vertical and the position of the planet <insert>the planet's vertical circle</insert>. The distance between the east points of these two circles <note>the prime vertical and the equator</note> at a distance of ninety degrees from where they intersect is the deflection. This distance is the same for the other directions as well. When the planet is in the eastern hemisphere <term>pūrvakapāla</term>, the east point of the equator is north of the east point of the prime vertical; therefore, the deflection is north. When in the western hemisphere, the east point of the equator is south of the east point of the prime vertical; therefore, it is south.

When the planet is on the horizon, that distance is equal to the degrees of latitude <term>akṣāṃśa</term>. When the planet is on the meridian <term>yāmyottaravṛtta</term>, there is no such distance. Therefore, the rule is established by proportion: if for a radius <term>trijyā</term> the sine of the latitude is the maximum deflection, then for the sine of the hour angle <term>natajyā</term>, what will it be? The resulting arc of the sine is the latitudinal deflection.

The second component is the "solstitial deflection" <term>āyana valana</term>, which is the distance by which the directions of the ecliptic are turned from the directions of the equator toward the north or south. To explain: Consider a circle passing through the celestial poles and the position of the planet. The distance between the east point of the equator and the east point of the ecliptic (which is three signs or 90 degrees away from the planet's position) is the solstitial deflection. This distance is the same for the other directions. It is north when the planet is in the northern transit <term>uttarāyaṇa</term> and south when in the southern transit <term>dakṣiṇāyana</term>.

This deflection is zero at the solstices <note>literally "at the end of the declination"</note> and equal to the maximum declination at the equinoxes <term>golasandhi</term>. Thus, it is correctly established that the deflection is derived from the declination of the planet's longitude plus three signs <note>90 degrees</note>. When both deflections are in the same direction, the "clear deflection" <term>sphuṭavalana</term>—representing the total shift of the ecliptic's east from the prime vertical's east—is their sum...

Now, he explains the conversion of the measurements of the celestial disks, latitudes, and so on, which are in minutes of arc <note>original: "kala"</note>, into fingers <note>original: "angulas"</note>.

->Add half of the day's duration to the altitude; divide by half the day's duration.<-
->By that result, divide the measures of latitude and the rest; these then become their values in fingers.<- || 26 ||

"Half of the day's duration" <note>original: "dinamanadhyardham"</note> means the half plus its own half <note>i.e., 1.5 times the half-day</note>. This is added to the "altitude" <note>the height of the planet above the horizon</note> in ghatis <note>a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> at the desired time, and divided by the half-day. The word "tu" <note>a Sanskrit particle used here for emphasis</note> implies that the altitude and day-length of the specific planet being calculated should be taken. The measures of the disk, latitude, and so on—which were previously stated in minutes of arc—as well as the magnitude of the eclipse <note>original: "grasa"</note>, should be divided. By the force of the word "tu," the results of these divisions become the values of those minutes in "fingers" <note>angulas</note>.

Here is the rationale <note>original: "upapatti"</note>: At the time of sunrise or sunset, because the rays of the celestial disk are obstructed by the Earth's sphere, the few rays that remain high are unable to strike the eye with full force; thus, the disk appears larger, like a physical body. In that state, a "finger" of the disk is measured at a rate of three minutes per finger. However, when the planet is at the zenith <note>directly overhead</note>, because all the rays of the disk are unobstructed and strike the eye directly, the disk appears smaller. In that state, a "finger" of the disk is measured at a rate of four minutes per finger. Since there is no gnomon shadow <note>original: "shanku"</note> at sunrise/sunset, and at the zenith it is equal to the radius...

When the sine-equivalent gnomon <note>original: "jyātulyaśaṅkau"; the gnomon is a vertical rod used to measure shadows</note> is at the time of rising, an increase of one digit <term>angula: a traditional unit of length, roughly a finger-breadth</term> is obtained for every three arc-minutes <term>kalā: a unit of angular measurement, 1/60th of a degree</term>. > plus two and a half, shall be the arc-minutes of the digit.

In this context, the Lord <note>referring to the divine origin of the Surya Siddhanta</note>, out of compassion for the world and because the difference is slight, accepted that one digit consists of four arc-minutes even at midday. The increase is desired at the time of maximum elevation (noon); therefore, by the proportion—"if this is the increase at the time of half-day, what is it at the desired time of elevation?"—the result added to three gives the arc-minutes of one digit at the desired time. Since the elapsed time of elevation divided by the half-day is the result, and by adding them with a common denominator, it is established that three times the half-day (which is the same as one and a half times the full day-length) plus the elapsed time of elevation, all divided by the half-day, [gives the value]. Then, the rule for converting arc-minutes into digits by the proportion—"if these many arc-minutes make one digit, what do the desired arc-minutes make?"—is proven. || 26 ||

# The Surya Siddhanta

Now, the chapter on the calculation of solar eclipses is explained. In this section, the author introduces the specific factors that distinguish a solar eclipse from a lunar eclipse. Since these factors arise from specific positional rules, he identifies them by describing the specific circumstances under which they do not occur.

->When the Sun is equal to the meridian ecliptic point, parallax in longitude does not occur.<-
->When the latitude of the observer and the declination of the meridian ecliptic point are equal, parallax in latitude also does not occur. || 1 ||<-

When the Sun, at the moment of the new moon's end, is equal to the **meridian ecliptic point** <note>Sanskrit: *madhyalagna*; the point of the ecliptic currently crossing the local meridian</note>. This point is defined in the chapter on the "Three Problems" <note>The *Triprasna* chapter, dealing with time, place, and direction</note> as the ecliptic point on the upper meridian. The result of this equality is that it is mid-day. **Parallax in longitude** <note>Sanskrit: *harija* or *lambana*; literally "born of the horizon," referring to the apparent shift in position due to the observer's location on Earth's surface</note> does not arise here. The term *harija* (horizon-born) is used for parallax because it originates from the observer's position on the Earth's surface relative to the horizon. The meaning is that in this position, there is an absence of parallax.

Now, one might argue that the Lord <note>The divine source of the *Surya Siddhanta*</note>, in His mercy, should have simply said "at mid-day" rather than using the indirect phrasing "equal to the meridian ecliptic point." However, considering the true meaning of the subsequent text, the absence of parallax does not always hold true exactly at mid-day <note>solar noon</note>. Therefore, disregarding the common traditional interpretation, the essential meaning is explained: it refers to the point midway between the rising horizon and the setting horizon on the ecliptic. This means the **nonagesimal** <note>Sanskrit: *tribhonalagna*; the point 90 degrees behind the ascendant</note>. The application is similar to the mid-day calculation. When the Sun is at that point, there is an absence of parallax.

As **Bhaskaracharya** <note>A famous 12th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note> clearly stated:

->First, having determined the ascendant at the end of the new moon, there is no parallax in longitude when the Sun is equal to the nonagesimal. When the Sun is less than or greater than that point, parallax occurs, and it should be known as positive or negative respectively.<-

Next, he describes the position where there is an absence of **parallax in latitude** <note>Sanskrit: *nati*; the north-south shift of the celestial body</note>.

# With the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings" commentary.

Regarding the phrase "In this context" and so forth: When the degrees of northern latitude are equal to the degrees of declination of the meridian ecliptic point <note>the *madhyalagna*, or the point of the ecliptic currently crossing the observer's meridian</note>. Here, by the term "meridian ecliptic point," one should understand either the cusp of the tenth house or the point of the ecliptic on the meridian; in both cases, there is no error. When these two are equal, the deflection <term>nati: the latitudinal component of parallax</term> is zero. By the use of the word "also," it is implied that this is a possibility—meaning, it is not an impossibility. However, the word "also" does not imply that parallax <term>lambana: the difference in apparent position due to the observer's location on the Earth's surface</term> is absent there as well. Even if the northern declination and latitude are equal, if the Sun is not equal to the meridian ecliptic point, parallax would still occur.

Here is the rationale: At the moment of the end of the new moon <note>the conjunction</note>, the Sun and Moon are at the same longitude. At that time, if the Moon has no latitude <note>is exactly on the ecliptic</note>, a line drawn from the center of the Earth to the Sun's position will certainly touch the Moon; thus, from the Earth's center, the Moon can act as the coverer and the Sun as the covered. However, because humans do not reside there but live on the Earth's surface, a line drawn from the Earth's surface toward the Sun does not necessarily touch the Moon. Rather, on the sphere where the Moon resides, it touches a point above the actual mark of the Moon. When the Moon arrives at that specific point, then for an observer on the Earth's surface, the Moon becomes the coverer of the Sun. 

But when the Sun is at the zenith, the line from the Earth's center and the line from the Earth's surface passing through the Sun are one and the same as they touch the Moon; therefore, at the end of the new moon, the Moon becomes the coverer even from the Earth's surface. This is precisely why parallax is defined as the interval between the lines from the Earth's center and the Earth's surface. This occurs because the Moon's mark is "dropped" <note>displaced</note> on the celestial sphere of the Moon's position relative to the surface-line passing through the Sun, or due to the Moon's actual latitude. This is why the teacher Bhaskaracharya <note>the famous 12th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note> said:

> "Because of the unity of the lines from the eye and the Earth's center, there is no parallax at the zenith."

Furthermore, on the sphere of the Moon's position, the degrees on the Moon's vertical circle where the Earth-surface line passing through the Sun touches above the Moon's mark—that parallax occurs on the ecliptic when it coincides with the vertical circle. But when the ecliptic is different from the vertical circle, then the point where the Earth-surface line touches the Moon's vertical circle above the Moon...

It cites the authority of Bhaskaracharya to explain why parallax disappears at the highest point of the sky.</summary>

# The Surya Siddhanta
<note>original: "सूर्यसिद्धान्तः" - The "Sun Precept," the foundational treatise of Indian astronomy.</note>

In that context, one must consider the secondary circle passing through the poles of the ecliptic <term>Kadamba-prota-vritta</term> <note>The circle passing through the ecliptic poles, used to measure celestial latitude</note> which represents the north-south direction relative to the lunar sphere. The distance on the ecliptic <term>Kranti-vritta</term> <note>The "Circle of Change," or the ecliptic</note> where it meets the lunar position—specifically the east-west interval between the true and apparent positions of the Moon—is defined as the base <term>Koti</term> of the triangle, representing the minutes of the **true longitude parallax** <term>Sphuta-lambana</term>.

Because the Moon moves according to the ecliptic, the north-south interval in minutes between the ecliptic and the vertical circle <term>Drig-vritta</term> <note>The altitude circle or vertical circle passing through the zenith</note> is the perpendicular <term>Bhuja</term>, known as the **latitude parallax** <term>Nati</term>. The distance between the lines of sight from the Earth's center and its surface, measured in minutes upon the vertical circle, is the hypotenuse <term>Karna</term>, known as the **total parallax** <term>Drig-lambana</term>.

If the vertical circle coincides with the circle passing through the ecliptic poles, there is no interval on the ecliptic, and thus **longitude parallax is absent**. In this case, the total parallax becomes identical to the latitude parallax. Conversely, if the ecliptic itself acts as the vertical circle, the total parallax exists entirely upon the ecliptic as longitude parallax, and **latitude parallax is absent**.

Furthermore, when the vertical circle aligns with the ecliptic pole circle, the Sun is at the **nonagesimal point** <term>Tribhona-lagna</term> <note>The point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the rising point (ascendant); the highest point of the ecliptic</note>. This is because that circle is perpendicular to the ecliptic and sits exactly between the rising and setting points, being three signs <note>90 degrees</note> distant from the ascendant.

One should not accept the prime vertical <term>Sama-prota-vritta</term> for calculating the north-south interval. If one did, it would imply that parallax disappears when the Sun is at the **meridian** <term>Dashama-bhava</term> <note>The 10th house or midheaven</note>, which is incorrect. Since the ecliptic is a celestial sphere circle and the prime vertical is a local directional circle, they lack that specific relationship.

For this reason, the Lord <note>The divine source of the Surya Siddhanta</note>, who is all-knowing, has established the **ecliptic zenith distance** <term>Drikkshepa</term> specifically at the nonagesimal point within the ecliptic pole circle to calculate the latitude parallax. When there is no ecliptic zenith distance, the nonagesimal point is at the **zenith** <term>Khamadhya</term> <note>The point directly overhead</note>; at that moment, it coincides with the meridian, and because there are no degrees of zenith distance, there is no ecliptic zenith distance.

In cases where there is a very small northern declination, for the sake of ease in calculation, some may roughly accept the zenith distance and the sine of the zenith distance of the **meridian** <term>Dashama-bhava</term> to calculate the ecliptic zenith distance and the motion-parallax. The Lord mentions this immediately after, but only for convenience, not as the true physical reality. With great effort...

Instead, it is understood to be established by the measure of a distinct circle's radius, which takes the form of the square root of the square of the radius diminished by the square of the "result." The <term>Drkksepa</term><note>The sine of the zenith distance of the highest point of the ecliptic (the Vitribha-lagna).</note>, when converted to the radius of the circle by being tied to the radius of the day-circle, represents the true <term>Drkksepa</term> of the point ninety degrees behind the rising sign. Some say that in the absence of the "rising sine," these two are the true values. That is not correct; since this is established by the aforementioned method, stating it otherwise is useless. 

The rationale here is as follows: because the point ninety degrees behind the rising sign is close to the tenth house, and the tenth house stays on the meridian circle, one may—for the sake of brevity—imagine the tenth house itself to be that ninety-degree point. Thus, the sine of its zenith distance (the "middle sine") becomes the <term>Drkksepa</term>, and the sine of its altitude (the "gnomon") becomes the <term>Drk-gati</term>. This is very approximate. ->The sines of the zenith distance and altitude<-

## The Surya Siddhanta

It is established by the method of calculating parallax <note>original: "lambana-nayana-prakāreṇa"</note> that the dividend should be divided by the square of the radius <term>Trijyā: the radius of a circle used in trigonometric calculations, typically 3438 minutes of arc</term>. In that context, by simplifying the multiplier and the divisor (which are four times the square of the radius), the square of the radius of a single sign <note>30 degrees</note> is established in the place of the divisor. Here too, the multiplier and divisor are the "driggati" <term>Driggati: the sine of the altitude of the highest point of the ecliptic</term> and the square of the radius; by simplifying with the multiplier, the divisor is established as the square of the sine, and so on. This is because the divisor is referred to as the "cheda." Therefore, the statement "when the Sun is at the meridian" <note>original: "madhyalagne'rke"</note> is justified.

The phrase "parallax of the Sun and Moon" is used to indicate that the movement of both by the ghatis <term>Ghati: a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</term> of parallax is necessary in the forthcoming calculations. Otherwise, at the end of the new moon <note>conjunction</note>, because the Moon's shadow is displaced from the line connecting the Earth's surface and the Sun's position by those ghatis of the lunar orbit, the statement regarding both would be inconsistent. 

Because there is no parallax when the Sun is at the "tribhonalagna" <term>Tribhonalagna: the nonagesimal, or the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the rising point</term>, it is said that parallax occurs in the eastern and western divisions when the Sun is present there; thus the terms "east" and "west" were used. 

Here, the following should be considered: In the calculation of parallax, if "madhyalagna" <note>literally 'middle sign'</note> is taken to mean the "tribhonalagna" <note>nonagesimal</note>, the divisor is accurate if using the previously calculated precise "driggati," but inaccurate if using the gross "driggati" derived from zenith distance <note>natāṃśa</note>. Conversely, if "madhyalagna" is taken to mean the "tenth house" <note>meridian ecliptic point</note>, the opposite is true. 

By this, the traditional view—that "madhyalagna" means the tenth house, where parallax is precise through laboriously calculated "driggati" and gross through zenith distance—is refuted. This is due to a lack of logical proof. Furthermore, even if the tenth house is taken as the "madhyalagna" here, since the demonstration exists through spherical geometry <note>gola-yukti</note>, how can the word "madhyalagna" used by the Sun <note>the divine author</note>, which usually signifies the universally accepted tenth house, be forcibly interpreted as the nonagesimal?

->The sines of the base and perpendicular of the zenith distance are the distinct "drikkshepa" and "driggati."<-

It might be argued that by using the word "distinct" <note>sphuṭe</note> here, the Lord's intention was made clear. Nevertheless, the mention of "drikkshepa" <term>Drikkshepa: the sine of the zenith distance of the nonagesimal</term> achieved through great effort remains within the Lord's intention regarding the three—

## Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings" <note>Sanskrit: Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka, a famous commentary on the Sūrya Siddhānta</note>

The use of the nonagesimal <term>tribhonalagna: the point 90 degrees behind the rising sign</term> is explained here. Otherwise, the effort spent calculating the ecliptic zenith <term>dr̥kkṣepa: the sine of the zenith distance of the nonagesimal</term> would be rendered useless; the wise should observe this carefully, so enough of this elaboration. || 8 || Now, he speaks regarding the knowledge of the time of the middle of the eclipse, the application of the parallax correction to the lunar day's end <note>tithyanta: the moment of the New Moon</note>, and how this must be done repeatedly.

---

-> When the Sun is greater than the meridian-point <note>madhyalagna: here referring to the nonagesimal</note>, one should subtract the parallax from the end of the lunar day. When it is less, add it. This process should be done repeatedly until all values become stationary. || 9 || <-

---

When the Sun is greater than the nonagesimal point, one should subtract the parallax—calculated from the time of the end of the lunar day—from that same end-time. When the Sun is less than the nonagesimal, the parallax should be added to the end-time of the lunar day. This mathematical operation must be performed repeatedly <note>asakr̥t: an iterative process used in Indian astronomy to reach a precise value</note>. 

The meaning is this: the Sun at the end of the lunar day is moved forward or backward in time by the hours of parallax. The Sun then exists at the parallax-adjusted end of the lunar day. From that adjusted time, one must again calculate the ascendant and the tenth house <note>the meridian</note> and find the parallax as previously described. This parallax, too, is applied to the original end-time. This continues until the parallax is applied again and again. He states the limit of the calculation: "until." This means until all the mathematics, such as the parallax, becomes stationary through the cycles of change. This means until there is no further difference <note>convergence</note>.

Here is the rationale <term>upapatti: proof or demonstration</term>: At the end of the New Moon, because the Moon is suspended below the line from the Earth's surface to the Sun, when the Sun is less than the nonagesimal, the conjunction—defined as being on the same line—occurs after the calculated end of the New Moon because there is no east-west difference on the ecliptic. This is because the fast-moving Moon is behind the slow-moving Sun. When the Sun is greater, the Moon is ahead...

# The Surya Siddhanta
<note>The Surya Siddhanta is one of the most important early Sanskrit texts on Indian astronomy, dating in its current form to approximately the 4th-5th century CE.</note>

In reality, the alignment <note>conjunction</note> occurs earlier than the end of the lunar day <term>amavasya</term> due to the time of parallax <term>lambana</term>. Therefore, the end of the lunar day, when adjusted by parallax, should be the time of the middle of the eclipse, because the moment of alignment is the middle of the eclipse. However, during that parallax interval, the Sun also moves along the ecliptic. Consequently, at the time of the lunar day's end adjusted by parallax, the Moon would still appear shifted <note>parallactic displacement</note> from the line connecting the Earth's surface to the Sun. Thus, the true middle of the eclipse is not yet established.

The Sun does not remain stationary during the Moon's parallax interval—whether the parallax is added or subtracted—so that their alignment would be perfectly consistent. Therefore, from that calculated time, one must calculate the instantaneous parallax again and apply it once more to the end of the lunar day. This would be the middle time. Yet, even at that parallax-adjusted end of the lunar day, the two bodies may not be perfectly on the line of sight from the Earth's surface; thus, parallax must be calculated yet again.

The end of the lunar day adjusted by that result is the middle of the eclipse. By this iterative process <term>asakrit-vidhi</term>, when the newly calculated parallax becomes equal to the previously calculated parallax, then necessarily, at that parallax-adjusted time, the two bodies are aligned on the line of sight from the Earth's surface. This is because, at that moment, there is no further discrepancy between the Moon and the line from the observer to the Sun, resulting in a parallax value identical to the one previously obtained. Otherwise, the parallax values would not match. Therefore, the middle time must be calculated repeatedly until the difference disappears; this explains the method of "middle parallax" and so forth. || 8 ||

Next, the calculation of the latitude-parallax <term>nati</term> is described:

-> The sine of the zenith distance of the ecliptic <term>drikkshepa</term> multiplied by the difference between the mean motions of the Moon and the Sun, <-
-> and divided by the product of fifteen and the radius, gives the result known as the latitude-parallax <term>nati</term>. || 10 || <-

The "sine of the zenith distance of the ecliptic" was calculated previously. This is multiplied by the difference between the mean motions of the Moon and the Sun <note>the "cool-rayed" and "hot-rayed" ones</note> expressed in minutes. When divided by the radius <note>multiplied by fifteen, as per the rule for <term>tithighna</term></note>, the result is that which is established in the celestial sphere for a specific place and time; in this calculation, that is the latitude-parallax <term>nati</term>.

# Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings" <note>original: "Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka," a famous commentary on the Sūrya Siddhānta</note>

It occurs. Now for the mathematical proof <note>original: "upapatti"</note>. As stated previously, when the ecliptic takes the form of the vertical circle, there is an absence of parallax in latitude <note>original: "nati"</note>. In that case, because the secondary ecliptic point <note>term: Tribhonalagna; the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the rising point</note> is at the zenith, there is an absence of the sine of the ecliptic zenith distance <note>term: dṛkkṣepa; the sine of the arc between the zenith and the highest point of the ecliptic</note>. In a place at sixty degrees <note>latitude</note>, where the secondary ecliptic point is on the horizon, the parallax in latitude is at its maximum. 

The maximum minutes of parallax in latitude are derived because the surface horizon is raised by the distance of the Earth's radius from the center-based horizon. By the proportion: "If the minutes of the difference in motion <note>between the Sun and Moon</note> are obtained by the yojanas <note>a traditional unit of distance</note> of their orbits, then what is obtained by the yojanas of the Earth's radius?" Since the mean daily motion and the Earth's radius are constants, the calculation is simplified by the Earth's radius. Therefore, the maximum minutes of parallax in latitude are approximately one-fifteenth of the minutes of the mean difference in motion. For this very reason, one-fifteenth of sixty ghatikas <note>a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note>, which is four ghatikas, is established as the maximum parallax in longitude <note>original: "lambana"</note>. 

Now, when the sine of the ecliptic zenith distance is equal to the radius <note>original: "trijyā"</note>, the Moon hangs to the north or south of the line from the Earth's surface passing through the Sun. Therefore, by the proportion: "If the parallax is one-fifteenth of the mean difference in motion when the ecliptic zenith distance sine equals the radius, then what is it for a given ecliptic zenith distance sine?" The result is the difference in motion multiplied by the ecliptic zenith distance sine and divided by the product of fifteen and the radius. This is the proven formula for the minutes of parallax in latitude. // 10 //

Now, for the sake of brevity, he states two other methods for calculating the parallax in latitude:

-> The result of the ecliptic zenith distance sine divided by seventy is the parallax. <-
-> Or, it is the result of multiplying by forty-nine and dividing by the radius. // 11 // <-

The parallax in minutes and so on is obtained by dividing the ecliptic zenith distance sine by seventy. Alternatively, by another method, it is multiplied by "seven times seven"—meaning the square of seven, which is forty-nine—and then divided by the radius to find the parallax in minutes. Now—

# The Surya Siddhanta

**Mathematical Proof:** The multiplier for the sine of the ecliptic zenith distance <note>original: "drkshepa"</note> is the difference in daily motion <note>original: "gatyantara"</note> measured in minutes, which is 73;27. The divisor is fifteen times the radius <note>original: "trijya"</note>, totaling 51,570. In the first method, when reduced by the difference in motion, the divisor becomes 70. In the second method, by reducing by fifteen, the multiplier becomes 49 (due to a slight approximation) and the divisor is the radius. Thus, it is proven. || 11 ||

Now, the author explains the direction of the parallax in latitude <note>original: "nati"</note> and the corrected latitude <note>original: "spashta-vikshepa" — the apparent distance of the Moon from the ecliptic as seen from the Earth's surface</note>.

-> The sine of the zenith distance of the meridian <note>original: "madhyajya"</note> determines the direction, <-
-> which is to be known as South or North. <-
-> If it is in the same direction as the Moon's latitude, they are added; <-
-> if in different directions, the difference is taken. || 12 ||

That parallax in latitude follows the direction of the sine of the meridian zenith distance; if the meridian sine is South, the parallax is South; if North, it is North. The word "and" <note>original: "cha"</note> implies a combination. Therefore, the meridian sine indicates the direction of the zenith distance. That South or North parallax, when in the same direction as the Moon's latitude <note>original: "indu-vikshepa"</note>—meaning they share the same cardinal direction—is "added" <note>original: "yukta"</note> to the latitude. Otherwise, if they are in different directions, the difference is taken. The resulting value, retaining the direction of the remainder, is the corrected latitude <note>original: "spashta-shara"</note> modified by the parallax. It should be noted here that the Moon's latitude is that which occurs at the time of the middle of the eclipse.

**The Proof:** Since the ecliptic zenith distance arises from the direction of the meridian zenith distance, it is logical that the parallax produced from it shares that direction. Furthermore, the parallax in latitude is the North-South distance from the line of sight of the Sun (from the Earth's surface) to the ecliptic in the lunar sphere. Since the latitude is the distance from the ecliptic to the Moon's disk, the North-South distance from the observer's line of sight to the Moon's disk is the corrected latitude. This is used in solar eclipses. Therefore, it is proven that when both are in the same direction, they are summed, and when in different directions, the difference is taken. || 12 ||

Next, the author applies the rules previously mentioned in the chapter on Lunar Eclipses to this context.

# Accompanied by the *Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka* <note>The "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings," a famous 17th-century commentary by Raṅganātha on the Sūrya Siddhānta</note>

Regarding the Sun: the word "but" <note>original: "tu-kāra"</note> is used here in the sense of "and" to connect the concepts. "Inversion" <note>original: "viparyaya"</note> refers to the opposite of what was previously stated. This means that the parallax <term>Lambana: the difference in the apparent position of a celestial body as seen from the Earth's center versus its surface</term> at the time of first contact <term>Sparsha: the beginning of an eclipse</term> is less than the parallax at the middle of the eclipse, and the parallax at the time of separation <term>Moksha: the end of an eclipse</term> is greater.

In such a case, the difference in parallax <note>original: "dṛgantara"</note> must be considered. The difference between the parallax at the middle and the parallax at the moments of contact or separation should be added to the half-duration of the eclipse <note>original: "sthit-yardha"</note>. Specifically, for the first half of the eclipse, the difference between the parallax at the beginning and the middle is added to the first half-duration. For the second half, the difference between the parallax at the middle and the end is added to the second half-duration.

Where this "inversion" occurs—meaning in the eastern hemisphere <term>Kapāla: literally "bowl," referring here to the eastern or western celestial hemispheres</term> the parallax at the beginning is less than at the middle, while in the western hemisphere the parallax at the beginning is greater than at the middle—the following rule applies:

The difference in parallax between the end and the middle, or the beginning and the middle, should be subtracted <note>original: "śodhyaṃ"</note> if the hemispheres are the same. This applies when the Sun's position relative to the "meridian ecliptic point" <term>Tribhonalagna: the point on the ecliptic 90 degrees behind the rising sign, used to calculate parallax</term> is consistently greater or consistently less at both times being compared.

It is stated that if there is a "difference" <note>original: "tad-bhede"</note>—meaning a change in hemisphere between the beginning and the middle, or the middle and the end—then the parallaxes should be added together <note>original: "lambanaikatā"</note>. This occurs, for example, if the Sun is greater than the meridian point at the beginning but less than the meridian point at the middle.

->As before, from the end of the lunar day, decreased or increased, the parallax is found again.<-

The reasoning here is as follows: the time of the middle of the eclipse, decreased or increased by the half-duration, results in the times of the beginning and end. Because the parallax correction at the specific times of the beginning and end is required—rather than just the parallax at the middle—this iteration is necessary. Indeed, a time that is corrected by the parallax of one moment cannot be considered "true" for a different moment, as there is no mathematical relation between them. Initially, the exact times of the beginning and end are unknown, and therefore the parallax for those specific moments is also unknown. Having repeatedly calculated the <term>parallax in longitude</term><note>original: "lambana"; the difference in the apparent positions of the Sun and Moon due to the observer's location on Earth</note> for each of the two phases, and having refined the time of the end of the <term>lunar day</term><note>original: "tithyanta"</note>, the times for the <term>contact</term><note>original: "sparśa"; the beginning of the eclipse</term> and the <term>separation</term><note>original: "mokṣa"; the end of the eclipse</note> are made accurate. In that context, when the contact, middle, and separation are determined using a negative parallax: if the parallax at contact is greater than the parallax at the middle, and the parallax at separation is less, then—because the time of contact is the end of the lunar day minus the half-duration of contact and further reduced by the greater parallax, and the middle time is the end of the lunar day reduced by the lesser parallax—the difference between them results in the loss of equality in the lunar day. Therefore, the difference between the two parallaxes is added to the half-duration of contact (specifically, the parallax at contact is added and the parallax at the middle is subtracted). 

Similarly, for the end of the lunar day increased by the half-duration of separation and reduced by the lesser parallax (which is the time of separation), the difference between the parallaxes at the middle and at separation is added to the half-duration of separation, following the previous logic.

However, when the parallax at contact is less than the parallax at the middle, and the parallax at separation is greater: then the difference between the parallaxes is subtracted from the half-duration of contact. Likewise, the difference between the parallaxes is subtracted from the half-duration of separation.

In the case where the contact, middle, and separation are determined using a positive parallax: when the parallax at contact is less than the parallax at the middle and the parallax at separation is greater, then—because the time of contact is the end of the lunar day minus the half-duration of contact plus the lesser parallax, and the middle time is the end of the lunar day plus the greater parallax—the difference between the parallaxes is added to the half-duration of contact. Similarly, for the time of separation, the difference between the parallaxes is added to the half-duration of separation.

# The Treatise of the Sun
<note>original: "Surya Siddhanta"</note>

Since the time of first contact <term>sparsha-kala; the moment the eclipse begins</term> is characterized by a greater negative parallax, and the middle of the eclipse <term>madhya-kala</term> by a lesser negative parallax, the difference between them—calculated according to the stated rule—is subtracted from the half-duration of the first contact. Similarly, since the time of separation <term>moksha-kala; the moment the eclipse ends</term> is characterized by a lesser negative parallax, it is established that the difference in parallax is subtracted from the half-duration of the separation relative to the middle of the eclipse.

Now, one might argue that this method of subtracting the difference in parallax is inconsistent due to a logical contradiction. For instance, because negative parallax <term>rina-lambana; "debt" or subtractive parallax</term> decreases sequentially, and because the times of contact, middle, and separation occur in a specific order, it is unproven that the parallax at contact and separation would be respectively less or more than the parallax at the middle. Likewise, because positive parallax <term>dhana-lambana; "wealth" or additive parallax</term> increases sequentially, it is unproven that the parallax at contact and separation would be respectively more or less than the middle parallax. Indeed, the times of contact and separation never occur respectively after and before the middle time in a way that would justify the stated rule. This would be a contradiction. Therefore, if the addition of the parallax difference is what is actually required, then this entire elaborate explanation is in vain.

If one asks: "How then does the statement of the All-Knowing Lord stand?"—which says:

-> The difference in parallax <term>hari-gyantara</term> is to be subtracted, and the reverse is also true. <-

Do not think so. Even though the "true" times of contact and separation—refined by parallax—must always occur before and after the middle time respectively, the "technical" times of contact and separation (used for calculating the half-duration <term>sthityardha</term> and based on the lunar day) are not the physical reality. Because these technical durations can sometimes be less than the middle time's negative or positive parallax, it is entirely possible for them to appear to occur after or before the middle time respectively. Thus, the explanation is clear. However, in the case of both negative and positive parallax, it is impossible for the parallax at separation and contact to be respectively greater than the middle parallax. From the middle time, the technical times of separation and contact occur respectively in the preceding and succeeding moments...

In the case of a positive parallax, the parallax at separation is certainly not less. This is because it is determined that the times of contact and separation taken from the middle of the eclipse <term>madhyakāla: the moment of maximum obscuration</term> do not occur at the subsequent or preceding times respectively. Otherwise, a stable parallax would be impossible.

Its only purpose is to gain that very knowledge.

It would be cumbersome, redundant, and the rule "the difference should be repeatedly refined" would be inconsistent. 

This objection is not valid because we do not accept the necessity of calculating the two parallaxes repeatedly. Even if the parallax calculated once contains a small discrepancy, the Lord <note>referring to the divine author of the Surya Siddhanta</note> has accepted it due to the difference being negligible. 

Therefore, the previous explanation of the word "again" <note>original: "punar"</note> in the verse "parallax again..." as meaning "repeatedly" is not appropriate. Rather, the explanation should be: "Since parallax was calculated for the middle of the eclipse, it must be calculated a second time for the sake of the times of contact and separation." Or, it is even more appropriate to view "again" as a mere poetic embellishment.

This is logical according to the method stated. ### The Treatise of the Sun

Since the time of the end of the <term>tithi</term><note>A lunar day, or the time required for the longitude of the Moon to increase by 12 degrees over the Sun.</note> is adjusted by the parallax at the middle of the eclipse, and the time of the end of the eclipse is found by adding the half-duration of the eclipse to that <term>tithi</term> end-point—further adjusted by the parallax at the moment of separation—it follows that the half-duration of the separation is combined with the sum of the parallax. This is logically established. 

One should not ask: "If the exact moments of contact and separation are achieved through repeated calculations of parallax, why did the Lord <note>Referring to the divine origin of the Surya Siddhanta</note>, in his omniscient scripture, adopt a method that allows for a slight discrepancy by accepting a single parallax calculation?" The answer is that the All-Knowing Lord accepted a very small margin of error to avoid the excessive effort required by repeated parallax calculations. For the sake of simplicity and to follow the method previously stated for lunar eclipses, he spoke only of the calculation of the corrected half-duration. This is the general direction of the argument.

In reality, when the initial contact occurs after sunrise and is followed by the middle of the eclipse, the parallax at contact—calculated from the fourth house of the zodiac <note>The meridian ecliptic point</note>—is sometimes less than the parallax at the middle. Where the middle occurs before sunrise and the separation occurs after, the parallax at the time of separation may be greater than the parallax at the middle. Where contact occurs before sunset and the middle occurs after, the parallax at contact (due to its relation to the night) is sometimes greater than the parallax at the middle. And where the middle occurs before sunset and the separation after, the parallax at separation—connected to the night—is not less than the parallax at the middle. 

The phrase "sometimes" is used because at the rising and setting of the eclipsed body, a reversal can occur; therefore, the difference in the horizon must be taken into account. By this, the solution which suggests that parallax should not be calculated repeatedly, or that a "reversal" is a specific type of exception, is refuted. This is the truth of the matter. This same logic applies to the half-duration of total darkness <note>Vimardardha</note>; thus, everything is consistent. 

The teacher Bhaskaracharya <note>A famous 12th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note>, however, stated:

->From the end of the lunar day, decreased or increased by the half-duration, calculate the parallax.<-
->The half-duration is then adjusted by the difference in parallax arising from that specific time.<-

# The Surya Siddhanta

By the method of determining the directions <note>diksādhana: the process of establishing the cardinal points—North, South, East, and West—on a circular diagram</note>, the directions are marked on the prime vertical circle. This is done because the directions of the ecliptic <note>krāntivṛtta: the apparent path of the Sun across the sky</note> exist at an interval determined by the deflection <note>valana: the angle between the ecliptic and the celestial equator</note> from these marks. In that context, to determine the directions of the first contact <note>sparśa: the beginning of the eclipse</note> and the last contact <note>mokṣa: the end of the eclipse</note>, the contact points of the Moon and Sun must be decided according to the East and West of the ecliptic. This is because the motion of the planets follows that circle.

The faster-moving Moon, coming from the West toward the Earth's shadow <note>bhūbhā: the shadow cast by the Earth, which causes a lunar eclipse</note>—which is located six signs away from the Sun and moves according to the Sun's pace—begins the meeting. Therefore, the first contact occurs on the **Eastern** side of the Moon's disk. When the Moon moves forward, surpassing the Earth's shadow, the separation from the shadow occurs at the Moon's **Western** side; thus, the last contact is in the West. In a solar eclipse, the Moon comes from the West and covers the Sun; therefore, the first contact is on the **Western** side of the Sun, and the last contact is on the **Eastern** side. || 4 ||

Now, he describes the application of the deflection on the circle of deflection:

-> The first contact deflection of the Moon is applied according to its direction; <-
-> but the last contact is the opposite. For the Sun, this is reversed. || 5 || <-

The deflection at first contact for the Moon (the body being eclipsed) should be applied from the Eastern mark according to its direction—if South, then facing South; if North, then facing North—along the circle of deflection, like a sine-segment <note>ardhajyā: literally 'half-chord', the standard trigonometric sine used in Indian astronomy</note> relative to the East-West line. For this reason, that circle is called the "Circle of Deflection."

The word "but" indicates that the Moon's deflection at the time of last contact is "opposite" or reversed. This means it is applied from the Western mark relative to the East-West line; if the deflection is South, it is applied facing the North, and if North, it is applied facing the South.

He then states the specific rule for a solar eclipse: "reversed." For the Sun (the body being eclipsed), these deflections for first and last contact are the inverse of the Moon's. The last contact deflection is applied from the Eastern mark relative to the East-West line; if South, then facing South; if North...

# Accompanied by the Illuminator of Hidden Meanings

The line drawn from the center <note>of the obscuring body</note> to the center of the body to be eclipsed is equal to the sum of their semi-diameters <term>mānaikyakhaṇḍa; the sum of the radii of the two disks</term>. Where this line touches the circle of the eclipsed body, the first contact <note>beginning of the eclipse</note> and the separation <note>end of the eclipse</note> occur on the circumference, due to the joining of their respective radii. || 7 ||

Now, in two verses, the author explains the arrangement of the directions of celestial latitude <term>vikṣepa; the angular distance of a planet north or south of the ecliptic</term> during an eclipse, and the application of the "deflection" <term>valana; the angle between the ecliptic and the local horizon/equator</term> at the time of the middle of the eclipse for the purpose of calculation.

> The latitudes of the Sun <note>original: *arkasya*</note> should always be drawn according to their actual direction.
> Those of the Moon <note>original: *śaśāṅkasya*</note> are reversed. Based on that, the middle— || 8 ||
> —deflection should be applied toward the East if the latitude and deflection are in the same direction.
> If they differ, it should be applied toward the West; for the Moon, it is the opposite of the Sun. || 9 ||

In a solar eclipse, the latitudes of the Moon should always be understood and drawn according to their actual directions <note>as they appear in the sky</note> for the purpose of illustrating the different types of eclipses. In a lunar eclipse, the latitudes of the Moon are reversed: if they are South, they are treated as North; if North, they are treated as South. The latitudes at the moments of first contact <insert>spārśika</insert> and separation <insert>maukṣika</insert> should be applied following this rule. It should be understood that they are not applied simply as they are calculated.

Furthermore, based on that—meaning, based on the direction of the latitude at the time of the middle of the eclipse—in a solar eclipse, one uses the direction of the true latitude at the middle of the eclipse, and in a lunar eclipse, one uses the opposite direction of the latitude at the middle. If—meaning "whenever"—there is "unity of latitude," meaning the deflection and the latitude at the middle of the eclipse are the same in terms of their directional relationship. This means they are in the same direction. Note that here, the direction of the Moon's latitude is taken as it actually is, not reversed. "Toward the East" means toward the eastern mark. The "middle deflection"—the true deflection at the time of the middle of the eclipse—should be applied like a sine-chord on the circle dependent on the deflection. In the case of "difference," meaning when the directions of the deflection and latitude are different, it is applied "toward the West." From the deflection—

# The Surya Siddhanta
<note>original: "Surya-Siddhanta" — The "Sun Treatise," a foundational text of Indian astronomy.</note>

On the circle of deflection, the deflection of the Moon at the time of the middle of the eclipse should be marked like a sine-chord, facing the western point. Now, he states a specific rule for solar eclipses: "Of the Sun..." <note>referring to a specific verse fragment</note>. In a solar eclipse, the deflection of the Sun is applied in the reverse of what was previously stated. This means that if the directions are the same, it is marked toward the western point; if the directions are different, it is marked toward the eastern point.

The practical result is this: In a lunar eclipse, if both the direction of the deflection at the middle of the eclipse and the direction of the actual latitude <term>vikshepa</term><note>The celestial latitude or angular distance of a planet from the ecliptic.</note> are South, then the middle deflection should be marked on the circle of deflection from the North point toward the East point, like a sine-chord. If both are North, the deflection should be marked from the South point toward the East. If the deflection is South and the latitude is North, then the deflection should be marked from the South point toward the West. If the deflection is North and the latitude is South, then the deflection should be marked on the circle of deflection from the North point toward the West.

However, in a solar eclipse: if both are South, the deflection should be marked on the circle of deflection from the South point toward the West. If both are North, it should be marked from the North point toward the West. If the deflection is South and the latitude is North, then it is marked from the North point toward the East. If the deflection is North and the latitude is South, then it is marked from the South point toward the East.

The teacher Bhaskaracharya <note>A famous 12th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer.</note> has stated this result more simply: the South and North deflections should be applied clockwise and counter-clockwise respectively.

The reasoning <term>upapatti</term> for this is as follows: The reasoning for the first verse was explained in the section on applying the latitude for the beginning and end of the eclipse. The center of the eclipsing body is located at a distance equal to the latitude from the center of the body being eclipsed. Since the latitude is oriented toward the pole of the ecliptic <term>kadamba</term><note>The "Kadamba" refers to the pole of the ecliptic, crucial for calculating celestial coordinates.</note>, knowledge of the pole's position on the circle of deflection is necessary to apply the latitude from the center toward the pole. Therefore, because the directions of the ecliptic exist at an interval of deflection from their own cardinal directions, the ecliptic directions are found from the North and South points by the interval of the middle deflection...

# The Treatise of the Sun

The meaning is that one should perform the projection. Here is the rationale: In a circle, the central line faces the <term>Kadamba</term> <note>the pole of the ecliptic</note>. There, the center of the eclipsing body is separated from the center of the eclipsed body by the deflection. A circle drawn with the radius of the eclipsing body represents its disk. The extent to which it overlaps the eclipsed disk at the middle of the eclipse is seen in the sky as the portion "seized" or covered; therefore, it is said to be "grasped by darkness." || 11 ||

Now, an objection arises: all that has been said is valid if the eclipses occur in the eastern hemisphere. However, if an eclipse occurs in the western hemisphere, the directions described in the diagram would appear reversed. Specifically, the directions of contact and separation shown in the diagram would appear opposite to the observer because they are facing west. To address this, the text says:

-> When a learned man draws the diagram on the ground or on a board, <-
-> he must reverse the directions for the eastern and western hemispheres. || 12 || <-

"On the ground or on a board" means on a wooden tablet. The mention of a "board" is made because a diagram drawn on the ground cannot be moved or rotated to suit the observer's eye. When the mathematician, a learned man <term>who knows the principles</term>, draws the previously mentioned diagram, he must perform a reversal or inversion of the directions (East, etc.) for the eastern and western hemispheres. 

For example, in the <term>eastern hemisphere</term>, the directions are written clockwise starting from the East. In the <term>western hemisphere</term>, one should not follow that same clockwise order starting from the East. Instead, East should be placed where West was, and West where East was. The North and South directions should be marked in their respective North and South positions <note>relative to the new East-West axis</note>. The intention is that even if an eclipse occurs in the western hemisphere, the <term>drawn diagram</term> will remain consistent with the visual observation. 

The rationale here is: since the directions appear reversed to the observer, by writing the directions in reverse beforehand, the <term>projection</term> will match the actual state of the sky. <term>Bhaskaracharya</term> <note>a famous 12th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note> also stated...

Now, he describes the perception of unobservable portions [of an eclipse].

->**Even if a twelfth part of the Moon is eclipsed, it is [not] seen because of its brightness.**<-

A twelfth part of the lunar disk is eclipsed, meaning covered. The word "even" implies that although there is a possibility of visibility due to the loss of light from the covering, it is not seen. Even if three minutes <term>minutes (liptā): a unit of angular measurement where 60 minutes make one degree</term> of the Sun are eclipsed, they are not seen. Here he gives the reason: "because of its intensity." This means that because the Sun's light is so sharp, it is capable of striking back (overpowering) the eyes of the observer. > If two digits of the Moon are eclipsed,
> or three minutes of the Sun, they are not perceived.
> Yet, they are somewhat visible at the time of rising or setting,
> because at those times, the two [luminaries] are devoid of a web of rays.

Thus, it should be understood that what is said to be invisible becomes visible at the time of rising or setting. || 13 ||

# The Treatise of the Sun

When less than half of the lunar disk is eclipsed <note>literally: "seized" by the shadow</note>, the eclipsed portion of the disk appears smoky in color. If more than half is eclipsed, the disk appears black. Following this, even if a larger portion is eclipsed, if it is facing liberation <note>the end of the eclipse</note>, meaning it is nearing the start of release and more than three-quarters is eclipsed but not yet fully, it takes on a dark-reddish hue <note>a mixture of black and red</note>. In a total eclipse, the disk becomes tawny or reddish-brown. These colors occur because the Earth's shadow, being a lack of light, covers the Moon.

However, in the case of the Sun, the Moon—which is a watery sphere—is the coverer. On the day of the new moon, the half visible to us is always black; therefore, the eclipsed portion of the Sun is always black. Because this color does not change, the Lord <note>the divine source of the text</note> has not specified different colors for solar eclipses. || 23 ||

Now, he speaks of the secrecy of the aforementioned diagrams <term>Cheidyaka: the graphical methods for representing eclipses</term>.

> This is a secret of the gods and should not be given to just anyone.
> It should be given to a well-tested student *who has resided with the teacher for a year. || 24 ||

This method of eclipse diagrams is a hidden treasure of the gods. It must not be given to just anyone who has not been tested. He explains who it *should* be given to: a well-tested student. He adds a qualifying reason for "well-tested": one who has resided for a year. The implication is that through a year of companionship, one truly comes to know the student's character. || 24 ||

Now, to prevent any inconsistency in the upcoming text, he concludes the chapter with a short prose statement.

Now begins the explanation of the Authority on Planetary Conjunctions <term>Graha-yuti-adhikara</term>, which is undertaken with refinements by describing the appearances of these unions. Regarding this, the author states the different types of conjunctions:

> Between the star-planets <note>The "star-planets" are Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn, distinguished from the Sun and Moon</note> themselves, there occur "Conflict" and "Association."
> "Association" is the term used for union with the Moon; union with the Sun is called "Setting." || 1 ||

When the five star-planets, beginning with Mars <note>original: "Bhauma"</note>, meet one another, they are classified as "Conflict" <term>Yuddha; literally 'war'</term> or "Association" <term>Samagama</term> based on characteristics to be described later. The union of any of the five stars with the Moon <note>original: "Shashanka"</note> is designated as "Association." The union of any of the five stars—or the Moon—with the Sun is called "Setting" <term>Astamana; heliacal setting or combustion</term>, which is a state of total invisibility. This is not an ordinary conjunction, as it exists in the time before and after the actual union. || 1 ||

Next, the author describes whether a conjunction is past or future in one and a half verses:

> If the faster planet has a higher longitude than the slower one, the conjunction is past; otherwise, it is in the future.
> This applies when both are moving eastward; however, if both are retrograde, the rule is reversed. || 2 ||

If a planet moving eastward has a higher longitude, the association is past; for retrograde planets, it is yet to come.

# The Surya Siddhanta

When a conjunction <note>original: "yoga"; a meeting of two celestial bodies at the same longitude</note> is desired between two planets, if the faster-moving planet <term>shighragati</term> is ahead of—meaning at a greater longitude than—the slower-moving planet <term>mandagati</term>, then their union, known as a conjunction <term>yuti</term>, is "past" <term>gata</term>; it has already occurred. Conversely, if the slower-moving planet is ahead of the faster-moving one, their conjunction is "future" <term>eshya</term>; it is yet to happen.

This rule for determining past or future status applies when both planets are moving eastward <note>direct motion</note>. However, for two planets in retrograde motion <term>vakragati</term>, the rule is reversed. This means that if the faster-moving planet is ahead of the slower one, the conjunction is "future," and if the slower one is ahead of the faster one, the conjunction is "past."

Now, the text explains the case where only one of the two planets is in retrograde motion. When one planet is retrograde and the other is moving eastward, if the eastward-moving planet is ahead of the retrograde one, the conjunction is "past." If the retrograde planet is ahead of the eastward-moving one, the conjunction is "future."

The reasoning <term>upapatti</term> is as follows:
Between two planets moving eastward, if the faster one is ahead, a future conjunction is impossible because the gap will only increase; therefore, the conjunction must have already happened. If the slower one is ahead, the faster one—being behind—will eventually catch up, so the conjunction will happen in the future.

In the case of two retrograde planets, if the faster one is ahead, a conjunction will occur in the future because its longitude is decreasing more rapidly toward the slower one. If the slower one is ahead, the faster one's longitude will continue to decrease away from it, making a future conjunction impossible; thus, it is "past."

Finally, if an eastward-moving planet is ahead of a retrograde planet, they are moving away from each other, so the conjunction is "past." If the retrograde planet is ahead of the eastward-moving one, they are moving toward each other, so the conjunction is "future." || 2 ||

Next, the method for calculating the exact positions of the planets at the moment of conjunction, and the calculation of the days elapsed or remaining until that moment, is described in the following three and a half verses.

## Accompanied by the *Illuminator of Hidden Meanings* <note>The *Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka*, a famous 17th-century commentary by Raṅganātha on the *Sūrya Siddhānta*</note>

The minutes of the interval between two planets are multiplied by their respective daily motions. || 3 ||
One should divide this by the difference between their daily motions when both are moving in direct or retrograde motion. If only one of the two is retrograde, one should divide by the sum of their daily motions. || 4 ||
The resulting minutes and seconds should be subtracted if the conjunction has passed, and added if it is in the future. In the case of two retrograde planets, this is reversed; if only one is retrograde, addition and subtraction are applied accordingly. || 5 ||
Those two planets, situated within the zodiac, will then be at equal minutes of longitude. By the non-exhaustion of that difference, the result is desired in days and further units of time. || 6 ||

The minutes of the interval between two planets involved in a conjunction at a desired time are separately multiplied by their respective daily motions <term>bhukti: the distance a planet travels in a day</term>. The calculator should divide this by the difference of their true motions, whether both planets are moving in direct <term>anuloma: "with the hair," meaning regular forward motion</term> or both are in retrograde <term>viloma: "against the hair," meaning backward motion</term>. He mentions a specific distinction: "If retrograde..." This means that if, between the two, one happens to be retrograde, he should divide by the sum of their motions. The result, in minutes and so on, should be subtracted from each planet's position if the conjunction has already occurred while the planets were in direct motion. If the conjunction is yet to come, it should be added to them. For two planets in retrograde motion, one must act "from the reverse," meaning the opposite of what was just said: add if the conjunction is past, and subtract if it is in the future. However, the word "but" <note>original: "tu"</note> implies that if only one of the two is retrograde while the other is direct, the resulting figures for each planet should be added and subtracted respectively. For example: if the conjunction is past, the result is subtracted from the direct planet and added to the retrograde planet. If the conjunction is in the future, it is subtracted from the retrograde planet and added to the direct planet. When this is done, those two planets involved in the conjunction will be "situated within the zodiac"—meaning their positions within the circle of signs—and will be at equal minutes <term>samaliptau: having the same longitude</term>, occupying the same point in the heavens.

# Surya Siddhanta
## Page 19

The term "position" <note>original: *ksiptapadasya*</note> is used here to characterize the fractional parts of a revolution, meaning that the two planets become equal in longitude. Now, the author explains the knowledge of the time of conjunction <term>Yutikala: the exact moment when two celestial bodies share the same longitude</term>. Regarding the "difference" <note>original: *vivaram*</note>: the difference between the two planets involved in the conjunction at the desired time is expressed in minutes of arc. Just as one calculates the result to find the equal minutes of arc, the difference is multiplied by the daily motion and divided by the sum of the motions or the difference of the motions <note>original: *gatyantarena*; the relative speed between two planets</note>.

The result obtained by that divisor, in days and fractions of days, is said to be "past" or "to come" relative to the desired time, depending on the nature of the conjunction. At that specific time—the moment of conjunction—those two planets are equal. The mathematical proof is as follows: If the difference in daily motions yields the daily motion in minutes, then what will the actual difference in minutes between the planets yield? In a "past" conjunction <note>original: *gatayutau*</note>, the result is subtracted from the planets. In a "future" conjunction <note>original: *esyayutau*</note>, it is added.

If both planets are in retrograde motion <term>Vakratva: the apparent backward motion of a planet as seen from Earth</term>, the result from the difference in motion is added to the planets for a past conjunction and subtracted for a future one. This is because a retrograde planet's longitude decreases over time. Now, if only one planet is retrograde, the distance between them increases daily by the sum of their motions. Therefore, the result obtained using the sum of motions as the divisor is subtracted from the direct-moving planet for a past conjunction (since it was previously less) and added to the retrograde planet (since it was previously greater). For a future conjunction, it is added to the direct planet (as it increases) and subtracted from the retrograde planet (as it will be less). By the proportion—if one day is gained by the sum or difference of motions, what is gained by the actual minutes of difference—one finds the days, etc., past or future. || 6 ||

Next, it is said that the tools for the visibility correction <term>Drikkarma: calculations to adjust the mathematical position of a planet to its actual visible position on the horizon</term> must be prepared:

> Having calculated the measure of day and night, as well as the minutes of celestial latitude,
> and having determined the zenith distance and altitude of the two planets based on their respective latitudes... || 7 ||

For those two planets at that time, one should calculate the measure of the day and the measure of the night individually, as well as the minutes of celestial latitude <note>original: *viksepalipsikah*; the angular distance of a planet north or south of the ecliptic</note>. This is what is meant by "having prepared." Here, the Lord <note>referring to the divine source of the Surya Siddhanta</note>...

# Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings"

Having established the calculation of the deflection minutes <note>original: "vicchepakalāḥ"; refers to the angular distance between two celestial bodies</note>, the length of day and night should then be established. It is indicated that the length of day and night should not be calculated using the ascensional difference <note>original: "cara"; the difference between the oblique and right ascension</note> derived from the "corrected declination." Instead, it must be calculated using the ascensional difference derived from the "pure declination," which has not been adjusted by the celestial latitude <note>original: "śara"</note> of the planets in conjunction.

After calculating the hour angle <note>original: "natakāla"; time elapsed since the meridian</note> and the altitude time <note>original: "unnatakāla"; time since rising</note> for each of the two planets having the same latitude, the word "likewise" is applied here to signify a combination of steps. For this very purpose, it was previously stated that the length of day and night must be established. The remainder of the sentence implies that the <term>visibility correction</term> <note>original: "dṛkkarma"; mathematical adjustments made to planetary positions to account for their visibility on the horizon</note> just mentioned must be performed.

Now, an objection arises: How can the hour angle and altitude be calculated when the rising sign <note>original: "udayalagna"</note> of the planet is unknown, and thus the duration of time relative to that rising is also unknown? Indeed, those values cannot be achieved through the mere lengths of day and night without knowing the elapsed time of the planet's day or night. To this, the author says: "By means of its own time." This means by means of the ascendant <note>original: "lagna"</note> at the specific time when the two planets reached the same longitude, as determined by the previously mentioned method. From that specific time and the planets in conjunction, the altitude time for each must be calculated. This is what is being said: designate the ascendant at the time of union as the "greater" value and the planet in conjunction as the "lesser" value.

> ->Subtract the breaths of the portion to be passed from the lesser, and the breaths of the portion already passed from the greater;<-
> ->adding these to the breaths of the intermediate signs, the calculation of time is achieved.<-

By this rule stated in the <term>Chapter on the Three Problems</term> <note>original: "Tripraśnādhikāra"; a standard section in Sanskrit astronomical texts dealing with time, place, and direction</note>, one should calculate the time elapsed in the day or night for the planet. In the daytime, the lesser of the elapsed time or the remaining time is the "altitude"; in the night, the lesser of the elapsed night or remaining night is the "altitude." The "hour angle" of the planet is the half-day or half-night minus that altitude. By using the singular form for "the measure of day and night" and "hour angle and altitude," it is indicated that for the two planets in conjunction, the length of day, length of night, hour angle, and altitude are identical. Therefore, the interval of time is not to be calculated separately for each using two different rising signs. Furthermore, it is clarified that the day and night measures are not calculated individually via the ascensional difference of the corrected declination, because the rising sign itself was not previously established. # The Surya Siddhanta

Just as the time elapsed since sunrise is established using the Sun’s longitude at a given moment and the rising sign <note>the *lagna* or the point of the ecliptic rising on the eastern horizon</note>, the time elapsed since a planet's rise is established using the planet's longitude and the rising sign at that moment. Although this calculation is perfectly accurate for the Sun—because the Sun always stays exactly on the ecliptic <note>the apparent path of the Sun across the sky</note>—it is technically inaccurate for planets. This is because planets do not strictly stay on the ecliptic, and the "elapsed time" calculated by the standard method refers to the point on the ecliptic associated with the planet, rather than the actual physical disk of the planet itself.

Therefore, the time derived from a planet that has undergone <term>Drkkarma</term> <note>visibility correction or "aspect-calculation" to account for the planet's latitude</note>, which will be explained later, refers to the actual planetary disk. Nevertheless, for the purpose of performing those very visibility corrections, the value associated with the ecliptic-point is required first, so there is no error in this approach. || 7 ||

Now, the author describes that visibility correction and its application to the planet in two verses:

> Multiply the celestial latitude of the planet by the equinoctial shadow and divide by twelve. 
> Multiply the result by the planet's own degrees of altitude <note>literally "bent-nadi" or time from the meridian</note> and divide by half of its own day-length. || 8 ||
>
> In the east, the result is subtracted if the latitude is northern, and added if the latitude is western <note>meaning the planet is in the western hemisphere</note>. 
> If the latitude is southern, it is added in the eastern hemisphere and subtracted in the western. || 9 ||

The result obtained from the planet's <term>Vikshepa</term> <note>celestial latitude</note> multiplied by the <term>Akshabha</term> <note>the shadow of a vertical gnomon at noon during the equinox</note> and divided by twelve, should be multiplied by the planet's own <term>Nataghati</term> <note>the time elapsed since the planet crossed the meridian</note>. This is then divided by the half-day length of that planet. By implication, if the calculation is done at night, one uses half the night-length. 

In this context, even though the day-length and altitude-time for two identical planets would be the same, the Lord <note>the divine author of the text</note> used the word "own" (*sva*) to ensure the calculation remains distinct for different celestial bodies, particularly when calculating planetary conjunctions. In reality, since the Lord discusses conjunctions later when the two "seen" planets are equal, and since the day-lengths and altitudes of the two planets at that specific moment may differ based on their distinct latitudes, the use of the word "own" is entirely appropriate. It does not refer to the day-length generated simply from the planet's declination...

# Accompanied by the *Gudharthaprakashaka* <note>The "Exposition of Hidden Meanings," a famous commentary by Ranganatha on the Surya Siddhanta.</note>

Because of the difference between the various divisions, it is said to be "void" <note>original: "kham"; referring to a zero value or nullification in specific mathematical contexts</note>. It should be understood that the means of achieving this does not proceed due to displacement. According to the stated method, the minutes of arc resulting from the latitude <note>original: "kshepa"</note> near the north and other directions are subtracted from the planet in the eastern hemisphere <note>original: "prak-pale"</note>. In the western hemisphere, they are to be added. The same applies to the southern latitude. By the use of the word "but" <note>original: "tu-karat"</note>, the resulting correction is to be added in the eastern hemisphere and subtracted in the western hemisphere. || 9 || Now, he describes the *Ayana-drkkarma* <note>The "ecliptic visibility correction" which accounts for the secondary correction needed due to the planet's latitude and the tilt of the ecliptic.</note>.

->The minutes of latitude multiplied by the degrees of declination of the planet plus three signs,<-
->are the seconds of arc. These are additive or subtractive when the declination and latitude are of different or like directions. || 10 ||<-

The minutes of latitude <note>original: "vikshepa-kala"</note> previously calculated, when multiplied by the degrees of declination <note>original: "kranti"</note> produced from the planet increased by three signs <note>90 degrees</note>, become seconds of arc <note>original: "vikala"</note>. In the position of the seconds of arc in the planet refined by the *Ayana-drkkarma*, these are to be made additive or subtractive respectively when the declination of the planet-plus-three-signs and the latitude are of different or the same directions.

Here is the rationale <note>original: "upapatti"</note>: The arc of the ecliptic <note>original: "kranti-vritta"</note> between the planet's position and the point where the secondary circle passing through the poles <note>original: "dhruva-prota-vritta"</note> touches the planet's disk on the latitude circle—those minutes are the <term>Ayana-kala</term> <note>Ecliptic correction minutes</note>. To calculate them, the field is as follows: the <term>Graha-shara</term> <note>The planet's celestial latitude</note> directed towards the <term>Kadamba</term> <note>The pole of the ecliptic</note> is the <term>Hypotenuse</term> <note>original: "karna"</note>. The distance between the intersection of the secondary circle and the corresponding region of the <term>Dhuravritta</term> <note>The diurnal circle; original uses "dhura" for "dyu"</note> is the <term>Base</term> <note>original: "bhuja"</note> on the diurnal circle. On the secondary circle through the poles, the <term>True Latitude</term> <note>original: "spashta-shara"</note> between the planet's disk and that intersection is the <term>Perpendicular</term> <note>original: "koti" or "upright"</note>.

Therefore, by the proportion: if the sine of the ecliptic polar deflection <note>original: "ayana-valana-jya"</note> is the base when the Radius <note>original: "trijya"</note> is the hypotenuse, then what is the base when the latitude is the hypotenuse? By this calculation, the minutes of the base are in the proportion of the <term>Dhyujya</term> <note>The radius of the diurnal circle</note>. These are not the minutes of the base on the ecliptic at the interval of the intersection of the planetary orbits, because of the slant of the ecliptic and the possibility of such a region of the ecliptic being part of that slant.
