<header>The Treatise of the Sun</header>

# The Treatise of the Sun

The figure formed by the square root of the difference between the squares of the <term>koti</term> <note>the perpendicular side of a right-angled triangle</note> and the radius is visible in the sphere. Therefore, there is no error in the proportion. In this context, the Lord <note>referring to the divine origin of the Surya Siddhanta</note>, out of compassion for the world and for the sake of ease in calculation, has accepted the arc-minutes of the <term>bhuja</term> <note>the base or sine-segment</note> located on the diurnal circle as being on the ecliptic, due to the very small difference between them.

Thus, while it follows that the sine of the <term>ayana-valana</term> <note>the deflection due to the obliquity of the ecliptic</note> should be multiplied by the minutes of the planetary latitude and divided by the radius, the Lord has accepted the degrees of the ecliptic's declination at a point three signs <note>90 degrees</note> ahead of the planet. Those degrees are to be multiplied by fifty-eight to find the sine. Since the maximum declination of twenty-four degrees multiplied by fifty-eight (minus five) results in the maximum sine of declination. This, multiplied by the latitude and divided by the radius, gives the <term>ayana</term> minutes. To obtain the result in seconds of arc, one multiplies by sixty. Thus, the planetary latitude multiplied by the declination degrees of the planet plus three signs, and then multiplied by the product of fifty-eight and sixty (which is 3480, or 3500 minus twenty), and divided by the radius, is established. Here too, for the sake of simplicity, since the multiplier is nearly equal to the radius, they are considered to cancel each other out. This explains the passage ending with "seconds of arc."

However, the teacher Bhaskaracharya <note>a famous 12th-century Indian mathematician</note> has stated more precisely:

> The <term>ayana-valana</term> multiplied by the corrected latitude and divided by the day-radius, then divided by 1800 <note>original: "purna-purna-dhriti", a numerical code where purna=0 and dhriti=18</note>, gives the <term>ayana</term> minutes based on the rising of the signs.

The logic for addition and subtraction is as follows: during the northward passage <note>the Sun's movement from Capricorn onwards</note>, the south pole of the ecliptic is below the south celestial pole, and the north pole of the ecliptic is above the north celestial pole. In that situation, when the latitude is southern, the planet's disk is directed toward the north pole of the ecliptic and is thus elevated from the north celestial pole. Consequently, the intersection of the planet's own vertical circle (passing through the ecliptic poles) with the ecliptic—which represents the position of the "equinoctial planet"—falls behind the actual position of the planet on the ecliptic. Therefore, the <term>ayana</term> seconds are subtracted from the planet's longitude to find the corrected longitude. Similarly, with southern latitude, because the planet's disk is directed toward the south pole of the ecliptic...

# Accompanied by the "Illumination of Hidden Meanings"
<note>original: "Gūḍhārthaprakāśa" — a famous 17th-century commentary by Raṅganātha on the Sūrya Siddhānta, the foundational text of Indian astronomy.</note>

Because of the elevation from the celestial pole, the position of the planet adjusted for precession <note>original: "āyana-graha"</note> is ahead of the actual planetary mark on the ecliptic <note>original: "krāntivṛtta"</note>; therefore, the minutes of the precession correction are additive <note>positive</note>. However, during the southward transit starting from Cancer, the south celestial pole is above the south ecliptic pole, and the north celestial pole is below the north ecliptic pole. In that case, if the planet's latitude <note>original: "śara"</note> is south, then because the planetary disk is inclined from the south pole, the precessional mark is behind the planetary mark on the ecliptic; thus, the correction is subtractive <note>negative</note>. 

If the latitude is north, then because the planetary disk is inclined from the north pole, the precessional mark is ahead of the planetary mark on the ecliptic; thus, the correction is additive. By the positioning of the celestial sphere, it is established that: when the direction of the precession and the latitude are the same, it is subtractive; when the directions are different, it is additive. Since the direction of precession follows the direction of the celestial sphere at a point three signs <note>90 degrees</note> ahead, it is logical that when the declination of that point and the planet's latitude are in the same direction, one subtracts; if in different directions, one adds.

Now follows the **<term>Rationalization of the Visibility Correction due to Latitude</term>** <note>original: "Akṣadṛkkarmopapatti" — the calculation to determine when a planet actually appears on the horizon, accounting for the observer's terrestrial latitude.</note>. When the planetary disk is attached to the circle of the horizon <note>specifically the circle passing through the intersection of the prime vertical and the meridian</note>, the planet is adjusted by the minutes of the latitude-visibility correction at the point where the ecliptic meets the planet. The distance on the ecliptic between that point and the precessional planetary position constitutes the "minutes of latitude-visibility." These are at their maximum when the planetary disk is on the horizon. When the planet is on the meridian <note>the north-south line</note>, the precessional mark itself becomes the mark adjusted for latitude-visibility; therefore, the correction is zero. 

Thus, when the planetary disk is on the horizon, the moving circle passing through the intersection of the meridian and the horizon is identical to the horizon circle itself. The minutes by which the intersection of the ecliptic and the polar-projection circle (the precessional mark) is separated above or below the ecliptic point on the horizon are the "minutes of latitude-visibility." To determine these, the time-degrees <note>original: "asavaḥ"</note> of the diurnal circle segment arising from the terrestrial latitude are calculated. To explain: on the moving circle passing through the two poles and the planetary disk, the distance between the celestial equator <note>original: "viṣuvadvṛtta"</note> and the planetary disk is the true declination.

# The Sūryasiddhānta

The distance between the celestial equator and the point of the planet on the ecliptic is the **mean declination** <note>original: "madhyamā krānti"; the angular distance of a celestial body north or south of the celestial equator</note>. The distance between that ecliptic point and the actual center of the planet's disk is the **true celestial latitude** <note>original: "sphuṭa-śara"; the angular distance of a planet from the ecliptic</note>. When both declinations are in the same direction, the **true declination** is greater. 

In the northern hemisphere, the point of the planet on the ecliptic lies below the horizon on its own diurnal circle by a number of respirations <note>term: "asu" (respiration); a unit of time equivalent to 4 seconds, used to measure the rotation of the celestial sphere</note> equal to the difference between the declination and the latitude. Because the ascensional difference <note>term: "cara"; the difference between the time of rising of a celestial body and the time of rising of the corresponding point on the equator</note> of the planet's disk is greater than the ascensional difference of the ecliptic point, there is a visible displacement. This displacement occurs toward the celestial pole from the point on the horizon associated with the mean ascensional difference. 

Because of the existence of this difference in ascensional periods at the interval of the horizon, a rectangular figure is formed. The sides of this figure are the true latitude and the difference in ascensional periods, allowing for the **true visibility** <note>original: "sphuṭa-darśanam"</note> to be calculated between these two diurnal circles. 

Similarly, in the southern hemisphere, the ecliptic point of the planet is above the horizon on its diurnal circle by respirations equal to the difference between declination and latitude. However, if the declinations are in different directions, the ecliptic point is below or above the horizon by respirations equal to the sum of the declination and latitude. This is because the ecliptic point exists at a distance equal to the true ascensional difference from the equatorial horizon <note>term: "unmaṇḍala"; the six-o'clock circle or the celestial horizon at the equator</note> in the north and south hemispheres. This was stated by the teacher **Bhāskarācārya** <note>A preeminent 12th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note>:

->**The respirations arising from the difference or sum**<-
->**of the two half-ascensional differences of the true and mean declinations,**<-
->**when they are in the same or different directions,**<-
->**are called the "terrestrial-born" corrections for the stars.**<-

In this way, the precise knowledge of the visibility correction for the ascensional difference is explained. By the grace of the Lord, following the previously mentioned method, the segment of declination—which takes the form of the true latitude produced by the refinement of the true and mean declinations—is accepted as being nearly equal to the latitude as it occurs. Thus, the following **rule of three** <note>term: "anupāta"; a mathematical proportion used to find an unknown value: if A results in B, what does C result in?</note> is applied: If, when the vertical side is twelve <note>The standard length of a gnomon or shadow-stick in Indian astronomy</note>, the "equinoctial shadow" <note>term: "palabhā"; the shadow cast by a vertical gnomon at noon on the day of the equinox, used to determine local latitude</note> is the horizontal side, then what will be the result when the latitude-declination is the vertical side?

# The Treatise of the Sun

<note>original: Sūryasiddhānta</note>

The values are increased by half of thirty and half of that again. Half of thirty is fifteen; half of that is seven and a half. When these are added successively to thirty, we get the diameters in <term>Yojanas</term><note>A traditional Indian unit of distance, roughly 5–9 miles</note> for Mars, Saturn, Mercury, and Jupiter respectively, as measured in the lunar orbit—meaning in the celestial sphere of the Moon, according to the scale of the Moon's orbit, and not according to their own orbits. The diameters of the disks <note>original: bimbavyāsa</note> are stated as follows: for Mars, 30; for Saturn, 37.5; for Mercury, 45; and for Jupiter, 52.5. Following this same progression, the value for Venus is 60. By stating "sixty for Venus," the interpretation that "half of a half" should be added to each previous value is clarified and the intended meaning is made manifest.

These stated diameters are doubled, multiplied by the <term>Radius</term><note>original: trijyā</note>, and divided by the sum of the "three and four chords." According to the traditional commentary, this means dividing by the sum of the two "chords" (distances) produced in the third and fourth operations—namely the <term>slow-chord</term><note>original: mandakarṇa; related to the planet's eccentricity</note> and the <term>fast-chord</term><note>original: śīghrakarṇa; related to the Earth's motion</note>. However, modern scholars <note>original: navyāstu</note> disregard the previous explanation because the third operation does not involve a ratio of chords and the "third chord" is not well-established, which contradicts logical reasoning. Instead, they interpret the word "three" to mean the Radius and "four-chord" to mean the fast-chord of the fourth operation; the diameter is divided by the sum of these two. The results are the "corrected" diameters of their respective disks. When divided by fifteen, these become the measure of the disk in minutes of arc <note>original: kalā</note>.

The reasoning <note>original: upapatti</note> here is as follows: The five star-planets, though situated in their own orbits, appear to people as if they are in the lunar sky due to their great distance. Therefore, the actual diameters of their disks in <term>Yojanas</term> are known through this method. Just as the Sun's diameter in <term>Yojanas</term> was calculated in the chapter on Lunar Eclipses by multiplying by its own revolutions and so on, these are likewise calculated in the lunar orbit according to their own revolutions. Thus, it is said in the *Compendium of Śākalya*:

->Like tall trees seen from afar standing at the edge of a forest.<-
<note>This metaphor explains why distant, large objects appear small and clustered on a single visual plane.</note>

Thus, the hypotenuse is taken as half the sum of the radius and the fast hypotenuse. By rearranging the divisor and the dividend, it is proven that the diameters multiplied by the radius and doubled are divided by the sum of the radius and the fast hypotenuse.

> Half the sum of the four hypotenuses is the true hypotenuse at its peak.
> The diameters, calculated through the true hypotenuse instead of the radius, are known as the "true" diameters.

This is the view of Śākaloka. Because the disk is located on the "fast" epicycle, only the fast hypotenuse—which connects the center of the Earth to the disk—is relevant; using the "slow hypotenuse" <note>original: "mandakarṇa," related to the planet's eccentric orbit</note> is incorrect. It has not been established by any authorities that the planetary disk exists at a distance equal to half the sum of the slow and fast hypotenuses. If that were the case, one would have to accept that same logic when calculating the "fast result" <note>the equation of center</note>. > These are individually multiplied by the difference between the radius and the planet's own hypotenuse,
> and then divided by the radius or the sine of the maximum equation...

# The Surya Siddhanta

In the absence of setting <note>heliacal setting</note> caused by proximity to the Sun, the two planets become visible for observation. At that time, two gnomons <term>Shanku: a vertical pillar or gnomon used for measuring shadows</term> should be raised to a height of five cubits <term>Hasta: a unit of measurement, approximately 18-24 inches; here defined as 24 digits</term>.

A cubit consists of twenty-four digits <term>Angula: a finger-breadth</term>. Thus, two straight wooden rods five cubits in length should be fashioned as gnomons. These are to be positioned according to the directions of the compass at the time of the planets' conjunction <term>Yuti: the alignment or conjunction of two celestial bodies</term>, following the specific directional rotation of the planets. Whether the planets are located in the eastern hemisphere or the western hemisphere due to the rotation of the "Provector Wind" <term>Pravaha-bhrama: the westward cosmic wind believed to carry the planets</term>, the gnomons must be placed in the direction of the hemisphere occupied by the planets, not in the unoccupied hemisphere. The distance between the planets is determined as being in the same or different directions; if the directions are the same, the difference is taken, and if different, the sum is taken. By this method, the north-south distance between the planets in minutes of arc <note>original: "kalatmakena"</note> is known, and the two gnomons should be placed separated by that north-south distance. Here, by using the method of "with elevation" <note>referring to a specific trigonometric calculation</note>, the planetary latitude <term>Vikshepa: celestial latitude</term> is converted into digits to determine the distance between the planets. "Below, within the earth" means they are buried one cubit deep. In a pit measured to the depth of one cubit, after planting the gnomons one cubit into the ground, the gnomons will stand four cubits high above the ground. Then, from the base of each gnomon, the tip of the shadow falls in the direction of the hemisphere not occupied by the planets. From each of these shadow-tips, the mathematician should extend the "shadow-hypotenuse" <term>Chhaya-karna: the line connecting the top of the gnomon to the tip of its shadow</term> so that it reaches the head or top of its respective gnomon. This is what is being expressed:

At the time of conjunction, having calculated the Ascendant <term>Lagna: the rising sign on the eastern horizon</term>, the time elapsed since the planet's rising is determined using the current Ascendant and the rising Ascendant, as previously described, in civil time <term>Savana: solar or civil timekeeping</term>. Thus, at the moment of the planets' conjunction, the shadow is to be calculated from the day-fraction using the method taught in the "Chapter on the Three Problems" <note>Tri-prashna-adhikara: a standard section in Sanskrit astronomy dealing with time, place, and direction</note> using the true declination. Then, whichever direction the planet is in (North or South), its shadow is placed in that direction from the base of the gnomon toward the unoccupied hemisphere, adjusted by the "base" <term>Bhuja: the polar sine or side of a triangle</term> distance from the east-west line. However, since the calculated shadow is for a gnomon of twelve digits, it must be proportioned for a gnomon of four cubits, and a line should be extended...

# With the "Illumination of the Hidden Meaning" <note>original: "Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka," a famous commentary on the Sūrya Siddhānta</note>

On the ground, one should work from the base of the <term>gnomon</term> <note>a vertical rod used to cast a shadow for astronomical measurement</note>. At the end of the line and at the end of the shadow, an identifying mark should be made. There, having tied a string with a pin or similar object and extending it through the tip of the gnomon, one proceeds. At the intersection of the shadow and the <term>hypotenuse</term> <note>the diagonal line from the tip of the gnomon to the end of the shadow</note>, the shadow's tip acts as the base of the hypotenuse. The mathematician should show the visibility—that is, bring into the range of sight—the planetary positions to a student who has entered a pit made at the location of the shadow, looking along the line of the student's own head at the top of the gnomon.

The reasoning here is as follows: For the purpose of viewing at a height, the gnomons are made five cubits <note>a cubit is roughly the length of a forearm</note> in length. One cubit is buried in the ground to ensure the stability of the gnomon. The remaining four cubits are above ground, equal to the height of a man, as they are named as a substitute for a person. Because the string from the gnomon is attached to the <term>planetary disk</term> <note>the visible circular shape of a planet</note>, it is said they are positioned according to the direction of the error. Since the position of the planetary disk is fixed by the straight line of the two gnomons, they are placed separated north-to-south by the distance between the planets. Here, although one could calculate using the distance between the respective gnomons and then by the two hypotenuses, and then by calculating the respective "arms" <note>the base of the right-angled triangle in shadow calculation</note> in the stated direction using the correction for the <term>equinoctial shadow</term> <note>the shadow cast at noon on the day of the equinox</note>:

-> "If the directions are the same, the difference is the distance; if different, the sum is the distance between the planets." <-

According to this rule, the distance between the planets should be the distance between the gnomons; however, the Lord <note>referring to the divine source of the Sūrya Siddhānta</note> has used the actual visual distance between the planets in the sky to remove mathematical confusion caused by small differences. Since the hypotenuse string from the tip of the gnomon to the tip of the shadow is the pointer for seeing the planetary disk, the planet must be seen by a person looking from the base of the hypotenuse. This is the direction of the method. || 17 ||

Now, regarding the previously promised "war" <note>planetary conjunction</note> and "meeting" of the five planets, described in two verses:

-> "An 'overlap' is declared when there is contact between the stars; a 'cleaving' occurs when there is a separation." <- || 18 ||

-> "A 'war' called 'clashing of rays' occurs when their rays mutually join." <-

# The Surya Siddhanta

If the distance is less than one degree, it is called a "counter-clockwise" <note>original: apasavya</note> planetary war, provided one of the planets is smaller in size. || 18 ||
If the distance is greater than one degree, it is a "conjunction" <note>original: samāgama</note>, and both planets are then considered endowed with strength.

Among the five star-planets <note>Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn</note>, when two meet and their disks touch—specifically when the edges of their circumferences meet—those who know the secrets of conjunctions call this a "contact" <note>original: ullekha</note> type of war. This occurs when the latitudinal distance between the two is equal to the sum of their semi-diameters. When there is an actual overlapping of the disks, it is called "cleaving" <note>original: bheda</note>; this sub-type of planetary war is described by those who understand the true nature of these encounters. Now, "cleaving" occurs when the north-south distance between the two is less than the sum of their semi-diameters. On this subject, the teacher Bhaskara <note>Bhaskara II, a famous 12th-century mathematician and astronomer</note> says:

> When the distance between two celestial bodies is less than the sum of their semi-diameters, a "cleaving" conjunction occurs.
> To find the precise time, one must perform all calculations like parallax, just as in a solar eclipse.
> For the purpose of calculating parallax, the lower planet should be imagined as the Moon and the one above it as the Sun.
> However, while this is usually done from the Sun, at the time of a planetary conjunction, it must be calculated from the "imagined" Sun.
> As before, the time of the planetary conjunction, when adjusted by that parallax, becomes precise.
> Only then are those two planets fit for observation; this should be done at the exact time of the conjunction.
> In a "cleaving" conjunction, the north-south distance between the celestial bodies is known as the "deflection" <note>original: bāṇa, literally 'arrow'</note>.
> Since the Moon-like planet is relative to the Sun-like one, that determines the direction of the latitude.
> Even if a planet is slow-moving or retrograde, when it is positioned below, the contact occurs on the east and the separation on the west; this should be understood through graphical representation.

This specific detail was mentioned by Bhaskara. However, it should be noted that the Lord <note>referring to the divine origin of the Surya Siddhanta</note> likely omitted this because the distinct separation of two tiny disks in the sky is impossible to see from a distance, making such effort unnecessary. When the rays of the two planets mix during a conjunction, it is a "clashing of rays" <note>original: aṃśumarda</note> type of war. If the north-south distance between the two is less than one degree (sixty minutes of arc)—

When the difference is not excessive, the encounter is called an *apasavya* <note>original: "apasavya"; literally "to the left" or "counter-clockwise," referring to a specific southern positioning in planetary combat</note> war. Here, the author mentions a specific detail. If one of the two planets involved in this *apasavya* war is an "atom" <note>original: "anu"; referring to a planet with a very small apparent disk or diameter</note>, then the *apasavya* war is considered "manifest" (clearly visible); otherwise, it is "unmanifest." The results of these four types of encounters are as follows:

> In an *apasavya* encounter, one should predict discord; in a "clash of rays" <note>original: "rashmisankula"</note>, a battle;
> In a "marking" encounter <note>original: "lekhana"</note>, there will be suffering for ministers; but in a "piercing" <note>original: "bhedana"</note>, there is a loss of wealth.

This should be understood as stated in the *Bhargaviya* <note>An ancient astrological treatise attributed to the sage Bhrigu</note>. Having described the types of planetary war, the author now describes "meeting" (*samagama*). When the north-south distance between two planets is greater than one degree (sixty minutes), a "meeting" or union occurs. Here too, a specific detail is mentioned. The two planets involved in the conjunction must be endowed with strength.

> Those devoid of positional and other strengths are considered useless by everyone;
> In this matter, the strength of "thickness and thinness" <note>original: "sthaulyasauksmya"; referring to the apparent size or magnitude of the planetary disk</note> is also recognized.

According to this statement from the *Brahma-Siddhanta* <note>A foundational 7th-century astronomical text by Brahmagupta</note>, if the two planets are joined with large disks—meaning they are of equal, large size—then their "meeting" is manifest. Otherwise, the meeting is unmanifest.

> If both are endowed with rays, large, and bright during a meeting,
> There is mutual affection between them; if they are the opposite, they destroy their own sides.

> If a war or a meeting is unmanifest according to the technical characteristics,
> Then one should likewise declare the results for the kings on earth to be unmanifest.

As it is said:

> Piercing, marking, the clashing of rays, and the *apasavya* is the other;
> Then "union" <note>original: "yoga"</note> occurs when these happen within one degree.

# The Surya Siddhanta
<note>The Surya Siddhanta is one of the most important early Sanskrit treatises on Indian astronomy.</note>

As stated by Kashyapa <note>An ancient sage and authority on astronomy</note>, everything is flawless. || 18 || Now, the author describes the characteristics of a planet defeated in "war" <term>yuddha: a planetary conjunction where two planets appear very close in the sky</term>.

->The one defeated in a "counter-clockwise" <note>original: apasavye</note> battle is covered, minute, and lacks luster. || 20 ||<-
->Rough, discolored, shattered, and situated to the south—such is the defeated.<-

Between two planets, the one who is "shattered" or struck by the other is to be known as the conquered or defeated. The author explains the signs of being "struck." Regarding "counter-clockwise": in a counter-clockwise battle, the one who is conquered lacks the characteristics of victory. By this, it is indicated that in the three types of conjunctions like "grazing" <note>original: ullekha</note>, the result is based on the specific name of the conjunction, not the result of a defeat. "Covered" means obscured or indistinct. "Minute" means having a smaller disk <term>bimba: the visible diameter of a celestial body</term> than the other planet. "Lacking luster" means without radiance. "Rough" means not glossy or bright. "Discolored" means deprived of its natural, inherent color. "Situated to the south" means located in the southern direction relative to the other planet.

>Dark, or with rays departed, or cruel;
>Overpowered, fallen down, or moved counter-clockwise;
>Such a planet is to be known as "struck" by a planet of equal time.

This is according to the statement of Bhargaviya <note>A work attributed to the sage Bhrigu</note>. || 20 || Now, with half a verse, the author describes the characteristics of the victorious planet.

->The one situated to the north, lustrous, and large is the victor; likewise, one who is powerful even in the south. || 21 ||<-

The one situated in the northern direction relative to the other planet; "lustrous" meaning endowed with radiance; "large" meaning having a broad disk relative to the other planet's disk—that one is the victor, possessed of victory.

Now, he states that victory and defeat are not determined simply by being situated in the northern or southern directions.

Regarding the "Southern" <note>original: "yāmye"</note>: The planet which is in the southern direction, if it is powerful, radiant, and possesses a large disk <term>bimbo; the visible diameter of a planet</term>, is the victor. The word "also" <note>original: "api"</note> is used to include the northern direction as well. Thus, the implication is that merely assigning directions is insufficient for defining the characteristics of victory and defeat. || 21 ||

### Now, he describes special cases in planetary combat.

->If both planets are close and radiant, it is a "Meeting."<-
->If both are small and lusterless, they are in "Secret Conflict." || 22 ||<-

"Both" refers to the two planets. "Close" means they have entered within one degree of each other. By the use of the word "also," it is implied they are characterized by the signs of planetary combat <term>yuddha; astronomical opposition or conjunction</term>. If they are both "radiant" (endowed with brilliance), then because they possess the characteristics of strength, it is a type of combat called a "Meeting" <term>samāgama; a peaceful conjunction</term>. If both planets are "small" (having minute disks) and "lusterless" (possessing the characteristics of defeat), then they are respectively known by the names "Secret Conflict" <term>kūṭa-vigraha; a deceptive or base encounter</term>—these are the different varieties of combat. || 22 || Now, stating that Venus generally possesses the characteristics of victory, he applies the previously promised rules of "Meeting" to the Moon.

->Whether situated to the North or to the South, Venus is usually the victor.<-
->One should calculate the conjunction of these planets with the Moon in the same way. || 23 ||<-

"Whether situated to the North or to the South" means in either direction relative to other planets. Venus <note>original: "Bhārgava," a name for the planet Venus as the son of Bhrigu</note> is "usually" the victor because it generally possesses the characteristics of victory. The underlying meaning is that it only occasionally possesses the characteristics of defeat. Regarding "these" (Mars and the others)—

# The Surya Siddhanta
## Chapter on the Conjunction of Planets

The calculator should perform the calculation of the union—the method of conjunction—of the twenty-seven stars <note>original: "dvipañcatārāṇāṃ," referring to the lunar mansions or Nakshatras</note> with the Moon according to the previously stated rules. Here, there is a specific half-verse to consider:

> "In a conjunction with the Moon, the latitude is to be known as corrected by the parallax in latitude." <note>term: parallax in latitude (avanati) — the apparent shift in the position of a celestial body when viewed from the Earth's surface versus its center</note>

This half-verse is seen in some manuscripts but not everywhere; it is strange that it was overlooked by Malla <note>likely referring to the commentator Mallāri</note>. Furthermore, this would result in the chapter having an incomplete verse. It should be understood that in other types of conjunctions, the prohibition of the parallax correction is established by its omission here. If it is not explicitly mentioned, the latitude is determined generally according to the method taught in the section on solar eclipses. // 23 //

Now, an objection is raised: since these planets are always at great distances from one another in terms of height (vertical distance), a physical union is impossible. How then is a "conjunction" consistent with reality? To answer this, the text says:

-> This theory has been presented for the well-being or ill-fortune of the world. <-
-> Moving in their own paths, these planets pass at a great distance from one another. // 24 // <-

These planets move in their own paths—staying within their respective orbits—and yet at the time of conjunction, they appear to pass together as if joined, due to the lack of perceptible vertical distance from our perspective. Therefore, this "theory of planetary conjunction" is described in the preceding text as being conceptual <note>original: "kalpanātmikā," meaning modeled or symbolic rather than physically touching</note> rather than a physical reality, because they are seen at a great distance. If it is not physically real, why was it taught? The purpose is stated: "For the well-being or ill-fortune." This means that even though the conjunction is not a physical collision, it is described for the purpose of predicting the good results <note>original: "śubha-phala"</note> or evil results <note>original: "aśubha-phala"</note> for the living beings inhabiting the Earth. // 24 //

Now, to prevent any inconsistency in the upcoming text, the conclusion of the chapter is stated in a brief prose remark <note>term: phakkikā — a concise statement or scholarly explanation</note>:

-> Thus ends the Chapter on the Conjunction of Planets. <-

<summary>This page concludes the technical rules for lunar conjunctions, explaining that while planets never physically touch in space, their apparent alignment is calculated to predict astrological effects on Earth.</summary>

Regarding the phrase "at the end of Vaishva" <note>Vaishva is another name for the nakshatra Uttarashadha, whose presiding deity is the Vishvedevas</note>: the position of the junction star of **Shravana** is to be known as being at the end of **Uttarashadha**. This means the polar longitude of **Shravana** is 9 signs and 10 degrees.

He then states the polar longitude of **Dhanishtha** with the phrase "in the third and fourth quarters." At the junction of the end and beginning of the third and fourth quarters of **Shravana** respectively, at the 20th degree of the sign **Capricorn**, <unclear>Avishtha</unclear> <note>Likely a scribal error or variant for Shravishtha, another name for Dhanishtha.</note> **Dhanishtha** is to be known. This means the polar longitude of **Dhanishtha** is 9 signs and 20 degrees.

By the word "but" <note>original: "tu"</note>, the position of **Dhanishtha** within the sign of **Aquarius** is subtracted by 7 degrees minus 20 minutes. He then states the span <term>bhoga: the portion of the ecliptic occupied by a nakshatra</term> of **Shatatara**. With the phrase "from its own span": this means from the span of **Dhanishtha** up to the limit of 7 degrees minus 20 minutes of **Aquarius**. The span of **Shatatara** is 80 degrees. Therefore, to indicate that the polar longitudes are as before, he said "from its own span." The position of **Shatatara** results in the polar longitude of the hundred-star mansion.

He then states the spans of the remaining stars with the phrase "six-thirty" <note>original: "ṣaṭtriṃśat" (thirty-six)</note>. The span of **Purva Bhadrapada** is 36 minutes. That of **Uttara Bhadrapada** is 22. That of **Revati** is 79.

Now, the calculation of the polar longitudes is as follows:
The span of **Ashvini** is 48. Multiplied by ten, it is 480. Since there are no preceding stars, there is no addition of spans. Thus, the polar longitude of **Ashvini** in minutes is 480. In signs and degrees, it is 8 <note>8 degrees, as 480 minutes divided by 60 equals 8</note>.
The span of **Bharani** is 40. Multiplied by ten, it is 400. Because there is one preceding star, 800 is added; by definition, the polar longitude of **Bharani** in signs and degrees is 0 [signs] 20 [degrees].
Similarly, the span of **Ardra** is 4. Multiplied by ten, it is 40. Because there are five preceding stars, it is added to five times 800, which is 4000. The polar longitude in minutes is 4040. In signs and degrees, it is...

## With the Illuminator of Hidden Meanings Commentary

### By eight and by thirty, those two are displaced to the North.
### Having constructed the armillary sphere, one should examine the true latitude and longitude. || 12 ||

From its own position on the ecliptic <note>the sun's apparent path</note>, **Agastya** <note>the star Canopus</note> is situated at eighty degrees to the South, at the end of Gemini and the beginning of Cancer. This means the **longitude** <term>dhruvaka: the coordinate of a star measured along the ecliptic</term> of the star Agastya is three signs <note>90 degrees</note>, and its southern **latitude** <term>vikṣepa: the angular distance of a star north or south of the ecliptic</term> is eighty degrees.

**Mrigavyadha** <note>the "Deer-Hunter," known as the star Sirius</note>, also called the Hunter, is situated at the twentieth degree of the sign of Gemini. The word "and" in the verse implies a collection. This means the longitude of the star Sirius is two signs and twenty degrees <note>80 degrees total</note>. Its latitude is measured as forty degrees to the South from the ecliptic.

In the sign of Taurus, **Vahni** <note>the star Elnath</note> and **Brahmahridaya** <note>the star Capella</note> are both situated at the twenty-second degree. Thus, the longitude for both Vahni and Brahmahridaya is one sign and twenty-two degrees <note>52 degrees total</note>. Regarding those two, Vahni and Brahmahridaya: "by eight and by thirty"—the word "and" here indicates the sequence, and the word "only" is used to exclude any more or less. They are "displaced to the North," meaning they possess northern latitude. The northern latitude of Vahni is eight degrees, and the northern latitude of Brahmahridaya is thirty degrees.

Now, one might ask: are these longitudes and latitudes fixed for all time, or do they change? To this, the author says: "Having constructed the sphere." Having constructed the **armillary sphere** <term>gola-yantra: a model of objects in the sky consisting of a spherical framework of rings</term> using bamboo strips and other materials, one should examine the **true latitude** <note>adjusted for calculation</note> and the **true longitude** <note>corrected for the precession of the equinoxes</note>. One should accept what is proven by observation in one's own time. 

Because the latitudes suitable for declination circles and the longitudes adjusted for the equinoxes are unstable due to the shifting of the equinoxes, I have stated these fixed longitudes and latitudes—adjusted for visibility—according to the requirements of the present time for the sake of simplicity. In other times, these should be known through actual observation with the armillary sphere. This is the intent. Observation with the armillary sphere is performed according to the rules mentioned in the construction of the sphere...

# The Surya Siddhanta

<note>The Surya Siddhanta is one of the oldest and most significant Sanskrit treatises on Indian astronomy, dating in its current form to approximately the 4th or 5th century CE.</note>

An instrument should be constructed. Upon the sphere of the sky <note>original: "khagola," the celestial sphere</note>, place the sphere of the constellations <note>original: "bhagola," the star-sphere</note>; upon the supporting circle, place the equatorial circle. Having fixed the ecliptic <note>original: "kranti-vritta," the sun's path</note> as described, marked with the degrees of the zodiac, another moving circle—the sighting circle <note>original: "vedha-valaya"—should be attached, pierced by the poles of the axis. This sighting circle should also be marked with the degrees of the zodiac.

Then, having fixed that sighting circle so that its axis is correctly directed toward the celestial pole and the horizon circle is level with the water, one should look at the star Revati <note>Zeta Piscium, the traditional starting point for Indian longitude</note> at night through a sight-hole in the center of the sphere. One should align the point on the ecliptic ten minutes <note>arc-minutes</note> behind the end of the sign Pisces with the star Revati. 

Then, looking through that same central sight-hole at the junction star <note>term: "yoga-tara," the principal star of a lunar mansion used for measurement</note> of a constellation such as Ashvini, one should bring the sighting circle over it. When this is done, the number of degrees on the ecliptic from the end of Pisces to the point where the sighting circle intersects it are to be known as the polar longitude <note>term: "dhruvamsha," the longitude measured along the ecliptic from a fixed point</note> of that star. The degrees on the sighting circle between that intersection and the junction star are its degrees of latitude <note>term: "vikshepamsha," celestial latitude</note>, to be known as either south or north.

Now, if the observation were made with a sighting circle passing through the poles of the ecliptic <note>original: "kadamba," the ecliptic pole</note>, the longitudes would always be fixed and corrected for the precession of the equinoxes <note>original: "ayana-drik-karma"</note>. However, because the ecliptic poles are not marked by stars, this is impossible. Therefore, by the method of observation described, the longitudes and latitudes are established as corrected for precession and directed toward the celestial poles. This is the direction. || 12 ||

->Now he describes the piercing of the Cart of Rohini.<-

> ->In the seventeenth degree of Taurus, that planet whose<-
> ->southern latitude is greater than two degrees<-
> ->will pierce the Cart of Rohini. || 13 ||<-

In the seventeenth degree of the sign Taurus, if a planet has a southern latitude greater than two degrees, that planet [is said to pierce] the Cart of Rohini—the cart-shaped configuration <note>The "Cart of Rohini" refers to the V-shaped Hyades star cluster in Taurus. In Hindu astrology, a planet "piercing" this cart is considered a dire omen of famine or catastrophe.</note>.

Its southern latitude is 2 degrees; this is the clear logic established by observation. || 13 ||

Now, for the purpose of calculating the conjunction of planets, he states the extended rule for the method of calculating planetary conjunctions:

> **The astronomer should perform the visibility correction for the stars at the time of conjunction as he does for the planets. The remainder of the process is like the meeting of two planets, and the days are calculated by the planet's motion.** || 14 ||

"At the time of conjunction as he does for the planets" means that just as the measures of day and night are calculated for the planets for the sake of the visibility correction <term>Aksha-drikkarma: the correction for the observer's latitude</term>, the calculator should do the same for the polar longitudes of the lunar mansions (nakshatras). After that, having calculated the daily rising and setting of the stars as before, and having determined the "natam" <note>the hour angle or distance from the meridian</note> from the elapsed or remaining parts of the day at the desired time, he should perform the visibility correction using the formula "multiplied by the equinoctial shadow," etc. 

<margin>Here, in the example, the visibility correction for the precession of the equinoxes <term>Ayana-drikkarma</term> was also applied to the star's polar longitude by Parvata <note>likely a reference to a specific commentator or previous authority</note>; that is improper. Because that correction is already inherently established in the star's fixed polar longitude.</margin>

Following that, the "remainder"—the method for calculating the conjunction of a star and a planet where the planet becomes equal to the star's longitude—should be done according to the rules for planetary conjunctions, using the "minutes of distance between the two," and so on. 

But one might ask: in that context, the rule states:

> "The minutes of distance between the planets are multiplied by their respective motions and divided by the difference in their motions."

Since a star has no motion, what motion should be used? To this, he says: "By the planet's motion." Using only the planet's daily motion, the result (the time correction) is applied to the planet's position relative to the star's longitude until the planet becomes equal to the star's fixed position. Because the star lacks eastward motion...

# The Treatise of the Sun

The meaning is that the fixed star <term>Dhruva</term> remains in its established position relative to the ecliptic. Now, a minor doubt may arise: how can one calculate the time of conjunction between a planet and a star since there is no "difference in motion" <note>usually, conjunctions are calculated by the closing speed of two moving bodies; here, the star is stationary</note>? To address this, the text says: "The days..." and so on. By using the motion of the planet alone, the days of conjunction between the planet and the star are to be calculated. The word "and" implies the inclusion of other factors. This is because the stars lack motion of their own. || 14 ||

Now, to prevent confusion regarding whether the time of conjunction between a planet and a star has passed or is yet to come relative to the desired time, the author says:

-> If the planet's position is less than the star's longitude, the conjunction is in the future; if greater, it has passed. <-
-> In the case of a planet in retrograde motion, the opposite is to be understood. || 15 || <-

The planet's position refers to the planet as processed by the "visibility corrections" <term>Drikkarma</term> <note>mathematical adjustments to account for the observer's latitude and the ecliptic's tilt</note> relative to the fixed star's longitude. To be precise: the planet is processed by both types of visibility corrections. When this value is less than the star's longitude, the conjunction between the star and the planet will occur after the desired time. When it is greater, the conjunction has already occurred. In the case of a planet with retrograde motion <term>Vakragati</term>, the conjunction is known by the reverse of what was stated: if the planet's position is less, it has passed; if greater, it is in the future. The logic here is very easy to understand: since the star is always fixed due to its lack of motion, the conjunction occurs solely through the movement of the planet. || 15 ||

Now, since constellations like Ashvini consist of many stars, one might ask: "To which specific star do these coordinates belong?" Keeping the answer "the coordinates of the Junction-Star" <term>Yogatara</term> in mind, and wishing to specify the Junction-Stars for Ashvini and the others, the author first identifies the Junction-Stars for these specific groups:

-> Of the two Phalgunis, the two Bhadrapadas, and likewise the two Ashadhas, <-
-> as well as of Vishakha, Ashvini, and Saumya <note>another name for Mrigashira</note>, the northern star is recorded as the Junction-Star. || 16 || <-

Thus ends the Chapter on the Conjunction of Stars and Planets in the *Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka* composed by the poet Ranganātha, son of the venerable Ballāla Daivajña, the sovereign of all calculators <note>term: "gaṇaka" (astronomer-mathematician)</note>.

Now, the Chapter on Rising and Setting <note>term: "Udayāstādhikāra"</note> is explained. One might ask: since it was previously stated that "setting occurs with the Sun," shouldn't the chapter on rising and setting have been described immediately after the chapter on planetary conjunctions, rather than after the chapter on star-planet conjunctions? To demonstrate the proper connection here, the author first introduces that chapter:

> Now, the knowledge of the rising and setting is proclaimed,
> regarding those bodies of little luster whose forms are overcome by the rays of the Sun. || 1 ||

"Now," meaning after the chapter on the conjunction of stars and planets. "Whose forms"—their disks—"are overcome by the rays of the Sun" refers to the six planets beginning with the Moon, as well as the stars. For this reason, they possess "little luster" or diminished brilliance. Regarding their "rising and setting": because of the possibility of them being more or less near to the Sun in the coming time, the rising and setting occur in sequence. For one who has emerged from the Sun, at whatever time and at whatever distance the first visibility is possible—

# The Surya Siddhanta
<note>original: "सूर्यसिद्धान्तः" - The "Sun Treatise," one of the most foundational texts of Indian astronomy.</note>

That is the rising. The time at which a planet, being at a certain distance from the Sun, is first capable of being seen is its rising; the opposite is its setting. By this, the distinction between their daily rising and setting is meant. The method of precise knowledge—the manner of subtle calculation—is now proclaimed. The meaning is that it is being told by me with extreme precision. And so, although the "planets" were mentioned in the introductory sequence, because their visibility is only possible when near the Sun, this topic is discussed following the section on planetary conjunctions <note>original: "ग्रहयुति" - the alignment of two celestial bodies</note>. The conjunction of stars and planets was said to be like the conjunction of planets. Therefore, even if the curiosity of the student has been satisfied, this must be spoken of as it is the proper occasion; following the chapter on the conjunction of stars and planets, the previously mentioned "setting" and, by association, the "rising" are now established. || 1 ||

First, he speaks of the western setting and eastern rising of the five stars <note>The "five stars" refer to the visible planets: Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn.</note>.

> When their longitude is greater than the Sun's, Jupiter, Mars, and Saturn set in the west.
> When their longitude is less, they rise in the east. So too do Venus and Mercury when moving in retrograde. || 2 ||

Venus and Mercury in retrograde motion <note>term: "वक्रगति" (Vakragati) - Retrograde motion, where a planet appears to move backward against the stars from Earth's perspective.</note> act similarly. When greater than the Sun, they go to a western setting. When less than the Sun, they attain an eastern rising. The rest is clear. || 2 || Now, he speaks of the eastern setting and western rising of the Moon, Mercury, and Venus.

> When their longitude is less than the Sun's, the Moon, Mercury, and Venus set in the east.
> When their longitude is greater, these fast-moving bodies rise in the west. || 3 ||

"Fast-moving" <note>original: "शीघ्रयायिनः" (Shighrayayinah)</note> means those whose motion is greater than the Sun's motion. By this, it is said that when Mercury and Venus move slower than the Sun's motion, they do not attain an eastern setting when less than the Sun, nor a western rising when greater. The rest is clear. Here is the rationale: when a body moving slower than the Sun is less than the Sun, it becomes capable of being seen in the east.

<header>Accompanied by the Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka <note>The "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings," a famous 17th-century commentary by Raṅganātha</note>.</header>

Because of the difference in speed between the Sun and a planet, and because the faster motion leads to an ever-increasing separation <note>original: "viprakarṣa"</note>, there is a rule that the one with the lesser longitudinal position rises first due to the power of the *Pravaha* wind <note>The cosmic wind believed in ancient Indian astronomy to drive the daily rotation of the celestial sphere</note>, and the one with the greater position rises after. Visibility is possible during that interval of separation between the time the planet is connected to its declination and the time the Sun reaches a similar position. 

Thus, when a slow-moving planet has a greater longitude than the Sun, the Sun rises first due to the *Pravaha* wind, and the planet is seen rising afterward. Similarly, the Sun (having lesser longitude) sets first, and the planet (having greater longitude) sets later. Even though the planet might be seen in the western sky after the Sun, if the Sun is moving faster and is behind the planet, it will continually get closer <note>original: "sannikarṣa"</note> until the planet becomes invisible in the west. These planets are Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn <note>original: "Bhauma-Guru-Śani"</note>. Mercury and Venus <note>original: "Budha-Śukra"</note> also behave this way when they are in retrograde motion <note>term: retrograde (vakra) - when a planet appears to move backward in the sky from the perspective of Earth</note> due to their reduced speed. 

Now, if a planet moving faster than the Sun has a lesser longitude than the Sun, it will become invisible in the east because it is continually getting closer to the Sun. When such a planet has a greater longitude than the Sun, it rises in the west because the separation is continually increasing. These fast-moving bodies are the Moon, Mercury, and Venus. Thus, the explanation is consistent. || 3 ||

Now, the author explains that on the desired day, the positions of the Sun and the "visible planet" <note>the planet adjusted for observational reality</note> must be calculated for the time of sunrise or sunset to determine the visibility at that moment:

---

-> **For the west, the Sun and the planet should be calculated for the time of sunset;** <-
-> **For the east, they should be calculated for the time of sunrise, specifically for the visibility correction of the planet. || 4 ||** <-

---

In the calculation of the western setting or rising, the astronomer should calculate the positions of the Sun and the planet for the time of sunset on the chosen day. For the calculation of the eastern setting or rising, he should calculate them for the time of sunrise. He should perform this for the desired time of day. The word "and" <note>original: "ca"</note> implies...

...meaning the purpose of the calculation. After this, the <term>visibility correction</term><note>Sanskrit: drkkarma; the process of adjusting a planet's longitude to account for its latitude and the observer's location on Earth</note> of the planet is performed. One should perform both types of visibility corrections: the <term>ecliptic correction</term><note>Sanskrit: ayana-drkkarma; correction for the obliquity of the ecliptic</note> and the <term>terrestrial correction</term><note>Sanskrit: aksha-drkkarma; correction for the observer's latitude</note>.

The syllable "tu" <insert>in the verse</insert> is used for emphasis, referring specifically to what was stated in the first half of the verse regarding the terrestrial correction. Here is the rationale: In calculating the rising and setting in the west, the observation occurs in the western direction; therefore, the Sun and the planet at the time of sunset are established to calculate the desired <term>degrees of time</term><note>Sanskrit: kalamsas; units used to measure the distance between the Sun and a planet required for visibility</note>. In calculating the rising in the east, the observation occurs in the eastern direction; therefore, the Sun and the planet at the time of sunrise are required to be precise for calculating the remaining degrees of time, though even if they are slightly approximate, they are used. A planet processed by the visibility correction is rendered capable of touching the horizon just like the Sun; thus, the planet must be processed by these corrections. || 4 ||

Now, he describes the calculation of the desired degrees of time:

-> Then, the <term>respirations</term><note>Sanskrit: pranas; a unit of time equal to 4 seconds, or 1 minute of arc of the celestial equator</note> of the difference in their rising signs, divided by sixty, are the degrees of time. <-
-> In the west, the same is done for the two <insert>the Sun and the planet</insert> increased by six signs. || 5 || <-

Then, from those two—the Sun and the planet corrected for visibility—the respirations of the difference in their rising signs are found. As previously stated in the method "by the remaining respirations of the sign to be passed," the respirations of the interval of time are divided by sixty to become the desired degrees of time. This applies to calculating the rising and setting in the east. In the west, for calculating the western rising and setting, the respirations of the difference in rising signs are calculated from the Sun and the corrected planet both increased by six signs <note>original: "shadrasi-yuktayoh"; adding six signs or 180 degrees effectively looks at the opposite point on the zodiac to calculate setting times using rising tables</note>. The meaning is that those interval-respirations, similarly divided by sixty, become the desired degrees of time.

Here is the rationale: The interval of time between the planet corrected for visibility and the Sun is used for the purpose of eastern rising and setting, representing the time elapsed in the day at the moment of sunrise. Similarly, for the purpose of western rising and setting, the interval of time between the Sun and the corrected planet—calculated via the respirations of the setting time—represents the time remaining in the day for the planet at the moment of sunset. Since there is no separate formula for calculating setting times, the Sun and the corrected planet are increased by six signs so that <insert>the calculation can be performed using rising times</insert>. # Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings"
<note>original: "Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka" — this refers to the famous commentary by Raṅganātha on the Sūrya Siddhānta.</note>
## 21

Time is expressed in degrees. Since the degrees of the celestial circle are obtained through the breaths <note>term: Prāṇa/Asu — a unit of time equal to 4 seconds, or the time taken for one breath</note> of a full day and night, which are equal to the minutes of the circle, we use a proportion: if the total breaths of a day yield the full circle, what do the desired breaths yield? By simplifying the ratio of the measure and the result, the number sixty remains in the place of the divisor. Therefore, the interval of time in degrees divided by sixty gives the desired time-degrees; this is logically proven.

Here, the following should be considered: The visible planet <note>term: Dṛggraha — the planet's position as corrected for observation</note> should first be moved backward by the elapsed portion of the day calculated from the positions of the Sun and the visible planet at the time of sunrise. Using the positions of the Sun and the visible planet (each increased by six signs <note>note: adding six signs or 180 degrees finds the point exactly opposite on the zodiac, used for sunset calculations</note>) at the time of sunset, the visible planet increased by six signs should be moved forward by the remaining portion of the day. 

In this sequence, the eastern and western visible planets are determined at the times of the planet's rising and setting. From these and from the Sun (or the Sun plus six signs), the interval of time is calculated as before at the times of sunrise and sunset. These elapsed or remaining portions of the day are sidereal <note>term: Nākṣatra — based on the stars rather than the solar day</note>; when divided by sixty, they yield the precise desired time-degrees. 

Now, the time-degrees calculated from positions at a single moment are nearly precise. However, because they lack a direct connection to the specific moment of sunrise or sunset, the resulting time-degrees are only approximate. Furthermore, time-degrees calculated only once from sunrise/sunset positions are "gross" <note>note: "sthūla" — meaning mathematically unrefined or approximate</note>, and those calculated from any random desired time are extremely gross, because in both cases the time used is civil time <note>term: Sāvana — the time from one sunrise to the next</note>. The completion of the celestial circle does not occur in exactly sixty civil hours <note>term: Ghaṭī — a unit of 24 minutes; 60 ghaṭīs make one day</note>, which is why the traditional doctrine states they are not precise. || 5 ||

Next, wishing to describe the specific time-degrees at which a planet rises or sets, the author first states the time-degrees for Jupiter, Saturn, and Mars:

---

-> **Eleven for Jupiter, and the number of lunar days (fourteen) for Saturn.** <-
-> **Eight degrees for the son of the Earth (Mars); then, ten plus seven (seventeen) for the others.** <-
<note>This verse defines the "visibility gap"—how many degrees away from the Sun a planet must be to be seen by the naked eye.</note>

|| 6 ||

Then, after understanding the degrees of the desired time, the degrees of setting are discussed. The degrees by which the setting occurs should also be understood as the degrees of rising, based on the characteristics of the setting. For Jupiter <note>original: "Amarejya" or "Guru"</note>, there are eleven <term>degrees of time</term> <note>Kālāṃśas: units used to measure the distance from the Sun required for a planet to become visible to the naked eye</note>. For Saturn, the number of degrees of time is fifteen. The word "and" implies a grouping. For Mars, it is ten plus seven, meaning seventeen degrees of time. || 6 ||

### Now, regarding Venus:

> Venus sets in the west and rises in the east at eight degrees due to its great size.
> It sets in the east and rises in the west at ten degrees due to its smallness. || 7 ||

Because of the greatness of Venus—being near its perigee <note>lowest point in its orbit relative to Earth</note> while in retrograde—it has a thick disk; therefore, its setting in the west and its rising in the east occur at eight degrees of time. Not more. When Venus is "small" <note>appearing smaller in the sky</note> due to having a minute disk, the calculator should determine its setting in the east at ten degrees of time. Not otherwise. Its rising in the west, when the disk is minute, is also to be known at exactly ten degrees of time. || 7 || ### Now, regarding Mercury:

> Similarly, Mercury, at twelve and fourteen degrees,
> being retrograde or fast-moving, performs its settings and risings from the Sun. || 8 ||

Retrograde and fast-moving. The word "and" implies a grouping. Mercury performs its settings and risings from the Sun at twelve and fourteen degrees of time. It does so in the same manner as Venus. Mercury performs its western setting and eastern rising at twelve degrees of time due to its large disk. It performs its eastern setting and western rising at fourteen degrees of time due to its minute disk—

This is what the wise practitioner does. || 8 || Now, the author explains how to determine whether the rising or setting of a planet has already occurred or is yet to happen, based on the calculated <term>time-degrees</term> <note>kalabhaga: a measure of the arc of separation between the Sun and a planet expressed in time units</note> at the desired moment.

->When the <term>time-degrees</term> are greater than these, the <term>planets</term> <note>khachara: literally 'sky-goers'</note> are visible;<-
->when less, they are invisible in the world, their forms overwhelmed by the Sun's brilliance. || 9 ||<-

When the calculated <term>time-degrees</term> at the desired time are greater than those mentioned in the previous three verses (beginning with "Eleven for Jupiter..."), the planets are visible—that is, capable of being seen—at that time. The implication is this: in the calculation for "setting," if the planet is visible, the setting is yet to come <note>future/prospective</note>. In the calculation for "rising," if the planet is visible, the rising has already occurred <note>past</note>. 

With fewer <term>time-degrees</term>, the planets are "invisible" in the world—meaning they are not within the range of sight at the desired time. If one asks why they are invisible, the text says: "their forms are overwhelmed by the Sun's brilliance." This means their bodies or disks are overpowered by the intensity of the Sun's rays due to their proximity to it, making them impossible for the eye to perceive as the light strikes the observer. 

The implication here is: in the calculation for "setting," if the planet is invisible, the setting has already occurred. In the calculation for "rising," if the planet is invisible, the rising is yet to come. Therefore, the statement by the teacher Bhaskara <note>Bhaskaracharya, the famous 12th-century mathematician and astronomer</note> is consistent:

> If the calculated degrees are less or more than those stated,
> then the <term>rising of the planet</term> <note>khetodyo</note> is respectively yet to come or already past.
> The opposite is to be understood for the setting.

The underlying logic <note>upapatti</note> is as follows: At the moment when the calculated <term>time-degrees</term> are exactly equal to the stated required degrees, the rising or setting of the planet caused by the Sun occurs. This is because the stated <term>time-degrees</term> are established as the cause for the first or last visibility of a planet due to its proximity to the Sun. Thus, if the calculated degrees are less than those stated, the planet is certainly obscured. Therefore, in the calculation of rising, if the calculated degrees...

# The Treatise of the Sun

If the degrees at the desired time are less than those stated, the rising of the planet occurs after that desired time. If the degrees at the desired time are greater than those stated, the rising of the planet has already occurred before the desired time. Similarly, in the calculation of the setting: if the degrees at the desired time are greater, the setting of the planet will occur after the desired time. If the degrees at the desired time are less, the setting of the planet has already occurred before the desired time. This is the established explanation. || 9 || Now, he describes the method for bringing forth the days and other units of time that have passed or are yet to come for the rising and setting.

-> The minutes of the difference between the degrees of that time are divided by the difference in the daily motions <note>original: "bhuktyantara"</note>. The result obtained is the days and other units. In the case of a planet in retrograde motion <note>original: "vakriṇas"</note>, the division is by the sum of the daily motions. || 10 || <-

The minutes of the difference between the stated degrees and the degrees at the desired time are divided by the difference in minutes of the daily motions of the Sun and the planet. The result is the days and other units of the rising and setting; this means it is the time passed or remaining for the rising and setting. He mentions a specific rule for a planet with retrograde motion: "The result obtained." For a retrograde planet, the minutes of the difference are divided by the sum of the daily motions <note>term: "bhukti" - the daily angular motion of a celestial body</note> of the Sun and the planet, and the result should be known as the days passed or remaining.

Here is the underlying logic <note>original: "upapatti"</note>: If one day is obtained by the difference in the motions of the Sun and the planet, then what is obtained by the minutes of the difference between the desired and stated degrees of time? By this proportion <note>term: "anupāta" - rule of three or mathematical proportion</note>, one understands the days passed or remaining for the rising and setting from the desired time. However, for a retrograde planet, because the distance between them increases daily by the sum of the motions of the Sun and the planet, the proportion using the sum of motions is logical; thus, the explanation is established. || 10 ||

Now, keeping in mind that the minutes of the planets' motions are located on the Ecliptic <note>term: "krāntivṛtta" - the sun's apparent path</note>, while the difference in the degrees of time is located on the diurnal circle <note>the circle of daily rotation</note>, a proportion between them might be considered improper due to the difference in the nature of the measure and the requirement. To make them of the same class, he describes the daily motions as being of the same nature as the requirement, and states that the proportion using their difference is indeed proper.

-> The two daily motions are multiplied by the shadow <note>the equinoctial midday shadow</note> and divided by 1,800. These become the "time-motions." With these two, the days and other units of the past and future are determined. || 11 || <-

# With the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings" <note>original: "Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka," the name of Ranganatha's famous commentary on the Surya Siddhanta</note>

Regarding the motion of the Sun and Moon during the period of consumption <note>the time they are obscured by the horizon or light</note>, the motion is expressed in minutes of arc. To determine the time, multiply the motion of the planet by the rising time of the zodiac sign <note>original: "rāśyudaya"</note> in which the planet is situated, and divide the product by 1800 <note>the number of minutes in one zodiac sign, 30 degrees × 60 minutes</note>. The resulting values represent the time-degrees <note>original: "kālāṃśa," a unit where 1 degree equals 4 minutes of time</note> for the Sun and the planets. Using these two motions, the days elapsed or remaining until the rising or setting should be calculated according to the previously stated method. One should not use the raw, instantaneous motions as previously described, as that would lead to inaccuracy. 

The mathematical proof is as follows: If the minutes of one zodiac sign correspond to the rising time of that sign in breaths <note>original: "asava," a unit of time</note>, then how many breaths correspond to the minutes of the planet's motion? By this proportion, the motion-breaths on the diurnal circle are determined to be equal to the minutes; thus, the statement is proven. || 11 ||

Now, wishing to explain the knowledge of the rising of the stars <note>original: "nakṣatras"</note> due to their proximity to the Sun, the author first states the following:

-> Arcturus, Canopus, Orion, Sirius, Spica, Antares, Pollux, <-
-> Vega, and Capella become visible at thirteen degrees. <- || 12 ||

"The Hunter" <note>original: "Mṛgavyādha"</note> refers to Sirius. At thirteen time-degrees, these stars become visible or invisible <note>depending on whether they are emerging from or entering the Sun's glare</note>. The rest is clear. || 12 ||

# The Surya Siddhanta
<note>The Surya Siddhanta is one of the most important early Sanskrit treatises on Indian astronomy, dating in its current form to roughly the 4th-5th century CE.</note>

> The Pleiades, Anuradha, Mula, Ashlesha, and Ardra,
> as well as the three beginning with Ashadha,
> are seen at fifteen degrees. || 14 ||

The stars <term>Krittika</term> <note>the Pleiades</note>, <term>Anuradha</term> <note>in Scorpio</note>, and <term>Mula</term> <note>near the galactic center</note> become visible when they are fifteen <term>degrees of time</term> <note>Kalanshas; units of time where 1 degree equals 4 minutes, representing the sun's distance below the horizon</note> away from the Sun. By implication, they also become invisible at this same distance. The word "only" <note>original: "evakāra"</note> is used to exclude any more or less than this amount. <term>Ashlesha</term> <note>in Hydra</note> and <term>Ardra</term> <note>Betelgeuse</note> are also included here. The word "and" <note>original: "ca"</note> serves to group them together. Likewise, the "three beginning with Ashadha"—meaning the two <term>Ashadhas</term> <note>Purva and Uttara Ashadha in Sagittarius</note>—become visible at fifteen degrees of time. || 14 || Now, the author speaks of the remaining stars.

> Bharani, Pushya, and Mrigashira,
> due to their faintness, at twenty-one degrees;
> the remaining stars become visible or invisible at seventeen. || 15 ||

<term>Tishya</term> <note>another name for the star Pushya in Cancer</note> and <term>Mrigashira</term> <note>the "Deer's Head" in Orion</note>, whose deity is Soma—these stars, because of their "faintness" <note>original: "sauksmya"</note> or the small size of their discs, become visible or invisible at twenty-one degrees of time <note>literally "three times seven"</note>. This means they rise or set heliacally at that distance. The "remaining" stars—those not mentioned in the previous categories, such as <term>Shatabhisha</term> <note>in Aquarius</note>, the two <term>Bhadrapadas</term> <note>Pegasus/Andromeda</note>, and <term>Revati</term> <note>Pisces</note>, as well as the stars named <term>Vashistha</term>, <term>Brahma</term>, <term>Apamvatsa</term>, and <term>Apa</term>—become visible or invisible at seventeen degrees of time. The word "but" <note>original: "tu"</note> here serves to connect the states of visibility and invisibility. || 15 || Now, for the purpose of calculating the day and time, the author describes the conversion of these degrees into "degrees of the ecliptic."

> The degrees of visibility multiplied by eighteen hundred,
> and divided by the rising period of the sign in breaths,
> result in the degrees of the ecliptic; by these, visibility is determined. || 16 ||

The "degrees of visibility" (the degrees of time) are multiplied by 1,800. These are then divided by the "rising period in breaths" <note>original: "svodayasubhih"; the time it takes for a zodiac sign to rise at a specific latitude, measured in pranas or breaths</note>. The result is the "degrees of the ecliptic" <note>Kshetramshas</note> for the desired star <unclear>...desired star...</unclear>

# With the Gudharthaprakashaka commentary.

The visibility or invisibility [of planets] is determined by their previous positions. Their rising and setting should be understood according to the method previously described. By taking the degrees of time <note>original: "kalansha"; these are units of time converted into arc to determine how far a planet must be from the sun to be visible</note> and deriving the degrees of the planet, the difference in minutes—divided by the sum or difference of their daily motions—yields the days past or remaining until the rising or setting. This is exactly as stated before. 

The reasoning here is as follows: If the rising time of a zodiac sign corresponds to the minutes of one sign, then what would correspond to the minutes of the degrees of time? The resulting minutes on the ecliptic <note>the sun's apparent path</note>, when divided by sixty, give the degrees. In the previous explanation, the degrees of time were used directly for the sake of brevity. Thus, what was stated is logically established. || 16 ||

Now, it has been stated in which direction the planets set and in which they rise. However, this has not been specified for the fixed stars <note>original: "nakshatras"</note>. Since they lack independent motion, the calculation of days past or remaining (based on the closing of a gap between two moving bodies) seems impossible. To address this, the author says:

->Their rising is in the East and their setting is in the West; the visibility correction is as before.<-
->The determination of days past or remaining is always through the motion of the Sun alone. || 17 ||<-

The rising of these stars is in the East and their setting is in the West, because they lack the motion that planets have. The visibility correction <term>Drkkarma: a mathematical adjustment to account for the latitude of a star or planet to find its true rising/setting time</term> for these stars should be performed as previously described. However, one should keep in mind what was stated in the first half of the verse. "Always" means eternally; the word "indeed" emphasizes that it is never otherwise. The calculation of days past or remaining is achieved solely through the motion of the Sun, since the stars do not move. In the case of planetary conjunctions, the motion of both bodies is used, but here only the Sun's motion applies. || 17 ||

Next, he names certain stars that never set <note>i.e., they are circumpolar or far enough north to remain visible</note> despite their proximity to the Sun:

->Abhijit, Brahmahrdaya, Svati, Vaishnava, Vasava,<-
->and Ahirbudhnya, because of their northern position,<-
->are not obscured by the rays of the Sun. || 18 ||<-

<note>These stars correspond to: Abhijit (Vega), Brahmahrdaya (Capella), Svati (Arcturus), Vaishnava (Shravana/Altair), Vasava (Dhanishta/Delphinus), and Ahirbudhnya (Uttara Bhadrapada/Pegasus-Andromeda). Their high northern declination keeps them above the horizon in northern latitudes even when the Sun is nearby.</note>

<summary>This page explains the mathematical calculation for the rising and setting of stars, noting that unlike planets, stars are fixed and their visibility depends entirely on the Sun's motion. It also lists specific northern stars that remain visible year-round and are never "lost" in the Sun's glare.</summary>

# The Surya Siddhanta

Abhijit <note>The star Vega</note>. Brahma-hridaya <note>The star Capella</note>. By this term, even a portion of the Creator [Brahma] is understood. Svati <note>Arcturus</note>, Shravana <note>Altair</note>, and Dhanishtha <note>Alpha Delphini</note>. Ahirbudhnya is Uttara-bhadrapada <note>Gamma Pegasi/Andromedae</note>. These lunar mansions <note>nakshatras</note>, because of their northern position—meaning their high northern latitude—are not obscured by the rays of the Sun. This means they do not undergo "setting" <note>heliacal setting, where a star becomes invisible due to the Sun's proximity</note>. Here is the mathematical rationale:

->When the setting-sun value is greater than the rising-sun value,<-
->produced by the great length of the northern latitude,<-
->then by the influence of the Sun's proximity,<-
->there is no possible way for that star to set.<-

This was stated by the teacher Bhaskaracharya <note>A famous 12th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note>. However, this specific point was mentioned in the *Ashtabhraya*. Otherwise, one would fall into the error of assuming the same for Purva-bhadrapada as well. This is the general direction of the argument. || 18 ||

Now, to prevent any inconsistency in the subsequent text, the concluding phrase of the chapter is stated:

## Thus ends the Chapter on Rising and Setting.

Because the rising and setting of both the lunar mansions and the planets have been described, this is collectively called the "Chapter on Rising and Setting" <term>Udayastadhikara: the section of astronomical treatises dealing with the visibility of celestial bodies relative to the Sun</term>.

->In this commentary on the Surya Siddhanta composed by Ranganatha,<-
->this Chapter on Rising and Setting is completed in the "Gudharthaprakashaka" <note>The Illuminator of Hidden Meanings</note>.<-

Thus ends the Chapter on Rising and Setting in the *Gudharthaprakashaka*, composed by the astronomer Ranganatha, son of the astronomer Ballala, the sovereign of all calculators <note>mathematicians/astronomers</note>.
