<meta>This page continues the commentary on the Sūrya-Siddhānta, specifically focusing on the dialogue between the demon-architect Maya and the emanation of the Sun God regarding the nature of solar radiation and time.</meta>

<page-num>28</page-num>
<header>Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings" <note>original: Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka, the title of the commentary</note>.</header>

<sig>2 p 2</sig>

## Accompanied by the Illuminator of Hidden Meanings.

Why is it that in the summer season the Sun possesses such sharp and hot rays, whereas in the winter it is not so? What is the reach and the path of travel of the Sun's rays, and what is their measurement? The essence is that these measurements have been stated and are thus properly understood. What is the purpose of these measurements? The word "and" <note>original: "ca"</note> is used in a cumulative sense and applies to each point individually. || 8 || Now, he concludes his question:

->**O Blessed Lord, Creator of Beings, cut through this doubt of mine.**<-
->**Other than You, there is no one to be found who can remove it, for You see all. || 9 ||**<-

O Blessed Lord <note>original: Bhagavan</note>, endowed with the six-fold lordly powers. The implied meaning is "O Teacher of All." Creator of Beings <note>original: Bhūtabhāvana</note>—one whose contemplation <note>original: bhāvanā</note> encompasses the past <note>original: bhūta</note>. By implication, since he knows the past, it is established that he is the knower of the present and future as well. For me—that is, for my sake. This aforementioned doubt. The singular form is used here to represent a category; therefore, it means "these questions asked by me." Cut through—meaning, destroy the doubt. Now, if one were to say, "I cannot speak further having just said this, seek the removal of your doubts from another," he responds with: "Other than." Without You. No other "All-Seeing One"—meaning one who perceives everything. An omniscient being, in other words. A "cutter"—one who removes doubts. Does not exist—is not found. And so, the sentiment is: "Just as You have spoken until now, please kindly speak on the rest as well." || 9 ||

Now, the Sage <note>the narrator</note>, having repeated the questions asked by Maya to the other sages, describes what the Man-who-is-a-part-of-the-Sun <note>original: Sūryāṃśa-puruṣa</note> said in return to Maya:

->**Having heard these words spoken by Maya with devotion,**<-
->**He then spoke to him again regarding the supreme, hidden spiritual mystery. || 10 ||**<-

<summary>This page features the conclusion of Maya's inquiry into the varying intensity of solar heat and his plea for the Sun's emanation to resolve his doubts, highlighting the teacher's omniscience. It marks the transition to the revelation of "supreme spiritual mysteries" in response to Maya's devotion.</summary>

# The Treatise of the Sun

That being who is an incarnation of the Sun's own rays <note>original: "Suryansha-purusha"</note>—as previously mentioned—having heard the words spoken by Maya, who had attained knowledge through devoted worship, spoke again. After the conclusion of the first part, he addressed the demon-sage Maya <note>Maya is often described as an 'Asura' or architect of the gods/demons in Vedic lore</note> regarding the second part of the text. This means he spoke the latter section of the book. He spoke with great clarity, revealing the secret essence <note>original: "rahasyam"</note> of the first part of this work. || 10 || Now, he describes how Maya must listen attentively to what the solar being is about to say:

> Listen with a focused mind to the secret known as the Supreme Self <note>original: "adhyatma"</note>.
> I shall speak to those who are deeply devoted; for me, there is nothing that cannot be given to them. || 11 ||

For this reason: to those who are extremely devoted, who perform my worship like you do, there is nothing that I, the solar being, should withhold. Therefore, I shall tell you the secret known as the knowledge of the Supreme Self. You must listen with a "one-pointed mind"—meaning a mind entirely fixed on my words—by joining your inner self and mind through the gateway of your ears. || 11 || Regarding the "secret" he promised to speak of, he says:

> Vasudeva is the Supreme Absolute <note>original: "Brahman"</note>; His form is the Supreme Spirit.
> He is unmanifest, without qualities, peaceful, beyond the twenty-five principles, and imperishable. || 12 ||

He is called "Vasu" because the entire universe dwells within Him, or He dwells within the entire universe. He is "Deva" because of His shining or illuminating nature. Thus, He is "Vasudeva" <note>A name for the Divine, often identified with Vishnu or Krishna, representing the omnipresent consciousness</note>. And so it has been said:

# Accompanied by the Illuminator of Hidden Meanings

> Because He dwells everywhere and everything dwells in Him,
> Therefore, He is sung of by the wise as "Vasudeva."
<note>original: "वासुदेवाख्यो" (Vasudevakhyo). The author is providing a philosophical etymology: 'Vas' means to dwell, and 'Deva' means the shining one/Lord.</note>

Thus it is said. The term is not to be analyzed here as "the son of Vasudeva" <note>original: "वसुदेवस्यापत्यमिति" (Vasudevasyapatyamiti). In common mythology, Vasudeva is the father of Krishna, but in this high-philosophy context, the author rejects the patronymic definition in favor of a cosmic one.</note>. This is because such a definition is useless when describing Him as the Cause of the Universe. However, even without repeating the material cause, He is indeed suitable as the substratum of the effect, or because the material cause is woven into the effect.

As it is said in the *Shruti* <term>Shruti: "That which is heard," referring to the Vedas as authoritative revealed scripture</term>: "All this is inhabited by the Lord," and so on. And in the *Bhagavata*: "That from which the world is born is not separate from it, O King." Even for individual souls, because they are essentially Brahman <note>original: "ब्रह्मात्मकतया" (brahmatmakataya)</note>, the term "Supreme" is used to mean "the highest of all" for their support.

> Because I transcend the perishable and am higher than even the imperishable,
> Therefore, in the Vedas and in the world, I am celebrated as the Supreme Person.
<note>original: "पुरुषोत्तमः" (Purushottama). This is a famous quote from the Bhagavad Gita 15.18.</note>

Thus says the *Smriti* <term>Smriti: "That which is remembered," referring to secondary scriptures like the Gita or Puranas</term>. "His form" refers to a portion or manifestation of that Vasudeva. This adjective applies to Sankarshana <note>The second of the four primary emanations in Vaishnava theology</note>, who will be discussed next. The reading "Form of Consciousness" <note>original: "चिन्मूर्तिरिति" (cinmurtiriti)</note> is a scribal error. This is because the intended meaning—that Sankarshana arises from Vasudeva—would not be understood from such a reading. "Unmanifest" <note>original: "अव्यक्त" (avyakta)</note> means beyond the reach of the senses. As the *Shruti* says:

> You do not know Him who created these things; something else has come between you.
> Enveloped in mist and idle talk, the singers of hymns wander, seeking to satisfy their appetites.

> His form does not stand within the range of sight; no one perceives Him with the eye.

The reason for His being unmanifest is that He is "without qualities" <note>original: "निर्गुण" (nirguna)</note>. He is "Peaceful" because He is free from the six waves of existence <note>The six "waves" (urmi) are hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, old age, and death.</note>. He is "Beyond the twenty-fifth." The twenty-four principles <term>Tattvas: the building blocks of reality in Samkhya philosophy</term> consist of the sixteen transformations, the seven nature-transformations, and Primordial Nature. The twenty-fifth is the individual soul; He is "Beyond" that. In the version that reads "Consisting of the twenty-five," it means He is the essence of the entire world. || 12 ||

Since the Pure Brahman cannot [directly] be the cause of the world, the author says:

It uses Vedic and Gita citations to establish the Supreme Being as transcending both the material world and the individual soul.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the cosmological narrative of the Surya Siddhanta, detailing the transition from the unmanifest divine to the creation of the Golden Egg and the emergence of the solar deity.</meta>

### The Divine, residing within Nature, both outside and within, all-pervading;
### This Sankarshana, at the beginning of the creative process, cast his seed into the waters. || 13 ||

"Residing within Nature" means being covered by the creative illusion <note>Sanskrit: Maya</note>. He is "outside and within" and "all-pervading" because he is the material cause of the universe. All these attributes of Sankarshana <note>A form of the divine associated with cosmic ego and strength</note> should be understood as identical to Vasudeva <note>The supreme, absolute deity</note>, through the realization of their essential oneness. Sankarshana, as an expansion of Vasudeva, first created the waters. In those waters, he "cast his seed"—a specific creative power. || 13 || What happened then? The text explains:

### That became a Golden Egg, enveloped everywhere by darkness;
### Within it, Aniruddha, the Eternal, first became manifest. || 14 ||

That water, combined with that power, became a "Golden Egg"—a golden sphere—enveloped everywhere, both inside and out, by darkness. The meaning is that in the space accompanied by darkness, the Golden Egg was produced. Within that Golden Egg, Aniruddha <note>The third expansion of the divine, associated with the mind and preservation</note>, the eternal and constant expansion of Sankarshana (who is himself an expansion of Vasudeva), became "manifest" or visible. He was not "born" or "produced" in the literal sense, because this text follows the doctrine of Pre-existent Effect <term>Satkaryavada: the philosophical theory that the effect already exists within its cause, like oil within a sesame seed</term>. Just as oil is already present in sesame seeds and is merely made manifest, he was not newly created. || 14 || Now, for the easy understanding of the world, the text provides his other names:

### He is recited in the Vedas as the Lord Hiranyagarbha;
### He is called Aditya because he is the first being, and by nature, he is called Surya. || 15 ||

This Lord Aniruddha, an expansion of Sankarshana, who is endowed with the six divine fortunes <note>The Shad-gunya: lordship, power, glory, splendor, knowledge, and dispassion</note>, is recited in the "Vedas" <note>original: Chandasi</note> as "Hiranyagarbha" <note>The Golden Womb/Embryo</note> because he resided within the interior of the Golden Egg.

<summary>This passage describes the Vedic creation myth where the divine manifests as Sankarshana and Aniruddha to create a Golden Egg (Hiranyagarbha) amidst cosmic darkness. It establishes the solar deity, Surya, as the first manifest being and the material cause of the universe.</summary>

# Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings"

<note>The title refers to the *Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka*, a well-known commentary on the *Sūrya Siddhānta*.</note>

It is being described. In the Vedas, "Hiranyagarbha" <note>literally "The Golden Womb" or "Golden Egg," the source of the universe</note> is his well-known alternative name. Indeed, he is called the Sun because he was the first to be manifested. Through his birth, this Aniruddha <note>a form of Vishnu associated with the sun and cosmic mind</note> is also called the Sun because of his manifestation from this world.

> In the beginning, the Golden Womb existed; once born, he was the sole Lord of all that exists.

This is the Scripture <note>original: *Śruti*; referring to Rig Veda 10.121.1</note>. || 15 || Now, the author describes his nature and state:

> He is the Supreme Light beyond the darkness, and he is this very Sun.
> He traverses the worlds, the creator of beings, bringing them into existence. || 16 ||

This Aniruddha, named the Sun, is the "Impeller" <term>Savita: the sun as a stimulating or life-giving power</term>. This is his name. The word "and" indicates the inclusion of his various attributes. He is well-known. "Beyond the darkness" means at the end of obscurity; he is the "Supreme Light," the very form of radiance. The essential meaning is that he is the destroyer of darkness. The Scripture says: "He is of the color of the sun, beyond the darkness." This Impeller, the "Creator of Beings"—the cause of the previously mentioned creation, maintenance, and dissolution—traverses the worlds (which will be described later), illuminating them and constantly revolving within the Golden Egg <note>original: *suvarṇāṇḍa*; the cosmic egg of creation</note>. || 16 || Now, explaining the phrase "Supreme Light," the author describes his nature in two verses:

> He is the soul of light, the slayer of darkness, and is renowned as the "Great One."
> The Rig-Veda verses are his orb, the Sama-Veda chants are his form, and the Yajur-Veda formulas too. || 17 ||

> This Lord consists of the Three Vedas; he is the soul of time, the maker of time, and the all-pervading Lord.
> He is the soul of all, the all-pervading, the subtle; everything is established in him. || 18 ||

Being the form of light and the destroyer of darkness, this Sun named Aniruddha is called the "Great One" or the "Great Principle" <term>Mahat-tattva: in Indian philosophy, the first product of primal nature, the cosmic intellect</term>. Thus he is renowned and defined in the Vedas and the Puranas <note>ancient mythological texts</note>—

# The Surya Siddhanta
<note>The Surya Siddhanta is a foundational Sanskrit treatise on Indian astronomy, dating in its current form to approximately the 4th-5th century CE.</note>

Of this defined Sun: The *Rig* <note>original: "Ṛcaḥ"</note> are the hymns of the Rigveda; the *Saman* <note>original: "Sāmāni"</note> are the hymns of the Samaveda, which are the rays; and the *Yajus* <note>original: "Yajūṃṣi"</note> are the hymns of the Yajurveda, which constitute its form or essence. The word "and" <note>original: "ca"</note> indicates a collection. Therefore, this defined Lord is endowed with the six divine attributes of the Sun. He is composed of the three Vedas <note>original: "trayīmayo"</note>. He is the nature of Time and the cause of Time. He is the All-pervading Lord <note>original: "vibhu"</note>, capable of the creation, preservation, and destruction of the universe. Consequently, he is the Soul of All, the form of the world, omnipresent, and all-encompassing, yet he also holds a subtle, non-pervading form. In this defined Sun, the entire universe is established. By this, there is no contradiction between his pervasive and non-pervasive aspects. || 18 || Now, the meaning of "he traverses the worlds" is explained:

> Having made the year-cycle his wheel upon a chariot composed of the universe,
> with the seven meters harnessed as horses, he traverses [the worlds] forever.* || 19 ||

Upon a chariot consisting of the three worlds, having fixed the wheel of the year consisting of the twelve months, and having harnessed the seven <term>meters</term> <note>The rhythmic structures of Vedic poetry</note>—namely Gayatri, Ushnih, Anushtubh, Brihati, Pankti, Trishtubh, and Jagati—as the horses. In the reading "the meters and the horses are joined," it means having yoked the seven horses to the chariot. Forever, eternally, this one—named the Unobstructed <note>original: "Aniruddha"</note>—traverses or revolves. || 19 || Now, his nature and the birth of Brahma are described:

> Three-quarters of him are immortal and secret; one quarter became manifest.
> That Lord, for the sake of creating the world, created Brahma, who is Ego. || 20 ||

Of this Vedic Soul, three-quarters <note>original: "tripādaṃ"</note> are the immortal portion to be known in heaven. Therefore—

# Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings" <note>original: "Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka," the title of the commentary</note>

Indeed, this is a secret and inaccessible mystery. A "quarter" <note>original: "pāda"</note> refers to a single portion or foot. This visible, perceptible world, consisting of both stationary and moving beings, became manifest from that portion. The sacred scripture <note>original: "Śruti," referring here to the Purusha Sukta of the Rig Veda</note> is explicit: "The three-quarters of the Supreme Being ascended above, while one quarter of Him manifested here again." That Lord, known by the name Aniruddha <note>A form of Vishnu associated with the preservation of the universe and the cosmic mind</note>, is capable of all origination. For the purpose of creating the universe, He brought forth the Being known as Brahma, who is the embodiment of the principle of self-consciousness <term>Ahaṅkāra-tattva: the cosmic element of "I-ness" or ego that allows for individualization in creation</term> || 20 || Now, it is described how, after appointing the created Being, Brahma, to the task of world-creation, the Lord Himself remains pervading the whole:

->Having given the excellent Vedas to him, the Grandfather of all worlds,<-
->And having established him within the Cosmic Egg, He Himself moves about, contemplating. || 21 ||<-

Then, after the production of Brahma, He who is named Aniruddha—having established that Brahma, the "Grandfather" of all worlds, within the Golden Egg <note>original: "suvarṇāṇḍa," the Hiranyagarbha or cosmic womb</note> and having granted him the excellent <insert>Vedas</insert> to serve as the path for creating the universe—He moves about, illuminating and sustaining all things. The word "and" is to be understood here as connecting these actions. || 21 || Next, it is described how Brahma, desiring to bring forth creation, produced the Moon and the Sun, which are the perceptible witnesses of the world:

->Then Brahma, bearing the form of Self-Consciousness, set his mind upon creation;<-
->From his mind, the Moon was born, and from his eyes, the Sun, the reservoir of light. || 22 ||<-

Then, after receiving his authority, Brahma, who holds the form of the principle of self-consciousness, directed his mind <note>original: "antaḥkaraṇa," the internal instrument of thought</note> toward creation. This means the desire arose in Brahma: "I shall perform the act of creation." Subsequently, from that mind, the Moon was born. The meaning is that by the mere thought "Let there be a Moon," the Moon came into existence.

# The Surya Siddhanta
<note>The Surya Siddhanta is one of the most important early Sanskrit treatises on Indian astronomy, dating in its current form to approximately the 4th-5th century CE.</note>

From the two eyes <note>original: "akṣṇornetrābhyāṃ"</note> of the Supreme Being, the Sun—the storehouse and source of all light—was produced. This is because the sense of sight is composed of the element of light. || 22 || Next, the author describes the origin of the Great Elements <term>Mahābhūtas; the five fundamental physical elements of Indian cosmology</term>.

> From the Mind came Space; from that, Air, Fire, Water, and Earth followed in succession.
> Through the increase of one quality each, these five Great Elements were born. || 23 ||

By the will of the Supreme Self, desiring "Let there be Space," Space <note>original: "kha" or "ākāśa"</note> arose from the Mind. From Space, in successive order, came Air, Fire, Water, and Earth. Specifically: from Space came Air; from Air, Fire; from Fire, Water; and from Water, Earth. These five Great Elements were born through the "increase of one quality" <note>original: "guṇaikavṛddhyā"</note>, meaning each subsequent element adds a new sensory characteristic to those of the previous one. The word "only" <note>original: "eva"</note> in the verse is used to exclude the possibility of there being more or fewer than five. They were born or produced as follows: Space possesses the quality of sound; Air possesses two qualities, sound and touch; Fire possesses three qualities, sound, touch, and form; Water possesses four qualities, sound, touch, form, and taste; and Earth possesses five qualities, sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. This is the clear meaning. || 23 || Now, while describing the nature of the Moon and Sun, the author speaks of the origin of the five planets.

> The Sun and Moon are Fire and Soma; from them, Mars and the others
> Were born respectively from Fire, Earth, Space, Water, and Air. || 24 ||

The Sun and Moon, whose births were mentioned previously, are of the nature of Fire and Soma <note>Soma is associated with the cooling, nourishing lunar nectar</note>. The Sun is of the nature of Fire, a sphere of light <term>tejogolaka</term>, because it is visible to the eye. The Moon, however, is of the nature of Soma; since the word "Soma" can refer to a liquid, it is a sphere of water <term>jalagolarūpa</term>. The grammatical usage of "Agni-ṣomau" <note>Fire and Soma joined</note> follows archaic Vedic rules <term>chāndasika</term>.

---

<margin>* An alternative reading for this line is: "The planets Mars and the others were born from the elements."</margin>

# Page 87
### Accompanied by the "Illuminator of the Hidden Meaning" <note>The *Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka*, a famous 17th-century commentary by Ranganatha</note>

Immediately after that, the five "star-planets" <term>tārā-graha; the planets visible as stars, excluding the Sun and Moon</term> beginning with Mars <note>original: *aṅgārakādayo*</note> were produced respectively from Fire, Earth, Ether, Water, and Air. The word "but" <note>original: *tu*</note> in the verse implies that for each planet, there is a predominance of its specific element while the other elements remain in equal proportions. Mars was produced from Fire <term>tejas</term>; for this very reason, he is called "The Burning Coal" <note>original: *aṅgāraka*</note>. Mercury was produced from Earth; Jupiter from Ether <term>ākāśa</term>; Venus from Water; and Saturn from Air. // 24 //

Now, he describes the zodiac signs and the lunar mansions:

->Furthermore, the Self-Controlled One divided himself twelve-fold into what are called the Zodiac Signs,<-
->and again into twenty-seven parts in the form of the Lunar Mansions. // 25 //<-

Furthermore, immediately after, he divided himself twelve-fold—into twelve locations—known as the Zodiac Signs <term>rāśi</term>. The meaning is that he created a mentally-conceived circle divided into twelve parts, known as the Zodiac Circle. Then, for a second time, he divided himself into twenty-seven parts in the form of the Lunar Mansions <term>nakṣatra</term>. This means he made that same mentally-conceived circle into twenty-seven divisions. 

One might ask: "Why were there not more or fewer divisions? There seems to be no rule governing these specific numbers." To this, the text says: "The Self-Controlled One" <note>original: *vaśī*</note>. This refers to one whose will is entirely under his own control; because he possesses independent will, he is not subject to external commands. The implication is that these specific numbers of divisions were made according to his own desire. It is established by the context that the Lunar Mansions, which manifest these twenty-seven divisions, were created in the form of stars. // 25 //

Next, he describes how he created the world of moving and unmoving beings:

->Then he fashioned the entire universe of moving and unmoving things, beginning with the gods,<-
->creating the various natures from the upper, middle, and lower streams. // 26 //<-

Then, after the creation of the zodiac and the planets, he created the various natures—characterized by the distinctions of Lucidity, Passion, and Inertia <term>sattva, rajas, and tamas; the three fundamental qualities of nature in Indian philosophy</term>—from the upper, middle, and lower "streams" or individual manifestations...

# The Surya Siddhanta

<insert>MINISTRY OF CULTURE GOVERNMENT OF INDIA
Ministry of Culture - Government of India</insert>

Therefore, creating and repeatedly manifesting the universe—beginning with the gods and including deities, humans, demons, and so on—he fashioned the world of moving and unmoving things, consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious. || 26 || Now, the author explains how he established the positions of the created objects.

-> Having created them in sequence as before, through the division of qualities and actions, <-
-> he ordained their respective distributions according to the vision of the Vedas. || 27 || <-

The "qualities" <term>guna: the three fundamental tendencies of nature</term> are Goodness, Passion, and Darkness <note>original: "Sattva, Rajas, Tamas"</note>. "Action" <term>karma</term> refers to the good or evil deeds accumulated in previous births. By the "division" of these two—meaning their specific combinations—and "in sequence as before"—referring to the previously mentioned creation of the Moon, Sun, and so forth—he performed the creation of gods, humans, demons, the earth, mountains, and all moving and unmoving things. Then, "according to the vision of the Vedas"—meaning the methods declared in the sacred scriptures—he "ordained their distributions"—that is, he established their specific positions according to their respective regions and times. || 27 || He now specifies for whom this was done:

-> The Lord ordained the positions of the planets, asterisms, and stars, of the earth, and of the whole universe; <-
-> as well as of the gods, demons, humans, and perfected beings, in their proper order. || 28 || <-

The "Lord" refers to Brahma, who is capable of assigning all things to their places. He established the positions in space for the spheres of the planets and asterisms <note>asterisms: the 27 lunar mansions or Nakshatras</note>, for the earth, and for the "three worlds" <term>trailokya: the triad of earth, atmosphere, and heaven</term>. The word "and" <note>original: "va"</note> is used here in a cumulative sense. Among these, the planets and asterisms have positions that vary according to time. The earth, however, has a fixed position. Within the earth, the three worlds are positioned according to their respective regions. There, in "proper order"—meaning according to what is appropriate—he established the locations for the gods, demons, humans, and "perfected beings" <term>siddhas: semi-divine beings of great purity and power</term>. The word "and" <note>original: "ca"</note> is again cumulative. He established their positions according to their respective regions. || 28 || Now, since space exists everywhere, one might ask how Brahma, situated in the middle of the Golden Egg <note>the Brahmanda or cosmic egg/universe</note>, established the positions of the planets, stars, and the earth...

->### Accompanied by the *Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka* <note>The "Revealer of the Hidden Meaning," a famous 17th-century commentary by Raṅganātha on the Surya Siddhanta</note> <-

Regarding the question of whether this was created in the space outside the Universe or within the space of the Universe, the author says:

> This Universe is hollow; within it is this world, consisting of the Earth, the Atmosphere, and so on. It is like the joining of two halves of a jar, forming a spherical shape. || 29 ||

This previously mentioned Golden Egg <note>original: "Brahmāṇḍa"</note>, presided over by Brahma, is hollow, meaning it consists of open space. Within that space, this world—consisting of the Earth <note>Bhūr</note>, the Atmosphere <note>Bhuvaḥ</note>, and the Heavens <note>Svar</note>—is situated, not outside of it. Now, one might argue that if the Egg is spherical, it is impossible for it to contain an internal void; to this, the author says: *of two halves of a jar*. A "jar" <note>original: "kaṭāha," usually referring to a shallow vessel or cauldron</note> is a hemispherical, hollow vessel. Two equal halves of such a vessel, joined face-to-face <insert>the word "exactly" is used to exclude any overlap or gap</insert>, form a spherical shape. Thus, there is no contradiction. || 29 || Now, while describing the inner circumference of the Universe, he explains in two verses how the stars and planets revolve in their proper places within that space.

> The circumference within the Universe is called the Orbit of the Sky. Within that, the stars revolve, and below them, one after another, revolve: || 30 ||
> Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon. Below them are situated the Perfected Beings, the Celestial Musicians, and the Clouds. || 31 ||

The circumference within the Universe—the measure of the equal circle—is called the "Orbit of the Sky" <term>Vyomakakṣā: the outermost limit of the planetary system</term>, a name which will be further defined. In the middle of that, in the space of the Universe, occurs the revolution of the stars <note>the "fixed" stars or constellations</note>, which are all spaced at equal distances. Similarly...

# The Treatise of the Sun
<note>original: "Surya Siddhanta"</note>

Below the stars, at various distances, Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon revolve in descending order. The <term>Siddhas</term><note>perfected beings</note>, <term>Vidyadharas</term><note>wisdom-holders or celestial musicians</note>, and <term>Sadhyas</term><note>a class of minor deities</note> are situated below the Moon, positioned one beneath the other in space. Because these beings lack the <term>Pravaha</term><note>the procreative or driving wind that moves the planets</note> and other such stabilizing forces, they do not revolve in the same manner as the Moon. || 31 || Now, the author describes the position of the Earth:

->In the very center of the Universe, the terrestrial globe stands in space,<-
->bearing the supreme power of Brahma, which is characterized by the capacity to support. || 32 ||<-

In the center of the "Egg" <note>original: "Anda," referring to the Brahmanda or Cosmic Egg/Universe</note>, in the middle of all regions, the globe of the Earth stands in space as the central point. If one asks, "How can the terrestrial globe remain fixed, since it is impossible for an object without support to stay in space?" the author provides a description of the Earth to answer. He says "bearing": it bears—or holds—the supreme power of Brahma, which is "characterized by support," meaning the power to remain in place without a physical foundation. Thus, there is no falling. By this, the two questions—"What is the shape of the Earth?" and "What is its support?"—are answered. || 32 || Now, he answers the question regarding the seven subterranean realms:

->Within its interior are seven cavities, the abodes of Serpents and Demons;<-
->filled with divine medicines and elixirs, these subterranean realms are beautiful. || 33 ||<-

Within the interior layers of that terrestrial globe, there are seven "folds" or cave-like spaces, such as <term>Atala, Vitala, Sutala</term><note>the traditional names of the lower worlds in Hindu cosmology</note>, and so on; these are the subterranean lands or regions, which are lovely and enchanting. If one asks who dwells there, as humans and others dwell upon the Earth, the author provides a description: they are the "abodes of Serpents <note>original: "Nagas"</note> and Demons <note>original: "Asuras"</note>." # Accompanied by the Illuminator of Hidden Meanings

The leaders of the demons, such as Shuki and others, all find their refuge in these <note>the subterranean realms or Patala</note>. Now, a question arises: since the sun does not travel there, and those regions are filled with darkness, how do the people living there conduct their daily affairs? To answer this, the author provides a second description: **"Endowed with the essence of divine herbs."** These are divine plants that are self-luminous; they are filled with such essences. Thus, by that light, daily activities are carried out, and by the power of those herbs, the lives of the people in those worlds are sustained. This is the intended meaning. || 33 ||

Now, having described the terrestrial globe <term>Bhugola: the sphere of the earth</term>, the author describes the position of Mount Meru, which exceeds the measurement of the earth's north-south diameter:

->**The mountain is a mass of many jewels, made of Jambu-river gold.**<-
->**Situated in the middle of the earth-globe, Meru emerges on both sides.**<- || 34 ||

The mountain named Meru, situated in the middle of the earth-globe, is a "mass of many jewels"—meaning a collection of various kinds of gems such as rubies, diamonds, and the like. It is also "made of Jambu-river gold" <note>original: Jambunada</note>. Regarding this gold:

> From the juice dripping from the ripe fruit of the Jambu tree,
> the Jambu river was formed; the clay touched by its waters became gold.
> Because it comes from that river, it is called Jambunada; the hosts of gods and perfected beings
> constantly drink it, turning away even from the consumption of nectar.

According to this statement by the teacher Bhaskaracharya <note>A famous 12th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note>, Meru is composed of this gold—it is fashioned of gold. It "emerges on both sides," meaning it extends outward from the two surface points of the earth separated by its diameter. The terrestrial globe is pierced through the middle by this rod-shaped golden mountain. Therefore, the name "Earth-Bearer" <note>original: Bhubhrad</note> is a literal and appropriate title for the mountain. This is the deeper significance. || 34 ||

Next, the author explains that the gods and the demons reside at the upper and lower portions of Meru, respectively.

## The Surya Siddhanta
<note>original: "Surya Siddhanta" — The "Sun Precept," one of the most important historical Sanskrit treatises on Indian astronomy.</note>

> Located upon the upper part of it <note>Mount Meru</note> are the gods, including Indra, and the great sages.
> Likewise, the demons are located below it; they are mutual enemies, residing on opposite sides. || 35 ||

Upon the upper part of it—meaning at the top of Mount Meru—are located the gods, including Indra <note>the king of the gods</note>, and the great sages. The word "and" should be understood here to connect these groups. They are stationed there. Below—meaning in the region beneath Meru—are the demons <note>original: "Asuras" or "Daityas"</note>. "Likewise" means in the same manner as the gods are in the upper portion. They are "residing" or stationed there. Now, one might ask: why do the gods and demons not stay in the same place? To this, the author says: "they are mutual enemies." They harbor hatred toward one another. Thus, because of the existence of mutual hatred between the gods and demons, it is impossible for them to stay together. The superior gods stay in the upper part, and the great sages, fearing the demons, stay there as well. In the lower part, the inferior demons are located. This is the intended meaning. || 35 ||

Next, he describes the location of the oceans on the globe:

> Then, all around the circumference, in order, is this great ocean.
> It stands like a girdle for the Earth, creating the division between gods and demons. || 36 ||

Starting from the staff-like Mount Meru, all around is this visible great ocean. In sequence, it forms a continuous circumference like a "girdle" <note>original: "mekhala" — a decorative waist-belt or sash</note> for the Earth. It is the "divider of gods and demons," meaning it acts as the circumferential boundary line between the two halves of the terrestrial globe. By this, it is established that the northern hemisphere of the globe, containing the continent of Jambu <note>original: "Jambudvipa"</note>, belongs to the gods, while the southern hemisphere—consisting of the other six continents and six oceans—belongs to the demons. In the middle of the globe, aligned with the axis of Meru, lies the Salt Ocean <note>original: "Lavanasamudra"</note> in the form of a circumference. The northern hemisphere is the edge of the ocean contained within the southern hemisphere...

<summary>This page describes the mythological and geographical division of the Earth, placing gods at the North Pole (Meru) and demons at the South Pole, separated by a central great ocean that acts like a belt around the world.</summary>

# Accompanied by the *Illuminator of Hidden Meanings* <note>original: "Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka," the name of the commentary by Raṅganātha</note>

"Touching the circumference" means that the girdle <note>the Earth's equator</note> is situated below the poet <note>referring to the observer's position or the pole</note>; this is the intended meaning. || 36 ||

Now, he states that on the northern shore of the ocean, which forms the circumference at the beginning of Jambu-island <note>the central continent in Hindu cosmology</note>, there are four cities located in the four divisions.

> At equal distances all around from the center of Meru, in the oceans, in the islands, and in the directions starting from the East, there are cities built by the gods. || 37 ||

"From the center of Meru" means from the middle region of the staff-like Meru, or rather, from the center of the terrestrial globe. "All around" means on the surface of the globe. "In equal parts of the ocean" refers to the ocean that forms the circumference. "In the islands" refers to the beginnings of Jambu-island. "In the directions" means in the four divisions. In the four directions—East, South, West, and North—relative to Meru, there are four cities "built by the gods," meaning they were created by divine beings. The essential meaning is that on the northern shore of the ocean, which constitutes the first part of Jambu-island, there are four cities at equal intervals in the designated cardinal directions of the globe. || 37 ||

Now, in three verses, he explains their names and their locations within the technical divisions called "regions" <term>Varṣa: a geographical division or continent-tract</term> arising from the island.

> At a quarter of the Earth's circumference to the East, in the region of Bhadrāśva, is the famous city known as Yamakoṭi, possessed of golden walls and arches. || 38 ||
>
> To the South, in the region of Bhārata <note>India</note>, is the great city of Laṅkā. Likewise, to the West, in the region called Ketumāla, the city named Romaka is celebrated. || 39 ||
>
> To the North, in the region of Kuru, the city named Siddhapuri is proclaimed. In it dwell the Great-Souled Perfected Ones, free from all suffering. || 40 ||

# The Treatise of the Sun
<note>original: "Surya Siddhanta"; the foundational text of Indian astronomy, traditionally dated to the end of the Golden Age (Satya Yuga).</note>

The globe of the Earth has Mount Meru passing through it on both sides like a rod <note>referring to the Earth's axis</note>. By a circular line passing through its two poles, the globe is divided into two halves. By another circular line running east to west <note>the equator</note>, the Earth is divided into two further sections. Thus, on the globe, there are four rampart-like quarters of the Earth.

In the eastern quarter, at a distance of one-fourth of the ocean's circumference, in the region known as Bhadrasva, at the junction of the upper and lower sections, there is a city with palaces and gateways made of gold. This city is famously known by the name **Yamakoti**.

To the south, at the junction of the two upper sections, lies the great city named **Lanka** in the region known as Bharata <note>ancient India</note>. Because it is south of Meru, it is likewise famous for its golden walls and gateways.

To the west, at the junction of the western and lower sections, in the region known as Ketumala, the city named **Romaka** is described.

To the north, at the junction of the two lower sections, in the region known as Kuru, the city named **Siddhapuri** is proclaimed. The name "Siddhapuri" <note>City of the Perfected</note> is literal; in that city dwell the *Siddhas* <note>beings who have attained spiritual perfection</note>, whose souls are superior to those of ordinary men, who are free from pain and sorrow, and who reside there eternally.

Now, the distance between these four cities and their distance from Meru is described:

->**These cities are situated at intervals of one-fourth of the Earth’s circumference from each other. To the north of them stands Meru, the abode of the gods, at that same distance.**<-

These aforementioned cities are placed at intervals of one-fourth of the Earth's circumference <note>90 degrees apart</note>. Meru, as stated, is the abode of the gods.

<meta>This page continues the astronomical commentary on the Earth's geography and the movement of celestial bodies, specifically focusing on the equatorial cities and the visibility of the Pole Stars from different latitudes.</meta>

# Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings" <note>Sanskrit: Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka; a famous 17th-century commentary by Raṅganātha on the Sūrya Siddhānta</note>

Because these cities are presided over by gods, they are situated at a distance of one-fourth of the Earth's circumference from each other. The word "only" <note>Sanskrit: eva</note> is used here to exclude any greater or lesser distance. The word "and" <note>Sanskrit: ca</note> serves to connect this with the previous half-verse. || 41 || Now, he explains that these cities have no latitude <note>literally "without eyes/axis," referring to the equatorial line</note>:

->The Sun, staying on the equator, passes directly above them.<-
->In those cities, there is no equinoctial shadow, nor is any elevation of the pole observed. || 42 ||<-

"Of those," meaning the aforementioned cities, the Sun "staying on the equator"—that is, staying on the celestial equatorial belt, the path along which the Sun moves on the day when day and night are equal—passes "directly above" them as it wanders. For this reason, in those cities, there is no "equinoctial shadow" <term>Akṣabhā: the shadow cast by a vertical gnomon at noon on the day of the equinox</term>. This is because for those at that location, the East-West circle is identical to the equatorial circle. Since the Sun is directly overhead at midday, no shadow is observed. Consequently, in those cities, the "elevation of the pole" <note>the height of the Pole Star above the horizon</note> in the form of degrees of latitude is not accepted or acknowledged. The point is that their status as equatorial regions <term>Nirakṣadeśa: "places without latitude"</term> is established by the absence of latitude degrees. || 42 || Now, wishing to explain the absence of colatitude and latitude in the cities mentioned and at Mount Meru respectively, he first describes the position of the two poles:

->At the two poles of Meru, the two Pole Stars are stationed in the sky.<-
->For those situated in the equatorial regions, both stars are seen on the horizon. || 43 ||<-

At the two sides of Meru—the North and the South—the two Pole Stars <note>the North Star, Polaris, and the corresponding southern celestial point</note> are situated in the sky, specifically at the "middle" or zenith of the sky respectively. For those "situated in the equatorial regions"—the people living in the cities previously described—both the North and South Pole Stars are resting on the "horizon" <term>Kṣitija: the circle where the earth meets the sky</term>.

<summary>This page explains the astronomical conditions at the Earth's equator, noting that the Sun passes directly overhead during equinoxes, resulting in no shadow, and that the Pole Stars appear on the horizon rather than overhead.</summary>
<keywords>Equator, Equinox, Pole Star, Latitude, Sūrya Siddhānta, Indian Astronomy, Meru, Horizon</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the astronomical discourse on the relationship between the horizon, the poles, and geographic latitude, specifically focusing on the conditions at the terrestrial equator and the poles.</meta>

# The Surya Siddhanta
<note>The Surya Siddhanta is one of the most celebrated ancient Indian treatises on astronomy, dating back to at least the 4th-5th century CE.</note>

This means that [the poles] are located on the circle of the horizon at that central point. (43) Now, for this very reason, he explains the absence of latitude and the maximum value of the colatitude in those places.

->Therefore, there is no elevation of the pole in those cities, as the two poles are located on the horizon.<-
->The degrees of colatitude are ninety; however, at Meru, the degrees of latitude are the same. (44)<-

"In those" refers to the previously mentioned cities <note>original: "tāsu", referring to the cities on the terrestrial equator like Lanka</note>. "Therefore," because both poles rest on the horizon, there is no "elevation of the pole," meaning no polar altitude. The sense is that since the elevation of the pole above the horizon constitutes the degrees of latitude, and that elevation is absent here, the latitude is zero. 

By the word "however" <note>original: "tu"</note>, it is meant that in those cities, while the two poles remain on the horizon, the degrees of colatitude <term>lamba-amsha: the complement of latitude, or the angle between the zenith and the celestial equator</term> are ninety, because ninety minus zero latitude equals ninety. Furthermore, because the distance from the zenith to the poles on the horizon represents the nature of colatitude, at Meru <note>the North Pole</note>, the degrees of latitude are likewise ninety, because the pole is at its highest point <note>the zenith</note>. 

The meaning established is this: just as at the equator <note>original: "niraksha-desha", the place without latitude</note> there is an absence of latitude and the colatitude is at its maximum, so at Meru, because the latitude is at its maximum, there is an absence of colatitude. By this, the following is indicated:

> If one city is north of another,
> what is the difference in their degrees of latitude?
> By the proportion of the degrees of the circle,
> the measurement of the circumference is rightly declared.

This indicates the answer to the first question posed by the teacher Bhaskaracharya <note>A famous 12th-century Indian mathematician and astronomer</note>. It is also indicated that the calculation of the "clear circumference" <note>the radius of the local parallel of latitude</note>, which decreases in accordance with the position of the imaginary zenith until it becomes zero at Meru, is not inconsistent. (44) 

Now, wishing to answer the questions regarding the arrangement of day and night and so forth, he first describes the commencement of the day for the Gods and the Demons.

<summary>This page explains the inverse relationship between latitude and colatitude at the equator and the North Pole, citing Bhaskaracharya to justify how Earth's circumference is measured.</summary>

# Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings" <note>The *Gudharthaprakashaka*, a famous 17th-century commentary by Ranganatha on the *Surya Siddhanta*</note>

## When the Sun is at the beginning of Aries, in the section of the Gods, it becomes visible to the Gods.
## But for the Demons, when the Sun moves through their section starting from the beginning of Libra, it becomes visible to them. || 45 ||

At the boundary of the "Rose-Apple Island" <note>Jambudvipa, the central continent in traditional Indian cosmology</note> and the Salt Ocean, there is a circumferential circle. In the middle of the terrestrial globe, aligned with that same thread in the sky, is the circle known as the Equator <note>original: *vishuvadvrittam*</note>. The Ecliptic <note>original: *krantivrittam*, the sun's path</note> is attached to it at two places at a distance of six signs; these are the locations of Aries and Libra. By the force of the Provector Wind <note>original: *pravahavayu*, the cosmic wind believed to drive the celestial bodies</note>, it rotates along the path of the Equator. From the point of Aries, the point of Cancer is twenty-four degrees to the north of the Equator. The point of Capricorn is twenty-four degrees to the south of the Equator.

These rotate in their own places by the Provector Wind. In this way, the regions of the Ecliptic rotate in their respective places by the Provector Wind. In that context, "at the beginning of Aries, in the section of the Gods" refers to the previously mentioned division between the Gods and Demons at Jambudvipa. The zodiac signs connected to that, from the beginning of Aries to the end of Virgo, constitute the Northern Hemisphere <note>original: *uttaragolah*</note>. The Sun, situated there at the beginning of Aries—the region of Aries—goes to, or attains, its "visibility" for the Gods residing at the northern peak of Mount Meru <note>the North Pole</note>; this refers to the first sighting after a period of six months. This is because the Equator serves as their horizon.

Similarly, for the Daityas <note>Demons</note> residing at the southern peak of Meru, the same logic applies. "Moving through their section" refers to the section of the Demons, the southern division starting from the ocean; the signs from the beginning of Libra to the end of Pisces constitute the Southern Hemisphere <note>original: *dakshinagolah*</note>. The Sun, traveling through those signs, attains its first visibility at the region of Libra after a period of non-visibility. This is because the Equator is also their horizon. || 45 || Now, following this topic, the author provides the answer to the question posed in the first half of the verse beginning with "Why is the Sun's ray intense in summer?"

# The Surya Siddhanta
<note>original: "सूर्यसिद्धान्तः" — The "Sun Treatise," one of the foundational texts of ancient Indian astronomy.</note>

> Because of that extreme proximity, the rays of the Sun are intense during the summer
> In the land of the gods; however, in the winter, there is a dullness, and the opposite is true for the others. || 46 ||

"Because of that" means by reason of the Sun’s movement between the northern and southern hemispheres. "In the land of the gods" <note>original: "देवभागे" (Devabhaga) — traditionally referring to the Northern Hemisphere or the North Pole</note> refers here to the continent of Jambu <note>original: "जम्बूद्वीपे" (Jambudvipa) — the central continent in traditional Indian cosmology</note>. Because of the extreme proximity—meaning the Sun being situated very close—during the summer season, the rays of the Sun's orb of light are sharp and very hot. By applying the logic of "the land of the gods" to the "land of the demons" <note>original: "असुराणां" (Asuranam) — referring to the Southern Hemisphere or South Pole</note>, in the region of the Daityas <note>demons</note> such as the southern oceans, the Sun's rays are very hot during the winter season because of the Sun's extreme proximity to them. 

"Otherwise" means that due to the Sun being far away, there is a "dullness" or a lack of heat in the rays. In the land of the gods, there is a dullness of rays during the winter season; therefore, there is an excess of cold there. In the land of the demons, there is a dullness of rays and an excess of cold during the summer. The underlying meaning is that the Sun's distance from the land of the gods in the southern hemisphere and its proximity in the northern hemisphere is due to the gradual increase and decrease of the midday solar rays. || 46 || 

Now, having stated that the land of the gods begins with the sign of Aries <note>the vernal equinox</note>, the author clarifies this under the pretext of describing the day and night of the gods and demons.

> The gods and demons, at the equinox, behold the Sun
> Situated upon the horizon; for these two, day and night are respectively left-handed and right-handed. || 47 ||

At the time of the equinox <note>original: "विषुवति" (Vishuvati)</note>, the gods and demons see the Sun staying upon the horizon. Because the Sun is on the equatorial circle, it appears on the horizon for both of them, as they are situated at the poles of the Earth. For these gods and demons, day and night occur mutually in "left-handed and right-handed" <note>original: "वामसव्ये" (Vama-savye)</note> or counter-clockwise and clockwise order. The meaning is this: For the gods...

The northern part of the Earth is "left" <note>Sanskrit: *savya*, often meaning left or clockwise in ritual contexts</note> for the gods because it is their own domain, while it is "right" <note>Sanskrit: *apasavya*, right or counter-clockwise</note> for the Daityas because it is not their own. Similarly, the southern part of the Earth is "left" for the Daityas as their own domain, and "right" for the gods as it is not theirs. Therefore, the northern and southern hemispheres, which are the left and right sides for the Daityas, are respectively the day and night of the gods. The southern and northern hemispheres, which are the left and right sides of the gods, are the day and night of the Daityas. Otherwise, the mutual relationship of "left" and "right" would not make sense. This is why it was previously stated, "starting from Aries," and so on. || 47 ||

At the beginning of Aries—the point where the celestial equator and the ecliptic intersect, near the star Revatī—the Sun, having risen or become visible, moves through three signs located in the northern part: Aries, Taurus, and Gemini. In doing so, he completes the "first half of the day" for the gods residing on Mount Meru. The implied meaning is that when the Sun reaches the end of Gemini, it is midday for those on Meru. Moving through the signs starting with Cancer—namely Cancer, Leo, and Virgo—that Sun completes the "latter half" or the second portion of the day. The word "only" <note>Sanskrit: *eva*</note> is used to exclude any other possibility. When the Sun is at the end of Virgo, for those on Meru...

# Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings" <note>original: "Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka," a famous commentary on the Sūrya Siddhānta</note>

At the end of the sun's course <note>the solstices</note> and at the intersection of these courses <note>the equinoxes</note>, due to the inversion of the days of these gods and demons, there occurs a half-day and a half-night. The practical meaning is this: where it is midday and midnight for the gods, there it is respectively midnight and midday for the demons; and where it is midday and midnight for the demons, there it is respectively midnight and midday for the gods. He <note>the author</note> states the reason for this with the word "Above." The gods and demons, residing in the northern and southern halves of Mount Meru <note>the terrestrial axis</note>, each imagine themselves to be on the "upper" part. In reality, because the earth is a sphere, it is the same everywhere; therefore, absolute "up" and "down" positions are impossible. Thus, the gods, considering themselves to be above relative to the demons, regard the demons as being in the lower position. The demons, considering themselves to be above relative to the gods' position, place the gods below. This is the intended meaning. And so, because of the inverted positions of the gods and demons, the inversion of day and night is entirely logical. || 51 || Now, he applies this principle of "up" and "down" regarding the gods and demons to others as well, using an illustration:

-> Others also, situated on the same diameter, consider each other to be "below"; <-
-> such as those staying in Bhadrāśva and Ketumāla, or those residing in Laṅkā and Siddhapura. || 52 || <-

"Others" refers to humans on the terrestrial globe other than the gods and demons. The word "also" is used to include them with the demons. Men situated on the same diameter <note>antipodes, separated by the diameter of the earth</note> consider each other to be underneath. The fourth quarter of the verse is self-evident. || 52 || Now, confirming that the aforementioned concepts are merely imaginary, he says:

-> Everywhere on the terrestrial globe, one considers their own place to be "up"; <-
-> since this globe is in space, what is "up" or where indeed is "down"? || 53 || <-

Everywhere on the terrestrial globe, in all regions, one's own place—the place where one is situated—is considered the center and "up"...

# The Treatise of the Sun

Those humans situated upon the Earth accept their own position as being "upward" due to their own perspective. For this reason, on the globe, everyone is indeed standing "up." There are no people who are truly "downward." The reality is that being "up" or "down" is relative and not an absolute physical property. Otherwise, if one were truly "downward," there would be a fear of falling, making human habitation on the globe impossible. Here, the reason is stated: "In the sky." Because the globe of the Earth is located in the center of the space of the universe <note>Sanskrit: *brahmāṇḍākāśa*, the cosmic egg or celestial sphere</note>. And since the universe is equidistant from the Earth on all sides, it follows that in reality, there is no such thing as an absolute "up" or "down" part of the globe. The author clarifies his intention: "Of that." For the Earth situated in the middle of space, in which part is "upwardness"? Or in which part is "downwardness"? The word "also" is used to group these together. Thus, because space is equal on all sides, it is impossible to define "up" and "down" parts of the Earth by which "upper" and "lower" worlds could be fixed. This is because of the impossibility of absolute upward or downward divisions of the Earth. || 53 ||

But if this Earth appears to the eyes to be flat like a mirror, how can it be spherical? To this, he says:

->Because of the smallness of their bodies, people from their own positions<-
->see this Earth as a flat disc, even though it is a sphere. || 54 ||<-

People, from the place where they stand, look in all directions. They see this visible Earth—which is actually a sphere <note>Sanskrit: *vṛttām*, rounded or globular</note>—as being shaped like a disc <note>Sanskrit: *cakrākārām*, like a wheel or circular plate</note>, meaning flat. The word "even" here carries the sense of "certainly." Therefore, even though the Earth is actually spherical, the fact that it is not seen in that shape but is seen as mirror-like is not a contradiction. He gives the reason here: "Because of the smallness of their bodies." This means because of having a short stature <note>The author explains that humans are so small relative to the Earth's diameter that the curvature is imperceptible to the naked eye</note>. And so—

# With the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings" commentary.

Because the Earth's surface is so vast and a human being is so small with a limited range of vision, the Earth does not appear as a sphere, but rather appears as a flat plane. This is because a small arc of a great circle appears straight. <note>The commentator explains that on a local scale, the curvature of a large sphere is indistinguishable from a flat surface.</note> Otherwise, the mathematical principle that the first sine is equal to its arc would be inconsistent. This is the intended meaning. || 54 ||

Now, wishing to describe the length of day and night in places such as the equator <term>niraksha; literally 'without latitude'</term> and other regions besides Mount Meru <note>The North Pole in ancient Indian cosmology</note>, the author describes the rotation of the celestial axis at the two poles and at the equator.

-> It rotates clockwise for the Gods, and counter-clockwise for the enemies of the Gods. <-
-> Above the equator, this celestial sphere in the sky always moves westward. <- || 55 ||

This visible celestial sphere <term>bhagola; the sphere of the stars</term>, the physical globe inhabited by the constellations, rotates "clockwise" for the Gods—those residing at the northern tip of Meru. This means it moves in the order of East and so on. For the Daityas <note>The Asuras or 'enemies of the Gods' residing at the South Pole</note>, it rotates "counter-clockwise," meaning in the reverse order of the directions starting from the East. This means the order is East, North, West, and South. In the sky at the equatorial regions <note>The text uses the singular 'region' to refer to the class of all places on the equator</note>, the celestial sphere always rotates westward directly overhead. This is because the celestial sphere rotates around the two poles, and at the equator, those poles lie exactly on the horizon. || 55 ||

-> Therefore, there the day is thirty units of time, and the night is the same. <-
-> Increase and decrease always occur in opposite ways for the two divisions of Gods and Demons. <- || 56 ||

# The Surya Siddhanta

At the terrestrial equator <note>original: "niraksha-deshe," literally 'the place without latitude'</note>, the day consists of thirty *nadikas* <note>a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note>, measuring exactly thirty *ghatis*. The night, or the duration of darkness, is also measured at thirty *ghatis*. This is because the horizon circle there passes through both poles and the center of the celestial sphere; therefore, the equality of day and night is entirely logical.

In the regions of the Gods and Demons <note>referring to the North and South Poles</note>, and in the southern lands beyond the Jambu-island <note>the central continent in traditional Indian cosmology</note> and its oceans, the increase and decrease of day and night should be understood as occurring inversely <note>original: "vamam vyastam"</note> at all times except during the equinoxes. This means: when the day decreases and the night increases in Jambu-island, then in the southern lands, the day and night respectively increase and decrease. Conversely, when the day increases and the night decreases in Jambu-island, the day and night in the southern lands respectively decrease and increase. Thus, the decrease and increase in the southern lands correspond to the increase and decrease of day and night in Jambu-island. The proof for this is that since their horizon circles do not connect to the poles and do not pass through the center of the celestial sphere, the day and night are never equal except on the day of the equinox; rather, they are lesser or greater, while the full day-and-night cycle always remains sixty *ghatikas* in total.

Now, the author clarifies the meaning of the latter half of this verse with two more verses:

> When the sun is in the signs beginning with Aries, there is always an increase in day length, which becomes greater as one moves further north in the section of the Gods. Alternatively, there is a decrease, which is reversed in the section of the Demons. || 57 ||

> When the sun is in the signs beginning with Libra, the increase and decrease of day and night are the opposite in those two halves. This knowledge is always determined by the latitude of the place and the declination of the sun, as explained previously. || 58 ||

When the sun is in the six signs beginning with Aries <note>the northern hemisphere signs</note>, it is in the northern celestial hemisphere. As one moves further north in the section of the Gods (Jambu-island), the increase becomes progressively greater—

...is greater. In a region on the equator <note>original: "nirakṣadeśa," literally "a place without latitude"</note>, as the sun moves progressively northward, the increase in the length of the day continues until the sun reaches its maximum northern point and then turns back. This means the increase then progressively diminishes. "Decrease" refers to the reduction of the night. The word "and" implies a combination of these effects. In the "Asura" regions <note>referring to the southern hemisphere, traditionally associated with the Asuras in ancient Indian cosmography</note>, such as the southern parts of the ocean, the increase and decrease of day and night are reversed or inverted. This means there is a decrease in the day and an increase in the night. When the sun is in the six signs beginning with Libra <note>the southern celestial hemisphere</note>, for both Jambūdvīpa <note>the northern hemisphere/India</note> and the southern oceanic regions, the increase and decrease of day and night are contrary to one another. The meaning is this: in Jambūdvīpa, the decrease and increase of day and night follow the pattern established for the northern hemisphere, while in the southern oceanic regions, the increase and decrease are the opposite.

Now, to explain how fixed these increases and decreases are, the author elaborates: "By means of the local latitude and declination." The knowledge of these two—the daily understanding of the increase and decrease—is always dependent on the local latitude <note>original: "palabhā," the length of the equinoctial midday shadow used to determine latitude</note> and the sun's declination. In accordance with both of these, as explained previously in the chapter on the True Places of the Planets:

> The sine of declination multiplied by the equinoctial shadow and divided by twelve is the "earth-sine" <term>Kṣitijyā: the sine of the arc of the celestial sphere between the equator and the horizon at the sun's rising</term>.
> This, multiplied by the radius and divided by the hypotenuse of the equinoctial midday shadow, gives the "ascensional difference" <term>Carajāsavaḥ: the difference between right ascension and oblique ascension, used to calculate the length of the day</term>.

By taking the arc of that result, the half-day and half-night are determined. It follows that doubling these gives the full length of the day and night. The mathematical proof is as follows: at the equator, the horizon circle passes through both poles. North of that, the local horizon—passing through the center of one's own globe—is below the North Pole and elevated above the South Pole. Consequently, in the northern hemisphere, it is below the equatorial horizon, and in the southern hemisphere, it is above it. Therefore, the fifteen *ghatikas* <note>a unit of time equal to 24 minutes; 15 ghatikas equal 6 hours or a quarter-day</note> which constitute the half-day at the equator are increased or decreased by the "ascensional difference" <note>cara</note> depending on the hemisphere to find the local half-day and half-night. # The Treatise of the Sun
<meta>Institutional seals: Ministry of Culture/National Library of India seal at top left; "CSL" stamp at top right.</meta>

...elevated from the North Pole and depressed from the South Pole. This refers to the horizon of the equator <note>original: "nirakṣa-kṣitija"; literally "the horizon where there is no latitude"</note>. According to the order of the celestial sphere, it is said to be above and below from the northern part. || 58 || Now, wishing to describe the boundary regions of what has been mentioned, the author first states the distance in terrestrial leagues <term>yojanas: a traditional Indian unit of distance, roughly 5 to 9 miles</term> corresponding to the degrees of declination <term>krānti: the angular distance of a heavenly body north or south of the celestial equator</term>.

-> Multiply the Earth's circumference by the degrees of declination, and divide by the degrees of the circle. <-
-> By the resulting leagues, the Sun moves situated above the equator. || 59 || <-

The circumference of the Earth in leagues, as previously stated, is multiplied by the desired degrees of declination and divided by the three hundred and sixty degrees that make up the passage of the twelve signs of the zodiac. By the leagues thus obtained, the Sun, being situated in the sky above, moves either to the south or to the north. However, in the absence of declination, it revolves exactly over the equatorial region. 

The logic <note>original: "upapatti"</note> here is as follows: From the equatorial region toward the North or South Pole <note>original: "Meru"; the sacred mountain at the center of the world, representing the North Pole</note>, the Sun moves by degrees of declination. To find that distance in leagues, the proportion is: if the leagues of the Earth's circumference touched by the equatorial region correspond to the total degrees of the circle, then how many leagues correspond to the degrees of declination? Thus it is proven. || 59 || Now, in two verses, he describes the knowledge of the boundary regions for the calculation of the length of the day.

-> In this same way, one should subtract the leagues derived from the maximum declination <-
-> from one-quarter of the Earth's circumference. By those leagues which remain, || 60 || <-
-> at the end of the Sun's progress <term>ayanānta: the solstice</term>, in the regions of the Gods and the Demons <note>The North and South Poles respectively</note>, <-

->Accompanied by the *Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka* <note>original: "गूढार्थप्रकाशकेन सहितः"; this is the title of the commentary, meaning "The Illuminator of Hidden Meanings"</note><-

By "people," it is meant those in the two regions belonging to the divisions of the gods and demons <note>The "division of gods" refers to the Northern Hemisphere, and the "division of demons" to the Southern Hemisphere in traditional Indian cosmology</note>, located respectively north and south of the **equatorial region** <term>nirakṣadeśa: literally "the place without latitude," or the Earth's equator</term>. In such a region, near that same solstice, there is likewise once a night measured at sixty ghatis by the same reversal. The word "also" in the text serves to group the day and night together.

This is what is being said: When the sun is at the beginning of Cancer, in a region at a certain distance in yojanas <note>an ancient unit of distance</note> north of the equator, the day lasts sixty ghatis; at that same time, in a region at the same distance south of the equator, the night lasts sixty ghatis. When the sun is at the beginning of Capricorn, in that same northern part, the night is sixty ghatis, and in the southern part, the day is sixty ghatis.

The mathematical proof is as follows: The yojanas corresponding to the **maximum declination** <term>paramakrānti: the obliquity of the ecliptic, roughly 24 degrees in ancient Indian astronomy</term> are subtracted from the yojanas of a quarter of the Earth's circumference. From those northern and southern regions at that distance from the equator, the northern and southern tips of **Mount Meru** <note>the celestial North and South poles</note> are respectively distant by the yojanas of maximum declination. Therefore, at that location, the **colatitude** <term>lambāṃśa</term> is 24 degrees and the **latitude** <term>palāṃśa</term> is 66 degrees.

In that region, the **horizon** <term>kṣitija</term> follows the path of the ecliptic. At the solstice, a quarter-segment of the day-night circle—measuring fifteen ghatis and representing the interval between the equator and the horizon—becomes, according to the previously stated method, either half the day or half the night. Thus, doubling that gives thirty <insert>for the half-day</insert>, and the total measure of sixty ghatis is mathematically proven. This is logical. Because the day-night circle at the solstice touches the horizon at only one point rather than two, the sun is either seen or not seen for the full sixty ghatis of the **diurnal revolution** <note>the 24-hour rotation driven by the *Pravaha* wind</note>. This is a fact established by direct observation according to the conditions of those regions. || 61 || Now—

# The Surya Siddhanta
<note>original: "सूर्य्यसिद्धान्तः" - The "Sun Treatise," one of the most important historical texts on Indian astronomy.</note>

The author explains that the calculation for the measure of day and night should be applied to the regions north and south up to a certain limit:

> Within that interval, up to the limit of sixty <note>sixty ghatis, or a full 24-hour day</note>, the decrease and increase of day and night occur. Beyond that, this celestial sphere revolves in a reverse manner. || 62 ||

In that interval—the regions situated to the north and south between the equator <note>original: "निरक्षदेश" - literally 'the land without latitude'</note> and the polar limits—the decrease and increase (the loss and gain of duration) of day and night occur appropriately within the span of sixty *ghatis* <note>a ghati is 24 minutes; 60 ghatis equal one full day</note> according to the rules mentioned. Beyond that limit, in the regions further north and south near the abodes of the Gods and Demons <note>the North and South Poles</note>, this visible celestial sphere—the physical sphere inhabited by the stars and constellations—revolves in a "reverse" way compared to the regions within the limits, contradicting the standard calculations. This means that the increase and decrease of day and night do not occur there in the previously described manner. This is because it is impossible to calculate the "ascensional difference" <term>charajya: the difference between the equatorial and local rising of a celestial body</term> when it exceeds the radius, and because the very form of that difference becomes impossible to realize. || 62 || Now, he demonstrates that "reverse" state of the sphere in two verses:

> When the quarter of the earth's circumference is diminished by the distance in yojanas corresponding to the sine of two signs' declination, the Sun, when situated in Sagittarius or Capricorn, is not seen in the region of the Gods. || 63 ||

> Likewise, in the region of the Demons, the Sun is not seen when situated in Gemini or Cancer. One should point out the visibility of the Sun at the quarter-circle of the earth where the shadow is lost. || 64 ||

When the quarter of the earth's circumference is reduced by the *yojanas* <note>an ancient unit of distance</note> derived from the degrees of declination of the sine of two signs <note>60 degrees</note>: at that distance from the equator, in the "Region of the Gods" (the Northern Hemisphere), the Sun is not seen by the inhabitants of that place when it is in the signs of Sagittarius or Capricorn. This implies that when the Sun is in Sagittarius or Capricorn, it is always night for them...

## Accompanied by the *Illuminator of the Hidden Meaning* <note>original: "Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka," a famous 17th-century commentary by Ranganatha</note>

> At the fifteenth part of the Earth's circumference, whether in the region of the gods or the demons,
> the Sun passes directly overhead when it reaches the end of its northern or southern course. || 68 ||

"In the region of the gods" refers to the northern hemisphere. "Or in the region of the demons" refers to the southern hemisphere. At a distance of one-fifteenth of the Earth's circumference from the equator <note>original: "nirakṣadeśa," literally the place with no latitude</note>—which is the distance in leagues <term>yojanas: a traditional unit of distance, roughly 8-9 miles</term> resulting from that fraction—the Sun passes directly overhead <note>at the zenith</note> when it reaches the end of its northern progress <term>Uttarāyana: the summer solstice</term> or the end of its southern progress <term>Dakṣiṇāyana: the winter solstice</term> respectively. The practical meaning is that just as the Sun passes overhead at the equator <note>during the equinoxes</note>, it does so at these two specific latitudes at the solstices.

The mathematical proof is as follows: When the Sun is at the end of its solstice, the maximum declination <note>obliquity of the ecliptic</note> is twenty-four degrees. The distance in leagues is calculated by:

> The Earth's circumference multiplied by the degrees of declination and divided by the degrees in a circle.

Since the multiplier is twenty-four and the divisor is the degrees in a circle <note>360</note>, if we simplify the fraction by dividing both by twenty-four, the divisor becomes fifteen. Thus, the statement "at the fifteenth part of the Earth's circumference" is mathematically proven. || 68 ||

Now, having described the Sun's movement to the north and south up to the fifteenth part of the Earth's circumference from the equator, the author explains the behavior of the shadows:

> In the regions between those points, the shadow may fall both south and north;
> beyond those points, the shadow always moves toward its own respective pole. || 69 ||

In the regions between the equator and those fifteenth-part latitudes to the north and south, the midday shadow of a twelve-digit gnomon <term>śaṅku: a vertical pillar used for timekeeping and solar observation</term> (or the shadow at any desired time) may have its tip pointing either north or south. This means: in the northern region between the equator and the fifteenth-part latitude, if the midday zenith distance is southern, the tip of the shadow points north; if the zenith distance is northern, the tip of the shadow points south. Similarly, in the southern region between the equator and the fifteenth-part latitude, the Sun—

# The Surya Siddhanta

When the Sun is in the north, the shadow falls to the south; when it is in the south, the shadow falls to the north.
Beyond that, in the regions within an interval of fifteen degrees, in the two divisions of the sky—the southern and northern divisions—the shadow goes toward the front, facing Mount Meru <note>The sacred mountain at the center of the universe in Hindu cosmology</note>, respectively toward the south and toward the north. This is the meaning. The shadow "goes," meaning it moves or occurs. The word "also" <note>original: "api"</note> is used to connect this with the meaning of the first half of the verse. || 69 || Now, the answer to the question "How does he revolve, illuminating the worlds?" is given in two verses:

-> When the Sun is above Bhadrasva, he produces sunrise in Bharata; <-
-> midnight in Ketumala, and sunset in Kuru. || 70 || <-

-> Revolving in the same manner through the regions of Bharata and the others, <-
-> he produces midday, sunrise, midnight, and sunset, moving clockwise. || 71 || <-

The Sun, having gone above the region of Bhadrasva <note>The eastern continent</note>, would produce sunrise in the region of Bharata <note>India/The southern continent</note>. By the word "but" <note>original: "tu"</note>, it is implied he produces midday in Bhadrasva. At that same time, he produces midnight in the region of Ketumala <note>The western continent</note> and sunset in Kuru <note>The northern continent</note>. By the word "but," it is meant that in the intervals between the aforementioned regions, he produces the elapsed or remaining portions of the day and night as appropriate. If taking very large regions, this is to be understood as heard; however, if taking somewhat more precise locations, these names refer to the cities of Yamakoti, Lanka, Romaka, and Siddhapura, which are contained within them.

-> When there is sunrise for the Sun in the city of Lanka, <-
-> then it is midday in the city of Yamakoti; <-
-> it is then midnight in Siddhapura, and sunset <-
-> occurs at that very time in Romaka. <-

<note>The text describes a global clock where four cities are placed 90 degrees apart: Lanka (on the equator), Yamakoti (East), Romaka (West), and Siddhapura (Antipodal to Lanka).</note>
