Thus, the geography described by the teacher Bhaskaracharya <note>Bhaskaracharya II, author of the Siddhanta Shiromani</note> is consistent, because the aforementioned cities are separated by one-fourth of the Earth's circumference. Now, regarding the three regions known as "Varshas"—namely Bharat, Ketumala, and Kuru—as well as Bhadrasva: the sun, as it revolves <note>literally "wandering around"</note>, positions itself above each respective location. Moving in a clockwise direction <note>original: "pradakshinam," the traditional circumambulation from left to right</note> from its starting position, the sun creates the specific times of midday, sunrise, midnight, and sunset within these four regions.

This is what is being said: When the sun is directly over **Bharat-varsha** <note>India</note>, it is simultaneously midday in Bharat, sunrise in **Ketumala**, midnight in **Kuru**, and sunset in **Bhadrasva**. When the sun is over Ketumala, it is midday in Ketumala, sunrise in Kuru, midnight in Bhadrasva, and sunset in Bharat. When the sun is over Kuru, it is midday in Kuru, sunrise in Bhadrasva, midnight in Bharat, and sunset in Ketumala. || 71 ||

One might ask: "Since the planets are in motion, their movement toward the north or south appears different at every moment and in every country. However, since the stars <note>the Nakshatras</note> do not have their own independent motion, why is it that their positions do not appear the same in every country, even if they are constantly revolving? Furthermore, since the two celestial poles <note>the North and South Poles</note> do not revolve at all, shouldn't they be seen in the exact same position everywhere and at all times?" To answer this, the text says:

-> As one travels toward Meru, the elevation of the Pole Star increases and the inclination of the celestial sphere changes. For one traveling toward the Equator, the elevation and inclination are reversed. || 72 || <-

"Toward Meru" means a person traveling toward either the North or South Pole. For such a traveler, the "elevation of the Pole" <term>Dhruva-unnati: the latitude of the observer, expressed as the height of the Pole Star above the horizon</term> refers to the increasing height of the North or South celestial poles respectively. <margin>As one moves toward the Equator <note>Niraksha: literally "the place without latitude"</note>, the Pole Star appears to sink lower toward the horizon.</margin>

# The Surya Siddhanta
<note>original: "सूर्यसिद्धान्तः" — The "Sun Treatise," the most celebrated ancient Indian astronomical text.</note>

This occurs. Because the center of the celestial sphere <note>original: "bhachakra" — literally the 'wheel of stars' or the zodiacal belt</note> is established by the stars, its inclination <note>term: nati — the angular depression or dip</note> becomes progressively tilted toward the south and north. For a person traveling toward the equatorial region <note>term: niraksha-desha — literally 'the place without latitude,' the terrestrial equator</note>, the previously mentioned depression and elevation become reversed. For a person located in the northern part traveling toward the equator, the North Pole appears depressed compared to their previous position, and the celestial sphere appears elevated compared to their previous position. Similarly, for a person in the southern part traveling toward the equator, the South Pole appears depressed compared to their previous position, and the celestial sphere appears elevated. || 72 || Now, as to why this is so:

-> How does this entire revolution of the stars and planets turn, and what is its support? <-

In response to this question, the author explains the physical reality of the celestial sphere's rotation:

-> The celestial sphere, bound at the two poles, is impelled by the Provector winds; <-
-> It revolves unceasingly, and the planetary orbits are attached to it in their respective order. || 73 || <-

The celestial sphere, which is the physical manifestation of the globe inhabited by the stars, is "bound at the two poles"—the fixed stars situated in the south and north. It was fastened by the Creator <note>original: "Brahma"</note> and is held in place by a spherical mechanism of constant wind-motion. It is "impelled by the Provector winds" <note>term: pravaha-anila — the 'Provector' or 'Forward-carrying' wind, believed in ancient Indian cosmology to drive the celestial bodies from east to west</note>; that is, being struck by the parts of the Provector wind situated in their own places, it "revolves unceasingly" or rotates without interruption. The meaning is that it rotates facing westward.

Now, one might ask: "The circle of stars rotates by the wind, but the planets are situated further and further below; since they lack a direct connection, how do they rotate?" To this, he says: "They are attached to it." The orbits <note>original: "kaksha"</note> or paths of the planets—the Sun and the others—which consist of portions of wind and are situated in the space within the celestial sphere, are "attached to it in their respective order" one below the other. They are tied by "wind-threads" <note>original: "vayu-sutra"</note> to the celestial sphere, which is itself established in the great globe of the Provector wind. Therefore, they rotate along with the celestial sphere. What is so strange about the planets situated there rotating as well? Thus, in the middle of the globe of Provector wind, called the equinoctial...

This fits perfectly with the explanation. || 74 || Now, by way of context, the reasoning for the fewer revolutions of the higher planets and the greater revolutions of the lower planets is presented—

# The Surya Siddhanta

To explain the motion, he first describes the relative sizes of the orbits in order from top to bottom, and the resulting large or small areas occupied by their respective divisions.

->The orbit of the planet situated above is large, and that of the one below is small.<-
->In a large orbit, the degrees are large; likewise, in a small orbit, they are small. || 75 ||<-

The orbit of a planet situated higher up—which takes the form of a path within the circle of the winds <note>The text refers to the 'Vayu-marga' or the atmospheric/celestial currents believed to carry the planets.</note>—is large, meaning it has a great circumference. The orbit of a planet situated below is small, having a small circumference. The word "and" <note>original: "ca"</note> is used for emphasis. Because smaller orbits are contained within larger ones, and larger orbits encompass the smaller ones, the orbits of those situated above and below have large and small circumferences respectively. Otherwise, the described structure would be impossible. 

Thus, when the twelve signs and their degrees are marked equally upon a large circular circumference, the individual degrees <term>bhaga: a 360th part of a circle</term> created by that large orbit are "large," meaning they occupy a great deal of physical space. In a small circle, when those same divisions are marked, the degrees created by that small orbit are "small," meaning they occupy little physical space. Consequently, the actual size of a single degree is greater or lesser respectively; they are not equal in physical extent, as otherwise the completion of the parts of the circle would be inconsistent. This is the inner meaning. || 75 ||

Now, he speaks of the greatness or smallness of the time taken for a planet to complete a revolution, following the order from top to bottom.

->Moving in a small orbit, a planet completes a revolution in a short time.<-
->Moving in a great circle, a planet completes it in a long time. || 76 ||<-

"Moving in a small orbit" refers to the lower orbit, the measure of whose circumference is small. A planet situated there completes or traverses a revolution <term>bhagana: a full circuit of the zodiac</term> consisting of the twelve signs in a short amount of time. "In a great circle" means in a higher orbit. Moving there, it travels for a great or long time through the twelve—

# Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings" <note>The *Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka*, a famous commentary on the Surya Siddhanta</note>

The planets traverse the zodiac signs. Because the motion in terms of *yojanas* <note>a traditional Indian unit of distance, roughly 8 miles</note> to be described later is uniform for all planets, they cover different angular distances. // 76 //

Now, the author explains with an example how, in the same amount of time, there are many revolutions for planets arranged in order from top to bottom:

->The Moon, traveling in a small orbit, completes many revolutions.<-
->Saturn, moving in a very large orbit, completes fewer than that. // 77 //<-

"In a small orbit" refers to the circumference of the path. The Moon, crossing through this, completes many "revolutions"—meaning it traverses the twelve signs of the zodiac many times. Saturn, moving in a very large orbit, completes "fewer" revolutions than the Moon. <note>The original uses the singular 'revolution' to refer to the category of motion</note>. It traverses the twelve signs fewer times. For this very reason, it is called *Shanaishchara* <note>literally "the slow-mover"</note>. // 77 //

Now, the answer to the question:

->Why are the lords of the days, years, months, and hours not the same?<-

is given in two verses:

->The lords of the days follow the fourth in order downwards from Saturn.<-
->The lords of the years are likewise declared to be every third planet in that same order. // 78 //<-
->The lords of the months are recorded in upward order from the Moon.<-
->The lords of the hours follow the downward order starting from the son of the Sun <note>Saturn</note>. // 79 //<-

The planets counted as fourth in descending order <note>from slowest to fastest</note> become the lords of the days (the rulers of the days of the week). That sequence is as follows: Saturn, Sun, Moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus. The lords of the year (consisting of three hundred and sixty-five days) are said to be every third planet in that same descending order from Saturn. The word "likewise" implies the same method of counting. That sequence is: Saturn, Mars, Venus, Moon, Jupiter, Sun, and Mercury. From the Moon upwards—

# Commentary on the Surya Siddhanta

The lords of the months, consisting of thirty days each, are described according to the descending order of their orbital spheres <note>The text refers to the ancient geocentric model where planets are arranged by their distance from Earth</note>. That sequence is: Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn. This is the order from the lowest to the highest. The lords of the hours <term>Hora: an hour, or half of a zodiac sign</term> are determined by the descending order starting from Saturn.

->The term *Hora* refers to the rising sign and is half of a zodiacal sign.<-

This means that in a full day and night <term>Ahoratra: a 24-hour solar day</term>, there are twenty-four hours, with twelve occurring during the day and twelve during the night, each consisting of fifteen degrees.

->A *Hora* is equal to two and a half *Ghatikas*.<-
<note>A Ghatika is 24 minutes; thus, a Hora is exactly 60 minutes.</note>

In a full day-and-night cycle of sixty *Ghatikas*, others state there are twenty-four hours. The lords of these hours are described as being separated from one another, much like the lords of the months. Their sequence is: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon. Here, because Saturn is the highest and the Moon is the lowest, the descending and ascending orders are stated starting from them. If any other planet were assumed as the starting point, it would lead to logical inconsistency.

One might ask: "Does Saturn not hold lordship over the days, years, and hours from the beginning of creation? Or does the Moon not hold lordship over the months from the beginning of creation? This would seem to contradict the lords mentioned in the previous section." The mathematical justification is as follows: Since the rising signs <term>Lagnas</term> in the form of hours occur in the ecliptic in a descending order starting from Aries <note>original: "Mesha"</note>, it is appropriate that the lordship of the hours follows the descending order of the orbital spheres.

Thus, in a day and night of twenty-four hours, when divided by seven <note>the seven planets</note>, three cycles of lords pass. The fourth lord at the start of the second day becomes the first lord of that hour, and consequently, the lord of that second day. This pattern continues hereafter. Similarly, in this sequence of weekdays, there are three weekdays remaining in a solar year <term>Savana-varsha: a civil year of 360 days</term>; therefore, the lord of the next year is the third planet in descending order from the current one. Likewise, in a civil month, there are two weekdays remaining beyond the full weeks; thus, the lord of the month is determined by skipping one in the order of the planetary spheres.

<summary>This text explains the mathematical and astronomical basis for assigning planetary "lords" to hours, days, months, and years, using the geocentric orbital order to justify the sequence of the seven-day week.</summary>
<keywords>Surya Siddhanta, Hora, planetary hours, Ahoratra, civil year, lords of the month, orbital spheres, Indian astronomy</keywords>

...in ascending order, the Lord of the Month <note>the presiding deity of a specific month in the Hindu calendar</note> follows one after another; thus the two verses beginning with "Saturn, the Sun, etc." are explained. || 79 || Now,

-> What is the measurement of the planetary orbits? <-

Wishing to answer this question, the author first states the measurement of the orbit of the asterisms <note>the Nakshatras or lunar mansions/stars</note>.

The revolution of the Sun—that is, the measurement of the circumference of its orbit in leagues <term>yojanas: an ancient Indian unit of distance, roughly 5 to 9 miles</term>—is:

-> 4,331,500. <- <note>original: "kha-kha-artha-eka-sura-arnavah," using a numerical code where words represent numbers: sky=0, sky=0, senses=5, earth=1, gods=33, oceans=4</note>

As will be stated later, this value multiplied by sixty becomes the orbit of the stars, which is the middle circle of the sphere where the stars reside. By those leagues measuring the stellar orbit, the circle of the stars <note>original: "Bhamandala"</note>—the middle circle of the sphere of the stars—revolves at the very top, far above the seven planets beginning with the Moon, circling around the terrestrial globe.

The logic <note>original: "upapatti"</note> here is as follows: Since the stars lack their own motion, the stellar sphere is at the highest point. There, the Sun's orbit is determined by the Sun's motion. Even though the stars do not move, by assuming a motion of one minute <note>one-sixtieth of a degree</note> for the sake of calculation, and because the proportion would otherwise be inconsistent—

> The divisor should be assumed from the total mass of the collection.

—and because a decrease in the height requires an increase in the result, or for the sake of simplicity in the calculation of the shadow, the Sun's motion was set at sixty minutes by the Lord <note>the Sun God, the revealed speaker of this text</note>. Because the stars lack motion, the multiplier of sixty is logically proven. || 80 || Now, to understand the measurement of the planetary orbits, the measurement of the orbit of space <note>the universe's limit</note> is discussed:

-> How far does that reach? <-

# The Surya Siddhanta

He now provides the answer to the question:

->**The lunar revolutions mentioned for a Kalpa, multiplied by the Moon’s orbit,**<-
->**is known as the Orbit of the Skies; it is the extent of the Sun’s rays. || 81 ||**<-

<note>A Kalpa is a vast cosmic time cycle consisting of 4,320,000,000 years.</note> The "lunar revolutions mentioned for a Kalpa" refers to the total number of times the Moon orbits the Earth in this period. By the rule stating "these revolutions in a cycle multiplied by a thousand are the revolutions in a Kalpa," it means the lunar revolutions of a Yuga <note>a smaller age</note> multiplied by one thousand. When these are multiplied by the "Moon’s orbit" (the circumference of the Moon's path, which will be defined later as 324,000 <term>Yojanas</term> <note>a traditional unit of distance, roughly 8-9 miles</note>), the result is the circumference of the "Orbit of the Skies." This should be understood by the wise.

Now, one might ask: how can infinite space have a circumference? To this, he says: "the extent of the rays." This means the reach of the Sun’s light is limited by this measurement of the celestial orbit. The idea is that the circumference of the celestial sphere—contained within the "Shell of the Brahma-Egg" <note>original: "Brahmanda-kataha," referring to the boundary of the physical universe</note>—is defined by the area reached by the Sun's rays. 

The proof is as follows: Since it was stated that the celestial orbit divided by a planet's revolutions equals that planet's specific orbit, it follows that the product of a planet's revolutions and its orbit equals the celestial orbit. Thus, the product of the Moon's revolutions and its orbit is indeed equal to the celestial orbit. || 81 ||

Next, he explains the method for calculating the orbits of the planets and their daily speed in <term>Yojanas</term>:

---

->**That same [celestial orbit] divided by the Kalpa-revolutions of a planet is its orbit.**<-
->**Dividing that by the number of Earth-days, the result is the eastward motion of all. || 82 ||**<-

That same "Orbit of the Skies," which consists of the reach of the Sun's rays, when divided by the revolutions of a specific planet in a Kalpa, gives the orbit (circumference) of that planet as the result. The word "same" is used for emphasis. When the celestial orbit is divided by the number of terrestrial (solar) days in a Kalpa, the resulting quotient is the "eastward motion" <note>the actual daily distance traveled in space</note> for all the aforementioned planets.

<summary>This text defines the "Orbit of the Skies" (the boundary of the universe) as the product of the Moon's revolutions and its orbital path, equating this limit to the reach of solar radiation. It further provides the formula for determining individual planetary orbits and their daily orbital velocity.</summary>

# Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings" <note>original: "Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka," a famous commentary on the Surya Siddhanta</note>

The term "of the days" refers to that which relates to the day. The forward motion <note>eastward motion of the planets</note> has been described in terms of <term>yojanas</term> <note>a traditional Indian unit of distance, roughly 8-9 miles</note>. Here is the proof: The "Sky-Circle" <note>the circumference of the universe</note>, which is the product of the revolutions in a <term>Kalpa</term> <note>an eon of 4.32 billion years</note> and the specific orbit, when divided by the revolutions in a Kalpa, results in the orbit itself. Since a planet traverses the distance of the Sky-Circle in the solar days of a Kalpa, then by proportion—if it covers the Sky-Circle in a full Kalpa, how much does it cover in one solar day?—it is proven that the daily forward motion in yojanas is constant for all planets. || 82 ||

Now, he describes how to convert this motion in yojanas into his own motion in <term>minutes of arc</term> <note>kalās</note>:

> **The number resulting from the motion in yojanas, multiplied by the Moon's orbit**
> **and divided by the Sky-Circle; that result, divided by fifteen, gives the minutes of motion.** || 83 ||

The number produced from the motion-yojanas is multiplied by the Moon's orbit and divided by the "Sky-Circle" <note>the circumference of the cosmic shell</note>—or rather, divided by the orbit of the specific planet intended. That result is then divided by fifteen <note>original: "tithyāptā," divided by the number of lunar days in a fortnight</note>. The word "but" <note>tu</note> implies that the final result is the minutes of motion for that desired planet. 

Here is the proof: If the yojanas of the full orbit equal the minutes in a circle <note>21,600 minutes</note>, then how many minutes do the motion-yojanas equal? By this proportion, the minutes of motion are found. In this calculation, the Moon's orbit divided by fifteen is used as a substitute for the form of the total minutes in a circle; thus, it is proven. || 83 ||

Now, he answers the question: "What are the altitudes <note>distances from Earth</note>?"

> **The orbit multiplied by the Earth's diameter and divided by the Earth's circumference**
> **is the distance (radius). The planet's own distance is half the diameter of its orbit.** || 84 ||

The orbit of the planets in yojanas is multiplied by the Earth's diameter—which is 1,600 yojanas, as it was stated that the Earth's diameter is twice eight-hundred <note>800 x 2</note>—and divided by the known circumference of the Earth. The result is the "ear" <note>radius/distance</note> of that orbit...

<margin>The calculation of planetary heights</margin>
These values result. When these are diminished by the diameter of the Earth and halved, the result is the height of the planet <term>Graha; any celestial body including the Sun and Moon</term> relative to its own specific diameter, measured from the surface of the Earth. Here is the proof <note>upapatti: a mathematical demonstration or rationale</note>: If the Earth's circumference gives the Earth's diameter, then what diameter does the orbital circumference in <term>Yojanas; a traditional unit of distance, roughly 5-9 miles</term> give? By this proportion, the diameters of the orbits are found. These are halved to find the radius of the orbit, which represents the distance from the center of the Earth to the orbital circle. To find that distance from the surface of the Earth, it is diminished by the Earth's radius; thus, the orbital height from the Earth's surface is obtained. In this calculation, the orbital diameters are diminished by the Earth's diameter and then halved. Both methods yield the same result. The height of the orbit is indeed the height of the planet, as the planet is stationed there. By this, the knowledge of the mutual distances between the established planetary heights is easily understood. The answer to the question "How much is the distance?" is self-evident. This is the general direction of the argument. || 84 ||

The orbit of the Moon is 324 multiplied by a thousand. The word "but" <note>original: "tu"</note> implies this should be accepted based on the authority of tradition <note>Agama</note>. Otherwise, a fallacy of mutual dependence <note>circular reasoning</note> would occur. Above the Moon, the orbit of Mercury's conjunction is 1,040,560. Although Mercury's conjunction is not directly visible in the sky and thus describing its orbit might seem improper, nevertheless, Mercury moves in an orbit above the Moon, determined by its motion derived from the revolutions of its conjunction. -> The Sun, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, and the Moon. <-

This was the order mentioned. The revolution of the shell of the cosmic egg <note>original: "brahmāṇḍa-sampuṭa"; the universe is traditionally envisioned as a golden egg</note> occurs all around, and within it is the expansion of the rays of the Sun<gloss>\*</gloss>. || 90 ||

The numbers—the limbs of the Vedas (6), eighty-eight (88), the nails (20), the earth (1), the seven (7), and the supports (18) <note>This uses the "bhūtasaṃkhyā" system where words represent numbers: 18,712,088,600,000</note>—multiplied by a million are the leagues <term>yojanas: a traditional measure of distance, roughly 8-9 miles</term> mentioned in the first half. The "revolution of the shell of the cosmic egg" refers to the circumference of the sphere of the universe. Since the circumference of space was previously described as the product of the revolutions in a Kalpa <note>a vast cosmic age</note> and the orbit, there is no repetition here. "Within it" means inside the sphere of the universe, the expansion of the rays of the Sun <note>the Sun is referred to here as "Dinakara," the Day-Maker</note> occurs in all directions; the circumference of the region where the sunbeams travel is equal to that. By this, it is indicated that this is the internal circumference of the cosmic sphere, not the external. || 90 ||
Now, to avoid any inconsistency in the subsequent text, he concludes the chapter with a formal statement.

### Thus ends the Chapter on Geography in the Sūrya Siddhānta.

This means that the topic started in a different meter is now finished. In the first section of this work, the divisions were called "Authorities" <term>adhikāra</term>. In this latter section, the divisions are called "Chapters" <term>adhyāya</term> due to the change in subject matter; this should be noted.

->this Chapter on Geography in the second half is completed.<-

# The Surya Siddhanta
<note>The "Sun-Treatise," the foundational text of Indian astronomy.</note>

Now, he <note>the teacher, the Sun's representative</note> addresses the sages again through two verses:

> Then, in a secluded and pure place, having bathed and being purified and adorned;
> Having worshipped the Sun with devotion, as well as the planets, the stars, and the Guhyakas; || 1 ||

> Through the traditional instruction received from the mouth of the teacher, according to his knowledge;
> The Teacher, having perceived everything directly, speaks for the enlightenment of the disciple. || 2 ||

The word "Then" <note>original: "Atha"</note> is used here for the sake of auspiciousness. The second "then" indicates the sequence following what was previously stated. In a "secluded" (private) and "pure" (sacred) place, the Teacher—who is the personified portion of the Sun <note>original: "Suryamsha-purusha"</note>—acts as the instructor to Mayasura. "Having bathed" means he has performed his ritual ablutions; "purified" means he possesses a clean mind. "Adorned" means he is decorated with ornaments on his hands, ears, and neck; this description signifies a state of being free from anxiety. Otherwise, if one's mind were agitated by worldly affairs or the movements of the planets, mental stability would be impossible.

"Having worshipped the Sun" <note>original: "Bhaskara"</note>—the venerable Sun who is the source of his livelihood—with "devotion" (defined here as the form of spiritual knowledge), and having made him the object of salutation and praise. He also worships the "planets" (the Moon and others); the Sun is mentioned separately to indicate his primary importance. He worships the "stars" (the lunar mansions and zodiac signs) and the "Guhyakas" <note>original: "Guhyakan," a class of supernatural beings/yakshas</note> and other minor deities. The connective "and" should be understood here.

"From the mouth of the teacher" means from the lotus-like face of the Sun. "Through traditional instruction" <note>original: "Paramparayopadeshena"</note> refers to the lineage: the Sun spoke to the sages, and the sages spoke to the Sun's representative. In reality, this phrasing is used to generate interest in the disciple and to indicate the extreme secrecy of this knowledge. For why else would the Sun, who was ready to speak to the distant sages, not speak directly to his own representative? It is due to the nature of the transmission. "According to his knowledge" means according to his own capacity...

## Accompanied by the *Illuminator of Hidden Meanings* <note>original: "Gudhartaprakashaka," a famous 17th-century commentary by Ranganatha</note>

The teacher has personally demonstrated everything mentioned in the previous chapter to produce a clear understanding in the student and to dispel any confusion for Mayasura <note>The mythical figure to whom the Sun God revealed astronomical secrets</note>. This means he showed it through direct observation. || 2 ||

How did he show it? In repeating the words of the Man-Who-Is-Part-of-the-Sun <note>original: "Suryamshapurusha," the divine messenger of the Sun God</note> spoken to Mayasura, he describes the purpose and the beginning of the construction of the globe <term>armillary sphere: a model of objects in the sky, consisting of a spherical framework of rings</term> in two verses:

->One should fashion a wondrous model of the celestial sphere.<-
->Having first caused a desired terrestrial globe to be made of wood,<- || 3 ||
->A staff should be passed through its center, protruding on both sides of Meru <note>The sacred mountain at the North Pole</note>.<-
->There should be two supporting circles and likewise the equatorial circle.<- || 4 ||

A wise mathematician or a craftsman skilled in globe-making should create a model—an illustrative globe—of the celestial sphere <note>original: "bhagola," the sphere of the fixed stars</note> which surrounds the terrestrial globe <note>original: "bhugola"</note>, in order to understand the positions described in the previous chapter. Now, one might ask: if knowledge is gained simply by what was spoken, isn't building a physical model useless? To this, he says: "wondrous." It is intended to produce an astonishing realization of the truths previously mentioned. For instance, the mind does not easily grasp the idea of people living on the sides or bottom of the earth, or the specific regions of the celestial sphere corresponding to those parts, or the fact that the Earth remains unsupported in space. Since a physical model makes such certain knowledge possible, its construction is necessary.

How should it be made? He says: "desired." This means a globe of the Earth should be made by a woodworker out of wood, with a hole through it, according to a circumference of one's own choosing. A wooden rod, representing the axis of Meru, is placed through the middle of that wooden terrestrial globe.

The rod is placed loosely within the central hole. This means it extends outward from both ends of the hole, which is sized according to the diameter of the earth-globe <note>original: *bhūgola*</note>. The portion of the rod remaining outside one end should be equal to the portion outside the other. One should ensure that the rod sections are identical on both sides. 

Next, he describes the two supporting circles for securing the earth-globe: "a pair of supporting orbits" <note>original: *ādhārakakṣā-dvitayam*</note>. To secure the earth-globe, one first creates a pair of circles as a support, one positioned vertically and the other horizontally. One circle should be threaded through the rod at an equal distance from both sides of the earth-globe. A second, identical circle should be threaded through the rod, intersecting the first at its midpoint. This is the established method, as the earth-globe cannot be properly secured without these two circles. 

He then begins the description of the binding of the orbits: "The orbit..." <note>original: *kakṣā*</note>. The equatorial <note>original: *vaiṣuvatī*</note> orbit refers to the circumference of the circle related to the equator—the equatorial circle itself. This is bound by the mathematician <note>term: *gaṇaka* (astronomer/mathematician)</note> through the midpoints of the two supporting circles, following the model of the earth's central circle. || 4 ||

Now, in the following five verses, he describes the construction of the diurnal circles <note>term: *ahorātra-vṛtta* (circles representing the daily path of stars/planets)</note> for the twelve zodiac signs beginning with Aries.

> -> These three [circles] should be made using the degrees of the zodiacal circle converted into finger-breadths <note>term: *aṅgula* (a traditional unit of measurement)</note> and divided by two, <-
> -> and by the half-chords of the diurnal circles, according to their estimated proportions. || 5 || <-
> -> By the degrees of declination <note>term: *krānti* (distance north or south of the celestial equator)</note> and celestial latitude <note>term: *vikṣepa*</note>, halved, in the south and north, <-

> -> These same orbits are reversed for Cancer and the following signs; <-
> -> similarly, three for Libra and the following, and in reverse for Capricorn and the following. || 7 || <-
> -> These should be attached to both supporting orbits, situated within the southern hemisphere. <-

> One should arrange the positions of the stars located in the southern and northern hemispheres, as well as Abhijit <note>The star Vega, often treated as the 28th lunar mansion</note> || 8 ||
> And the Seven Sages <note>The Big Dipper/Ursa Major</note>, Canopus, and the stars of Brahma and others. The equinoctial circle is situated in the middle of all of these || 9 ||

This means they are marked with the degrees of the zodiacal signs converted into finger-breadths <term>angulas: a traditional unit of measurement roughly equal to a finger's width</term>, specifically by three hundred and sixty units divided into equal parts. These "orbits" or circles consist of three rings made of bamboo strips. There are exactly three of them. The use of the word "exactly" in the text excludes any number more or less than this in the marking of the circles. These should be crafted by a skilled artisan who is also an expert in the mathematics of the celestial sphere. 

The text explains that these should not be made according to the measurements of the previous circles. He says: *By the half-chords of their own day and night.* By the word "own," he refers to the three signs starting with Aries. The "half-chord of the diurnal circle" for each sign refers to the radius of that specific day-circle, known as the <term>dyujya: the radius of the diurnal circle of a planet or star</term>. The word "and" implies they must be constructed this way. One should make three circles for the first three signs (Aries, Taurus, Gemini) using radii equal to their respective diurnal radii. 

Now, one might ask: since there is no explicit logic given here for calculating these diurnal radii as mentioned in the chapter on "True Places," how can one construct the circles? To this, he says: *By estimation from that measurement.* The three circles should be made by estimating from the measurement of the equinoctial circle. Just as the equinoctial circle is equal to the prime vertical, the circle at the end of Aries is smaller than that, the circle at the end of Taurus is smaller still, and the circle at the end of Gemini is the smallest of all. Thus, the circles have progressively smaller radii. 

The logic for constructing these circles using the diurnal radius is sound, because the radius of a diurnal circle is the square root of the difference between the square of the total radius <term>trijya: the radius of the celestial sphere, usually 3438 minutes of arc</term> and the square of the sine of declination <term>krantijya: the distance of a celestial body north or south of the equator</term>. Having prepared these three circles, he now fixes them onto the model sphere *by the degrees of declination and latitude...*

From those specific regions, by the degrees <note>original: "amshaih"</note>. And by the segments of the supporting circle, divided into equal parts and marked. The result is that the circle for the end of Gemini serves for the start of Cancer; the circle for the end of Taurus serves for Leo; and the circle for the end of Aries serves for Virgo.

These must be fastened by the astronomer to the two supporting circles in the southern portion of the celestial equator.

## The Surya Siddhanta

Above the point of intersection <note>original: "sampata"</note>. At the intersection of the final diurnal circles <note>the paths stars and planets take daily</note>, the two solstitial points—the northern and southern transitions—are located. Here, because of the movement described as "above," the supporting circle should be understood as vertical <note>meridional</note>, not horizontal like the celestial equator <note>original: "unmandala"</note>. 

The result is this: In the vertical supporting circle of the equinoctial circle, there is an upper middle intersection. From that upper intersection, the diurnal circle of Capricorn <note>the Winter Solstice</note> is located twenty-four degrees south on that supporting circle; where it meets, that is the point of the Winter Solstice <note>original: "uttarayana-sandhi," the start of the sun's northern progress</note>. Similarly, from the lower intersection, the diurnal circle of Cancer <note>the Summer Solstice</note> is twenty-four degrees north on that supporting circle; where it meets, that is the point of the Summer Solstice <note>original: "dakshinayana-sandhi," the start of the sun's southern progress</note>. 

Because the equinox is positioned opposite to the solstice, and through the relationship of the word "below" (implied by the word "above"), the two equinoxes are formed. The essential meaning is that the two intersections of the horizontal equatorial circle and the supporting circle are the East and West points, which represent the start of Aries and Libra respectively at the equinoctial positions.

Now, the author describes the arrangement of all the zodiac signs <note>original: "rashi"</note>. Starting from the equinoctial position: by using the precise thirty-degree segments related to the signs—following the movement of the celestial sphere—the arrangement of all the signs is made. By using transverse chords <note>sines</note> and the specific regions of their respective circles (which follow the pattern of the circles mentioned), the positions of Aries and the other signs are determined. 

In this manner, following the method of imagining the solstices and equinoxes, a wise mathematician should calculate and mark the other positions in the intervals between them. For example: from the equinoctial point in the East, using a segment of one-twelfth of the celestial circle, one finds the position on the diurnal circle of the end of Aries. From there, at the same interval on the diurnal circle of the end of Taurus, one finds the position of the end of Taurus. From that point, one reaches the solstitial point. Then, by that same interval, the end of Gemini. From there, moving toward the Western side on the diurnal circle of the end of Cancer, one finds the position of the end of Cancer. From there, the end of Leo...

<meta>This page continues the technical description of the celestial sphere and the positioning of the zodiac signs along the diurnal circles, following the previous discussion on the intersection of the ecliptic and the equator.</meta>

<page-num>252</page-num>
<header>Accompanied by the *Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka* <note>The "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings," a famous commentary by Raṅganātha on the Surya Siddhanta</note>.</header>

...on the diurnal circle <note>original: "ahorātravṛtta"</note>; by that same interval is the end of Leo <note>Simha</note>. From this, by that same interval, is the western equinoctial point <note>the autumnal equinox</note> at the end of Virgo <note>Kanya</note>. From this, in the eastern part, on the diurnal circle of the end of Libra <note>Tula</note>, by that same interval, is the position of the end of Libra. From this, on the diurnal circle of the end of Scorpio <note>Vrishchika</note>, by that same interval, is the position of the end of Scorpio. From this, by that same interval, is the solstice point <note>ayana-sandhi</note> at the end of Sagittarius <note>Dhanu</note>. From this, on the diurnal circle of the beginning of Aquarius <note>Kumbha</note>, by that same interval, is the position of the end of Capricorn <note>Makara</note>. From this, on the diurnal circle of the beginning of Pisces <note>Meena</note>, by that same interval, is the position of the end of Aquarius and the beginning of Pisces. From this, at the eastern equinox, is the position of the end of Pisces and the beginning of Aries <note>Mesha</note>; it is clear that this is by that same interval. || 10 ||

Now, an objection is raised: since the twelve zodiac signs exist on the circles of the celestial sphere <note>Gola</note>, and otherwise the minutes of the circle <note>the 360 degrees/21,600 minutes of the zodiac</note> would be inconsistent, how can there be a marking of the signs or a division of the signs when there is no single, unified circle <note>because the previous description used multiple diurnal circles</note>? Since the space between these circles is merely the sky <note>void</note>, the author, while clarifying the previous statement under the guise of describing a specific circle, states that the Sun completes its revolution <note>bhagaṇa</note> in that specific circle:

---

-> From solstice to solstice, there is another slanted orbit. || 11 || <-
-> Known as the Ecliptic <note>term: Kranti; literally "the path of transition" or declination</note>, the Sun always travels along it, illuminating the world. <-

---

The phrase "starting from the solstice point and returning to that same solstice point" uses the word "and" to exclude any solstice point other than the one where the motion began and ended. There is "another" orbit <note>kakṣā</note> in the celestial sphere, equal in size to the base circle <note>the equator</note>, which serves as the path for marking the zodiac signs. The word "certainly" <note>implied in the Sanskrit 'eva'</note> is used to exclude any other path. It is "slanted" <note>tiryak</note>, meaning its inclination is distinct from the previously mentioned circles. The name "Kranti" <note>Ecliptic</note> refers to the act of "stepping" or "transitioning" <note>kramaṇa</note>. For the purpose of knowing the motion and position of the planets, a circle by that name has been conceptualized. The essential meaning is that one should fix on the celestial sphere the Ecliptic circle, which is connected to the two solstices and the two equinoxes, and is marked with the twelve signs of the zodiac.

# The Surya Siddhanta
<meta>Seal: MINISTRY OF CULTURE GOVERNMENT OF INDIA</meta>
<meta>Logo: SL</meta>

Illuminating the worlds, that Sun shines forth. By this description, the Moon and other celestial bodies are excluded <note>original: "candrādīnāṃ nirāsaḥ"; the Sun is unique as the primary light source</note>. Always and continuously, he travels along the orbit known as the ecliptic <note>original: "krānti-sañjñayā kakṣayā"</note>, moving by his own power to complete the full cycle of the zodiac. The sense is that the ecliptic is a fixed path imagined in accordance with the Sun's motion. || 11 ||

Now, one might ask why the Moon and other planets do not travel exactly along this same ecliptic path. To this, the text says:

->**The Moon and the others, by their own nodes situated on the ecliptic, || 12 ||**<-
->**are seen pulled away from that path at the ends of their latitudes.**<-

The Moon and the other planets—excluding the Sun—are influenced by their own "nodes" <term>Pata: the points where a planet's orbit crosses the ecliptic</term>. These nodes are personified as deities situated upon the ecliptic at the specific positions of the planets' longitudes. Because of these nodes, the planets are "pulled away" <note>original: "apakṛṣṭā"</note> or drawn toward the north or south by the distance of their latitude. For this reason, they are seen by people on Earth at the points of their calculated celestial latitude <note>original: "vikṣepa"</note>, rather than on the ecliptic itself. Just as the ecliptic is situated in relation to the celestial equator, there is a separate "latitude circle" <note>original: "vikṣepa-vṛttam"</note> imagined for the motion of the Moon and each planet. This circle is attached to the ecliptic at the node and at a point six signs away, reaching its maximum distance (north or south) three signs away from the nodes. || 12 ||

Next, the text describes the nature of the "Rising Sign" and the "Meridian Sign" as mentioned in the chapter on the three problems of direction, time, and place:

->**The point on the ecliptic at the eastern horizon is the Ascendant; the point setting is determined by it. || 13 ||**<-
->**The "Middle" point is that which is above in the middle of the sky, as established by the rising times at Lanka.**<-

<note>Lanka refers to the hypothetical city on the equator used as the prime meridian in Indian astronomy.</note>

# Accompanied by the "Illuminator of the Hidden Meaning"

<note>original: "Gudartha-prakashaka"</note>

At the rising horizon means at the eastern point of the horizon circle. The **Rising Sign** <term>Lagna: the point of the ecliptic rising on the eastern horizon</term> is defined as that point of the **Ecliptic** <term>Kranti-vritta: the sun's apparent path</term> which is connected to that location by the **Provector Wind** <note>In ancient Indian cosmology, the Pravaha-vayu is the celestial wind responsible for the constant rotation of the stellar sphere</note>, measured by its longitude starting from Aries. 

In this context, he describes the nature of the **Setting Sign**: "The Setting." By virtue of that—following the logic of the rising sign—the setting horizon refers to the western point of the horizon circle. As the ecliptic moves, the point where it is connected by the provector wind is called the **Setting Sign**, measured by its longitude starting from Aries. 

And so, because the ecliptic is always present on the horizon's path, it is established that there is an interval of six signs <note>180 degrees</note> between the rising and setting signs. This is calculated using the **Rising Times at the Equator** <term>Lankodaya: the time taken for signs to rise at the terrestrial equator</term>. As established in the manner described in the "Chapter on the Three Problems," the **Culminating Sign** <term>Madhya Lagna: the 'Middle Lagna' or Meridian House Cusp</term> is that which is "above one's own middle." 

This "middle" refers to the center of one's visible sky, a region following the North-South meridian circle; it does not refer to the **Zenith** <term>Khasvastika</term> as favored by the teacher Bhaskaracharya, because the ecliptic does not always pass through the zenith. The essential meaning is that the point where the ecliptic meets the meridian circle is called the **Culminating Sign**, measured by its longitude starting from Aries. || 13 ||

Next, he describes the principles mentioned in the "Chapter on the Three Problems" and the nature of the **Sine of Ascensional Difference** <term>Carajya: a value used to calculate the variation in daylight length</term> mentioned in the "Chapter on True Motions."

->The sine which is between the meridian and the horizon is called the **Antya**. || 14 ||<-
->The **Sine of the Earth-Sine** <term>Caradalajya</term> is known as the interval between the Equator and the Horizon.<-

In the Northern Hemisphere, this is the sum of the **Radius** <term>Trijya</term> and the Sine of Ascensional Difference; in the Southern Hemisphere, it is the Radius minus the Sine of Ascensional Difference, as stated in the "Chapter on the Three Problems." That *Antya* is the meridian...

<meta>This page continues the technical commentary on the Surya Siddhanta, specifically focusing on the mathematical definitions of the horizon and the calculation of the "ascensional difference" (charajya) used to determine the length of day and night.</meta>

# The Surya Siddhanta <note>The "Sun-Treatise," the foundational text of Indian astronomy.</note>

The sine <note>original: "jya"; in Indian trigonometry, this refers to the "half-chord" of an arc.</note> is located in a specific portion of the diurnal circle <note>the daily path of a star or planet</note> within the interval between the meridian circle and the horizon of one's desired location. This is a string-like chord representing the distance from the intersection of the rising-setting line and the meridian line, up to the intersection of the diurnal circle and the meridian; however, it is not a "true" sine in the strictest sense. This is because the rising-setting line, which connects the two points where the diurnal circle meets the horizon, does not function as the diameter of the diurnal circle. Therefore, in the northern hemisphere, another value for the sine is found to be greater. This is declared and explained by those learned in the study of the celestial sphere <note>the "Golajnas" or sphere-experts</note>. Now, one might ask: what is the nature of this "ultimate" sine of ascensional difference <note>original: "charajya"</note> upon which everything depends, and how is it established? To answer this, the author says: "It should be known..."

> The polar horizon <note>original: "unmandala"; the horizon at the Earth's equator</note> and the celestial equator <note>original: "vishuvandala"</note> are proclaimed as such.

According to the chapter on the "Three Problems" <note>referring to the problems of time, direction, and place</note>, these two terms refer to the same concept. The polar horizon is the fixed equatorial horizon that mimics a transverse supporting circle; the "horizon" mentioned here is the horizon of one's own specific location. The interval between these two is the subject. The word "and" <note>original: "cha"</note> here carries a specific meaning, implying the straight-line chord that represents half of that portion of the diurnal circle situated between them. Thus, the practical result is the vertical distance between the rising-setting lines of the equator and one's own location. The "sine of the semi-ascensional difference" <note>original: "charadalajya"</note> refers to the sine of that segment called "ascensional difference" <note>chara</note> located in that interval. It does not mean "half" <note>dala</note> in a literal sense here; it means the sine of the ascensional difference itself. This must be understood by those learned in the celestial sphere. || 14 ||

Now, because the content of the previous two verses might be difficult to grasp without knowing the nature of the horizon, the author explains the form of the horizon in half a verse:

> Having placed one's own location at the top, the horizon circle is in the middle. || 15 ||

On the globe of the Earth, having placed or imagined one's own specific location at the very top—above all other regions—then in the middle of such a globe, in the vertical center...

# Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings"

The circle known by the name *Ed* <note>original: "ed-sanjnau"; likely referring to the horizon or a specific technical designation in the preceding verse</note> is the <term>Horizon Circle</term> <note>original: "ksitija-vrttam"</note>. The sense is that, in accordance with that, the horizon circle should be made fixed and attached to the <term>demonstration globe</term> <note>original: "drstanta-gole"; a physical model used to illustrate celestial movements</note>. || 15 || Now, having completed this demonstration globe, the author describes the method by which it may rotate westward of its own accord:

->Covered with cloth, and also surrounded on the outside by the "Light-and-Shadow" circle,<-
->the instrument for time-rotation is achieved through the application of the "flow of nectar."<- || 16 ||

"On the outside" means upon the surface of the globe. The <term>demonstration globe</term> is to be "covered" or draped with a cloth in a spherical shape. The word "and" <note>original: "ca"</note> implies that the various celestial circles should be marked or drawn upon that cloth. It is "surrounded by the Light-and-Shadow" <note>original: "lokalokena"</note>, meaning it is attached to the circle known as the horizon, which sits at the junction of the visible and invisible realms. The word "also" <note>original: "api"</note> is used for conjunction. The implication here is that the horizon itself should not be covered by the cloth; rather, the horizon should be made fixed to the globe over the cloth by some means so that it remains stable. 

"Through the application of the flow of nectar" <note>original: "amrta-srava-yogena"; a poetic reference to water or mercury used in hydraulics</note>: having constructed such a globe, one should create a mechanism—a <term>means for time-rotation</term>—using the impact of a water stream or similar force, so that the demonstration globe rotates exactly according to the <term>sixty sidereal hours</term> <note>original: "sasti-naksatra-ghatibhih"; the traditional Indian measurement of a full day-night cycle</note>. One should personally construct this <term>globe-instrument</term> <note>original: "gola-yantram"</note>. 

The meaning is as follows: Having covered the demonstration globe with cloth, the ends of its supporting axle should be placed in channels on the north and south walls. This must be done so that the tip of the axle is <term>facing the Pole Star</term> <note>original: "dhruvabhimukham"</note>. Then, a <term>water stream</term> <note>original: "jala-pravaha"</note> moving in a straight path toward the east should strike the lower back part of the axle. The instruction to "cover with cloth" is specifically to hide this mechanism. Otherwise, if the impact of the water were visible through the gaps between the circles of the globe, the "miracle" <note>original: "camatkara"</note> or wonder of the self-rotating movement would not be produced. From the sky...

# The Surya Siddhanta
<note>original: "Sūryasiddhānta"; the "Sun's Treatise," the foundational text of Indian astronomy.</note>

To ensure the rotation is smooth, it is mentioned that the device should be covered with a cloth. This cloth should not be damp; rather, it should be coated with a smooth substance such as wax <note>original: "madanādinā" - literally "with beeswax and such"</note>. A wall in the form of a trench should be constructed so that the globe is visible below the horizon circle. However, the part of the southern axis <term>yaṣṭi: the central rod or axle of the globe</term> must be kept loose there. Otherwise, the rotation would be impossible. One must understand through their own intelligence that the water flow should be made invisible, exiting from the outer section of the trench located in the eastern direction, and so forth. || 16 ||

Now, if a water flow is not possible in that location, how can the illustrative globe become self-rotating? To address this self-rotation, and noting that this must be kept secret, the text says:

### One should equip the globe-instrument with the "Seed of the High One."
### This must be kept secret; if revealed, it would become common knowledge here. || 17 ||

The instrument in the form of the illustrative globe should be equipped with the "Seed of the High One" <note>original: "tuṅgabīja"</note>. "The High One" <note>original: "tuṅga"</note> refers to Mahadeva <note>Lord Shiva</note>, and his "seed" or "potency" <note>original: "vīrya"</note> means mercury <note>original: "pārada"</note>. The mathematician or skilled craftsman should prepare it using that. He should accomplish it through the application of mercury in such a way that the globe rotates exactly in sixty <term>ghaṭīs: a unit of time equal to 24 minutes; 60 ghaṭīs make a full 24-hour day</term>.

The meaning of what has been said is as follows: At two or three desired locations on the ends of the axis protruding outside the fixed globe, one should carve a rim in the shape of a circumference. Having covered that with palm leaves or a coating of smooth material, a hole should be made. Through that path, mercury should be filled into half of the circumference, and water should be placed in the other half of the circumference. Then, having sealed the hole, the ends should be placed into two tubes fixed in a wall so that the globe remains suspended in the air. Then, the axis, pulled by the mercury and water, rotates on its own. Then—

## With the "Illuminator of the Hidden Meaning" Commentary

...attached to the sphere. If it is asked whether this object is covered simply to achieve the appearance of the sky <note>original: "ākāśākāratā", referring to making the model look like the celestial void</note>, then why is this self-rotating mechanism not described explicitly? To this, the author replies: **"It is to be kept secret."** This method of creating a self-moving device is a secret, not to be revealed. Why? He says: **"Because if stated openly..."** If the construction of the self-rotating machine were described too clearly, it would become common knowledge for everyone here on earth. And so, because no sense of wonder arises from a thing that is known to everyone, the intention is that it should not be revealed everywhere for the sake of preserving that wonder; this is why the construction was not explicitly stated. || 17 ||

Now, one might ask: "If you say it is a secret, how am I to understand it, and how are others like me to understand it?" He answers this with a verse and a half:

> ->Therefore, one should construct the excellent sphere through the instruction of a teacher.<-
> ->In age after age, this construction of the Sun God is lost.<-
> ->By the grace of someone, it appears again according to their desire.<-

Therefore, because the construction of the <term>self-mover</term> <note>original: "svayaṃvaha", a perpetual motion or self-rotating mechanism</note> is a secret, a <term>calculator</term> <note>original: "gaṇaka", an astronomer-mathematician</note> should create the excellent sphere—the self-rotating model—through the instruction of a teacher, meaning through the honest explanation of a teacher received via tradition. The implication is: "I have told it to you, but it is not stated too explicitly in the book because it is a secret." How is this to be known by others? He says: **"In age..." etc.** This self-moving construction of the Sun <note>original: "vivasvataḥ", the Sun God or the presiding spirit of the solar orb</note> is, in every age—meaning over long periods of time—lost or disappeared from the world. By the grace or favor of someone like me, it appears or becomes manifest again and again according to their will. Thus, just as you have understood it from me, others must understand it from others like me.

# The Treatise of the Sun
<note>original: "Surya Siddhanta"</note>

This is because time is limitless and creation is beginningless. ||18|| Now, following the previously mentioned method of self-moving mechanisms, he explains that other self-moving instruments—distinct from the self-moving celestial globe—should be constructed for the knowledge of time, and that their construction should be carried out in secret:

->For the purpose of determining time, one should likewise construct instruments. || 19 ||<-

"Likewise" means in the same manner as the self-moving celestial globe was constructed. "For the purpose of determining time" means for the sake of precise knowledge of the elapsed portion of the day and so forth. One should construct "instruments," meaning self-moving devices other than the celestial globe. The mathematician <note>term: Ganaka (mathematician/astronomer)</note> should have these made through skill in craftsmanship and related arts. In the "wondrous instrument" used for determining time—which causes amazement among people because of its self-moving nature—one should apply the "seed" (the cause that achieves self-motion) while "solitary," meaning alone and without a second person. This means he should produce it himself through his own knowledge of craftsmanship. Otherwise, if a second person knows of it, the secret heart of the instrument might become known to the public through that person's mouth; if that were to happen, the sense of wonder would be lost. || 19 || Now, because these self-moving instruments are difficult to construct, he says that the knowledge of time should be gained through instruments such as the gnomon:

->By means of the gnomon, the staff, the arc, and the wheel, and by various shadow-instruments, || 20 ||<-
->The knowledge of time is to be understood from the instruction of a teacher by those who are untiring.<-

By means of the gnomon <note>term: Sanku (a vertical pillar used to measure shadows)</note>, the staff, the arc <note>term: Dhanus (a semi-circular instrument)</note>, and the wheel <note>term: Chakra (a circular instrument)</note>—which are well-known—and by various shadow-instruments (instruments that utilize shadows) through many types of mathematical methods, and from the "instruction of a teacher" (from one's own professor)...

# The Treatise of the Sun

On the circumference, there is a support consisting of holes and chains. ## Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings"

By means of instruments such as the peacock, the man, and the monkey. The "peacock" refers to a self-rotating instrument <note>original: svayaṃvaha-yantra; a device designed to move on its own without external force</note> that operates independently. The "man" refers to the gnomon instrument <note>original: śaṅkhākhyaṃ chāyā-yantra; literally a "shadow instrument" used to measure time by the sun's position</note> previously mentioned. The "monkey" is another self-rotating independent instrument. These are equipped with "fine sand within their interiors" <note>original: sasūkṣmareṇugarbhaiḥ</note>, meaning they contain finely sifted dust or sand. It is well known in the world that sixty small earthen jars are finely threaded and placed within the belly of the peacock; these exit from the mouth one after another at intervals of one *ghatika* <note>a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</note> by their own accord. Such is the meaning of these instruments.

Alternatively, it refers to an instrument that has fine grains of sand in its interior or "belly," which is the famous sand-clock <note>term: vālukā-yantra; an hourglass-like device</note>. The meaning established here is that one should use the peacock and other mentioned instruments along with the sand-clock. The word "and" <note>original: cakāraḥ</note> is used to include other devices like the water-clock <note>term: toya-yantra; a clepsydra</note> and the hemispherical bowl. With these, one should accurately and precisely determine the time, such as the portion of the day already elapsed. This means one should know it with extreme precision. // 21 //

Now, one might ask: how are these self-rotating instruments like the peacock and others to be constructed? To this, the author explains that the methods for achieving this are numerous and difficult to master:

> Mercury, spokes, water, threads, copper, oil, and water;
> These are the "seeds" <note>driving forces or components</note>, as are sands; but the practical applications of these are difficult to attain. // 22 //

In those peacock-like instruments, these applications must be employed with great skill for the purpose of self-rotation. This "skill" should be applied until the desired result is achieved. What are these components? He lists them: "Mercury, spokes, water, threads," and so on. These are spokes filled with mercury. As it is stated in the *Siddhanta Shiromani* <note>a major 12th-century astronomical treatise by Bhaskara II</note>:

> On a balanced wheel made of light wood,
> there are hollow spokes placed at equal intervals on the rim...

By accurately determining the shadow using the <term>Gnomon</term> <note>original: "Shanku"; a vertical rod used in sundials to cast a shadow for measurement</note>—which is the "human instrument"—and by understanding the methods of calculation, one gains the best means for determining time, such as the portion of the day already passed. This instrument is far superior to all others. Furthermore, because it functions specifically by calculating the shadow, the Gnomon’s role as a time-keeper is achieved through that shadow; thus, there is no contradiction in its function as an instrument. ->Having known the movements of the planets and stars, and the Sphere in its true essence,<-

"The movements of the planets and stars" refers to the mathematical knowledge contained in the first half of the book. "The Sphere" <note>original: "Gola"</note> refers to the nature of the terrestrial and celestial spheres explained in the latter half of the book. The word "and" serves to connect these two. "In its true essence" means according to the actual state and nature of reality. "Having known" means having fully understood. "The man" refers to the practitioner. "The world of the planets" refers to the realm of the Moon and other planets, as well as the realm of the stars. "Attains" means he reaches it. 

Now, one might ask: what human goal is served by reaching the world of the planets? To this, the author states the ultimate goal in the form of liberation <note>original: "Moksha"</note>. "Eventually" means that in a subsequent birth, the man becomes a "knower of the Self" <note>original: "Atma-jnani"</note>. # The Surya Siddhanta

**In this world, practical dealings are conducted using four measures: Solar, Lunar, Sidereal, and Civil.**
**The sixty-year cycle should be understood through the Jovian measure, and not through the others, as a constant rule. || 2 ||**

In this world of mortals, practical dealings—the organization of ritual and daily actions—are carried out using four measures: Solar, Lunar, Sidereal <note>original: *nakshatra*</note>, and Civil <note>original: *savana*</note>. The "sixty-year cycle" refers to the cycle of sixty years beginning with *Prabhava* <note>The first year of the 60-year Hindu Jupiter cycle</note>; the singular form is used here to denote the class of years. This should be understood through the Jovian measure <note>original: *barhaspatya*</note>, which is the time it takes for the mean motion of Jupiter to pass through one sign of the zodiac. By "not through the others," the text refers to the remaining measures: the Brahma, Pitrya <note>Ancestral</note>, and Prajapatya measures. "As a constant rule" means always. There is no regular practical dealing with those other measures. The word "but" <note>original: *tu*</note> implies that those other measures might be used for practical dealings only on very rare occasions. || 2 || Now, the author demonstrates the practical use of the Solar measure.

**By the Solar measure, the length of days and nights, the "Eighty-six Mouths,"**
**the Solstices, the Equinoxes, and the auspicious times of the Sun's entry into a sign are determined. || 3 ||**

The length of a full day and night <note>original: *ahoratra*</note> is to be known by the Solar measure. This means a day and night result from the daily motion and transit of the Sun. The "Eighty-six Mouths" <note>original: *shadashitimukha*</note> will be explained shortly. The word "and" <note>original: *cha*</note> is used for conjunction; therefore, these are all known by the Solar measure. The Solstice <note>original: *ayana*</note> and the Equinox <note>original: *vishuvat*</note> are also included. The "auspicious time of entry" <note>original: *sankranti*</note> refers to the sacred period associated with the specific position of the Sun's disk, determined by the Solar measure. || 3 || Now, he describes the "Eighty-six Mouths."

**Starting from Libra, every eighty-sixth degree is an "Eighty-six Mouth" in sequence.**
**There are four of these, occurring specifically in the "Dual-natured" signs. || 4 ||**

Starting from the beginning of Libra, a period of eighty-six solar days constitutes an "Eighty-six Mouth." There are four such points, and they occur in sequence within the four "Dual-natured" <note>original: *dvisvabhava*; also known as mutable signs: Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, and Pisces</note> signs as will be described. || 4 || He explains this further:

# The Treatise of the Sun

At the center of the circle of stars <note>original: "bhachakra-nabhau"</note>, equidistant from the two poles of the terrestrial globe, lies the celestial equator. There are two equinoctial points <note>original: "vishuvat-dvitayam"</note> located on a straight line passing through the center, separated by the diameter of the circle. Because the equinoctial circle is described as being midway between the poles, the two points where the ecliptic <note>the path of the sun</note> intersects that circle are known respectively as the Eastern and Western equinoxes, specifically named Aries and Libra.

There are also two solstices <note>original: "ayana-dvitayam"</note>, which are the beginnings of Cancer and Capricorn. The word "and" in the text implies a grouping. Thus, these four locations—the two equinoxes and the two solstices—are situated on a straight line relative to the center and are well-known in astronomical calculations as the starting points of the four quarters of the zodiac. The word "only" is used to exclude other zodiac signs from being these primary markers. The word "but" implies that although other points might align, they are not famous as the "beginnings of the quarters" because they lack the specific properties of the equinoxes and solstices. || 7 ||

Next, the author describes the names and natures of the remaining points:

> Between those points, there are two entries <note>original: "samkranti"</note> each;
> Furthermore, due to the continuous progression of the sun's entry,
> these are known as the two "Steps of Vishnu" <note>original: "vishnupadi"</note>. || 8 ||

"Between those" refers to the intervals between the equinoxes and solstices. The plural is used here because there are four such intervals in the circle. In each interval, there are two "entries" or transitions <note>term: Samkranti; the moment the sun enters a new zodiac sign</note>, meaning the sun occupies two signs between each cardinal point.

For example:
*   Between the equinox of **Aries** and the solstice of **Cancer**, lie the beginnings of **Taurus** and **Gemini**.
*   Between **Cancer** and the equinox of **Libra**, lie the beginnings of **Leo** and **Virgo**.
*   Between **Libra** and the solstice of **Capricorn**, lie the beginnings of **Scorpio** and **Sagittarius**.
*   Between **Capricorn** and the equinox of **Aries**, lie the beginnings of **Aquarius** and **Pisces**.

Thus, after an equinox come two transitions, then a solstice; after that, two transitions, then an equinox; then two transitions, then a solstice...

...and so on, this should be understood as occurring repeatedly. Regarding the first transit <term>Saṅkrānti: the moment the sun enters a new zodiac sign</term> among two consecutive transits, the author explains the specific detail: "Due to continuity." This means that from the transit occurring in continuous succession, two "Vishnupada" <note>A specific astronomical division occurring when the sun enters fixed signs: Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, and Aquarius</note> points occur in that interval. The essential meaning is that the first transit is designated as Vishnupada, and two of these occur within that internal period. It should be noted that the second type of transit, known as "Shadashiti" <note>The "eighty-six" division occurring in dual signs: Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, and Pisces</note> previously indicated, also has two occurrences within that interval. || 8 ||

Now, he describes the two solstices <term>Ayana: the half-year journey of the sun north or south</term>.

> From the Sun's entry into Capricorn <note>Makara-saṅkrānti</note>, six months are the Northern Progress <note>Uttarāyaṇa</note>.
> Likewise, from the beginning of Cancer <note>Karka-saṅkrānti</note>, six months are the Southern Progress <note>Dakṣiṇāyana</note>. || 9 ||

From the moment of the Sun's entry into Capricorn, there are six solar months of the Northern Progress. From the beginning of Cancer—that is, from the transit into Cancer—the same occurs due to the Sun's transit. The use of the word "only" <note>implied by the particle 'eva' in the commentary</note> excludes other planets from this calculation. These six months—the word "but" <note>tu</note> implies they are solar months—constitute the Southern Progress. || 9 ||

Now, he describes the seasons, months, and the year.

> These twelve, starting with Aries <note>Meṣa</note>, are the months; from these alone, a year is formed. || 10 ||

"From then" means starting from the entry into Capricorn. The word "also" is used to include the limit of the Northern Progress. "Governed by two signs" means they consist of the Sun's transit through two zodiac signs. The seasons—Dewy <note>Śiśira</note>, Spring <note>Vasanta</note>, Summer <note>Grīṣma</note>, Rainy <note>Varṣā</note>, Autumn <note>Śarad</note>, and Winter <note>Hemanta</note>—are specific divisions of time. # Surya Siddhanta
<note>The Surya Siddhanta is one of the most important early Sanskrit treatises on Indian astronomy.</note>

...by months. The word "only" <note>original: "evakāra"</note> is used here to exclude any more or less. This constitutes a year, specifically a solar year. || 10 ||

Now, in this context, the author describes the calculation of the auspicious time <term>Punya-kala: a period considered spiritually potent for rituals</term> during a transit <term>Sankranti: the moment the Sun enters a new zodiac sign</term>.

->**The minutes of the Sun's diameter, multiplied by sixty and divided by its daily motion,**<-
->**half of those resulting ghatikas are auspicious before the transit, and likewise after. || 11 ||**<-

The meaning is: the minutes <note>arc-minutes</note> of the measure of the Sun's disk <note>original: "bimba"</note> are multiplied by sixty and divided by the Sun's daily motion <note>original: "bhukti"</note>. Half of that result is the number of <term>Ghatikas: a unit of time equal to 24 minutes</term> of that name. From the moment of the transit—meaning the time the Sun enters a new zodiac sign—the time before <note>original: "arvāk"</note> is auspicious for religious acts like ritual bathing, meaning these minutes increase one's merit. Likewise, the time after <note>original: "apare"</note> the transit is also merit-giving for religious acts.

The mathematical rationale <note>original: "upapatti"</note> is as follows: The exact moment of transit is when the center of the Sun's disk moves into the beginning of a zodiac sign. Because that moment is extremely subtle and difficult to perceive, a certain duration must be accepted. That duration is recognized as the time the entire disk takes to move across the transition point, due to the physical contact of the disk. Therefore, the proportion is: if the Sun's daily motion takes sixty civil <term>Savana: terrestrial or solar-day based</term> ghatikas, then how much time do the minutes of the Sun's disk take? The resulting "disk-ghatikas" represent the gross transit period, from the time the front edge <note>original: "nemi"</note> touches the sign-boundary until the back edge passes it. Half of those ghatikas represent the time for the radius to pass. Thus, because the front and back edges move across the boundary in sequence, the times before and after the central transit moment are considered auspicious. || 11 ||

Having spoken of solar measurement, the author now describes lunar measurement <note>original: "candramāna"</note> in its proper order.

->**When the Moon, having moved away from the Sun, travels eastward day by day,**<-
->**that is lunar measurement. A lunar day is known by twelve degrees of separation. || 12 ||**<-

Having left the conjunction with the Sun and becoming separate, the Moon—

## Accompanied by the *Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka* <note>The "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings," a famous 17th-century commentary by Raṅganātha on the Surya Siddhanta.</note>

Day by day, that which occurs daily. The specific amount by which [the Moon] moves toward the eastern direction daily is the lunar measure; however, that is measured by the difference in their respective motions. Now, just as a solar day is defined by the Sun's degree, one might ask: how many of these degrees make a complete lunar day? To this, he says: "By degrees." By the degrees—the word "but" implies the degrees produced by the interval between the Sun and the Moon, as that is its nature. By twelve—meaning the number twelve—a *tithi* <note>A lunar day, specifically 1/30th of a lunar month.</note> is to be known. This means one lunar day is to be understood. This is what is being said: since the lunar day begins from the conjunction of the Sun and Moon and the month ends at their next conjunction, a lunar month consists of thirty lunar days based on the difference in their revolutions. Therefore, if thirty days equal the difference in degrees of a full circle [360°], what does one day equal? One lunar day equals twelve degrees.

-> The New Moon (*Darśa*) is the union of the Sun and Moon. <-

Because of this definition, since the month ending with the New Moon consists of thirty *tithis*, the *tithi* is the form of the lunar day. || 12 || Now, he describes the practical use of lunar time:

> The lunar day (*tithi*), the half-lunar day (*karana*), marriage, tonsure, and all such rites;
> The performance of vows, fasts, and pilgrimages are governed by lunar time. || 13 ||

The *tithi* refers to the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pratipada*) and so on; the *karana* refers to *bava* <note>The first of the eleven karanas or half-tithis.</note> and so on; marriage is the wedding ceremony; tonsure is the ritual cutting of hair (*caula*). These and all other such actions, including the initiation of vows and so on, as well as the performance of rules, fasts, and departures for journeys. The word "and" is used for inclusion. All these are accepted—that is, governed—by lunar measurement. || 13 ||

Now, following the lunar month, he describes the measurement of the Manes <note>The *Pitris* or ancestral spirits.</note> by association:

> A lunar month consists of thirty *tithis*; it is declared to be a day and night of the Manes.
> Their division into day and night occurs at the end of the two fortnights. || 14 ||
