# The Surya Siddhanta

A lunar month consists of thirty lunar days <note>original: "tithis"</note>. That which pertains to the **Pitris** <note>The Pitris are the deified souls of ancestors in Hindu cosmology</note> is called "Paitrya." A "day" refers to the daylight portion, and "night" refers to the dark portion belonging to the ancestors. The word "and" <note>original: "ca"</note> in the text acts as a regulator; therefore, it is remembered that the two together—not each individually—form a single unit. Following the grammatical gender, this applies to both. Thus, the result is that a lunar month is equivalent to a day and night of the ancestors.

The "end of the month" and the "end of the festival" refer to the end of the New Moon <note>original: "darshanta"</note> and the end of the Full Moon <note>original: "purnimanta"</note>. These two points serve as the division. In the middle of that ancestral day and night, these two points occur: the end of the New Moon is the **midday** for the ancestors, and the end of the Full Moon is the **midnight** for the ancestors. Consequently, it is established that their day begins at the middle of the eighth day of the dark fortnight, and their day ends at the middle of the eighth day of the bright fortnight.

|| 14 || Now, having reached the proper sequence, the author explains the sidereal measurement <note>term: "nakshatra mana" - time measured by the stars</note> and, in this context, the naming of the months:

->The constant revolution of the star-circle is called a sidereal day.<-
->The months are to be known by the names of the lunar mansions, based on their connection to the end of the Full Moon. || 15 ||<-

"Constant" means daily. The "revolution of the star-circle" <note>original: "bhachakra-bhramanam"</note> refers to the rotation of the entire collection of stars caused by the *Pravaha* wind <note>In ancient Indian astronomy, the 'Pravaha' is the celestial wind believed to drive the planets and stars around the Earth</note>. This is called a "sidereal day" by those who know measurement. By using the word "constant," the author dismisses the idea that a sidereal day is based on the moon's passage through a single lunar mansion, as that would not fit the definition of a full revolution of the star-circle.

Regarding the naming of the months: they are named after the "Great Lunar Mansions." This is determined by the "connection to the end of the Full Moon." The months are named according to the lunar mansion <note>term: "nakshatra" - one of the 27 sectors of the sky the moon passes through</note> in which the moon is located at the end of the Full Moon. The word "but" <note>original: "tu"</note> implies that these are to be understood as lunar months. The essential meaning is: a month is known by the name of the lunar mansion in which the moon stays at the moment of the Full Moon. For example, in a lunar month bounded by the end of the New Moon, if the moon is near the star **Chitra** at the Full Moon, the month is called **Chaitra**. If near **Vishakha**, it is called Vaishakha...

<header>The Treatise of the Sun</header>

# The Treatise of the Sun

<note>original: "Surya Siddhanta"</note>

Because of the connection with the three asterisms <note>lunar mansions or constellations</note> starting with Phalguni and Hasta, the month is established as Phalguna.
|| 16 || Now, in this context, the author describes the years of Jupiter starting with Kartika.

> In the months starting with Vaishakha, during the dark fortnight on the fifteenth lunar day,
> the years starting with Kartika are determined by the setting and rising of Jupiter. || 17 ||

Just as a month receives its name from its connection to a specific asterism on the full moon day, the same logic applies here. The word "and" <note>original: "tatha"</note> is used for the sake of conjunction. Based on Jupiter's proximity to or distance from the Sun—that is, from its setting or rising—during the twelve months starting with Vaishakha, on the fifteenth lunar day of the dark fortnight (meaning the new moon day <note>original: "amavasya"</note>), the connection occurs. The word "and" <note>original: "ca"</note> implies a conjunction with the full moon relationship previously discussed. This connection with the asterism of that day defines the twelve years starting with Kartika.

When the setting or rising of Jupiter occurs on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Vaishakha (the new moon), that Jupiter year is named Kartika due to its connection with the Krittika asterism. In this same manner, during the months of Jyeshtha, Ashadha, Shravana, Bhadrapada, Ashvina, Kartika, Margashirsha, Pausha, Magha, Phalguna, and Chaitra, the years such as Margashirsha and others occur through their connection with the daily asterisms: Mrigashirsha, Pushya, Magha, Purva-Phalguni, Chitra, Vishakha, Jyeshtha, Purva-Ashadha, Shravana, Purva-Bhadrapada, and Ashvini. Here too, the previously mentioned connection to groups of two or three asterisms should be understood.

This description is illustrative. The core meaning is that the Jovian year is named after whichever asterism the Moon is stationed in on the day Jupiter rises or sets. In the books of the *Samhitas* <note>encyclopedic collections of astral science</note>, the year is declared based on both setting and rising, but currently, the practice of naming the year based on the rising is favored by <term>calculators</term> <note>original: "ganaka"; traditional astronomers or astrologers who perform mathematical computations</note>, as it is said, "by the risen Jupiter." || 17 ||

Next, the author describes the Civil <note>original: "savana"</note> day in its proper order.

# Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings" <note>The Gudharthaprakashaka, a famous 17th-century commentary by Ranganatha on the Surya Siddhanta</note>

-> From one sunrise of the Sun to the next, that is declared as "Civil" (Savana) time. <-
-> Civil days are determined by this; the rules for the timing of sacrifices are set by them. || 18 || <-

The duration of time beginning from the moment of one sunrise of the Sun until the moment of the immediately following sunrise is called "Civil" (Savana) time by those knowledgeable in measurement. By this calculation of the interval between two sunrises, the Civil days—such as the large numbers mentioned in the "Chapter on Mean Motions" <note>referring to the total number of civil days in a Kalpa or great cycle</note>—are derived. He explains its practical application with the phrase: *The rules for the timing of sacrifices.* The calculation of the proper time for a Vedic sacrifice is done by those Civil days. The word "but" (tu) in the verse is used in the sense of "only," serving to exclude other systems of measurement for this specific purpose. || 18 || Now, he describes other practical uses:

-> The determination of impurity periods and the like, as well as the lords of the day, month, and year; <-
-> and the mean motion of the planets is grasped only by Civil time. || 19 || <-

"Impurity" (Sutaka) refers to that associated with birth or death. <unclear>By the word "and the like," purity</unclear>, medical treatments, and penances like the *Chandrayana* <note>a fast regulated by the moon's waxing and waning</note> are included. The "determination" is the decision or calculation of these periods. The "lords of the day, month, and year" <note>the presiding planetary deities of these time units</note> are also determined this way. Likewise, in the aggregate, the "motion of the planets" refers to their *mean* (average) motion. By the word "but" (tu), the "true" (apparent) motion is excluded. This is because true motion varies from moment to moment, whereas Civil time is based on the nature of the day's connection. By this, it is indicated that calculating a planet's position using true motion for these purposes is rejected because it is too imprecise <note>literally "gross" or "thick"</note>. By "Civil measurement" and the word "only," the exclusion of other measurements is emphasized. It is "grasped," meaning accepted by the wise. Here, in accordance with the plural context, "is grasped" should be understood in the plural sense. || 19 || Now, he describes "Divine" measurement:

# The Surya Siddhanta
<note>original: "Surya Siddhanta" — The "Sun Treatise," one of the most important foundational texts of Indian astronomy.</note>

The attainment of the world of the planets was mentioned previously; now, the author explains what the specific fruit or result of these two attainments is:

> This celestial knowledge of the stars and the planets has been shown as the highest wisdom. By understanding it, one attains an eternal place in the worlds of the Sun and the other celestial bodies. || 23 ||

"Of the stars" refers to knowledge related to the lunar mansions <note>original: "Nakshatra" — the 27 or 28 divisions of the sky along the ecliptic</note>. "Of the planets" refers to their specific movements. The word "and" serves as a conjunction. This knowledge is "highest," meaning it is superior to all other sciences. The reason for this is given in the adjective "celestial," meaning it originated in the heavenly world. Having been "shown"—that is, taught by me to you—and having "understood" it, one attains a "place" or residence in the worlds of the Sun and other planets. This place is "eternal," meaning a permanent state of union with the Supreme Absolute <note>original: "Brahmasayujya" — the final liberation where the soul merges with the divine</note>. The second "and" in the first half of the verse connects these ideas, implying that both results occur in sequence. In some manuscripts, the verse beginning with "That which was told to you as the supreme..." does not appear before this verse, but rather at the end of the chapter on time measurements, following this verse.

<meta>This page continues the technical astronomical discourse of the Surya Siddhanta, specifically focusing on the "Beeja" corrections (secular equations) required to align calculated planetary positions with observed reality.</meta>

## Accompanied by the "Illuminator of Hidden Meanings" <note>original: "Gūḍhārthaprakāśaka," a famous commentary by Ranganatha</note>

The mean position <term>Madhya: the average position of a planet ignoring its elliptical orbit</term> arises from the proportion of the cycle; the true position <term>Sphuta: the actual observed position after corrections</term> arises from the degrees of the true circle. Because these do not match observation over time, the "Seed Action" <term>Beeja-kriya: a corrective factor applied to astronomical constants to account for long-term changes</term> is now described. || 5 ||

Multiply the Moon's position (in signs and degrees) by the Sun, and divide by the orbit of the stars <note>original: "Nakshatra-kaksha"</note>. Subtract the remainder from the orbit of the stars; this provides the correction for each. || 6 ||

Whichever is smaller, multiply that by the orbit of the "Elephants of the Directions" <note>a poetic reference to the number 8</note> and by the lunar days <note>the number 15</note>. That result, in degrees and minutes, is the "Seed." One should apply its multiplier to the Sun. || 7 ||

Subtract three times the amount from the Moon; add twenty-four times <note>original: "Jina," referring to the 24 Tirthankaras</note> the amount to Mars. Subtract twice the amount from Mercury; subtract thirty times <note>original: "Kha-rama," where Kha=0 and Rama=3</note> the amount from Jupiter. || 8 ||

Subtract ninety times <note>original: "Vyoma-nava," where Vyoma=0 and Nava=9</note> the amount from the "Apex of Motion" <term>Chalocha: the apogee or the point of highest velocity</term> of Venus. Add seven times the amount to Saturn. Now, the circumferences <note>original: "Paridhi"</note> are described. || 9 ||

The circumferences stated for the end of even quadrants are always considered "True" <note>already corrected</note>. However, those stated for the end of odd quadrants are to be understood as refined by the "Supreme Seed" correction. || 10 ||

I shall now state the degrees of the circles at the end of the odd quadrants without the seed correction. For the Sun and Moon, they are 14 and 32 <note>original: "Manavas" (14) and "Dantas" (32)</note>, reduced by minutes of 18 and 25 <note>original: "Dhriti" (18) and "Tattva" (25)</note>. || 11 ||

For Mars, they are 65 <note>original: "Bana" (5) and "Tarka" (6)</note>; for Mercury, 27 <note>original: "Achala" (7) and "Bahu" (2)</note>. For Jupiter, 82 <note>original: "Ashta" (8) and "Netra" (2)</note>; for Venus, 10 <note>original: "Vyoma" (0) and "Shitanshu" (1)</note>. || 12 ||

For Saturn, they are 60 <note>original: "Shunya" (0) and "Ritu" (6)</note>. One should apply the seed correction to these. For the Sun's circumference degrees, divide the seed by 30 <note>original: "Kha-agni"</note> and subtract. || 13 ||

For the Moon, divide by 2 and add. For Mars, divide by 2 and add. For Mercury, divide by 1 and add. For Jupiter, divide by 14 <note>original: "Indra"</note> and add. || 14 ||

For Venus, multiply by 1 and add. For Saturn, multiply by 12 <note>original: "Ravi"</note> and subtract. Thus, the corrected circumferences of the "Slow Apex" <term>Manda: the correction for the eccentricity of the orbit</term> are made, and one should do the same for the "Fast Apex" <term>Shighra: the correction for the planet's motion relative to the Sun</term>. || 15 ||

## The Surya Siddhanta
<note>The Sun's Precept: The foundational Sanskrit treatise on Indian astronomy.</note>

For Mars, the values are two hundred thirty-eight <note>original: "abhra-guṇa-akṣīṇi" (0-3-2), read right-to-left as 232; however, the text likely refers to specific correction factors</note>; for Mercury, one hundred thirty-four; for Jupiter <term>Devapūjya</term>, fifty-five; for Venus <term>Bhārgava</term>, two hundred sixty-one. || 16 ||

For Saturn, forty-one. These are the <term>śīghra</term> <note>fast-motion or kinetic</note> corrections at the end of the odd quadrants, excluding the seed-correction <term>bīja</term>. Double the value for Mars's degrees; for Mercury, double the value and subtract it. || 17 ||

Multiply by seventeen <note>original: "atyaṣṭi"</note> and add for Jupiter; for Venus, multiply by one and subtract. For Saturn, multiply by one and subtract. By these corrections, the planets become equal to their observed positions. || 18 ||

This "seed" <term>bīja</term> <note>the correction factor required to align calculated positions with observed reality</note> has been declared by me to you out of great affection. This must always be kept secret; it is not to be taught here and there <note>to just anyone</note>. || 19 ||

It should be given to a tested disciple who is devoted to the teacher and virtuous, or to a learned priest <term>vipra</term>, and to no one else—certainly not to one who acts as a mere pretender. || 20 ||

This "seed" is the ultimate, clear secret of the entire Siddhanta. It grants the successful accomplishment of works such as journeys, marriage, and other rites. || 21 ||

The text found at the end of this "Chapter on the Application of the Seed" <term>Bījopanayanādhyāya</term> in some books does not seem appropriate. Because the <term>Uttara-khaṇḍa</term> <note>the latter section of the work</note> lacks a description of planetary mathematics, it is improper to write a chapter there that requires such context. It would be more fitting to write this at the end of the "Chapter on True Motion" <term>Spaṣṭādhikāra</term>. Furthermore:

->How many measures are there, and what is their use?<-

Since there are no further questions following this one, writing this in the <term>Uttara-khaṇḍa</term> (which consists of answers to questions) is inconsistent. Moreover, since the "seed" correction did not exist at the time of the original instruction, and the observation of discrepancies occurred later, how could it have been taught then? Otherwise, it would have been included in the original text itself. Considering this, it appears some clever person added this to suggest the "seed" has a divine, sage-given origin...

The commentator also argues that this specific chapter is likely a later interpolation rather than part of the original ancient text.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the concluding verses of the Surya Siddhanta, specifically the departure of the solar messenger and the reaction of the demon-architect Maya.</meta>

->Accompanied by the *Gudharthaprakashaka* <note>The "Revealer of Hidden Meanings," a famous commentary by Ranganatha</note><-

...it should be understood that the chapter on the application of corrections <note>original: "Bijopanayanadhyaya"</note> is considered an interpolation here, and therefore has not been commented upon. || 23 || Now, he begins the conclusion of the dialogue spoken to the Sages.

> Having spoken thus, and taking leave of Maya, being duly honored by him, the part of the Sun <note>original: "Arkanshah"; referring to the divine messenger sent by the Sun God</note> ascended to heaven and entered the solar orb. || 24 ||

The Person who was a portion of the Sun, having taken leave of the demon Maya <note>original: "Mayasura"</note> after duly teaching the true nature of the motions of the planets and so on—having spoken the two verses beginning with "This to you..." and so forth—the word "and" should be understood here to connect the actions. He "ascended to heaven," meaning he made the celestial realm the object of his journey. Now, one might ask: what purpose did this Person, a portion of the Sun, achieve by giving this instruction? To this, he says: "By him." He was "honored" by Maya. The meaning is that he was made the object of worship through offerings of incense, perfumes, food, garments, and ornaments. Through Maya, he attained fame in the mortal world as being equal to the Sun himself. If one asks where exactly in heaven he went, he says: "He entered." He entered the "solar orb" <note>original: "Khamandalam"</note>, occupying his own abode. Here too, the word "and" should be understood in a conjunctive sense. || 24 || Now, he describes the state of Maya at that moment.

> Then Maya, having learned that divine knowledge directly from the Sun <note>original: "Vivasvat"</note>, considered himself as one who had accomplished his life's purpose, with his sins washed away. || 25 ||

Then, after the disappearance of the Person who was a portion of the Sun, Maya, having understood that "divine knowledge"—the previously mentioned knowledge of the movements of the planets and so on—which exists in heaven and was received directly from the Sun...

# The Treatise of the Sun

<note>original: "Surya-Siddhanta"</note>

...meaning "from the sun." It is appropriate that the person who is a partial incarnation of the Sun is spoken of as being non-different from the Sun itself, as he was produced from him; thus, even if there is a distinction, they are essentially the same. Having known his own self to be like the sky <note>pure and all-pervading</note>, and being washed of all taints <note>original: "nirdhuta-kalmasham"</note>—meaning his sins were removed—he considered himself to have accomplished his purpose, having completed his task. || 25 ||

Now, being asked by the listening sages, "How did you obtain this knowledge?", the sage <note>the commentator or narrator</note> explains to them that the Rishis <note>sages</note> present there, such as Atri and others, asked Maya for this knowledge.

> Then the Rishis, having known that Maya had received a boon from the Sun,
> approached and surrounded him, and then respectfully asked for that knowledge. || 26 ||

Now, after Maya the Asura <note>a class of powerful beings in Vedic cosmology</note> had obtained the knowledge, the sages such as Atri and others—who were located in the lands adjacent to the place where the conversation between the solar incarnation and Maya took place—recognized that Maya had accomplished his goal. They knew him to be one who had received a boon from the Sun <note>original: "surya-labdha-varam"</note>, meaning the grace of divine knowledge. They approached near to him. The word "and" <note>original: "ca"</note> indicates the gathering together. They surrounded him. Then, with great respect and intense desire to learn, they questioned him regarding that knowledge—the movements of the planets and so forth. || 26 ||

Next, it is described how Maya, being pleased, spoke his knowledge to those sages like Atri and others:

> Being pleased, he bestowed upon them the great motion of the planets,
> which is most wonderful in the world, a secret equal to the Vedas. || 27 ||

Maya, being satisfied, gave to those Rishis like Atri and others the knowledge of the positions and movements of the planets. This knowledge is "great" because it is immeasurable, and for that very reason, it is "equal to the Vedas" <note>original: "brahma-sammitam"; implying it carries the same divine authority as sacred scripture</note>.

# The Surya Siddhanta
## Page 399

->With his mind fixed upon the feet of the Lord of the Universe <note>original: "Vishvesha"; referring to Shiva, the patron deity of Varanasi</note>,<-
->the resident of Kashi <note>modern-day Varanasi</note>, respected by all,<-
->the illustrious Ranganatha—the elder brother of the wise Mahadeva—<-
->having composed this commentary named *Gudha-Prakasha* <note>The Illumination of Hidden Meanings</note><-
->on the science originating from the Sun <note>original: "Arka-mukha"; referring to the Surya Siddhanta, traditionally revealed by the Sun God</note>,<-
->has now offered it to the Lord of the Universe. It is pleasing to the heart.<-

In the Shaka year measured by the "Principles" and the "Lunar Days" <note>A chronogram where "Tattva" (Principles) equals 25 and "Tithi" (Lunar Days) equals 15, signifying the Shaka year 1525, or 1603 CE</note>, in the month of Chaitra, during the bright fortnight on the day of Shambhu <note>the 11th or 14th lunar day</note>, on a Wednesday at the end of sunrise; at that moment, the *Gudha-Prakasha* on the *Siddhanta* of the Sun and the great Sage was completed.

By observing this *Gudha-Prakasha* born of Ranganatha upon this earth, may the mathematicians and astronomers <note>term: "Ganaka" - those who calculate the movements of heavenly bodies</note> easily attain the natural wisdom of the Lord of Sages.

Thus ends the *Gudha-Artha-Prakashaka* <note>The Illumination of Hidden Meanings</note> of the *Surya Siddhanta*, composed by Ranganatha, the son of Ballala Daivajna <note>term: "Daivajna" - an astrologer or one who knows the divine will through the stars</note>, the emperor of all mathematicians.

**Completed.**
